that is, the statement of Kourovka Problem 11.94 holds.

This was proved by Kazarin and Chankov; the Kourovka Archive answers 11.94 "Yes, it is".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.94 (S. P. Strunkov); resolution: L. S. Kazarin and E. I. Chankov, Sb. Math. 201, no. 5 (2010), 655-668, Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.94: "Yes, it is", https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Solubility of finite simply reducible groups (Kourovka 11.94)
articles.statement:
The statement, asked by
S. P. Strunkov as Kourovka Problem 11.94, that every finite simply reducible group is soluble.

articles.title: Breuillard–Green–Tao structure theorem for approximate subgroups
articles.statement:
For every real number
$K$ there is a natural number $C \ge 1$ with the following property. Let $G$ be a group and let
$A \subseteq G$ be a $K$-approximate subgroup, that is, $1 \in A$, $A^{-1} = A$, and $A^2$ is
covered by at most $K$ left translates of $A$. Then there are a subgroup $H$ of $G$, a normal
subgroup $N$ of $H$, a finite set $F \subseteq G$ and a finite set $S \subseteq H/N$ such that
$H/N$ is nilpotent of class at most $C$ (the $C$-th term of its upper central series is all of
$H/N$), $S$ has at most $C$ elements and generates $H/N$, $N$ is contained in the $C$-fold
product set $(AA^{-1})^C$, $F$ has at most $C$ elements, and $A \subseteq FH$.

## Sources

- S. Machado, *Topics in Geometric Group Theory* lecture notes, <https://sites.google.com/view/simonmachado/teaching>, Theorem 4.4; original B. Breuillard, B. Green, T. Tao, *The structure of approximate groups*, Publ. Math. IHÉS 116 (2012).

articles.title: Breuillard–Green–Tao theorem (small doubling form)
articles.statement:
For every real number $K$ there is a
natural number $C > 0$ with the following property. Let $G$ be a group and let $A$ be a nonempty
finite subset of $G$ such that the product set $A A = \{ab : a, b \in A\}$ satisfies
$|A A| \le K |A|$. Then there are a subgroup $N$ of $G$, a normal subgroup $D$ of $N$ and a finite
subset $S$ of $N / D$ with at most $C$ elements such that $N / D$ is nilpotent of class at most
$C$ (its upper central series reaches $N / D$ at step $C$), $S$ generates $N / D$, every element
of $D$ is a product of four elements of $A A^{-1} = \{ab^{-1} : a, b \in A\}$, and there are
$a_1, \dots, a_C \in G$ such that $A$ is contained in the union of the left cosets
$a_1 N, \dots, a_C N$ of $N$.

## Sources

- S. Machado, *Topics in Geometric Group Theory* lecture notes, <https://sites.google.com/view/simonmachado/teaching>, Theorem 1.8; original B. Breuillard, B. Green, T. Tao, *The structure of approximate groups*, Publ. Math. IHÉS 116 (2012).

articles.title: Uncountable abelian groups of odd exponent have coset-free partitions
articles.statement:
Every uncountable
abelian group $G$ of finite odd exponent can be written as $G = A_1 \cup A_2$ with $A_1$ and $A_2$
disjoint, so that for every infinite subgroup $H$ of $G$ and every $g \in G$, the coset $gH$ is
contained neither in $A_1$ nor in $A_2$. This answers Kourovka Problem 13.46 in the affirmative.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 13.46 (I. V. Protasov); resolution: E. G. Zelenyuk, Math. Notes 67 (2000), 599-602, Kourovka Archive, Problem 13.46 (answer: Yes, it can).

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 13.46: coset-free partitions
articles.statement:
The proposition that every uncountable
abelian group $G$ of finite odd exponent can be written as $G = A_1 \cup A_2$ with $A_1$ and $A_2$
disjoint, so that for every infinite subgroup $H$ of $G$ and every $g \in G$, the coset $gH$ is
contained neither in $A_1$ nor in $A_2$. The problem is due to I. V. Protasov.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 13.47 has a positive answer
articles.statement:
Every countable abelian group $G$ with only
finitely many elements of order $2$ can be partitioned into two disjoint sets $A_1$ and $A_2$ with
$A_1 \cup A_2 = G$ such that $A_1$ and $A_2$ are both dense in every non-discrete Hausdorff group
topology on $G$.

The Kourovka Archive answers 13.47 "Yes, it can", citing Zelenyuk.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 13.47 (I. V. Protasov); resolution: E. G. Zelenyuk, Ukrain. Math. J. 51 (1999), no. 1, 44-50, Kourovka Archive, Problem 13.47 (answer: Yes, it can).

articles.title: Protasov's question on absolutely dense partitions (Kourovka 13.47)
articles.statement:
The proposition that
every countable abelian group $G$ with only finitely many elements of order $2$ can be partitioned
into two disjoint sets $A_1$ and $A_2$ with $A_1 \cup A_2 = G$ such that $A_1$ and $A_2$ are both
dense in every non-discrete Hausdorff group topology on $G$.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 15.80 has a negative answer
articles.statement:
It is not true that every topological group $G$
admitting a sequence $(P_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ of pairwise disjoint dense subsets with union $G$
has an expansive sequence, that is, a sequence $(F_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of pairwise disjoint
finite subsets of $G$ such that every nonempty open set $U \subseteq G$ meets $F_n$ for all $n$
larger than some $m$.

S. Corson's counterexample: $\prod_{\mathbb{N}} \mathbb{R}$ with the box topology has no countable
dense subset, hence no expansive sequence (the union of one is countable and dense), but its base
of $2^{\aleph_0}$ open sets of size $2^{\aleph_0}$ lets a transfinite induction partition it into
countably many dense subsets.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 15.80 (I. V. Protasov); resolution: S. Corson, letter of 19 May 2025, as recorded in the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue), Problem 15.80, G = ∏_ℕ ℝ with the box topology: not separable, hence without expansive sequences, but partitionable into countably many dense subsets by transfinite induction; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 15.80 solved (answer: Not necessarily), https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 15.80: dense partitions and expansive sequences
articles.statement:
Every topological group
$G$ admitting a sequence $(P_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ of pairwise disjoint dense subsets with union
$G$ has an expansive sequence.

articles.title: Expansive sequence
articles.statement:
In a topological space $G$, a sequence $(F_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of
finite subsets of $G$ is expansive if the sets $F_n$ are pairwise disjoint and for every nonempty
open set $U \subseteq G$ there is $m \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $F_n$ meets $U$ for all $n > m$.

articles.title: No infinite group has equicardinal maximal direct factors
articles.statement:
For every infinite group $G$ there
are subsets $A, B_1, B_2 \subseteq G$ such that $B_1$ and $B_2$ are both maximal under inclusion
among the subsets $B$ for which the product $AB$ is direct, but $B_1$ and $B_2$ have different
cardinalities. That is, the answer to Kourovka Problem 21.58 is negative.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 21.58 (M. H. Hooshmand); resolution: M. I. Kabenyuk, Factors in infinite groups, preprint, arXiv:2602.22876 (2026); M. H. Hooshmand, preprint, arXiv:2604.08724 (2026), Remark 1.16, Kabenyuk, Section 6, Theorem: every infinite group is unstable, i.e. has a subset A whose maximal subsets U with AU direct do not all have the same cardinality; Kourovka Notebook (21st issue), Problem 21.58: No, there are no such groups, https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.22876.

articles.title: Infinite groups with equicardinal maximal direct factors (Kourovka 21.58)
articles.statement:
The statement
that there is an infinite group $G$ such that for every subset $A \subseteq G$, any two subsets
$B_1, B_2 \subseteq G$ that are maximal under inclusion among the subsets $B$ for which the
product $AB$ is direct have the same cardinality.

articles.title: Direct product of subsets
articles.statement:
For subsets $A$ and $B$ of a group $G$, the product
$AB = \{ab \mid a \in A,\ b \in B\}$ is direct when each element of $AB$ is $ab$ for unique
$a \in A$ and $b \in B$: whenever $a_1 b_1 = a_2 b_2$ with $a_1, a_2 \in A$ and $b_1, b_2 \in B$,
we have $a_1 = a_2$ and $b_1 = b_2$.

articles.title: Constructing a G-harmonic tuple
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group and $a = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$ a tuple
of natural numbers with every $a_i$ positive. If $U_1, \dots, U_n$ are subgroups of $G$ such that
$U_i$ has index $a_i$ in $G$ for every $i$, and $g_1, \dots, g_n \in G$ are elements such that the
left cosets $g_1 U_1, \dots, g_n U_n$ are pairwise disjoint, then $a$ is $G$-harmonic.

articles.title: The empty tuple is G-harmonic
articles.statement:
For every group $G$, the empty tuple of natural numbers is
(vacuously) $G$-harmonic.

articles.title: Characterization of G-harmonic tuples
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group and $a = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$ a
tuple of natural numbers. Then $a$ is $G$-harmonic if and only if every $a_i$ is positive and
there are subgroups $U_1, \dots, U_n$ of $G$ and elements $g_1, \dots, g_n \in G$ such that $U_i$
has index $a_i$ in $G$ for every $i$ and the left cosets $g_1 U_1, \dots, g_n U_n$ are pairwise
disjoint.

articles.title: The tuple (1) is G-harmonic
articles.statement:
For every group $G$, the one-entry tuple $(1)$ is
$G$-harmonic; the subgroup $G$ itself, of index $1$, with coset representative $1$ witnesses
this.

articles.title: G-harmonic tuples
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group and $a = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$ a tuple of natural
numbers. The tuple $a$ is $G$-harmonic if every $a_i$ is positive and there exist subgroups
$U_1, \dots, U_n$ of $G$ and elements $g_1, \dots, g_n \in G$ such that $U_i$ has index $a_i$ in
$G$ for every $i$ and the left cosets $g_1 U_1, \dots, g_n U_n$ are pairwise disjoint.

articles.title: Tuples with a zero entry are not G-harmonic
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group. If a tuple
$a = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$ of natural numbers has $a_i = 0$ for some $i$, then $a$ is not
$G$-harmonic.

articles.title: Entries of a G-harmonic tuple are positive
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group. If a tuple
$a = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$ of natural numbers is $G$-harmonic, then $a_i > 0$ for every $i$.

articles.title: Witnesses for a G-harmonic tuple
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group. If a tuple $a = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$
of natural numbers is $G$-harmonic, then there exist subgroups $U_1, \dots, U_n$ of $G$ and
elements $g_1, \dots, g_n \in G$ such that $U_i$ has index $a_i$ in $G$ for every $i$ and the
left cosets $g_1 U_1, \dots, g_n U_n$ are pairwise disjoint.

articles.title: Factorization of a group into subsets of given sizes
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group, $k$ a natural
number and $a_0, \dots, a_{k-1}$ natural numbers. The group $G$ has a subset factorization of
type $(a_0, \dots, a_{k-1})$ when there are finite subsets $A_0, \dots, A_{k-1}$ of $G$ with
$|A_i| = a_i$ for every $i$ such that $G = A_0 A_1 \cdots A_{k-1}$, that is, every $g \in G$ can be
written as $g = x_0 x_1 \cdots x_{k-1}$ with $x_i \in A_i$ for every $i$.

articles.title: Finite groups without subset factorizations exist for every length
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$k \ge 3$ there are a finite group $G$ and natural numbers $a_0, \dots, a_{k-1}$, each at least
$2$, with $a_0 a_1 \cdots a_{k-1} = |G|$, such that there are no subsets $A_0, \dots, A_{k-1}$ of
$G$ with $|A_i| = a_i$ for every $i$ and $G = A_0 A_1 \cdots A_{k-1}$, that is, with every element
of $G$ a product $x_0 x_1 \cdots x_{k-1}$ where $x_i \in A_i$ for every $i$.

In McCulloch's Theorem 2.3, $G$ is a Frobenius group of order $2^{k-1}(2^{k-1} - 1)$ and the
factors are $(2, \dots, 2, 2^{k-1} - 1, 2)$; the case $k = 3$ is Bergman's example in the
alternating group $A_4$. This answers Kourovka Problem 19.35 (M. H. Hooshmand) in the negative.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 19.35 (M. H. Hooshmand); resolution: R. McCulloch, Some answers regarding factorizations of finite groups, arXiv:2607.20569 (2026); counterexamples first given by M. Kabenyuk, Factorizations of finite groups, arXiv:2102.08605, Kourovka Archive, Problem 19.35: No (Bergman's A4 example for k = 3); counterexamples for all k ≥ 3 are constructed in (McCulloch); paper, Theorem 2.3: the Frobenius group of order 2^(k-1)(2^(k-1) - 1) has no k-fold factorization for (2, …, 2, 2^(k-1) - 1, 2), https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20569.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 19.35: counterexamples to subset factorization of every length
articles.statement:
The
statement that for every natural number $k \ge 3$ there are a finite group $G$ and natural numbers
$a_0, \dots, a_{k-1}$, each at least $2$, with $a_0 a_1 \cdots a_{k-1} = |G|$, such that $G$ has
no subset factorization of type $(a_0, \dots, a_{k-1})$: there are no subsets
$A_0, \dots, A_{k-1}$ of $G$ with $|A_i| = a_i$ for every $i$ and $G = A_0 A_1 \cdots A_{k-1}$.

articles.title: Monochromatic symmetric subsets in finite colourings (Jayadevan)
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an infinite
abelian group, written additively, let $\alpha$ be a cardinal with $\alpha < |G|$, and let $n$ be
a natural number. For every colouring $\chi \colon G \to \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ there are a set
$A \subseteq G$ of cardinality $\alpha$ on which $\chi$ is constant and an element $g \in G$ such
that $2g - a \in A$ for every $a \in A$.

This answers Kourovka Problem 15.77 (I. V. Protasov) affirmatively; the Kourovka Notebook (21st
issue) marks it solved, "Yes, it is true" (AI solution confirmed by I. V. Protasov).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 15.77 (I. V. Protasov); resolution: A. Jayadevan, Monochromatic symmetric subsets in finite colourings of infinite abelian groups, preprint, Zenodo record 22909420 (2026), AI-generated solution confirmed by I. V. Protasov, main theorem (for G infinite abelian and α < |G|, every finite colouring has a monochromatic S with |S| = α and 2g - S = S for some g); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 15.77 solved, https://zenodo.org/records/22909420.

articles.title: Monochrome symmetric subsets (Kourovka 15.77)
articles.statement:
The statement, written additively, that for
every infinite abelian group $G$, every cardinal $\alpha < |G|$, every natural number $n$ and every
colouring $\chi \colon G \to \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, there are a set $A \subseteq G$ of cardinality
$\alpha$ on which $\chi$ is constant and an element $g \in G$ such that $2g - a \in A$ for every
$a \in A$; that is, $A$ is a monochrome set symmetric with respect to $g$.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 17.3 has a negative answer
articles.statement:
There is a group $G$ in which every $4$-element
subset contains two distinct elements generating a nilpotent subgroup, but some subgroup of $G$
generated by two elements is not nilpotent.

The Kourovka Archive answers 17.3 "No, not always", citing Sozutov (2019).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 17.3 (A. Abdollahi); resolution: A. I. Sozutov, Siberian Math. J. 60 (2019), 1099-1100, Kourovka Archive, Problem 17.3 (No, not always).

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 17.3 (Abdollahi's question on nilpotent pairs)
articles.statement:
The proposition that for
every group $G$ in which every $4$-element subset contains two distinct elements generating a
nilpotent subgroup, every subgroup of $G$ generated by two elements is nilpotent.

articles.title: A partition of $\bigoplus_{\omega_1} \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ into three parts meeting every infinite coset
articles.statement:
**A partition of $\bigoplus_{\omega_1} \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ into three parts meeting every
infinite coset.** Let $I$ be a set of cardinality $\aleph_1$ and let $A = \bigoplus_{i \in I}
\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ be the group of finitely supported functions from $I$ to
$\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$. Then $A$ can be partitioned into three subsets $A_0, A_1, A_2$ such that
for every infinite subgroup $H$ of $A$ and every $x \in A$, the coset $x + H$ meets each $A_i$.

The Kourovka Archive records more: every infinite abelian group with finitely many involutions can
be partitioned into infinitely many subsets such that every coset modulo an infinite subgroup meets
each subset of the partition.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 16.43 (E. G. Zelenyuk); resolution: Y. Zelenyuk, J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 115 (2008), 331-339, Kourovka Archive, Problem 16.43 (Yes; moreover every infinite abelian group with finitely many involutions can be partitioned into infinitely many subsets such that every coset modulo an infinite subgroup meets each subset).

articles.title: Kourovka 16.43: partitioning $\bigoplus_{\omega_1} \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ into three parts meeting every infinite coset
articles.statement:
**Kourovka 16.43: partitioning $\bigoplus_{\omega_1} \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ into three parts
meeting every infinite coset.** The proposition that for every set $I$ of cardinality $\aleph_1$,
the group $A = \bigoplus_{i \in I} \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ of finitely supported functions from $I$
to $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ can be partitioned into three subsets $A_0, A_1, A_2$ such that for
every infinite subgroup $H$ of $A$ and every $x \in A$, the coset $x + H$ meets each $A_i$.

articles.title: Some group of singular cardinality has no such partition
articles.statement:
There is an infinite group $G$
whose cardinality $\mathfrak{m} = |G|$ is singular (not regular) such that for all disjoint sets
$A_1$ and $A_2$ with $A_1 \cup A_2 = G$ there is a subset $F \subseteq G$ with
$|F| < \mathfrak{m}$ and $A_1 F = G$ or $A_2 F = G$, where $A F = \{a f : a \in A, f \in F\}$.
That is, the statement of Kourovka Problem 13.45 fails.

Protasov and Slobodianiuk show that the answer depends on the algebraic structure of $G$: such a
partition exists for every free group, but not for abelian groups of singular cardinality. The
Kourovka Archive answers 13.45 "No, not always".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 13.45 (I. V. Protasov); resolution: I. Protasov and S. Slobodianiuk, A note on partitions of groups, Quest. Answers Gen. Topology 33 (2015), no. 2, 61-70, arXiv:1408.5607, abstract and Theorem 2(iii): the statement fails for abelian groups of singular cardinality (it holds for free groups); Kourovka Archive, Problem 13.45, https://arxiv.org/abs/1408.5607.

articles.title: Partitions of groups of singular cardinality (Kourovka 13.45)
articles.statement:
The statement that every
infinite group $G$ whose cardinality $\mathfrak{m} = |G|$ is singular (not regular) can be split
into two disjoint sets $A_1$ and $A_2$ with $A_1 \cup A_2 = G$ such that $A_1 F \ne G$ and
$A_2 F \ne G$ for every subset $F \subseteq G$ with $|F| < \mathfrak{m}$, where
$A F = \{a f : a \in A, f \in F\}$.

articles.title: Product set of a finite set
articles.statement:
For a finite subset $A$ of a type with a multiplication, the
product set $A \cdot A$ is the finite set $\{ab : a, b \in A\}$ of all products of two elements
of $A$.

## Sources

- AIM-COMBINATORICS-0241, Problem 3.4, aim-combinatorics-notes.json notes[240].

articles.title: Sets of size about $p^{5/2}$ in $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$ grow under multiplication
articles.statement:
For
every real $C \ge 1$ there are a real $\delta > 0$ and a natural number $P_0$ such that for every
prime $p \ge P_0$ and every finite subset $A$ of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$, where
$\mathbb{F}_p = \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, with $C^{-1} p^{5/2} \le |A| \le C p^{5/2}$, the product
set $A \cdot A = \{ab : a, b \in A\}$ satisfies $|A \cdot A| > p^{5/2 + \delta}$.

Every nontrivial representation of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$ has dimension at least
$(p-1)/2$, and the product-mixing bound of Gowers and Babai–Nikolov–Pyber then gives
$|A \cdot A| \gg p^3$ for such $A$, so every $\delta < 1/2$ works. This answers AIM
additive-combinatorics Problem 3.4 (Green, after Venkatesh).

## Sources

- N. Nikolov and L. Pyber, Product decompositions of quasirandom groups and a Jordan type theorem, arXiv:math/0703343, https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0703343.

articles.title: Two-step product growth in $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$ (AIM Problem 3.4)
articles.statement:
The statement
that for every real $C \ge 1$ there are a real $\delta > 0$ and a natural number $P_0$ such that
for every prime $p \ge P_0$ and every finite subset $A$ of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$, where
$\mathbb{F}_p = \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, with $C^{-1} p^{5/2} \le |A| \le C p^{5/2}$, the product
set $A \cdot A = \{ab : a, b \in A\}$ satisfies $|A \cdot A| > p^{5/2 + \delta}$.

This is a large-$p$ reading of the question of Green, after Venkatesh: if
$A \subseteq \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$ satisfies $|A| \sim p^{5/2}$, does it follow that
$|A \cdot A| > p^{5/2 + \delta}$?

## Sources

- AIM-COMBINATORICS-0241, Problem 3.4, aim-combinatorics-notes.json notes[240], https://aimath.org/WWN/additivecomb/additivecomb.pdf.

articles.title: Product theorem for special linear groups
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number. For every real
$\varepsilon$ with $0 < \varepsilon < 1$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ such that the following
holds for every finite field $k$: if $A$ is a subset of $\mathrm{SL}(n, k)$ with $A^{-1} = A$ and
$1 \in A$ that generates $\mathrm{SL}(n, k)$, then $|A|^{1+\delta} \le |A^3|$ or
$|\mathrm{SL}(n, k)|^{1-\varepsilon} \le |A|$, where $A^3 = \{abc : a, b, c \in A\}$. Thus
$\delta$ depends only on $n$ and $\varepsilon$.

## Sources

- S. Machado, *Topics in Geometric Group Theory* lecture notes, <https://sites.google.com/view/simonmachado/teaching>, Theorem 1.9; originals B. Breuillard, B. Green, T. Tao, *Approximate subgroups of linear groups*, Geom. Funct. Anal. 21 (2011), and L. Pyber, E. Szabó, *Growth in finite simple groups of Lie type*, J. Amer. Math. Soc. 29 (2016).

articles.title: Pyber's conjecture for $\mathrm{PSL}(2, p)$ holds
articles.statement:
There is a natural number $N$ such that for
every prime $p$ the following holds. Let $G = \mathrm{PSL}(2, p)$ be the quotient of
$\mathrm{SL}(2, \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})$ by its center. If $G$ has a subset $S$ with
$g s g^{-1} \in S$ and $s^{-1} \in S$ for all $g \in G$ and $s \in S$, with more than
$|G| / \log_2 |G|$ elements, and with $S^2 = \{st : s, t \in S\}$ different from $G$, then
$p \le N$. In other words, only finitely many groups $\mathrm{PSL}(2, p)$ with $p$ prime have such
a subset.

Skresanov (Bull. London Math. Soc. 57 (2025), Corollary 3) proves that in a finite simple group $G$
of Lie type of bounded rank every inverse-closed normal subset $A$ with $|A| > |G| / \log_2 |G|$
satisfies $A^2 = G$ once $|G|$ is large, and notes that this settles the groups
$\mathrm{PSL}(2, p)$; the 21st issue of the Kourovka Notebook records 20.74(b) as proved for the
groups $\mathrm{PSL}(2, p)$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 20.74 (L. Pyber); resolution: O. Sheinfeld, On Shalev's quantitative version of Thompson's conjecture, preprint, arXiv:2609.22004 (2026) (part (a)); S. V. Skresanov, Bull. London Math. Soc. 57 (2025), no. 11, 3429-3440 (part (b)), (a) Sheinfeld, Theorem 1.6: for every odd n ≥ 5 there is an inverse-closed normal subset S ⊆ SL_n(5) = PSL_n(5) with |S| ≥ |SL_n(5)|/960 and diag(1, -I_{n-1}) ∉ S², which the paper states disproves Pyber's conjecture; (b) Skresanov, Corollary 3 (arXiv:2406.12506): in a finite simple group of Lie type of bounded rank every inverse-closed normal subset A with |A| > |G|/log₂|G| has A² = G once |G| is large in terms of the rank, and part (b) for PSL(2, p) follows; Kourovka Notebook (21st issue), Problem 20.74: a) No, there are infinitely many such groups; b) The conjecture is proved for the groups PSL(2, p), https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22004.

articles.title: Pyber's conjecture for $\mathrm{PSL}(2, p)$ (Kourovka 20.74(b))
articles.statement:
This proposition states
that there is a natural number $N$ such that $p \le N$ for every prime $p$ for which the group
$G = \mathrm{PSL}(2, p)$, the quotient of $\mathrm{SL}(2, \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})$ by its center,
has a subset $S$ closed under conjugation and under inversion with $|S| > |G| / \log_2 |G|$ and
$S^2 \ne G$, where $S^2 = \{st : s, t \in S\}$. In other words, only finitely many groups
$\mathrm{PSL}(2, p)$ with $p$ prime have such a subset.

articles.title: Pyber's conjecture for finite simple groups is false
articles.statement:
There is no natural number $N$ such that
every nonabelian finite simple group $G$ that has a subset $S$ with $g s g^{-1} \in S$ and
$s^{-1} \in S$ for all $g \in G$ and $s \in S$, with $|S| > |G| / \log_2 |G|$ and with $S^2 \ne G$,
where $S^2 = \{st : s, t \in S\}$, has order $|G| \le N$.

Sheinfeld (Theorem 1.6) gives, for every odd $n \ge 5$, an inverse-closed normal subset $S$ of the
simple group $G = \mathrm{PSL}_n(5) = \mathrm{SL}_n(5)$ with $|S| \ge |G| / 960$ and $S^2 \ne G$, so
infinitely many nonabelian finite simple groups have such a subset; the paper states that this
disproves Pyber's conjecture, and the 21st issue of the Kourovka Notebook records 20.74(a) as "No,
there are infinitely many such groups".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 20.74 (L. Pyber); resolution: O. Sheinfeld, On Shalev's quantitative version of Thompson's conjecture, preprint, arXiv:2609.22004 (2026) (part (a)); S. V. Skresanov, Bull. London Math. Soc. 57 (2025), no. 11, 3429-3440 (part (b)), (a) Sheinfeld, Theorem 1.6: for every odd n ≥ 5 there is an inverse-closed normal subset S ⊆ SL_n(5) = PSL_n(5) with |S| ≥ |SL_n(5)|/960 and diag(1, -I_{n-1}) ∉ S², which the paper states disproves Pyber's conjecture; (b) Skresanov, Corollary 3 (arXiv:2406.12506): in a finite simple group of Lie type of bounded rank every inverse-closed normal subset A with |A| > |G|/log₂|G| has A² = G once |G| is large in terms of the rank, and part (b) for PSL(2, p) follows; Kourovka Notebook (21st issue), Problem 20.74: a) No, there are infinitely many such groups; b) The conjecture is proved for the groups PSL(2, p), https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22004.

articles.title: Pyber's conjecture for finite simple groups (Kourovka 20.74(a))
articles.statement:
This proposition states
that there is a natural number $N$ such that every nonabelian finite simple group $G$ that has a
subset $S$ closed under conjugation and under inversion with $|S| > |G| / \log_2 |G|$ and
$S^2 \ne G$, where $S^2 = \{st : s, t \in S\}$, has order $|G| \le N$. Since there are only finitely
many groups of each order, this says that only finitely many such groups exist up to isomorphism.

articles.title: Large inverse-closed normal subsets with small square
articles.statement:
A group $G$ has this property when it
has a subset $S$ such that $g s g^{-1} \in S$ and $s^{-1} \in S$ for all $g \in G$ and $s \in S$,
$S$ has more than $|G| / \log_2 |G|$ elements, and $S^2 = \{st : s, t \in S\}$ is not all of $G$.

The definition is intended for finite groups $G$.

articles.title: Every number of distinct permuted products occurs (Kourovka 18.50)
articles.statement:
For all natural
numbers $n$ and $k$ with $1 \le k \le n!$ there are a group $G$ and pairwise distinct elements
$g_1, \dots, g_n \in G$ such that the set
$\lbrace g_{\sigma(1)} g_{\sigma(2)} \cdots g_{\sigma(n)} : \sigma \in S_n \rbrace$ of products
obtained by permuting the factors has exactly $k$ elements.

The Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) answers 18.50 "Yes, it is true", by an AI-generated solution
confirmed by S. Kohl (P. Monticone, 2026); van Doorn, Judin, Monticone and Morrison (2026) give
an independent account.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 18.50 (S. Kohl); resolution: P. Monticone, preprint, 2026 (AI solution confirmed by S. Kohl), https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/18_50.pdf; W. van Doorn, E. Judin, P. Monticone and D. Morrison, On some problems from the Kourovka Notebook, preprint, arXiv:2607.17477 (2026), arXiv:2607.17477 abstract: for every 1 ≤ k ≤ n! there is a group containing n distinct elements whose n! ordered products take exactly k distinct values (found and verified in Lean by the Aristotle agent); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 18.50 solved, https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17477.

articles.title: Kohl's permuted-products statement (Kourovka 18.50)
articles.statement:
The assertion that for all natural
numbers $n$ and $k$ with $1 \le k \le n!$ there are a group $G$ and pairwise distinct elements
$g_1, \dots, g_n \in G$ such that the set
$\lbrace g_{\sigma(1)} g_{\sigma(2)} \cdots g_{\sigma(n)} : \sigma \in S_n \rbrace$ of products
obtained by permuting the factors has exactly $k$ elements.

articles.title: Separated subsets of a group
articles.statement:
Two subsets $A$ and $B$ of a group $G$ are separated, in the
sense of I. V. Protasov, when there is an infinite subset $X \subseteq G$ with $1 \in X$,
$X^{-1} = X$ and $XAX \cap B = \emptyset$, where $XAX = \{x a y : x, y \in X,\ a \in A\}$.

articles.title: Small disjoint subsets of an infinite group need not be separated
articles.statement:
There exist an infinite
group $G$ and disjoint subsets $A, B \subseteq G$ with $|A| < |G|$ and $|B| < |G|$ such that $A$
and $B$ are not separated. That is, the statement of Kourovka Problem 17.102 is false.

Resolved false: Wan (Theorem 1.1) takes $G = \mathrm{Sym}(\mathbb{N})$ and splits the set of
transpositions into $A$ and $B$ using a graph on $\mathbb{N}$ with trivial automorphism group, so
that $|A| = |B| = \aleph_0 < 2^{\aleph_0}$. The Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) answers 17.102
"No, not always".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 17.102 (I. V. Protasov); resolution: S. Wan, Counterexamples to Problem 17.102 of The Kourovka Notebook, preprint, arXiv:2608.00504 (2026), Theorem 1.1 (an infinite group G with disjoint A, B, |A|, |B| < |G|, not separated; in the proof G = Sym(N) and A, B split the transpositions by a rigid graph on N); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 17.102 solved (No, not always), https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00504.

articles.title: Separation of small disjoint subsets of infinite groups (Kourovka 17.102)
articles.statement:
The statement,
posed by I. V. Protasov, that for every infinite group $G$ and all disjoint subsets
$A, B \subseteq G$ with $|A| < |G|$ and $|B| < |G|$, the sets $A$ and $B$ are separated.

articles.title: Equal commutators of basic commutators do not determine their entries
articles.statement:
The Gaglione–Spellman
claim on equal commutators of basic commutators (Kourovka Problem 11.20) is false: writing
$[x, y] = x^{-1} y^{-1} x y$, there are a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, a linear order $<$ on the
formal commutators in the letters $\alpha$ that orders the letters as in $\alpha$ and puts formal
commutators of smaller weight first, formal commutators $a$ and $b$ such that the formal commutator
$[a, b]$ is basic for $<$, and elements $c$ and $d$ of the free group $F(\alpha)$, each of the form
$[x, y]$ with $x, y \in F(\alpha)$, such that $[\bar a, \bar b] = [c, d]$ in $F(\alpha)$, where
$\bar a$ and $\bar b$ are the values of $a$ and $b$ in $F(\alpha)$, but $\bar a \ne c$ or
$\bar b \ne d$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.20 (A. Gaglione, D. Spellman); resolution: V. G. Bardakov, Abstracts of the IIIrd Intern. Conf. on Algebra, Krasnoyarsk, 1993, p. 33 (Russian), Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.20: "No, not always"; for free generators `x₁ < x₂ < x₃`, `a = [[x₂, x₁], x₃]`, `b = [x₂, x₁]`, `c = b⁻¹`, `d = b^{x₃ b}`, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Gaglione–Spellman claim on equal commutators of basic commutators
articles.statement:
The proposition
(Kourovka Problem 11.20, A. Gaglione and D. Spellman) that the following holds. Write
$[x, y] = x^{-1} y^{-1} x y$. For every linearly ordered type $\alpha$ and every linear order $<$
on the formal commutators in the letters $\alpha$ that orders the letters as in $\alpha$ and puts
formal commutators of smaller weight first (within one weight it is arbitrary), if $a$ and $b$ are
formal commutators such that the formal commutator $[a, b]$ is basic for $<$ (so $a$ and $b$ are
basic too), $c$ and $d$ are elements of the free group $F(\alpha)$, each of the form $[x, y]$ with
$x, y \in F(\alpha)$, and $[\bar a, \bar b] = [c, d]$ in $F(\alpha)$, where $\bar a$ and $\bar b$
are the values of $a$ and $b$ in $F(\alpha)$, then $\bar a = c$ and $\bar b = d$.

articles.title: Formal commutators
articles.statement:
The formal commutators (bracket arrangements) in an alphabet $\alpha$
are the formal expressions generated by two rules: every letter $a \in \alpha$ is a formal
commutator, and for formal commutators $u$ and $v$, the bracket $[u, v]$ is a formal commutator.

articles.title: Value of a formal commutator
articles.statement:
Each formal commutator in the letters $\alpha$ has a value in
the free group $F(\alpha)$ on $\alpha$: a letter $a$ has the value of the generator $a$, and
$[u, v]$ has the value $\bar u^{-1} \bar v^{-1} \bar u \bar v$, where $\bar u$ and $\bar v$ are the
values of $u$ and $v$.

articles.title: Basic commutators
articles.statement:
Let $<$ be a relation on the formal commutators in the letters $\alpha$
(in applications, a linear order). Every letter is basic for $<$, and a formal commutator $[u, v]$
is basic for $<$ when $u$ and $v$ are basic for $<$, $v < u$, and, in case $u = [y, z]$ is itself a
bracket, $v < z$ fails (for a linear order: $z \le v$). This is M. Hall's definition.

articles.title: Commutator, Kourovka–Hall convention
articles.statement:
For elements $x$ and $y$ of a group, their
commutator is $[x, y] = x^{-1} y^{-1} x y$ (the convention of the Kourovka Notebook and of Hall).

articles.title: Weight of a formal commutator
articles.statement:
The weight of a formal commutator is the number of
occurrences of letters in it: a letter has weight $1$, and $[u, v]$ has weight the weight of $u$
plus the weight of $v$.

articles.title: A commutator power identity need not make the derived subgroup periodic
articles.statement:
There exist an
integer $n \ge 1$ and a group $G$ such that $[x, y]^n = 1$ for all $x, y \in G$ but some element of
the derived subgroup $[G, G]$ has infinite order. This answers Kourovka Notebook Problem 13.34
(I. D. Macdonald; V. D. Mazurov) in the negative, by results of G. S. Deryabina and P. A.
Kozhevnikov from 1999 and of S. I. Adyan from 2000.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 13.34 (I. D. Macdonald; V. D. Mazurov); resolution: G. S. Deryabina and P. A. Kozhevnikov, Commun. Algebra 27 (1999), no. 9, 4525-4530; S. I. Adyan, Dokl. Math. 62 (2000), no. 2, 174-176, Kourovka Archive, Problem 13.34: No, not always.

articles.title: Derived subgroups under a commutator power identity (Kourovka 13.34)
articles.statement:
This is the
proposition that for every integer $n \ge 1$ and every group $G$ with $[x, y]^n = 1$ for all
$x, y \in G$, every element of the derived subgroup $[G, G]$ has finite order, that is, the derived
subgroup of $G$ is periodic.

This is Kourovka Notebook Problem 13.34 (I. D. Macdonald).

articles.title: Commutator length in Aut(Fₙ) is unbounded
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 3$ and let $F_n$ be the free group on
$n$ generators. For every natural number $k$ there is an element of the derived subgroup of
$\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)$ that is not a product of at most $k$ commutators $xyx^{-1}y^{-1}$ with
$x, y \in \operatorname{Aut}(F_n)$. Equivalently, the supremum $k_n$ of the commutator lengths of
the elements of the derived subgroup of $\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)$ is infinite.

This answers Kourovka Problem 14.15 (V. G. Bardakov): $\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)$ is acylindrically
hyperbolic (Genevois–Horbez), and acylindrically hyperbolic groups have infinite commutator width
(Bestvina–Bromberg–Fujiwara).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 14.15 (V. G. Bardakov); resolution: A. Genevois and C. Horbez, J. Topology 14 (2021), 963-991 (Aut F_n is acylindrically hyperbolic); M. Bestvina, K. Bromberg and K. Fujiwara, Algebr. Geom. Topol. 19 (2019), 477-489 (acylindrically hyperbolic groups have infinite commutator width), the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 14.15 solved: k_n = ∞ for n ≥ 3.

articles.title: Unbounded commutator length in Aut(Fₙ) (Kourovka 14.15)
articles.statement:
The proposition that for every
$n \ge 3$, writing $F_n$ for the free group on $n$ generators, and for every natural number $k$,
some element of the derived subgroup of $\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)$ is not a product of at most $k$
commutators $xyx^{-1}y^{-1}$ of elements of $\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)$. This is the answer
$k_n = \infty$ to Bardakov's question, which asks for the supremum $k_n$ of the commutator lengths
of the elements of the derived subgroup of $\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)$.

articles.title: Unbounded commutator length
articles.statement:
A group $G$ has unbounded commutator length when for every
natural number $n$ some element of the derived subgroup $[G, G]$ is not a product of at most $n$
commutators $x y x^{-1} y^{-1}$ with $x, y \in G$.

articles.title: Commutator width of the derived subgroup
articles.statement:
For a group $G$ with derived subgroup $G'$, the
commutator width $w(G')$ is the least positive integer $m$ such that every element of $G'$ is a
product of at most $m$ commutators $aba^{-1}b^{-1}$ with $a, b \in G$; it is $0$ when no such $m$
exists.

articles.title: A finitely presented simple group with unbounded commutator length
articles.statement:
There is a finitely
presented simple group $G$ such that for every natural number $n$ some element of the derived
subgroup $[G, G]$ is not a product of at most $n$ commutators $x y x^{-1} y^{-1}$ with
$x, y \in G$. This answers Kourovka Problem 14.13(b) in the affirmative; the Kourovka Archive cites
Caprace and Fujiwara.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 14.13 (V. G. Bardakov); resolution: (a) J. Barge and É. Ghys, Math. Ann. 294 (1992), 235-265, and A. Muranov, Int. J. Algebra Comput. 17 (2007), 607-659 (finitely generated examples); (b) P.-E. Caprace and K. Fujiwara, Geom. Funct. Anal. 19 (2010), 1296-1319, Kourovka Archive, Problem 14.13 (answers: a) constructed; b) Yes, there does).

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 14.13(b) (Bardakov)
articles.statement:
The statement that there is a finitely presented
simple group $G$ such that for every natural number $n$ some element of the derived subgroup
$[G, G]$ is not a product of at most $n$ commutators $x y x^{-1} y^{-1}$ with $x, y \in G$.

articles.title: Products of a bounded number of commutators
articles.statement:
For a group $G$, a natural number $m$ and
$g \in G$, $g$ is a product of at most $m$ commutators when there are $k \le m$ and
$a_1, b_1, \dots, a_k, b_k \in G$ with $g = [a_1, b_1] \cdots [a_k, b_k]$, where
$[a, b] = aba^{-1}b^{-1}$; for $k = 0$ the empty product is the identity.

articles.title: Products of at most $n$ commutators
articles.statement:
An element $z$ of a group $G$ is a product of at most
$n$ commutators when $z = [x_1, y_1] \cdots [x_k, y_k]$ for some $k \le n$ and some
$x_1, y_1, \dots, x_k, y_k \in G$, where $[x, y] = x y x^{-1} y^{-1}$; for $k = 0$ the product is
the identity.

articles.title: Products of at most $n$ commutators (Kourovka 14.15)
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group and $n$ a natural
number. An element $z \in G$ is a product of at most $n$ commutators when there are $m \le n$ and
elements $x_1, y_1, \dots, x_m, y_m \in G$ with $z = [x_1, y_1] \cdots [x_m, y_m]$, where
$[x, y] = xyx^{-1}y^{-1}$; for $m = 0$ the empty product is the identity.

articles.title: The maximal commutator width ratio is one sixth
articles.statement:
For every finite non-abelian group $G$,
the commutator width $w(G')$ of its derived subgroup satisfies $w(G')/|G| \le 1/6$, and for the
symmetric group $S_3$ equality holds, $w(S_3')/|S_3| = 1/6$; so Kourovka Problem 16.8 has a
positive answer.

The Kourovka Archive answers 16.8 "Yes, it is", citing Bonner (2008) for the bound; $S_3$ attains
it because its derived subgroup $A_3$ consists of commutators.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 16.8 (V. G. Bardakov); resolution: T. Bonner, J. Algebra 320 (2008), 3165-3171, Kourovka Archive, Problem 16.8 (Yes, it is).

articles.title: Bardakov's commutator width ratio claim (Kourovka 16.8)
articles.statement:
The proposition that for every
finite non-abelian group $G$ the commutator width $w(G')$ of its derived subgroup $G'$ satisfies
$w(G')/|G| \le 1/6$, and that for the symmetric group $S_3$ equality holds:
$w(S_3')/|S_3| = 1/6$.

articles.title: A simple group with unbounded commutator length
articles.statement:
There is a simple group $G$ such that for
every natural number $n$ some element of the derived subgroup $[G, G]$ is not a product of at most
$n$ commutators $x y x^{-1} y^{-1}$ with $x, y \in G$. This answers Kourovka Problem 14.13(a) in
the affirmative; the Kourovka Archive records examples constructed by Barge and Ghys, and finitely
generated ones by Muranov.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 14.13 (V. G. Bardakov); resolution: (a) J. Barge and É. Ghys, Math. Ann. 294 (1992), 235-265, and A. Muranov, Int. J. Algebra Comput. 17 (2007), 607-659 (finitely generated examples); (b) P.-E. Caprace and K. Fujiwara, Geom. Funct. Anal. 19 (2010), 1296-1319, Kourovka Archive, Problem 14.13 (answers: a) constructed; b) Yes, there does).

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 14.13(a) (Bardakov)
articles.statement:
The statement that there is a simple group $G$ such
that for every natural number $n$ some element of the derived subgroup $[G, G]$ is not a product of
at most $n$ commutators $x y x^{-1} y^{-1}$ with $x, y \in G$.

articles.title: Negative answer to Kourovka Problem 18.57
articles.statement:
There is no natural number $d$ such that
$G^{(d)} = 1$ for every finite group $G$ in which every element has order a power of $2$, which is
generated by its involutions, and in which $[[x, u], u] = 1$ for every $x \in G$ and every
involution $u \in G$; here $[x, u] = x^{-1} u^{-1} x u$ and $G^{(d)}$ is the $d$-th term of the
derived series of $G$. Thus the derived length of such groups is unbounded.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 18.57 (D. V. Lytkina); resolution: A. Abdollahi, J. Group Theory 18 (2015), no. 1, 111-114, Kourovka Archive, Problem 18.57: No, it is not, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 18.57 on the derived length of involution-generated 2-groups
articles.statement:
The
proposition (Kourovka 18.57, D. V. Lytkina) that there is a natural number $d$ such that
$G^{(d)} = 1$ for every finite group $G$ in which every element has order a power of $2$, which is
generated by its involutions, and in which $[[x, u], u] = 1$ for every $x \in G$ and every
involution $u \in G$; here $[x, u] = x^{-1} u^{-1} x u$ and $G^{(d)}$ is the $d$-th term of the
derived series of $G$.

articles.title: Involution-generated 2-groups with the Engel condition on involutions
articles.statement:
A group $G$ has
this property when every element of $G$ has order a power of $2$, $G$ is generated by its
involutions, and $[[x, u], u] = 1$ for every $x \in G$ and every involution $u \in G$, where
$[x, u] = x^{-1} u^{-1} x u$.

articles.title: Iterated commutators for Engel lengths
articles.statement:
For elements $h$ and $g$ of a group and a natural
number $l$, the iterated commutator $[h, g; l]$ is defined by $[h, g; 0] = h$ and
$[h, g; l + 1] = [[h, g; l], g]$, where $[x, y] = x^{-1} y^{-1} x y$; in particular
$[h, g; 1] = [h, g]$.

articles.title: Engel lengths of products admit no polynomial bound (Kourovka 11.88)
articles.statement:
There is a group $G$
such that for every polynomial $\varphi(x, y)$ in two variables with natural-number coefficients
there are $u, v \in G$ such that $u$, $v$ and $uv$ are Engel elements and
$l(uv) > \varphi(l(u), l(v))$. Here $g \in G$ is an Engel element if there is a $k \ge 1$ with
$[h, g; k] = 1$ for all $h \in G$, and its Engel length $l(g)$ is the least such $k$, where
$[h, g; 0] = h$, $[h, g; i + 1] = [[h, g; i], g]$ and $[x, y] = x^{-1} y^{-1} x y$.

For a prime $p$, Dolbak builds finite $p$-groups $G_n$ (wreath products of a cyclic group of
order $p$ by groups $K_n$) with elements $c_n$ and $c_n^{-1} b_0$ of Engel length at most
$(n + 1)p - n + 1$ whose product $b_0$ has Engel length at least $p^n$. He takes the direct
product of the $G_n$ in the restricted sense (the direct sum, whose elements have finite support).
It is a single Engel group: an element of finite support has Engel length at most the largest
Engel length of its coordinates, and each $G_n$ is a finite $p$-group, hence nilpotent. (The
unrestricted product is not Engel: the element with $b_0$ in every coordinate has unbounded Engel
length.) Let $u_n$ and $v_n$ be $c_n$ and $c_n^{-1} b_0$ in coordinate $n$ and $1$ elsewhere: they
are Engel elements of length at most $(n + 1)p - n + 1$, and $u_n v_n$ has length at least $p^n$,
which exceeds every polynomial in the lengths of the factors (Theorem 1: there are Engel groups in
which the Engel length of a product of two elements is bounded by no polynomial in the Engel
lengths of the factors). The refutation of this statement uses only that $u_n$, $v_n$ and
$u_n v_n$ are Engel elements of one group. The Kourovka Archive answers 11.88 "No, it does not".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.88 (V. A. Roman'kov); resolution: L. V. Dolbak, The Engel length of the product of Engel elements, Siberian Math. J. 47, no. 1 (2006), 55-57, Theorem 1 and its proof; Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.88: "No, it does not", https://doi.org/10.1007/s11202-006-0006-9.

articles.title: Roman'kov's problem on Engel lengths of products (Kourovka 11.88)
articles.statement:
The statement that every
group $G$ has a polynomial $\varphi(x, y)$ in two variables with natural-number coefficients such
that $l(uv) \le \varphi(l(u), l(v))$ for all $u, v \in G$ for which $u$, $v$ and $uv$ are Engel
elements. Here $g \in G$ is an Engel element if there is a $k \ge 1$ with $[h, g; k] = 1$ for all
$h \in G$, and its Engel length $l(g)$ is the least such $k$, where $[h, g; 0] = h$,
$[h, g; i + 1] = [[h, g; i], g]$ and $[x, y] = x^{-1} y^{-1} x y$.

Natural coefficients lose nothing: on $\mathbb{N}^2$ every real polynomial is bounded by one with
natural coefficients.

articles.title: Engel length
articles.statement:
For an element $g$ of a group $G$, the Engel length $l(g)$ is the least
$k \ge 1$ such that $[h, g; k] = 1$ for every $h \in G$, where $[h, g; 0] = h$,
$[h, g; i + 1] = [[h, g; i], g]$ and $[x, y] = x^{-1} y^{-1} x y$. If no such $k$ exists, that
is, if $g$ is not an Engel element, then $l(g) = 0$.

articles.title: Engel element
articles.statement:
An element $g$ of a group $G$ is an Engel element if for every $h \in G$
there is an $n \ge 0$ with $h_n = 1$, where $h_0 = h$ and $h_{i + 1} = [h_i, g]$ with
$[x, g] = x^{-1} g^{-1} x g$; that is, some iterated commutator $[h, g, \dots, g]$ is trivial.

articles.title: Bounded Engel element
articles.statement:
An element $g$ of a group $G$ is an Engel element if there is an
$l \ge 1$ such that $[h, g; l] = 1$ for every $h \in G$, where $[h, g; 0] = h$,
$[h, g; i + 1] = [[h, g; i], g]$ and $[x, y] = x^{-1} y^{-1} x y$.

articles.title: Right Engel element
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, an element $a$ of a group $G$ is a right
$n$-Engel element when $[a, {}_n x] = 1$ for every $x \in G$, where $[y, x] = y^{-1} x^{-1} y x$
and $[a, {}_n x] = [\dots[[a, x], x], \dots, x]$ is the left-normed commutator with $n$ copies of
$x$ (so $[a, {}_0 x] = a$).

articles.title: Commutator for Engel lengths
articles.statement:
For elements $x$ and $y$ of a group, the commutator is
$[x, y] = x^{-1} y^{-1} x y$ (the convention of the Kourovka Notebook).

articles.title: Positive answer to Abdollahi's question on right Engel subgroups (Kourovka Problem 17.12)
articles.statement:
There are functions $e, c \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $e(n) > 0$ for every $n$ such
that, for every natural number $n$, every nilpotent group $G$ and every normal subgroup $H$ of $G$
all of whose elements are right $n$-Engel elements of $G$, the subgroup $H^{e(n)}$ generated by the
$e(n)$-th powers of elements of $H$ is contained in the $c(n)$-th term $\zeta_{c(n)}(G)$ of the
upper central series of $G$.

Crosby and Traustason prove that there are positive integers $e(n)$, $c(n)$ such that
$[H^{e(n)}, {}_{c(n)} G] = 1$, that is $H^{e(n)} \le \zeta_{c(n)}(G)$, whenever $H$ is a normal
subgroup of $G$ consisting of right $n$-Engel elements and lying in some term of the upper central
series; in a nilpotent group every subgroup does. The Kourovka Archive answers 17.12 "Yes, there
are".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 17.12 (A. Abdollahi); resolution: P. G. Crosby and G. Traustason, J. Algebra 324 (2010), 875-883, main theorem as presented by G. Traustason, Right Engel subgroups (Ischia Group Theory 2010): for a normal right n-Engel subgroup H of G with H ≤ ζ_m(G) for some m, there are positive integers e(n), c(n) with [H^{e(n)}, _{c(n)} G] = 1; Kourovka Archive, Problem 17.12 (Yes, there are), http://www.dipmat2.unisa.it/ischiagrouptheory/IGT2010/talks/Traustason.pdf.

articles.title: Abdollahi's question on right Engel subgroups (Kourovka Problem 17.12)
articles.statement:
The statement that
there are functions $e, c \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $e(n) > 0$ for every $n$ such
that, for every natural number $n$, every nilpotent group $G$ and every normal subgroup $H$ of $G$
all of whose elements are right $n$-Engel elements of $G$, the subgroup $H^{e(n)}$ generated by the
$e(n)$-th powers of elements of $H$ is contained in the $c(n)$-th term $\zeta_{c(n)}(G)$ of the
upper central series of $G$.

articles.title: Non-abelian simple groups can have nontrivial Engel elements (Kourovka 16.17)
articles.statement:
There is a
non-abelian simple group $G$ (one with elements $a$, $b$ such that $ab \ne ba$) that contains
an Engel element $g \ne 1$. Here $g$ is an Engel element if for every $h \in G$ some iterated
commutator $[h, g, \dots, g]$ is trivial, where $[x, g] = x^{-1} g^{-1} x g$.

The Kourovka Archive answers 16.17 "No, it can" (Bludov): an involution is an Engel element in
any 2-group, so non-abelian simple 2-groups are counterexamples. Simple infinite 2-groups exist
by Archive 4.74(a), from the finitely generated infinite groups of exponent $2^n$ of Ivanov and
Lysënok and Zel'manov's solution of the restricted Burnside problem.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 16.17 (V. V. Bludov); resolution: V. V. Bludov, letter of 30 March 2006, as recorded in the Kourovka Archive; infinite simple 2-groups: Kourovka Archive, Problem 4.74(a) (S. V. Ivanov, Int. J. Algebra Comput. 4 (1994), 1-308; I. G. Lysënok, Izv. Math. 60 (1996), 453-654; E. I. Zel'manov, Math. USSR-Sb. 72 (1992), 543-565), Kourovka Archive, Problem 16.17 (No, it can: an involution is an Engel element in any 2-group, and non-abelian simple 2-groups exist).

articles.title: Bludov's problem on Engel elements in simple groups (Kourovka 16.17)
articles.statement:
The statement that no
non-abelian simple group contains an Engel element other than the identity: for every simple group
$G$ with elements $a$, $b$ such that $ab \ne ba$, every Engel element $g$ of $G$ satisfies $g = 1$.
Here $g$ is an Engel element if for every $h \in G$ some iterated commutator $[h, g, \dots, g]$ is
trivial, where $[x, g] = x^{-1} g^{-1} x g$.

articles.title: Groups with a unique product presentation
articles.statement:
A group $G$ has a unique product presentation if
there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and elements $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1} \in G$ such that every element of $G$
equals $a_0^{k_0} a_1^{k_1} \cdots a_{n-1}^{k_{n-1}}$ for exactly one tuple
$(k_0, \dots, k_{n-1}) \in \mathbb{Z}^n$.

articles.title: Almost polycyclic groups (Kourovka Problem 13.11)
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is almost polycyclic, or
virtually polycyclic, if some subgroup of finite index in $G$ is polycyclic.

articles.title: Polycyclic groups (Kourovka Problem 13.11)
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is polycyclic if it has a finite
series of subgroups $1 = H_0 \le H_1 \le \cdots \le H_n = G$ in which each $H_i$ is normal in
$H_{i+1}$ and each quotient $H_{i+1} / H_i$ is cyclic.

articles.title: A torsion-free group with a unique product presentation need not be almost polycyclic
articles.statement:
Not
every torsion-free group with a unique product presentation is almost polycyclic: there is a group
$G$ in which no element other than $1$ has finite order, which has a unique product presentation,
and which is not almost polycyclic.

Muranov's theorem gives such a group with $n$ generators for every $n \ge 63$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 13.11 (V. V. Bludov); resolution: A. Muranov, On torsion-free groups with finite regular file bases, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 359 (2007), 3609-3645, Theorem (Section 1, proved at the end of Section 5), https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9947-07-04256-0.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 13.11 (torsion-free groups with a unique product presentation)
articles.statement:
The
statement, asked by V. V. Bludov, that every group $G$ which is torsion-free (no element of $G$
other than $1$ has finite order) and has a unique product presentation is almost polycyclic.

articles.title: The intersection of the derived series need not be perfect
articles.statement:
There exists a finitely presented
group $G$ such that the intersection $D = \bigcap_{n} G^{(n)}$ of the terms $G^{(n)}$ of the
derived series of $G$ satisfies $[D, D] \ne D$. That is, the conjecture of Kourovka Problem 17.82
is false; the Kourovka Archive credits this answer to V. A. Roman'kov (2011).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 17.82 (R. Mikhailov); resolution: V. A. Roman'kov, Siberian Math. J. 52 (2011), 348-351, Kourovka Archive, Problem 17.82 (No, not always).

articles.title: Perfectness of the intersection of the derived series (Kourovka 17.82)
articles.statement:
The conjecture of
R. Mikhailov that for every finitely presented group $G$, the intersection
$D = \bigcap_{n} G^{(n)}$ of the terms $G^{(n)}$ of the derived series of $G$ satisfies
$[D, D] = D$, that is, $D$ has trivial abelianization.

articles.title: Local word identities need not hold globally in connected groups
articles.statement:
There are a connected
Hausdorff topological group $G$, a word $W(x, y)$ in the free group on two generators $x$, $y$ and
a nonempty open subset $U$ of $G \times G$ such that $W(a, b) = 1$ for all $(a, b) \in U$ but
$W(a, b) \ne 1$ for some $a, b \in G$. This answers Kourovka Notebook Problem 18.71 in the
negative.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 18.71 (J. Mycielski); resolution: I. N. Zyabrev and E. A. Reznichenko, On identities in connected topological groups, preprint, arXiv:2406.05203 (2024), abstract: a connected (indeed path-connected) Hausdorff topological group in which, for an odd n, the identity x^n = e holds in some neighbourhood of the identity but not in the whole group; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 18.71 solved (odd n > 10^10), https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.05203.

articles.title: Local word identities in connected groups (Kourovka 18.71)
articles.statement:
The statement that for every
connected Hausdorff topological group $G$ and every word $W(x, y)$ in the free group on two
generators $x$, $y$, if $W(a, b) = 1$ for all $(a, b)$ in some nonempty open subset of $G \times G$,
then $W(a, b) = 1$ for all $a, b \in G$.

The problem is posed for connected topological groups; here they are also taken to be Hausdorff,
which weakens the statement.

articles.title: $p$-local groups
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a natural number. A group $H$ is $p$-local when, for every
natural number $n$ coprime to $p$, the map $x \mapsto x^n$ is a bijection of $H$.

This is the notion of a $P$-local group of Hilton, Mislin and Roitberg, for $P$ the set whose only
element is $p$.

articles.title: $p$-localization of a group
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a natural number. A homomorphism of groups
$e \colon G \to L$ is a $p$-localization when $L$ is nilpotent and $p$-local, and every
homomorphism $f$ from $G$ to a nilpotent $p$-local group $H$ factors uniquely through $e$: there is
exactly one homomorphism $g \colon L \to H$ with $g \circ e = f$.

articles.title: Nilpotent extensions that split at every prime need not split
articles.statement:
It is not true that every
extension of nilpotent groups with finitely generated quotient that splits at every prime splits:
there are nilpotent groups $N$, $G$ and $Q$ with $Q$ finitely generated, an injective homomorphism
$i \colon N \to G$ and a surjective homomorphism $\pi \colon G \to Q$ with $\operatorname{im} i =
\ker \pi$, such that the extension splits at every prime $p$ (for some $p$-localizations $G_p$
of $G$ and $Q_p$ of $Q$, the localized quotient map $\pi_p \colon G_p \to Q_p$ has a homomorphic
section) but there is no homomorphism $s \colon Q \to G$ with $\pi \circ s = \mathrm{id}_Q$.

Lorensen constructed such extensions in which $N$, $G$ and $Q$ are finitely generated and
torsion-free.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 12.93 (P. Hilton); resolution: K. Lorensen, Nonsplit nilpotent group extensions that split at every prime, Math. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. 123 (1998), no. 2, 213-215, doi:10.1017/S0305004197002211, introduction (first page, shown on Cambridge Core): examples of nilpotent group extensions which split at every p-localization but fail to split, disproving Hilton's conjecture that any nilpotent group extension with finitely generated quotient which splits at every prime must split; in both families of counterexamples the groups are torsion-free and finitely generated. Kourovka Archive, Problem 12.93: 'No, not always', https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305004197002211.

articles.title: Hilton's splitting question for nilpotent extensions (Kourovka 12.93)
articles.statement:
The proposition
that every extension of nilpotent groups with finitely generated quotient that splits at every
prime splits: for all nilpotent groups $N$, $G$ and $Q$ with $Q$ finitely generated, every
injective homomorphism $i \colon N \to G$ and every surjective homomorphism $\pi \colon G \to Q$
with $\operatorname{im} i = \ker \pi$ such that the extension splits at every prime $p$, there is
a homomorphism $s \colon Q \to G$ with $\pi \circ s = \mathrm{id}_Q$.

articles.title: Splitting at a prime
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a natural number and $\pi \colon G \to Q$ a homomorphism
of groups (in the intended use, the quotient map of an extension). Then $\pi$ splits at $p$ when
there exist $p$-localizations $e_G \colon G \to G_p$ and $e_Q \colon Q \to Q_p$ and homomorphisms
$\pi_p \colon G_p \to Q_p$ and $s \colon Q_p \to G_p$ with $\pi_p \circ e_G = e_Q \circ \pi$ and
$\pi_p \circ s = \mathrm{id}_{Q_p}$; that is, the localized quotient map $\pi_p$ has a homomorphic
section.

Since $Q_p$ is nilpotent and $p$-local, $\pi_p$ is the unique homomorphism with
$\pi_p \circ e_G = e_Q \circ \pi$; since localizations are unique up to unique isomorphism, the
condition does not depend on the chosen localizations.

articles.title: Minimal condition on centralizers (Kourovka 13.16)
articles.statement:
For a subset $X$ of a group $G$, let
$C_G(X)$ be its centralizer, the subgroup of elements of $G$ that commute with every element of
$X$. The group $G$ satisfies the minimal condition on centralizers if every nonempty set of such
centralizers has a minimal element with respect to inclusion; equivalently, there is no infinite
strictly descending chain $C_G(X_0) > C_G(X_1) > \cdots$ of centralizers.

articles.title: Hirsch–Plotkin radical
articles.statement:
The Hirsch–Plotkin radical of a group $G$ is the subgroup
generated by all locally nilpotent normal subgroups of $G$. By the Hirsch–Plotkin theorem it is
the largest locally nilpotent normal subgroup of $G$.

articles.title: Hypercentral group (Kourovka 13.16)
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is hypercentral if for every proper normal
subgroup $N$ of $G$ there is some $g \in G$ with $g \notin N$ and $g h g^{-1} h^{-1} \in N$ for all
$h \in G$; that is, every nontrivial quotient $G/N$ has nontrivial centre (equivalently, the
transfinite upper central series of $G$ reaches $G$).

articles.title: Locally nilpotent group (Kourovka 13.16)
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is locally nilpotent if for every
finite subset $S \subseteq G$ the subgroup generated by $S$ is nilpotent, that is, every finitely
generated subgroup of $G$ is nilpotent.

articles.title: Locally nilpotent subgroup
articles.statement:
A subgroup $N$ of a group $G$ is locally nilpotent when every
subgroup generated by finitely many elements of $N$ is nilpotent.

articles.title: Locally nilpotent groups with the minimal condition on centralizers are hypercentral
articles.statement:
Every
locally nilpotent group satisfying the minimal condition on centralizers is hypercentral. This
answers Kourovka Problem 13.16 (F. O. Wagner) in the affirmative (V. V. Bludov, 1998).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 13.16 (F. O. Wagner); resolution: V. V. Bludov, Algebra and Logic 37 (1998), no. 3, 151-156, Kourovka Archive, Problem 13.16: Yes, it is.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 13.16 (Wagner)
articles.statement:
The proposition that every locally nilpotent group
satisfying the minimal condition on centralizers is hypercentral.

articles.title: A finite group with exactly one non-commutator
articles.statement:
There is a finite group $G$ of order greater
than $2$ in which exactly one element is not a commutator, that is, not of the form $x^{-1}y^{-1}xy$
with $x, y \in G$.

Resolved true: Skresanov constructs an infinite series of finite groups with exactly one element
that is not a commutator, the smallest of order 16609443840, and Hatem and Siniora find two such
groups of order 368640, the smallest possible order. The Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) answers
17.76 "Yes".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 17.76 (D. MacHale); resolution: S. V. Skresanov, Siberian Electron. Math. Rep. 23 (2026), 603-607 (preprint On finite groups with exactly one noncommutator, arXiv:2509.17587); O. Hatem and D. Siniora, Int. J. Group Theory 15 (2026), 161-167 (preprint A group with exactly one noncommutator, arXiv:2511.00541), Skresanov, abstract (an infinite series of such groups, the smallest of order 16609443840); Hatem-Siniora, abstract (two non-isomorphic groups of order 368640, the smallest order); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 17.76 solved (Yes, such groups do exist, and there are infinitely many examples), https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.17587.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 17.76 (finite groups with exactly one non-commutator)
articles.statement:
This is the
statement that there is a finite group $G$ of order greater than $2$ in which exactly one element is
not a commutator, that is, not of the form $x^{-1}y^{-1}xy$ with $x, y \in G$.

articles.title: Locally nilpotent group
articles.statement: A group is locally nilpotent if every finitely generated subgroup is nilpotent.

articles.title: No infinite perfect locally nilpotent $p$-group has only nilpotent proper subgroups
articles.statement:
There is
no prime $p$ and no infinite locally nilpotent $p$-group $G$ (every element of $G$ has order a
power of $p$) such that $G = [G, G]$ and every proper subgroup of $G$ is nilpotent.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 14.86 (J. Wiegold); resolution: A. O. Asar, Locally nilpotent p-groups whose proper subgroups are hypercentral or nilpotent-by-Chernikov, J. London Math. Soc. (2) 61 (2000), no. 2, 412-422, Kourovka Archive, Problem 14.86 (answer: No, it does not exist).

articles.title: Kourovka 14.86: perfect locally nilpotent $p$-groups with nilpotent proper subgroups
articles.statement:
The
proposition that for some prime $p$ there is an infinite locally nilpotent $p$-group $G$ (every
element of $G$ has order a power of $p$) such that $G = [G, G]$ and every proper subgroup of $G$
is nilpotent.

articles.title: Free central extensions need not be residually nilpotent
articles.statement:
There exist a free group $F$ and a
normal subgroup $R$ of $F$ such that $F/R$ is finitely presented and residually torsion-free
nilpotent, while $F/[F, R]$ is not residually nilpotent; here $[F, R]$ is the subgroup of $F$
generated by all commutators $[f, r]$ with $f \in F$ and $r \in R$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 16.65 (R. Mikhailov, I. B. S. Passi); resolution: V. V. Bludov, J. Group Theory 12 (2009), no. 4, 579-590, Kourovka Archive, Problem 16.65 (Yes, there does).

articles.title: Mikhailov–Passi question on free central extensions (Kourovka 16.65)
articles.statement:
The assertion that
there exist a free group $F$ and a normal subgroup $R$ of $F$ such that $F/R$ is finitely
presented and residually torsion-free nilpotent, while $F/[F, R]$ is not residually nilpotent,
where $[F, R]$ is the subgroup of $F$ generated by all commutators $[f, r]$ with $f \in F$ and
$r \in R$.

articles.title: Residually nilpotent group
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is residually nilpotent if for every element
$g \ne 1$ of $G$ there is a normal subgroup $N$ of $G$ with $g \notin N$ such that the quotient
$G/N$ is nilpotent.

articles.title: Residually torsion-free nilpotent group
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is residually torsion-free nilpotent
if for every element $g \ne 1$ of $G$ there is a normal subgroup $N$ of $G$ with $g \notin N$ such
that the quotient $G/N$ is nilpotent and torsion-free, that is, every nontrivial element of $G/N$
has infinite order.

articles.title: Mycielski's trace-range question for $\mathrm{GL}(2, \mathbb{R})$ has a negative answer
articles.statement:
There is a nontrivial element $w$ of the free group on two generators $x, y$ such that some real
number $t \ge -2$ is not the trace of $w(A, B)$ for any $A, B \in \mathrm{GL}(2, \mathbb{R})$, where
$w(A, B)$ is obtained by substituting $A$ for $x$ and $B$ for $y$.

Resolved false: the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) answers 16.69(a), posed for `x, y ∈ GL(2, ℝ)`,
"No, it need not" (AI solution confirmed by A. Thom), citing the Nilradical note, whose Theorem 2
gives an explicit word `W ≠ 1` with `tr W(A, B) > 7/4` for all `A, B ∈ SL(2, ℝ)`. Source: E. I.
Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st
issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 16.69 (J. Mycielski); resolution: Nilradical v1.0.0, Word
maps on PSL2: real and complex cases, result notes (21 September 2026); A. Thom, Convergent
sequences in discrete groups, Canad. Math. Bull. 56 (2013), 424-433, (a) Nilradical, Theorem 2 (an
explicit W ≠ 1 with tr W(A, B) > 7/4 for all A, B ∈ SL_2(ℝ)); (b) Thom, Corollary 1.2 (for every n
and ε > 0 a word w ≠ 1 with ‖1 - w(u, v)‖ ≤ ε for all u, v ∈ U(n)); the Kourovka Notebook (21st
issue) marks 16.69 solved (a: No, AI solution confirmed by A. Thom; b: No, Thom 2013),
https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/nilradical-kourovka-16-68-69.pdf.

articles.title: Mycielski's trace-range property for $\mathrm{GL}(2, \mathbb{R})$ (Kourovka 16.69(a))
articles.statement:
For
every nontrivial element $w$ of the free group on two generators $x, y$, the set of traces
$\operatorname{tr} w(A, B)$, where $A, B$ range over $\mathrm{GL}(2, \mathbb{R})$ and $w(A, B)$ is
obtained by substituting $A$ for $x$ and $B$ for $y$, contains the interval $[-2, \infty)$.

articles.title: Nontrivial word maps on $\mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{C})$ are surjective (Kourovka 16.68(b))
articles.statement:
For every nontrivial element $w$ of the free group $F_2$ on two generators, the word map
$\mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{C}) \times \mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{C}) \to \mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{C})$,
$(x, y) \mapsto w(x, y)$, is surjective. That is, Mycielski's question has an affirmative answer
for $\mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{C})$.

Nilradical (Theorem 1) proves that for every algebraically closed field $K$ of characteristic
zero, in particular $\mathbb{C}$, every nontrivial word $w \in F_2$ induces a surjective map
$\mathrm{PSL}(2, K)^2 \to \mathrm{PSL}(2, K)$; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) records the
affirmative answer for $\mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{C})$ (AI solution confirmed by A. Thom).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 16.68 (J. Mycielski); resolution: Nilradical v1.0.0, Word maps on PSL2: real and complex cases, result notes (21 September 2026); A. Thom, Convergent sequences in discrete groups, Canad. Math. Bull. 56 (2013), 424-433, Nilradical, Theorem 1 (every w ≠ 1 in F_2 induces a surjective map PSL_2(K)² → PSL_2(K) for K algebraically closed of characteristic 0) and Theorem 2 (an explicit W ≠ 1 with tr W(A, B) > 7/4 for all A, B ∈ SL_2(ℝ)); Thom, Corollary 1.2 (for every n and ε > 0 a word w ≠ 1 with ‖1 - w(u, v)‖ ≤ ε for all u, v ∈ U(n)), for SO(3, ℝ); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 16.68 solved (AI solution confirmed by A. Thom; SO(3, ℝ) from Thom 2013), https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/nilradical-kourovka-16-68-69.pdf.

articles.title: Surjectivity of word maps on $\mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{C})$ (Kourovka 16.68(b))
articles.statement:
The
statement, asked about by J. Mycielski, that for every nontrivial element $w$ of the free group
$F_2$ on two generators, the word map
$\mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{C}) \times \mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{C}) \to \mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{C})$,
$(x, y) \mapsto w(x, y)$, is surjective.

articles.title: Some nontrivial word map on $\mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{R})$ is not surjective (Kourovka 16.68(a))
articles.statement:
There is a nontrivial element $w$ of the free group $F_2$ on two generators whose word map
$\mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{R}) \times \mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{R}) \to \mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{R})$,
$(x, y) \mapsto w(x, y)$, is not surjective. That is, Mycielski's question has a negative answer
for $\mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{R})$.

Nilradical (Theorem 2) gives an explicit nontrivial word $W$ (cyclically reduced length 44) with
$\operatorname{tr} W(A, B) > 7/4$ for all $A, B \in \mathrm{SL}(2, \mathbb{R})$; a nonidentity
involution of $\mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{R})$ lifts to a matrix of trace $0$, so the word map of
$W$ misses it. The Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) records the negative answer for
$\mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{R})$ (AI solution confirmed by A. Thom).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 16.68 (J. Mycielski); resolution: Nilradical v1.0.0, Word maps on PSL2: real and complex cases, result notes (21 September 2026); A. Thom, Convergent sequences in discrete groups, Canad. Math. Bull. 56 (2013), 424-433, Nilradical, Theorem 1 (every w ≠ 1 in F_2 induces a surjective map PSL_2(K)² → PSL_2(K) for K algebraically closed of characteristic 0) and Theorem 2 (an explicit W ≠ 1 with tr W(A, B) > 7/4 for all A, B ∈ SL_2(ℝ)); Thom, Corollary 1.2 (for every n and ε > 0 a word w ≠ 1 with ‖1 - w(u, v)‖ ≤ ε for all u, v ∈ U(n)), for SO(3, ℝ); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 16.68 solved (AI solution confirmed by A. Thom; SO(3, ℝ) from Thom 2013), https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/nilradical-kourovka-16-68-69.pdf.

articles.title: Surjectivity of word maps on $\mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{R})$ (Kourovka 16.68(a))
articles.statement:
The
statement, asked about by J. Mycielski, that for every nontrivial element $w$ of the free group
$F_2$ on two generators, the word map
$\mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{R}) \times \mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{R}) \to \mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{R})$,
$(x, y) \mapsto w(x, y)$, is surjective.

articles.title: Mycielski's real-part question for quaternion word maps has a negative answer
articles.statement:
There is a
nontrivial element $w$ of the free group on two generators $x, y$ such that some real number $t$
with $-5/27 \le t \le 1$ is not the real part of $w(p, q)$ for any nonzero real quaternions $p, q$,
where $w(p, q)$ is obtained by substituting $p$ for $x$ and $q$ for $y$.

Resolved false: the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) answers 16.69(b) "No, it need not", citing Thom
(2013), whose Corollary 1.2 gives, for every `n` and `ε > 0`, a word `w ≠ 1` with `‖1 - w(u, v)‖ ≤
ε` for all `u, v ∈ U(n)`. Source: E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group
Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 16.69 (J. Mycielski);
resolution: Nilradical v1.0.0, Word maps on PSL2: real and complex cases, result notes (21 September
2026); A. Thom, Convergent sequences in discrete groups, Canad. Math. Bull. 56 (2013), 424-433, (a)
Nilradical, Theorem 2 (an explicit W ≠ 1 with tr W(A, B) > 7/4 for all A, B ∈ SL_2(ℝ)); (b) Thom,
Corollary 1.2 (for every n and ε > 0 a word w ≠ 1 with ‖1 - w(u, v)‖ ≤ ε for all u, v ∈ U(n)); the
Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 16.69 solved (a: No, AI solution confirmed by A. Thom; b: No,
Thom 2013),
https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/nilradical-kourovka-16-68-69.pdf.

articles.title: Mycielski's real-part property for quaternion word maps (Kourovka 16.69(b))
articles.statement:
For every
nontrivial element $w$ of the free group on two generators $x, y$, the set of real parts
$\operatorname{Re} w(p, q)$, where $p, q$ range over the nonzero real quaternions and $w(p, q)$ is
obtained by substituting $p$ for $x$ and $q$ for $y$, contains the interval $[-5/27, 1]$.

articles.title: Some nontrivial word map on $\mathrm{SO}(3, \mathbb{R})$ is not surjective (Kourovka 16.68(c))
articles.statement:
There is a nontrivial element $w$ of the free group $F_2$ on two generators whose word map
$\mathrm{SO}(3, \mathbb{R}) \times \mathrm{SO}(3, \mathbb{R}) \to \mathrm{SO}(3, \mathbb{R})$,
$(x, y) \mapsto w(x, y)$, is not surjective. That is, Mycielski's question has a negative answer
for $\mathrm{SO}(3, \mathbb{R})$.

The Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) answers 16.68 negatively for $\mathrm{SO}(3, \mathbb{R})$,
noting that this follows from Thom (2013), whose Corollary 1.2 gives, for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, a nontrivial word $w$ with $\|1 - w(u, v)\| \le \varepsilon$ for all unitary
$u, v$, in particular for all $u, v \in \mathrm{SO}(3, \mathbb{R})$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 16.68 (J. Mycielski); resolution: Nilradical v1.0.0, Word maps on PSL2: real and complex cases, result notes (21 September 2026); A. Thom, Convergent sequences in discrete groups, Canad. Math. Bull. 56 (2013), 424-433, Nilradical, Theorem 1 (every w ≠ 1 in F_2 induces a surjective map PSL_2(K)² → PSL_2(K) for K algebraically closed of characteristic 0) and Theorem 2 (an explicit W ≠ 1 with tr W(A, B) > 7/4 for all A, B ∈ SL_2(ℝ)); Thom, Corollary 1.2 (for every n and ε > 0 a word w ≠ 1 with ‖1 - w(u, v)‖ ≤ ε for all u, v ∈ U(n)), for SO(3, ℝ); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 16.68 solved (AI solution confirmed by A. Thom; SO(3, ℝ) from Thom 2013), https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/nilradical-kourovka-16-68-69.pdf.

articles.title: Surjectivity of word maps on $\mathrm{SO}(3, \mathbb{R})$ (Kourovka 16.68(c))
articles.statement:
The
statement, asked about by J. Mycielski, that for every nontrivial element $w$ of the free group
$F_2$ on two generators, the word map
$\mathrm{SO}(3, \mathbb{R}) \times \mathrm{SO}(3, \mathbb{R}) \to \mathrm{SO}(3, \mathbb{R})$,
$(x, y) \mapsto w(x, y)$, is surjective.

articles.title: Word map
articles.statement:
