For a group $G$ and an element $w$ of the free group $F_2$ on two generators
$x_0, x_1$, the word map of $w$ is the map $G \times G \to G$ sending $(x, y)$ to $w(x, y)$, the
image of $w$ under the group homomorphism $F_2 \to G$ with $x_0 \mapsto x$ and $x_1 \mapsto y$.

articles.title: Breadth of a finite group
articles.statement:
For a finite group $G$ and a natural number $p$, the breadth
$\operatorname{br}_p(G)$ of $G$ is the maximum of the element breadths $\operatorname{br}_p(g)$
over all $g \in G$.

articles.title: Conjugacy class sizes divide the group order
articles.statement:
In a finite group $G$, the number of
elements of the conjugacy class of any $g \in G$ divides the order $|G|$.

articles.title: The conjugacy class of the identity
articles.statement:
In every group, the conjugacy class of the identity
element $1$ is the singleton $\{1\}$.

articles.title: Breadth from an exact class size
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group, $p$ a prime, $k$ a natural
number and $g \in G$. If the conjugacy class of $g$ has exactly $p^k$ elements, then the breadth
$\operatorname{br}_p(g)$ of $g$ equals $k$.

articles.title: Element breadth is at most the group breadth
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group and $p$ a
natural number. For every $g \in G$, the breadth $\operatorname{br}_p(g)$ of $g$ is at most
the breadth $\operatorname{br}_p(G)$ of $G$.

articles.title: Breadth of the identity
articles.statement:
In a finite group, the breadth $\operatorname{br}_p(1)$ of the
identity element $1$ is $0$ for every natural number $p$.

articles.title: Breadth of an element
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group, $p$ a natural number and $g \in G$,
and write $g^G$ for the conjugacy class of $g$. When $p \ge 2$, the breadth
$\operatorname{br}_p(g)$ of $g$ is $\lfloor \log_p |g^G| \rfloor$, the largest natural number
$k$ with $p^k \le |g^G|$; when $p \le 1$, it is $0$.

If $p$ is prime and $G$ is a $p$-group, then $|g^G|$ is a power of $p$, so
$p^{\operatorname{br}_p(g)} = |g^G|$.

articles.title: The group breadth is attained
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group and $p$ a natural number.
There is an element $g \in G$ whose breadth $\operatorname{br}_p(g)$ equals the breadth
$\operatorname{br}_p(G)$ of $G$.

articles.title: Conjugacy classes of a finite $p$-group have $p$-power size
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and
$G$ a finite $p$-group. For every $g \in G$ there is a natural number $k$ such that the
conjugacy class of $g$ has exactly $p^k$ elements.

articles.title: Class sizes in a $p$-group via breadth
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime, $G$ a finite $p$-group and
$g \in G$, and write $g^G$ for the conjugacy class of $g$. Then the breadth
$\operatorname{br}_p(g)$ of $g$ satisfies $p^{\operatorname{br}_p(g)} = |g^G|$.

articles.title: Centralizers of maximal order need not contain normalized nilpotent subgroups
articles.statement:
For an element
$x$ of a group $G$ write $C_G(x)$ for its centralizer. There exist a finite group $G$, an element
$a \ne 1$ of $G$ with $|C_G(x)| \le |C_G(a)|$ for every $x \ne 1$ in $G$, and a nilpotent subgroup
$H$ of $G$ normalized by $C_G(a)$ (that is, $C_G(a)$ is contained in the normalizer of $H$) such
that $H$ is not contained in $C_G(a)$.

Jayadevan constructs a group $G$ of order $660602880$, an involution $a$ with
$|C_G(a)| = 41287680 \ge |C_G(g)|$ for every $g \ne 1$, and a nilpotent normal subgroup $H$ of
order $16384$ not contained in $C_G(a)$; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) answers Problem 14.67
"No, not always".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 14.67 (I. T. Mukhamet'yanov, A. N. Fomin); resolution: A. Jayadevan, Centralizers of maximal order and nilpotent normal subgroups, preprint, Zenodo record 22861469 (2026), main theorem: a group of order 660602880 with an involution a and a nilpotent normal subgroup H of order 16384 such that |C_G(a)| = 41287680 ≥ |C_G(g)| for every g ≠ 1 but H is not contained in C_G(a); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 14.67 solved (AI solution confirmed by K. Muliarchyk), https://zenodo.org/records/22861469.

articles.title: Mukhamet'yanov–Fomin problem on centralizers of maximal order
articles.statement:
For an element $x$ of a
group $G$ write $C_G(x)$ for its centralizer. This is the statement that for every finite group
$G$ and every element $a \ne 1$ of $G$ with $|C_G(x)| \le |C_G(a)|$ for every $x \ne 1$ in $G$,
every nilpotent subgroup $H$ of $G$ normalized by $C_G(a)$ (that is, $C_G(a)$ is contained in the
normalizer of $H$) is contained in $C_G(a)$.

This is Kourovka Notebook Problem 14.67 (I. T. Mukhamet'yanov, A. N. Fomin).

articles.title: The class number can exceed the order of every nilpotent subgroup
articles.statement:
There is a finite group
$G$ such that the number $k(G)$ of conjugacy classes of $G$ is greater than $|N|$ for every
nilpotent subgroup $N$ of $G$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 14.54 (M. W. Liebeck, L. Pyber); resolution: S. Tertooy, Class numbers and nilpotent subgroups of PGL(2,q), preprint, arXiv:2606.21404 (2026), abstract: for certain odd prime powers q, k(PGL(2,q)) exceeds the order of every nilpotent subgroup; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 14.54 solved (No, not always), https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.21404.

articles.title: Liebeck–Pyber problem on the class number and nilpotent subgroups
articles.statement:
The proposition that
every finite group $G$ has a nilpotent subgroup $N$ whose order $|N|$ is at least the number
$k(G)$ of conjugacy classes of $G$. This is Kourovka Problem 14.54 (M. W. Liebeck, L. Pyber).

articles.title: A finite group of maximal order with a given class number can be soluble
articles.statement:
There are an
integer $k \ge 1$, an insoluble finite group with exactly $k$ conjugacy classes, and a soluble
finite group $G$ with exactly $k$ conjugacy classes whose order is at least the order of every
finite group with exactly $k$ conjugacy classes. So it is not true that whenever some insoluble
finite group has exactly $k \ge 1$ conjugacy classes, every finite group of maximal order with
exactly $k$ conjugacy classes is insoluble.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 17.77 (R. Heffernan, D. MacHale); resolution: A. Vera-López and J. Sangroniz, Math. Nachr. 280 (2007), 676-694, Kourovka Archive, Problem 17.77 (No, it is not; see Table 1 in Vera-López-Sangroniz).

articles.title: Heffernan–MacHale problem on groups of maximal order with a given class number
articles.statement:
The
proposition that for every integer $k \ge 1$ such that some insoluble finite group has exactly $k$
conjugacy classes, every finite group $G$ with exactly $k$ conjugacy classes whose order is at
least the order of every finite group with exactly $k$ conjugacy classes is insoluble. This is
Kourovka Problem 17.77 (R. Heffernan, D. MacHale).

articles.title: The set of commuting probabilities is closed
articles.statement:
Let $\Pr(G)$ denote the commuting
probability of a group $G$: $\Pr(G) = |\{(x, y) \in G \times G : xy = yx\}| / |G|^2$ if $G$ is
finite, and $\Pr(G) = 0$ if $G$ is infinite. Then the set $\{\Pr(G) : G \text{ a group}\}$ is a
closed subset of $\mathbb{R}$.

## Sources

- https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.09402. Problem `commProb_closed` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Perfect centreless groups need not have order at most the square of the largest class size
articles.statement:
It is not true that every finite group $G$ that is perfect ($[G, G] = G$) and has trivial centre
contains an element $x$ with $|G| \le |x^G|^2$, where $x^G$ is the conjugacy class of $x$. That
is, some perfect centreless finite group $G$ satisfies $|G| > n^2$, where $n$ is the largest size
of a conjugacy class of $G$.

Muliarchyk (Theorem 1.1) constructs a perfect centreless finite group of order $120 \cdot 5^{68}$
whose largest conjugacy class has size $30 \cdot 5^{32}$, so $|G| / n^2 = 250/3 > 1$; the 21st
issue of the Kourovka Notebook marks 20.30 solved ("No, not always"). The preprint acknowledges
assistance from ChatGPT.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 20.30 (P. M. Neumann and M. R. Vaughan-Lee; I. B. Gorshkov); resolution: K. Muliarchyk, Perfect centreless groups with large centralizers, preprint (2026), Kourovka Notebook site, Theorem 1.1: an explicit perfect centreless finite group of order 120·5^68 whose largest conjugacy class has size 30·5^32, so |G|/n² = 250/3 > 1 (built from a class-three Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff group over F₅ and an SL₂(F₅)-action); Theorem 6.1: no bound |G| ≤ C n^c holds for all perfect centreless finite groups; Kourovka Notebook (21st issue), Problem 20.30: No, not always, https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/kourovka_20_30_solution.pdf.

articles.title: Kourovka 20.30: the order of a perfect centreless group and its largest conjugacy class
articles.statement:
The proposition that every finite group $G$ that is perfect ($[G, G] = G$) and has trivial centre
contains an element $x$ with $|G| \le |x^G|^2$, where $x^G$ is the conjugacy class of $x$.
Equivalently, $|G| \le n^2$, where $n$ is the largest size of a conjugacy class of $G$.

articles.title: Groups with a normal p-complement
articles.statement:
A group $G$ has a normal $p$-complement when it has a
normal subgroup $N$ and a Sylow $p$-subgroup $P$ that are complements of each other: every element
of $G$ can be written uniquely as $nq$ with $n \in N$ and $q \in P$.

articles.title: A maximal p-part of a class size does not force a normal p-complement
articles.statement:
For a prime $p$, the
$p$-part of a positive integer $m$ is the largest power of $p$ dividing $m$. There exist a finite
group $G$, a prime $p$ and a $p$-element $g$ of $G$ (that is, $g^{p^k} = 1$ for some natural
number $k$) such that for every $x \in G$ the $p$-part of the size of the conjugacy class of $x$
is at most the $p$-part of the size of the conjugacy class of $g$, but $G$ has no normal
$p$-complement.

Sambale's counterexample is the group $\mathrm{SL}(2, 3) \rtimes Q_8$ of order $192$ (number $945$
in the GAP library of small groups) with $p = 2$. In it an element of order $4$ has class size
$24$, whose $2$-part $8$ is the largest $2$-part of a class size, while the eight elements of
order $3$ form one conjugacy class, so there is no normal subgroup of order $3$, that is, no
normal $2$-complement.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 20.27 (I. B. Gorshkov); resolution: B. Sambale, letter of 16 February 2022, recorded in the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue), Problem 20.27: "No, not necessarily, a counterexample is given by SmallGroup(192,945)", https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Gorshkov's problem on maximal p-parts of class sizes
articles.statement:
For a prime $p$, the $p$-part of a
positive integer $m$ is the largest power of $p$ dividing $m$. This is the statement that for
every finite group $G$, every prime $p$ and every $p$-element $g$ of $G$ (that is, $g^{p^k} = 1$
for some natural number $k$), if for every $x \in G$ the $p$-part of the size of the conjugacy
class of $x$ is at most the $p$-part of the size of the conjugacy class of $g$, then $G$ has a
normal $p$-complement.

This is Kourovka Notebook Problem 20.27 (I. B. Gorshkov).

articles.title: Three large conjugacy classes multiply to the whole alternating group
articles.statement:
There are a real number
$\delta$ with $0 < \delta < 1$ and a natural number $N$ such that for every $n \ge N$ and all
conjugacy classes $A$, $B$, $C$ of the alternating group $\mathrm{Alt}(n)$, each of size at least
$|\mathrm{Alt}(n)|^{\delta}$, the product set $ABC$ is all of $\mathrm{Alt}(n)$. This is the
positive answer to Kourovka Problem 20.23.

Dona (2025, Theorem 1.2) proves this with the size bound written as
$|\mathrm{Alt}(n)|^{1-\varepsilon}$ for a small $\varepsilon > 0$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 20.23 (M. Garonzi, A. Maróti); resolution: D. Dona, Products of three conjugacy classes in the alternating group, preprint, arXiv:2505.06012 (2025), Theorem 1.2: there are δ > 0 and n₀ such that for n ≥ n₀ any three conjugacy classes of G = Alt(n) of size at least |G|^(1-δ) satisfy C₁C₂C₃ = G (a positive answer to Problem 20.23 with exponent 1 - δ); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 20.23 solved, https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06012.

articles.title: Products of three large conjugacy classes in alternating groups (Kourovka 20.23)
articles.statement:
The
statement that there are a real number $\delta$ with $0 < \delta < 1$ and a natural number $N$
such that for every $n \ge N$ and all conjugacy classes $A$, $B$, $C$ of the alternating group
$\mathrm{Alt}(n)$, each of size at least $|\mathrm{Alt}(n)|^{\delta}$, the product set $ABC$ is
all of $\mathrm{Alt}(n)$.

articles.title: The set of conjugacy class sizes
articles.statement:
For a group $G$, $N(G)$ is the set of natural numbers
$|\{y \in G : y \text{ is conjugate to } x\}|$ for $x \in G$, that is, the set of sizes of the
conjugacy classes of $G$, where an infinite class counts as size $0$.

articles.title: Thompson's conjecture on conjugacy class sizes is true
articles.statement:
For all finite groups $G$ and $H$, if
$G$ is simple and non-abelian, $H$ has trivial centre, and $G$ and $H$ have the same set of
conjugacy class sizes, then $G$ and $H$ are isomorphic.

Resolved true: the Kourovka Archive answers 12.38 "Yes, it is true" (Thompson's conjecture); the
final step is I. B. Gorshkov (Commun. Algebra 47 (2019)), completing a case-by-case proof over the
finite simple groups by many authors.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 12.38 (J. G. Thompson; A. S. Kondratiev, W. J. Shi); resolution: I. B. Gorshkov, Commun. Algebra 47 (2019), no. 12, 5192-5206 (final step), Kourovka Archive, Problem 12.38: Yes, it is true; earlier steps by many authors cited there.

articles.title: Thompson's conjecture on conjugacy class sizes
articles.statement:
Write $N(G)$ for the set of sizes of the
conjugacy classes of a group $G$. Thompson's conjecture is the statement that for all finite
groups $G$ and $H$, if $G$ is simple and non-abelian, $H$ has trivial centre, and
$N(G) = N(H)$, then $G$ and $H$ are isomorphic.

This is Kourovka Notebook Problem 12.38 (J. G. Thompson).

articles.title: Minasyan's theorem (Kourovka Problem 11.42)
articles.statement:
There is a torsion-free group $G$ (no element of
$G$ other than the identity has finite order) that has exactly three conjugacy classes and has a
subgroup of index $2$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.42 (A. V. Izosov); resolution: A. Minasyan, Comment. Math. Helv. 84 (2009), 259-296, Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.42: "Yes, there does", https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 11.42 (statement)
articles.statement:
The statement that there is a torsion-free group $G$ (no
element of $G$ other than the identity has finite order) that has exactly three conjugacy classes
and has a subgroup of index $2$.

The problem was posed by A. V. Izosov.

articles.title: Bagayoko's theorem (Kourovka Problem 11.67)
articles.statement:
There is a torsion-free group $G$ (no element of
$G$ other than the identity has finite order) with exactly three conjugacy classes in which no
element $g \neq 1$ is conjugate to its inverse $g^{-1}$.

Bagayoko's example is a linearly ordered group with exactly three conjugacy classes, the positive
transseries under composition; an ordered group is torsion-free, and conjugation preserves
positivity, so no $g \neq 1$ is conjugate to $g^{-1}$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 11.67 (B. Neumann); resolution: V. Bagayoko, Ordered groups of formal series, and a conjugacy problem, arXiv:2509.09186 (2025), main result: a linearly ordered group `(𝕋^{>ℝ}, ∘, <)` of transseries under composition with exactly three conjugacy classes; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 11.67 solved, https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.09186.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 11.67 (statement)
articles.statement:
The statement that there is a torsion-free group $G$ (no
element of $G$ other than the identity has finite order) with exactly three conjugacy classes in
which no element $g \neq 1$ is conjugate to its inverse $g^{-1}$, that is, no nontrivial conjugacy
class contains a pair of mutually inverse elements.

The problem was posed by B. Neumann.

articles.title: Base relators of the Kropholler group
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be the free group on $x, y$, viewed inside
the free group on $x, y, t$. The base relators are the elements $[[a, b], [c, d]]$ and $[a, b]^2$
for all $a, b, c, d \in F$.

These elements generate $F''(F')^2$ as a normal subgroup of $F$, so they are relators for
$K = F/F''(F')^2$.

articles.title: The Kropholler group
articles.statement:
The Kropholler group $G$ is the group with generators $x, y, t$ whose
relators are the base relators, namely $[[a, b], [c, d]]$ and $[a, b]^2$ for all $a, b, c, d$ in
the free group $F$ on $x, y$, together with the twist relators $t x t^{-1} y^{-1}$ and
$t y t^{-1} (x y)^{-1}$.

With $K = F/F''(F')^2$ and $\varphi$ the automorphism $x \mapsto y$, $y \mapsto x y$ of $K$, this is
the mapping torus of $\varphi$, that is, the semidirect product $K \rtimes \langle \varphi \rangle$
($\varphi$ has infinite order on $K$).

articles.title: The Kropholler group has rational cohomological dimension 4
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be the Kropholler group.
Then $H^4(G, M) \neq 0$ for some $\mathbb{Q}G$-module $M$, and $H^n(G, M) = 0$ for every
$\mathbb{Q}G$-module $M$ and every integer $n > 4$. This resolves Kourovka Notebook Problem 12.41
by P. H. Kropholler, which asks whether this cohomological dimension is 3 or 4.

The Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 12.41 solved: $G$ is not constructible, so by Theorem
III.8 of Bridson and Kropholler its cohomological dimension over $\mathbb{Q}$ is its homological
dimension plus 1, and the homological dimension is the Hirsch length 3 (U. Stammbach).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 12.41 (P. H. Kropholler); resolution: M. R. Bridson and P. H. Kropholler, J. Reine Angew. Math. 699 (2015), 217-243; U. Stammbach, J. London Math. Soc. (2) 2 (1970), 567-570, Theorem III.8 of Bridson-Kropholler (non-constructible groups: cd = hd + 1) and Stammbach (hd = Hirsch length = 3); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 12.41 solved: it is 4.

articles.title: Rational cohomological dimension 4 of the Kropholler group (Kourovka 12.41)
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be
the Kropholler group. This is the proposition that $H^4(G, M) \neq 0$ for some $\mathbb{Q}G$-module
$M$, and $H^n(G, M) = 0$ for every $\mathbb{Q}G$-module $M$ and every integer $n > 4$; that is, the
cohomological dimension of $G$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ is $4$.

This is the answer to Kourovka Notebook Problem 12.41 (P. H. Kropholler).

articles.title: Twist relators of the Kropholler group
articles.statement:
In the free group on $x, y, t$, the twist relators
are the two elements $t x t^{-1} y^{-1}$ and $t y t^{-1} (x y)^{-1}$; they encode the relations
$t x t^{-1} = y$ and $t y t^{-1} = x y$, so conjugation by $t$ acts as the automorphism
$\varphi \colon x \mapsto y,\ y \mapsto x y$.

articles.title: Mazurov's question on first cohomology (Kourovka 16.55) has a negative answer
articles.statement:
There exist a
field $k$, a finite group $G$ and a faithful absolutely irreducible representation of $G$ on a
finite-dimensional $k$-vector space $V$ such that the first cohomology group $H^1(G, V)$ has
dimension greater than $2$ over $k$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 16.55 (V. D. Mazurov); resolution: L. L. Scott, J. Algebra 260 (2003), 416-425; J. N. Bray and R. A. Wilson, J. Group Theory 11 (2008), 669-673, Kourovka Archive, Problem 16.55 (No, it is not).

articles.title: Mazurov's question on first cohomology (Kourovka 16.55)
articles.statement:
The proposition that for every
field $k$, every finite group $G$ and every faithful absolutely irreducible representation $\rho$
of $G$ on a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space $V$, the first cohomology group $H^1(G, V)$ has
dimension at most $2$ over $k$.

articles.title: Absolutely irreducible representations
articles.statement:
A representation $\rho$ of a group $G$ on a vector
space $V$ over a field $k$ is absolutely irreducible when $V \neq 0$, the only $G$-invariant
subspaces of $V$ are $0$ and $V$, and every $k$-linear endomorphism of $V$ commuting with
$\rho(g)$ for all $g \in G$ is a scalar multiple of the identity.

For a finite-dimensional irreducible module this is equivalent to irreducibility over an algebraic
closure of $k$.

articles.title: Extensions of a division ring's additive group by units need not split (Kourovka 18.76)
articles.statement:
There exist a division ring $A$, a subgroup $G$ of its unit group $A^\times$, a group $E$, an
injective homomorphism $i$ from the additive group of $A$ to $E$ and a surjective homomorphism
$\pi : E \to G$ whose kernel is the image of $i$, with $e \, i(a) \, e^{-1} = i(\pi(e) a)$ for all
$e \in E$ and $a \in A$, such that no homomorphism $s : G \to E$ satisfies $\pi(s(g)) = g$ for all
$g \in G$. That is, the splitting statement of Kourovka Problem 18.76 is false.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 18.76 (E. A. Palyutin); resolution: M. Kinyon and J. Urban, Results on problems from the Kourovka Notebook, preprint, version 4, 19 September 2026; Achyuth Jayadevan, preprint of 14 September 2026, https://zenodo.org/records/22751423, Kinyon-Urban Section 3.28: G = F × L with F, L free of rank 2, D the division closure of kG in a Mal'cev-Neumann division ring (k = Q or a prime field), and a nonsplit extension of (D, +) by G whose conjugation action on the kernel is left multiplication; AI solutions confirmed by B. A. F. Wehrfritz, accepted in the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue), https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/kourovka-mathematics.pdf.

articles.title: Palyutin's splitting problem for division rings (Kourovka 18.76)
articles.statement:
The statement that for
every division ring $A$, every subgroup $G$ of its unit group $A^\times$ and every group $E$, if
$i$ is an injective homomorphism from the additive group of $A$ to $E$ and $\pi : E \to G$ is a
surjective homomorphism whose kernel is the image of $i$, such that
$e \, i(a) \, e^{-1} = i(\pi(e) a)$ for all $e \in E$ and $a \in A$ (so $G$ acts on the kernel by
left multiplication), then the extension splits: there is a homomorphism $s : G \to E$ with
$\pi(s(g)) = g$ for every $g \in G$.

articles.title: Finitely generated metabelian groups with finitely generated integral homology have finite rank
articles.statement:
**Finitely generated metabelian groups with finitely generated integral homology have finite
rank.** Let $G$ be a finitely generated metabelian group, that is, its second derived subgroup
$G''$ is trivial, such that for every $n \ge 0$ the integral homology group $H_n(G, \mathbb{Z})$
with trivial coefficients is finitely generated. Then $G$ has finite Prüfer rank: there is a
natural number $r$ such that every finitely generated subgroup of $G$ is generated by at most $r$
elements. This answers Kourovka Problem 10.37 positively.

The Kourovka Archive records this answer, citing Kochloukova (2003); Groves had proved it when $G$
splits over its derived subgroup.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 10.37 (G. A. Noskov); resolution: D. H. Kochloukova, Groups with finitely generated integral homologies, in: Groups St. Andrews 2001 in Oxford, Vol. II, Cambridge Univ. Press, 2003, 332-343, Kourovka Archive, Problem 10.37 ("Yes, it is").

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 10.37 (statement)
articles.statement:
The statement that every finitely generated
metabelian group $G$ (that is, one whose second derived subgroup $G''$ is trivial) all of whose
integral homology groups $H_n(G, \mathbb{Z})$ with trivial coefficients, $n \ge 0$, are finitely
generated has finite Prüfer rank: there is a natural number $r$ such that every finitely generated
subgroup of $G$ is generated by at most $r$ elements.

articles.title: Integrability of finite groups is decidable
articles.statement:
Integrable group tables form a decidable set: some
computable function decides, for every finite list $t = (t_0, \dots, t_{n-1})$ of finite lists of
natural numbers, whether there is a group structure on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which, for all
$i, j < n$, the product of $i$ and $j$ is the entry of $t_i$ at index $j$, counting from $0$ (an
entry missing from a short row is read as $0$), and which is isomorphic to the derived subgroup of
some finite group. That is, the decidability part of Kourovka Problem 21.32 has a positive answer.

Kalithasan and Thomas bound the order of some integral of an integrable finite group $G$ (their
Theorem 3.3 and its Corollary), which makes the problem decidable; the 21st issue of the Kourovka
Notebook marks 21.32 solved ("Yes, it is decidable, in nondeterministic quasi-polynomial time").
The complexity bound is not part of this statement.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 21.32 (P. J. Cameron); resolution: S. Kalithasan and V. Z. Thomas, On the decidability of the integrability of finite groups, preprint, arXiv:2602.18829 (2026), Theorem 3.3 (an integrable finite group G has an integral, a group with derived subgroup ≅ G, of order bounded in terms of |Aut(G)|, |Z(G)|, μ(G) and d(Z(G))) and its Corollary: integrability of a finite group is decidable; Kourovka Notebook (21st issue), Problem 21.32: Yes, it is decidable, in nondeterministic quasi-polynomial time, https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.18829.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 21.32 (decidability of integrability)
articles.statement:
The statement that integrable group
tables form a decidable set: some computable function decides, for every finite list
$t = (t_0, \dots, t_{n-1})$ of finite lists of natural numbers, whether $t$ is an integrable group
table, that is, whether there is a group structure on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which, for all
$i, j < n$, the product of $i$ and $j$ is the entry of $t_i$ at index $j$, counting from $0$ (an
entry missing from a short row is read as $0$), and which is isomorphic to the derived subgroup of
some finite group.

articles.title: Integrable group tables
articles.statement:
A finite list $t = (t_0, \dots, t_{n-1})$ of finite lists of
natural numbers is an integrable group table when there is a group structure on
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ such that, for all $i, j < n$, the product of $i$ and $j$ is the entry of $t_i$
at index $j$, counting from $0$ (an entry missing from a short row is read as $0$), and some finite
group $H$ has derived subgroup $[H, H]$ isomorphic to this group. Lists that are not the
multiplication table of a group on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ do not satisfy the predicate.

articles.title: Zenkov's rank bound fails (Kourovka 21.150)
articles.statement:
Call a subgroup elementary abelian if it is
abelian and there is a prime $p$ with $x^p = 1$ for all its elements $x$. There are a finite group
$G$, elementary abelian subgroups $A$ and $B$ of $G$ with $A$ normal, $A \cap B = 1$ and
$\langle A, B \rangle = G$, and an element $a \in A$ whose centralizer $C_B(a)$ in $B$ is trivial,
such that, for $H = \langle a, B \rangle$, with centre $Z(H)$ and derived subgroup $H' = [H, H]$,
some finite generating set of $B$ has fewer elements than every finite generating set of
$Z(H) \cap H'$ (here $Z(H)$ is viewed as a subgroup of $G$).

Counterexample (Monticone; van Doorn, Judin, Monticone and Morrison, Theorem 9.1):
$A = \mathbb{F}_3[x, y]/(x, y)^3$, $B = \langle 1 + x, 1 + y \rangle$ acting by multiplication,
$G = A \rtimes B$ and $a = 1$; then $C_B(a) = 1$, while
$Z(H) \cap H' = \langle x^2, xy, y^2 \rangle$ has rank $3 > 2 = \operatorname{rank} B$. The 21st
issue of the Kourovka Notebook marks 21.150 solved ("No, not always").

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 21.150 (V. I. Zenkov); resolution: P. Monticone, letter of 21 March 2026 and solution note, Kourovka Notebook site; W. van Doorn, E. Judin, P. Monticone and D. Morrison, On some problems from the Kourovka Notebook, preprint, arXiv:2607.17477 (2026), Kourovka Notebook (21st issue), Problem 21.150: No, not always: A = F₃[x, y]/I³ (I = (x, y)), B = ⟨1 + x, 1 + y⟩ acting by multiplication, G = A ⋊ B, a = 1; then C_B(a) = 1 and Z(H) ∩ H' = ⟨x², xy, y²⟩ has rank 3 while B has rank 2; van Doorn-Judin-Monticone-Morrison, Theorem 9.1, https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17477.

articles.title: Zenkov's rank bound in elementary abelian extensions (Kourovka 21.150)
articles.statement:
Call a subgroup
elementary abelian if it is abelian and there is a prime $p$ with $x^p = 1$ for all its elements
$x$. This is the proposition that for every finite group $G$, all elementary abelian subgroups $A$
and $B$ of $G$ (possibly for different primes) with $A$ normal, $A \cap B = 1$ and
$\langle A, B \rangle = G$ (so $B$ is a complement to $A$ and $B \cong G/A$), and every $a \in A$
whose centralizer $C_B(a)$ in $B$ is trivial, the following holds for $H = \langle a, B \rangle$,
with centre $Z(H)$ and derived subgroup $H' = [H, H]$: whenever $B$ is generated by a finite set of
$k$ elements, $Z(H) \cap H'$ (with $Z(H)$ viewed as a subgroup of $G$) is generated by a finite set
of at most $k$ elements. That is, the rank of $Z(H) \cap H'$ is at most the rank of $B$.

The question is due to V. I. Zenkov.

articles.title: Elementary abelian subgroups
articles.statement:
A subgroup $H$ of a group $G$ is elementary abelian if any
two of its elements commute and there is a prime $p$ with $x^p = 1$ for all $x \in H$.

articles.title: Schur–Zassenhaus theorem: conjugacy of complements
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group and $N$ a normal
subgroup of $G$ whose order is coprime to its index, and suppose $N$ is solvable. If $K_1$ and
$K_2$ are complements of $N$ in $G$, then there is an element $g \in N$ with $g K_1 g^{-1} = K_2$.

## Sources

- I. Schur (1904); H. Zassenhaus, Lehrbuch der Gruppentheorie (1937); Isaacs, Finite Group Theory; standard solvability hypothesis for conjugacy.

articles.title: Existence of Hall groups (Göbel–Shelah; Kourovka Problem 12.44)
articles.statement:
There is a nontrivial group
$G$ that is isomorphic to every extension of itself by itself: every group $H$ with a normal
subgroup $N \cong G$ such that $H/N \cong G$ is isomorphic to $G$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 12.44 (P. Hall; J. C. Lennox); resolution: R. Göbel and S. Shelah, Philip Hall's problem on non-Abelian splitters, Math. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. 134 (2003), no. 1, 23-31, arXiv:math/0009091, Definition 1.1 and Corollary 1.5 (L^ω is a Hall group for every rigid group L), with the existence of rigid groups (Theorem 3.1); Kourovka Archive, Problem 12.44, https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0009091.

articles.title: Hall's problem on self-extensions (Kourovka Problem 12.44)
articles.statement:
There is a nontrivial group $G$
that is a Hall group, that is, isomorphic to every extension of itself by itself: every group $H$
with a normal subgroup $N \cong G$ such that $H/N \cong G$ is isomorphic to $G$.

articles.title: Hall group
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is a Hall group (in the sense of Göbel and Shelah) when it is
isomorphic to every extension of itself by itself: for every group $H$ and every normal subgroup
$N$ of $H$ with $N \cong G$ and $H/N \cong G$, also $H \cong G$.

articles.title: Burichenko's theorem on surjections injective on no nontrivial subgroup
articles.statement:
For every finite
group $G$ there are a finite group $F$ and a surjective homomorphism $f \colon F \to G$ such that
for every nontrivial subgroup $H$ of $F$ the restriction of $f$ to $H$ is not injective.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 17.50 (E. G. Zelenyuk); resolution: V. P. Burichenko, Math. Notes 92 (2012), 327-332, Kourovka Archive, Problem 17.50 (Yes, it is).

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 17.50: surjections injective on no nontrivial subgroup
articles.statement:
The statement
that for every finite group $G$ there are a finite group $F$ and a surjective homomorphism
$f \colon F \to G$ such that for every nontrivial subgroup $H$ of $F$ the restriction of $f$ to
$H$ is not injective.

articles.title: Equal normal closures forcing conjugacy does not make the derived subgroup of a finite $2$-group abelian (Kourovka 12.15)
articles.statement:
**Equal normal closures forcing conjugacy does not make the derived subgroup of a finite $2$-group
abelian (Kourovka 12.15).** There exists a finite $2$-group $G$ in which any two elements with the
same normal closure are conjugate, but whose derived subgroup $G'$ is not abelian.

Muliarchyk gives an explicit such group of order $2^{11} = 2048$, given by a power-commutator
presentation, whose second derived subgroup $G'' = (G')'$ is nontrivial (a ChatGPT-assisted
construction with a symbolic proof); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 12.15 solved, "No,
not always".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 12.15 (E. A. Golikova, A. I. Starostin); resolution: K. Muliarchyk, An explicit counterexample to Kourovka Notebook Problem 12.15, preprint (13 August 2026), main result: an explicit group of order `2¹¹ = 2048`, given by a power-commutator presentation, satisfies the hypothesis and has `G'' = ⟨z⟩ ≠ 1`; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 12.15 solved, https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/kourovka_12_15_counterexample.pdf.

articles.title: Golikova–Starostin question on finite $2$-groups in which normal closures determine conjugacy (Kourovka 12.15)
articles.statement:
**Golikova–Starostin question on finite $2$-groups in which normal closures determine
conjugacy (Kourovka 12.15).** The statement that for every finite $2$-group $G$ in which any two
elements with the same normal closure are conjugate, the derived subgroup $G'$ of $G$ is
abelian.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 20.75 has a negative answer
articles.statement:
The statement of Kourovka Problem 20.75 is
false: there are a prime $p$, a natural number $k$, a finite $p$-group $G$ all of whose abelian
normal subgroups can be generated by at most $k$ elements, and an abelian subgroup of $G$ that
cannot be generated by at most $2k$ elements.

Muliarchyk's counterexample (Theorem 1.1) is a finite $2$-group of order $2^{110N+1}$, with
$N = 2124210350$, whose abelian normal subgroups can be generated by $32N + 1$ elements while an
elementary abelian subgroup needs $65N > 2(32N + 1)$ generators; the 21st issue of the Kourovka
Notebook marks 20.75 solved ("No, it is not").

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 20.75 (L. Pyber); resolution: K. Muliarchyk, An explicit counterexample to Kourovka Notebook Problem 20.75, preprint (2026), Kourovka Notebook site, Theorem 1.1: for N = 2124210350 an explicitly specified finite 2-group of order 2^(110N+1) in which every abelian normal subgroup can be generated by at most 32N + 1 elements and some elementary abelian subgroup needs 65N generators; Kourovka Notebook (21st issue), Problem 20.75: No, it is not, https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/kourovka_20.75_solution.pdf.

articles.title: Pyber's question on generators of abelian subgroups (Kourovka 20.75)
articles.statement:
The proposition that
for every prime $p$, every natural number $k$ and every finite $p$-group $G$, if every abelian
normal subgroup of $G$ can be generated by at most $k$ elements, then every abelian subgroup of $G$
can be generated by at most $2k$ elements.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 20.76 has a negative answer
articles.statement:
The statement of Kourovka Problem 20.76 is
false: there are a prime $p$, a natural number $k$, a finite $p$-group $G$ all of whose abelian
normal subgroups have order at most $p^k$, and an abelian subgroup of $G$ of order greater than
$p^{2k}$.

Muliarchyk's counterexample (Theorem 1.1) is a finite $2$-group of order $2^{144e+1}$, with
$e = 256363762$, whose abelian normal subgroups have order at most $2^{42e}$ while it has an
elementary abelian subgroup of order $2^{85e} > 2^{84e}$; the 21st issue of the Kourovka Notebook
marks 20.76 solved ("No, it is not").

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 20.76 (L. Pyber); resolution: K. Muliarchyk, Abelian subgroups of finite 2-groups: counterexamples to Problems 20.75 and 20.76, preprint (2026), Kourovka Notebook site, Theorem 1.1: for e = 256363762 an explicitly specified finite 2-group of order 2^(144e+1) whose abelian normal subgroups have order at most 2^(42e), with an elementary abelian subgroup of order 2^(85e) (p = 2, k = 42e); Kourovka Notebook (21st issue), Problem 20.76: No, it is not, https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/kourovka_20_75-20_76_solution.pdf.

articles.title: Pyber's question on orders of abelian subgroups (Kourovka 20.76)
articles.statement:
The proposition that for
every prime $p$, every natural number $k$ and every finite $p$-group $G$, if every abelian normal
subgroup of $G$ has order at most $p^k$, then every abelian subgroup of $G$ has order at most
$p^{2k}$.

articles.title: Nilpotent Camina-type groups have unbounded class
articles.statement:
There is no natural number $c$ such that
every nilpotent group $G$ in which, for every $x \notin [G, G]$, the coset $x[G, G]$ of the
commutator subgroup $[G, G]$ equals the conjugacy class $x^G$ of $x$, has nilpotency class at
most $c$. So Kourovka Problem 17.47 has a negative answer.

Ionin and Semidetnov (Answer 4.2) construct, for every integer $c \ge 2$, a nilpotent group of
class exactly $c$ in which $x^G = x[G, G]$ for every $x \notin [G, G]$. The Kourovka Notebook
(21st issue) answers 17.47 "No, there is no such bound".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 17.47 (S. H. Ghate, A. S. Muktibodh); resolution: V. Ionin and A. Semidetnov, On some more problems from the Kourovka Notebook, preprint, arXiv:2608.29219 (2026; solutions found with the assistance of large language models and checked by the authors, per its abstract), Answer 4.2 (for every integer c ≥ 2 there exists a nilpotent Camina group of class exactly c); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 17.47 solved (No, there is no such bound), https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29219.

articles.title: Bounded class for nilpotent Camina-type groups
articles.statement:
Kourovka Problem 17.47 (S. H. Ghate,
A. S. Muktibodh) asks whether this proposition holds: there is a natural number $c$ such that
every nilpotent group $G$ in which, for every $x \notin [G, G]$, the coset $x[G, G]$ of the
commutator subgroup $[G, G]$ equals the conjugacy class $x^G$ of $x$, has nilpotency class at
most $c$.

articles.title: Rank of a group
articles.statement:
The rank of a group $G$ is the supremum, in the natural numbers, of the
minimal numbers of generators of the subgroups of $G$, where an unbounded set of natural numbers
has supremum $0$. For a finite group $G$ it is the largest minimal number of generators of a
subgroup of $G$.

articles.title: Cyclic lower central factors from the second on
articles.statement:
Let $\gamma_1(P) = P$ and
$\gamma_{i+1}(P) = [\gamma_i(P), P]$ be the lower central series of a group $P$. The group $P$
has cyclic lower central factors from the second on if for every $i \ge 2$ there is an element
$g \in \gamma_i(P)$ such that every $x \in \gamma_i(P)$ satisfies $x g^{-k} \in \gamma_{i+1}(P)$
for some integer $k$, that is, the factor $\gamma_i(P)/\gamma_{i+1}(P)$ is cyclic.

articles.title: Minimal number of generators of a subgroup
articles.statement:
For a subgroup $H$ of a group $G$, the
minimal number of generators of $H$ is the least natural number $n$ such that $H$ is generated by
some finite set of $n$ elements of $G$; it is $0$ when $H$ is not finitely generated.

articles.title: No rank analogue of the Shepherd-Leedham-Green-McKay theorem (Kourovka 16.103)
articles.statement:
For every
prime $p$ and every natural number $r$ there is a finite $p$-group $P$ generated by two elements,
whose lower central factors $\gamma_i(P)/\gamma_{i+1}(P)$ are cyclic for all $i \ge 2$, such that
for every normal subgroup $N$ of $P$ of nilpotency class at most $2$ the quotient $P/N$ has rank
greater than $r$. Here $\gamma_1(P) = P$ and $\gamma_{i+1}(P) = [\gamma_i(P), P]$, and the rank of
a finite group is the largest minimal number of generators of its subgroups. That is, the
statement of Kourovka Problem 16.103 fails for every prime.

Khukhro's groups even have no normal subgroup of bounded derived length with quotient of bounded
rank; the Kourovka Archive answers 16.103 "No".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 16.103 (E. I. Khukhro); resolution: E. I. Khukhro, Counterexamples to a rank analogue of the Shepherd-Leedham-Green-McKay theorem on finite p-groups of maximal class, Siberian Math. J. 54 (2013), no. 1, 174-184, Theorem (no functions r(p), l(p) give every such group a normal subgroup of derived length at most l(p) with quotient of rank at most r(p)), with examples for every fixed prime (Section 4); Kourovka Archive, Problem 16.103 (answer: No), https://eprints.maths.manchester.ac.uk/1937/1/.

articles.title: Rank analogue of the Shepherd-Leedham-Green-McKay theorem (Kourovka 16.103)
articles.statement:
The
statement that for some prime $p$ there is a natural number $r$ such that every finite $p$-group
$P$ generated by two elements whose lower central factors $\gamma_i(P)/\gamma_{i+1}(P)$ are
cyclic for all $i \ge 2$ has a normal subgroup $N$ of nilpotency class at most $2$ with $P/N$ of
rank at most $r$. Here $\gamma_1(P) = P$ and $\gamma_{i+1}(P) = [\gamma_i(P), P]$, and the rank
of a finite group is the largest minimal number of generators of its subgroups.

Kourovka 16.103 (E. I. Khukhro) asks for a bound $r(p)$ for each prime $p$; this form asks for
one prime, so its negation says that no prime has such a bound.

articles.title: Vanishing first cohomology of $G/\Phi(G)$ in $Z(\Phi(G))$
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group, let
$\Phi(G)$ be its Frattini subgroup and let $Z(\Phi(G))$ be the centre of $\Phi(G)$. The property
holds when every map $\delta \colon G \to Z(\Phi(G))$ with
$\delta(gh) = \delta(g)\, g\, \delta(h)\, g^{-1}$ for all $g, h \in G$ and $\delta(g) = 1$ for all
$g \in \Phi(G)$ is a coboundary: there is an $a \in Z(\Phi(G))$ with $\delta(g) = g a g^{-1} a^{-1}$
for all $g \in G$.

Such maps $\delta$ are exactly the inflations to $G$ of the 1-cocycles of $G/\Phi(G)$ with values
in $Z(\Phi(G))$ for the conjugation action, so the property says
$H^1(G/\Phi(G), Z(\Phi(G))) = 0$.

articles.title: Centre of the Frattini subgroup
articles.statement:
An element $x$ of a group $G$ lies in the centre
$Z(\Phi(G))$ of the Frattini subgroup $\Phi(G)$ when $x \in \Phi(G)$ and $xy = yx$ for every
$y \in \Phi(G)$.

articles.title: A non-abelian $p$-group with $H^1(G/\Phi(G), Z(\Phi(G))) = 0$ (Kourovka 17.2)
articles.statement:
There exist a
prime $p$ and a finite non-abelian $p$-group $G$ such that, writing $\Phi(G)$ for the Frattini
subgroup of $G$ and $Z(\Phi(G))$ for its centre, the first cohomology group
$H^1(G/\Phi(G), Z(\Phi(G)))$ for the conjugation action of $G/\Phi(G)$ on $Z(\Phi(G))$ is trivial.

This answers Kourovka Problem 17.2 in the affirmative: the Kourovka Archive answers "Yes, it does",
citing Abdollahi (2011).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 17.2 (A. Abdollahi); resolution: A. Abdollahi, J. Algebra 342 (2011), 154-160, Kourovka Archive, Problem 17.2 (Yes, it does).

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 17.2 (a non-abelian $p$-group with trivial $H^1$)
articles.statement:
The statement, a
question of P. Schmid recorded by A. Abdollahi, that there exist a prime $p$ and a finite
non-abelian $p$-group $G$ such that, writing $\Phi(G)$ for the Frattini subgroup of $G$ and
$Z(\Phi(G))$ for its centre, the first cohomology group $H^1(G/\Phi(G), Z(\Phi(G)))$ for the
conjugation action of $G/\Phi(G)$ on $Z(\Phi(G))$ is trivial.

articles.title: Composition series of finite p-groups
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and let $G$ be a finite
$p$-group of order $p^n$. Then there are subgroups
$G = H_0 \supseteq H_1 \supseteq \cdots \supseteq H_n = \{1\}$ such that for each $i < n$,
$H_{i+1}$ is a normal subgroup of $H_i$ and there is a surjective homomorphism
$H_i \to \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ with kernel $H_{i+1}$. By the first isomorphism theorem,
$H_i / H_{i+1} \cong \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ for each $i < n$.

articles.title: Finite p-groups are solvable
articles.statement:
For every prime $p$, every finite $p$-group is
solvable.

articles.title: Cossey–Hawkes theorem on conjugacy class sizes of p-groups
articles.statement:
For every prime $p$ and every
finite set $X$ of natural numbers that contains $1$ and consists of powers of $p$, there is a
finite $p$-group whose set of conjugacy class sizes is exactly $X$. This answers Kourovka
Problem 14.77 (Sangroniz) in the affirmative.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 14.77 (J. Sangroniz); resolution: J. Cossey and T. Hawkes, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 128 (2000), no. 1, 49-51, Kourovka Archive, Problem 14.77 (answer: Yes, it is).

articles.title: Prescribed sets of conjugacy class sizes of finite p-groups (Kourovka 14.77)
articles.statement:
The
statement that for every prime $p$ and every finite set $X$ of natural numbers that contains $1$
and consists of powers of $p$, there is a finite $p$-group $G$ whose set of conjugacy class sizes
$\{|C| : C \text{ a conjugacy class of } G\}$ equals $X$.

articles.title: Number of conjugacy classes of maximum size
articles.statement:
For a group $G$, the number of conjugacy
classes $c$ of $G$ such that every conjugacy class of $G$ has size at most the size of $c$. It is
meant for finite groups: sizes and counts are taken in $\mathbb{N}$, where an infinite set has
size $0$.

articles.title: Some odd $p$-group has exactly $p - 1$ conjugacy classes of maximum size
articles.statement:
There exist an odd
prime $p$ and a finite $p$-group with exactly $p - 1$ conjugacy classes of maximum size.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 14.92 (G. Fernández-Alcober); resolution: A. Jaikin-Zapirain, M. F. Newman and E. A. O'Brien, p-groups having the minimal number of conjugacy classes of maximal size, Israel J. Math. 172 (2009), no. 1, 119-123, abstract (a 3-group with exactly p - 1 = 2 conjugacy classes of the largest size); Kourovka Archive, Problem 14.92 (answer: Yes, there are, for p = 3), http://verso.mat.uam.es/~andrei.jaikin/preprints/articulos.htm.

articles.title: Odd $p$-groups with $p - 1$ conjugacy classes of maximum size (Kourovka 14.92)
articles.statement:
The
statement that there exist an odd prime $p$ and a finite $p$-group with exactly $p - 1$ conjugacy
classes of maximum size.

articles.title: Derived subgroups of p-groups need not be Frattini subgroups of p-groups
articles.statement:
There exist a prime
$p$ and a finite $p$-group $G$ such that for every finite $p$-group $H$, the Frattini subgroup
$\Phi(H)$ of $H$ is not isomorphic to the derived subgroup $[G, G]$ of $G$. That is, the conjecture
of Kourovka Problem 16.11 is false.

Ionin and Semidetnov take $p = 2$ and $G$ the group SmallGroup(256, 511), whose derived subgroup
is the Hall-Senior group 32/40 (a GAP computation); by a theorem of van der Waall and de Nijs, that
group is not isomorphic to the Frattini subgroup of any finite 2-group. The authors state that
their solutions were found with the assistance of large language models and checked by them.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 16.11 (Ya. G. Berkovich); resolution: V. Ionin and A. Semidetnov, On some more problems from the Kourovka Notebook, preprint, arXiv:2608.29219 (2026), Answer 3.2 with Lemma 3.4 and Theorem 3.3 (van der Waall-de Nijs, Theorem 1.15): for p = 2, G = SmallGroup(256, 511) has derived subgroup the Hall-Senior group 32/40, which is the Frattini subgroup of no finite 2-group; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 16.11 solved (No, not always), https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29219.

articles.title: Derived subgroups of p-groups as Frattini subgroups (Kourovka 16.11)
articles.statement:
The conjecture of
Ya. G. Berkovich that for every prime $p$ and every finite $p$-group $G$ there is a finite
$p$-group $H$ whose Frattini subgroup $\Phi(H)$, the intersection of the maximal subgroups of $H$,
is isomorphic to the derived subgroup $[G, G]$ of $G$.

articles.title: Metacyclic group
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is metacyclic if it has a cyclic normal subgroup $N$ such
that the quotient $G/N$ is cyclic.

articles.title: Derived length of $p$-groups whose $2$-generator subgroups have cyclic derived subgroups (Kourovka Problem 17.46)
articles.statement:
**Derived length of $p$-groups whose $2$-generator subgroups have cyclic derived subgroups
(Kourovka Problem 17.46).** Let $p$ be a prime and $G$ a finite $p$-group such that for all
$x, y \in G$ the derived subgroup $[H, H]$ of $H = \langle x, y \rangle$ is cyclic. Then $G$ has
derived length at most $4$, that is, the fourth term $G^{(4)}$ of the derived series of $G$ is
trivial.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 17.46 (B. M. Veretennikov); resolution: B. Wilkens, J. Group Theory 17 (2014), 151-174, Kourovka Archive, Problem 17.46 (Yes, it is at most 4).

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 17.46, with the bound $4$
articles.statement:
The statement that for every prime $p$ and
every finite $p$-group $G$ such that for all $x, y \in G$ the derived subgroup $[H, H]$ of
$H = \langle x, y \rangle$ is cyclic, $G$ has derived length at most $4$, that is, the fourth
term $G^{(4)}$ of the derived series of $G$ is trivial.

articles.title: Finite $2$-groups with metacyclic $2$-generator subgroups are metabelian (Kourovka Problem 15.33)
articles.statement:
**Finite $2$-groups with metacyclic $2$-generator subgroups are metabelian (Kourovka
Problem 15.33).** Let $G$ be a finite $2$-group such that for all $x, y \in G$ the subgroup
$\langle x, y \rangle$ generated by $x$ and $y$ is metacyclic, that is, has a cyclic normal
subgroup with cyclic quotient. Then $G$ is metabelian: its second derived subgroup $G''$ is
trivial.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 15.33 (Ya. G. Berkovich); resolution: E. Crestani and F. Menegazzo, J. Group Theory 15 (2012), no. 3, 359-383, Kourovka Archive, Problem 15.33 (answer: Yes, it is at most 2).

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 15.33, with the bound $2$
articles.statement:
The statement that every finite $2$-group $G$
such that for all $x, y \in G$ the subgroup $\langle x, y \rangle$ generated by $x$ and $y$ is
metacyclic has derived length at most $2$, that is, its second derived subgroup $G''$ is
trivial.

articles.title: $\Phi$-extension (Berkovich)
articles.statement:
For a natural number $p$ and groups $H$ and $G$, $H$ is a
$\Phi$-extension of $G$ when $H$ is a finite $p$-group with a normal subgroup $N$ of order $p$
such that $N \le \Phi(H)$, where $\Phi(H)$ is the Frattini subgroup of $H$, and $H/N \cong G$.

articles.title: Infinite chains of $\Phi$-extensions (Kourovka 16.12)
articles.statement:
For every prime $p$ and every
nontrivial finite $p$-group $G$ there are groups $G_0, G_1, G_2, \dots$ with $G_0 \cong G$ such
that, for every $i \ge 0$, $G_{i+1}$ is a $\Phi$-extension of $G_i$ for the prime $p$. This answers
Kourovka Problem 16.12 in the affirmative: the Kourovka Archive answers "Yes, it is", citing
Kamornikov (2008).

The trivial group is excluded: it has no $\Phi$-extension, since a group of order $p$ has trivial
Frattini subgroup.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 16.12 (Ya. G. Berkovich); resolution: S. F. Kamornikov, Izv. Gomel' Univ. 5 (2008), 200-201 (Russian), Kourovka Archive, Problem 16.12 (Yes, it is).

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 16.12 (infinite chains of $\Phi$-extensions)
articles.statement:
The statement, a question
of Ya. G. Berkovich, that for every prime $p$ and every nontrivial finite $p$-group $G$ there are
groups $G_0, G_1, G_2, \dots$ with $G_0 \cong G$ such that, for every $i \ge 0$, $G_{i+1}$ is a
$\Phi$-extension of $G_i$ for the prime $p$.

articles.title: Finite p-groups without a generating set of elements of equal order
articles.statement:
For some odd prime $p$
there is a finite $p$-group $G$ such that no generating set of $G$ consists of elements that all
have the same order. This answers Kourovka Problem 11.6 (Bagiński) in the negative (O'Brien,
Scoppola and Vaughan-Lee).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.6 (C. Bagiński); resolution: E. A. O'Brien, C. M. Scoppola and M. R. Vaughan-Lee, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 134, no. 12 (2006), 3457-3464, Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.6: "No, it is not true", https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Generating sets of equal order in finite p-groups (Kourovka 11.6)
articles.statement:
The statement that for
every odd prime $p$, every finite $p$-group $G$ has a generating set $S$ all of whose elements have
the same order.

articles.title: Generalized quaternion group
articles.statement:
A group $P$ is a generalized quaternion group if, for some
natural number $k \ge 1$, it is isomorphic to the quaternion group
$Q_{2^{k+2}} = \langle a, x \mid a^{2^{k+1}} = 1,\ x^2 = a^{2^k},\ x^{-1} a x = a^{-1} \rangle$
of order $2^{k+2}$. Thus $P$ has order $8$, $16$, $32$ or some larger power of $2$.

articles.title: Large automorphisms of p-groups force cyclic subgroups of given index
articles.statement:
For every prime $p$ and
all natural numbers $k$ and $m$ with $m \ge 64k + 2$, if a finite group $G$ of order $p^m$ has an
automorphism of order $p^{m-k}$, then $G$ has a cyclic subgroup of index $p^k$.

Resolved true: Jayadevan proved this with the threshold $f(k) = 64k + 2$; the Kourovka Notebook
(21st issue) marks 15.32 solved, "Yes, one can take $f(k) = 64k + 2$" (AI solution confirmed by
A. Caranti).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 15.32 (Ya. G. Berkovich); resolution: A. Jayadevan, Large-order automorphisms of finite p-groups force cyclic subgroups of prescribed index, preprint, Zenodo record 22910914 (2026), AI-generated solution confirmed by A. Caranti, main theorem (for every k ≥ 0, a group of order p^m with m ≥ 64k + 2 and an automorphism of order p^(m-k) has a cyclic subgroup of index exactly p^k); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 15.32 solved, https://zenodo.org/records/22910914.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 15.32: large automorphisms and cyclic subgroups
articles.statement:
For every prime $p$ and
all natural numbers $k$ and $m$ with $m \ge 64k + 2$, every finite group $G$ of order $p^m$ that
has an automorphism of order $p^{m-k}$ has a cyclic subgroup of index $p^k$.

Kourovka 15.32 (Ya. G. Berkovich) asks for some threshold $f(k)$ beyond which this holds; the
threshold $f(k) = 64k + 2$ is the one of its resolution.

articles.title: Normal subgroups of exponent p in p-groups when p > n
articles.statement:
For every prime $p$ and every natural
number $n < p$, if a finite $p$-group $G$ has a subgroup $H$ of order $p^n$ with $x^p = 1$ for all
$x \in H$, then $G$ has a normal subgroup $N$ of order $p^n$ with $x^p = 1$ for all $x \in N$.

The Kourovka Archive answers "Yes, it is true if $p > n$" (A. Mann): by induction a subgroup $H$
of exponent $p$ and order $p^n$ may be taken normal in a maximal subgroup $M$; then $H$ lies in
the $(p-1)$-st term $\zeta_{p-1}(M)$ of the upper central series of $M$, and the elements of
order $p$ of $\zeta_{p-1}(M)$ form a normal subgroup of $G$ containing $H$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 15.24 (Ya. G. Berkovich); resolution: A. Mann, letter of 1 October 2002, as recorded in the Kourovka Archive, Problem 15.24, Archive answer: Yes if p > n (H of exponent p and order p^n normal in a maximal subgroup M lies in ζ_{p-1}(M), whose elements of order p form a normal subgroup of G), https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Berkovich's question on normal subgroups of exponent p, for p > n
articles.statement:
For every prime $p$
and every natural number $n < p$, if a finite $p$-group $G$ has a subgroup of order $p^n$ all of
whose elements $x$ satisfy $x^p = 1$, then $G$ has a normal subgroup of order $p^n$ all of whose
elements $x$ satisfy $x^p = 1$.

Berkovich asked this for $p$ sufficiently large relative to $n$; the explicit bound $p > n$ is the
one of the resolution. For $n \ge 1$ the condition $x^p = 1$ on a group of order $p^n$ says that it
has exponent exactly $p$.

articles.title: Sambale's order bound for $2$-groups of bounded abelian rank fails (Kourovka 19.75)
articles.statement:
There
exist natural numbers $e$ and $r$ and a finite $2$-group $P$ of exponent $2^e$ in which every
abelian subgroup is generated by at most $r$ elements, such that $|P| > 2^{r(e+1)}$.

The Kourovka Archive answers 19.75 "No, it is not true", as follows from Olshanskii's examples of
finite $p$-groups whose abelian subgroups are small compared to the group (pointed out by Mann).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 19.75 (B. Sambale); resolution: A. Yu. Olshanskii, The number of generators and orders of abelian subgroups of finite p-groups, Math. Notes 23 (1978), no. 3, 183-185; A. Mann, letter of 23 April 2018, abstract: the least f(n) such that every finite p-group whose abelian subgroups are generated by at most n elements has at most f(n) generators grows quadratically in n; Kourovka Archive, Problem 19.75: No, it is not true, as follows from the examples constructed by Olshanskii (Mann), https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01651428.

articles.title: Sambale's question on the order of $2$-groups of bounded abelian rank (Kourovka 19.75)
articles.statement:
The statement that for all natural numbers $e$ and $r$, every finite $2$-group $P$ of exponent
$2^e$ in which every abelian subgroup is generated by at most $r$ elements has order
$|P| \le 2^{r(e+1)}$.

articles.title: Special group
articles.statement:
A group $H$ is special when its center, its commutator subgroup and its
Frattini subgroup coincide: $Z(H) = [H, H] = \Phi(H)$.

articles.title: Arbitrarily large $p$-groups all of whose maximal subgroups are special
articles.statement:
For every prime $p$
and every natural number $n$ there is a finite $p$-group $G$ of order greater than $n$ such that
every maximal subgroup $H$ of $G$ is special, that is, its center $Z(H)$, its commutator subgroup
$[H, H]$ and its Frattini subgroup $\Phi(H)$ coincide. This answers Kourovka Problem 16.13
positively.

The Kourovka Archive records this answer, citing Cossey (2014); for $p = 2$ a Sylow $2$-subgroup of
$L_3(4)$ is another example (Zenkov).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 16.13 (Ya. G. Berkovich); resolution: J. Cossey, Bull. Austral. Math. Soc. 89 (2014), 415-419, Kourovka Archive, Problem 16.13 (for all primes, groups of arbitrarily large size; for p = 2 also a Sylow 2-subgroup of L_3(4), V. I. Zenkov, 2014).

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 16.13, strong form (statement)
articles.statement:
The statement that for every prime $p$
and every natural number $n$ there is a finite $p$-group $G$ of order greater than $n$ all of whose
maximal subgroups $H$ are special, that is, have center $Z(H)$, commutator subgroup $[H, H]$ and
Frattini subgroup $\Phi(H)$ all equal. This is the form in which the problem was resolved; the
problem as posed asks only for one finite $p$-group all of whose maximal subgroups are special.

articles.title: Partition of a group
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group. A set $C$ of subgroups of $G$ is a partition of
$G$ when every member of $C$ is a proper subgroup of $G$, every element of $G$ lies in some member
of $C$, and any two distinct members of $C$ intersect in the trivial subgroup. The members of $C$
are called its components.

articles.title: Every partition of a finite $p$-group has an abelian component
articles.statement:
For every prime $p$, every
finite $p$-group $G$ and every partition $C$ of $G$ (a set of proper subgroups of $G$ whose union is
$G$ and any two distinct members of which intersect in the trivial subgroup), some member $H$ of $C$
is abelian, that is, $xy = yx$ for all $x, y \in H$.

Resolved true: by Theorem B of Cat's preprint, every partition of a finite $p$-group into nontrivial
components has an abelian component (for non-abelian $G$ an elementary abelian one meeting the
Frattini subgroup $\Phi(G)$ of $G$ trivially); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 15.26
solved, "Yes, it is true" (AI solution confirmed by E. I. Khukhro). Components are not required to
be nontrivial here: a trivial component is abelian, and removing it leaves a partition.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 15.26 (Ya. G. Berkovich); resolution: G. Cat, A Frattini-free component in every partition, and Kourovka 15.26, preprint (2026), AI-generated solution confirmed by E. I. Khukhro, Theorem B (a partition of a finite p-group into nontrivial components has an abelian component), derived from Theorem A; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 15.26 solved, https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/kourovka_15-26-ai.pdf.

articles.title: Berkovich's question on abelian components of partitions
articles.statement:
The statement that for every prime
$p$, every finite $p$-group $G$ and every partition $C$ of $G$ (a set of proper subgroups of $G$
whose union is $G$ and any two distinct members of which intersect in the trivial subgroup), some
member $H$ of $C$ is abelian, that is, $xy = yx$ for all $x, y \in H$.

This is Kourovka Notebook Problem 15.26 (Ya. G. Berkovich).

articles.title: Kourovka 21.137 fails for every odd prime
articles.statement:
For every odd prime $p$ there is a finite
$p$-group $G$ of exponent $p^2$ with a subgroup $P$ whose underlying set is exactly the set
$\{x^p : x \in G\}$ of $p$-th powers in $G$, such that $P$ is not abelian.

Muliarchyk's counterexample has order $p^{3p+1}$, and its subgroup of $p$-th powers is isomorphic
to $\mathrm{UT}_3(\mathbb{F}_p) \times C_p^{p-1}$. The 21st issue of the Kourovka Notebook marks
Problem 21.137 solved ("No, it need not be"), citing this preprint for all odd primes.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 21.137 (L. Wilson); resolution: K. Muliarchyk, A counterexample to Kourovka Problem 21.137 for p = 3, preprint (2026), and A non-powerful subgroup of p-th powers for every odd prime, preprint (2026), Kourovka Notebook site; letter of A. Chang of 1 August 2026, Muliarchyk (every odd prime), abstract and Section 1: for each odd prime p an affine group V ⋊ B_p (V = F_p[r]/(r^(2p))) of order p^(3p+1) and exponent p² whose set of p-th powers is a subgroup isomorphic to UT₃(F_p) × C_p^(p-1), non-abelian of exponent p, hence not powerful; Kourovka Notebook (21st issue), Problem 21.137: No, it need not be (p = 3: Muliarchyk, order 3^15; p = 2: the Sylow 2-subgroup of S₈ has exponent 8 and its squares form the non-abelian, non-powerful subgroup C₂ × D₈, letter of A. Chang), https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/kourovka_21.137_solution.pdf.

articles.title: Kourovka 21.137, odd-prime form
articles.statement:
The proposition that there is an odd prime $p$ such that
for every finite $p$-group $G$ of exponent $p^2$ and every subgroup $P$ of $G$ whose underlying
set is exactly the set $\{x^p : x \in G\}$ of $p$-th powers in $G$, the subgroup $P$ is abelian.

Kourovka Problem 21.137 (L. Wilson) asks this for each odd prime; it is stated here for some odd
prime, so that its refutation covers all of them.

articles.title: Kourovka 21.137 fails for every prime
articles.statement:
For every prime $p$ there is a finite $p$-group $G$
with a subgroup $P$ whose underlying set is exactly the set $\{x^p : x \in G\}$ of $p$-th powers in
$G$, such that $P$ is not powerful: the commutator subgroup $[P, P]$ is not contained in the
subgroup $P^m$ generated by the $m$-th powers of the elements of $P$, where $m = p$ for odd $p$
and $m = 4$ for $p = 2$.

For odd $p$ a counterexample is Muliarchyk's group of order $p^{3p+1}$ and exponent $p^2$, whose
$p$-th powers form a non-abelian subgroup of exponent $p$; for $p = 2$ it is the Sylow
$2$-subgroup of $S_8$, whose squares form $C_2 \times D_8$ (letter of A. Chang). The 21st issue of
the Kourovka Notebook marks Problem 21.137 solved ("No, it need not be").

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 21.137 (L. Wilson); resolution: K. Muliarchyk, A counterexample to Kourovka Problem 21.137 for p = 3, preprint (2026), and A non-powerful subgroup of p-th powers for every odd prime, preprint (2026), Kourovka Notebook site; letter of A. Chang of 1 August 2026, Muliarchyk (every odd prime), abstract and Section 1: for each odd prime p an affine group V ⋊ B_p (V = F_p[r]/(r^(2p))) of order p^(3p+1) and exponent p² whose set of p-th powers is a subgroup isomorphic to UT₃(F_p) × C_p^(p-1), non-abelian of exponent p, hence not powerful; Kourovka Notebook (21st issue), Problem 21.137: No, it need not be (p = 3: Muliarchyk, order 3^15; p = 2: the Sylow 2-subgroup of S₈ has exponent 8 and its squares form the non-abelian, non-powerful subgroup C₂ × D₈, letter of A. Chang), https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/kourovka_21.137_solution.pdf.

articles.title: Kourovka 21.137, main question
articles.statement:
The proposition that there is a prime $p$ such that for
every finite $p$-group $G$ and every subgroup $P$ of $G$ whose underlying set is exactly the set
$\{x^p : x \in G\}$ of $p$-th powers in $G$, the subgroup $P$ is powerful: its commutator subgroup
$[P, P]$ is contained in the subgroup $P^m$ generated by the $m$-th powers of the elements of $P$,
where $m = p$ for odd $p$ and $m = 4$ for $p = 2$.

Kourovka Problem 21.137 (L. Wilson) asks this for each prime; it is stated here for some prime, so
that its refutation covers all of them.

articles.title: Locally finite group, via finite subsets
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is locally finite when every finite
subset $S \subseteq G$ generates a finite subgroup; equivalently, every finitely generated subgroup
of $G$ is finite.

articles.title: Set of 3-transpositions
articles.statement:
A subset $D$ of a group $G$ is a set of 3-transpositions when it
is closed under conjugation ($g d g^{-1} \in D$ for all $g \in G$ and $d \in D$), every $d \in D$
is an involution ($d \ne 1$ and $d^2 = 1$), and for all $d, e \in D$ the product $de$ has order
at most $3$, that is, $de = 1$, $(de)^2 = 1$ or $(de)^3 = 1$.

articles.title: Groups generated by 3-transpositions are locally finite
articles.statement:
If a group $G$ is generated by a set
$D$ of 3-transpositions (a conjugation-invariant set of involutions whose pairwise products have
order at most $3$), then $G$ is locally finite: every finite subset of $G$ generates a finite
subgroup of $G$.

The Kourovka Archive answers 12.76 "Yes, it is" (H. Cuypers and J. I. Hall, 1992).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 12.76 (A. I. Sozutov); resolution: H. Cuypers and J. I. Hall, in: Groups, combinatorics and geometry (Durham, 1990), London Math. Soc. Lecture Note Ser. 165, Cambridge Univ. Press, 1992, 121-138, Kourovka Archive, Problem 12.76: Yes, it is.

articles.title: Sozutov's question on 3-transposition groups (Kourovka 12.76)
articles.statement:
The statement that for
every group $G$ and every set $D$ of 3-transpositions of $G$ that generates $G$, the group $G$ is
locally finite.

articles.title: Baer–Suzuki theorem for binary finite groups
articles.statement:
For every prime $p$, every group $G$ in
which any two elements generate a finite subgroup, and every element $a \in G$ such that any two
conjugates of $a$ generate a $p$-subgroup, there is a normal $p$-subgroup of $G$ containing $a$.
Here a $p$-subgroup is a subgroup in which every element has order a power of $p$.

This answers Kourovka Problem 11.11(b) affirmatively (Sozutov, 2000): by the Baer–Suzuki theorem
for finite groups, $\langle a_1, b \rangle$ is a finite $p$-group for every conjugate $a_1$ of $a$
and every element $b$ of $p$-power order, so by induction every product $a_1 \cdots a_n$ of
conjugates of $a$ has $p$-power order, and the normal closure of $a$ is a normal $p$-subgroup.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.11 (A. V. Borovik); resolution: V. D. Mazurov, A. Yu. Olshanskii and A. I. Sozutov, Algebra and Logic 54, no. 2 (2015), 161-166 (a); A. I. Sozutov, Siberian Math. J. 41, no. 3 (2000), 561-562 (b), Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.11.

articles.title: Baer–Suzuki property for binary finite groups
articles.statement:
The proposition that for every prime $p$,
every group $G$ in which any two elements generate a finite subgroup, and every element $a \in G$
such that any two conjugates of $a$ generate a $p$-subgroup, there is a normal $p$-subgroup of $G$
containing $a$. Here a $p$-subgroup is a subgroup in which every element has order a power of $p$.

This is the statement asked about in Kourovka Problem 11.11(b) (A. V. Borovik).

articles.title: Failure of the Baer–Suzuki theorem for periodic groups at the prime 2
articles.statement:
There is a group $G$
in which every element has finite order, together with an element $a \in G$ such that any two
conjugates of $a$ generate a finite $2$-subgroup, but no normal $2$-subgroup of $G$ contains $a$.
Here a $2$-subgroup is a subgroup in which every element has order a power of $2$.

This answers Kourovka Problem 11.11(a) negatively for $p = 2$ (Mazurov, Olshanskii and
Sozutov, 2015).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.11 (A. V. Borovik); resolution: V. D. Mazurov, A. Yu. Olshanskii and A. I. Sozutov, Algebra and Logic 54, no. 2 (2015), 161-166 (a); A. I. Sozutov, Siberian Math. J. 41, no. 3 (2000), 561-562 (b), Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.11.

articles.title: Baer–Suzuki property for periodic groups at the prime 2
articles.statement:
The proposition that for every
group $G$ in which every element has finite order and every element $a \in G$ such that any two
conjugates of $a$ generate a finite $2$-subgroup, there is a normal $2$-subgroup of $G$ containing
$a$. Here a $2$-subgroup is a subgroup in which every element has order a power of $2$.

This is the case $p = 2$ of Kourovka Problem 11.11(a) (A. V. Borovik).

articles.title: Baer–Suzuki theorem
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group, $p$ a prime and $x \in G$. Then $x$ lies
in the $p$-core $O_p(G)$ of $G$ if and only if, for every $g \in G$, the subgroup of $G$ generated
by $x$ and $g x g^{-1}$ is a $p$-group, that is, every element of it has order a power of $p$.

## Sources

- R. Baer, Engelsche Elemente Noetherscher Gruppen, Math. Ann. 133 (1957), 256-270; M. Suzuki, Finite groups in which the centralizer of any element of order 2 is 2-closed, Ann. of Math. (2) 82 (1965), 191-212. Problem `baer_suzuki` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: The $p$-core of a group
articles.statement:
For a natural number $p$ and a group $G$, the $p$-core $O_p(G)$
is the supremum, in the lattice of subgroups of $G$, of all normal subgroups $N$ of $G$ that are
$p$-groups, that is, such that every $y \in N$ satisfies $y^{p^k} = 1$ for some $k \ge 0$.

When $p$ is prime, $O_p(G)$ is itself a normal $p$-subgroup of $G$, hence the largest one, and no
finiteness hypothesis is needed: the join of two normal $p$-subgroups is again a normal
$p$-subgroup, so the family is directed and every element of the supremum lies in one of them.

articles.title: Bender–Suzuki theorem
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a finite simple group that has a strongly embedded
subgroup $M$. Then $X$ is a simple Bender group: $X$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{PSL}(2, 2^n)$ for
some $n \ge 2$, to the Suzuki group $\mathrm{Sz}(2^{2n+1})$ for some $n \ge 1$, or to
$\mathrm{PSU}(3, 2^n)$ for some $n \ge 2$.

## Sources

- D. Gorenstein, R. Lyons, and R. Solomon, The classification of the finite simple groups, Number 2. Problem `bender_suzuki` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Simple Bender groups
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is a simple Bender group if it is isomorphic to
$\mathrm{PSL}(2, 2^n)$ for some $n \ge 2$, to the Suzuki group $\mathrm{Sz}(2^{2n+1})$ for some
$n \ge 1$, or to $\mathrm{PSU}(3, 2^n)$ for some $n \ge 2$.

articles.title: Strongly embedded subgroups
articles.statement:
A subgroup $M$ of a group $X$ is strongly embedded in $X$
if $M \ne X$, the order of $M$ is even, and for every $g \in X$ outside $M$ the order of
$M \cap g M g^{-1}$ is odd. Here an infinite group is assigned order $0$, so an infinite $M$
counts as having even order and an infinite intersection never has odd order.

articles.title: The group $\mathrm{PSL}(2, 2^n)$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n \ge 1$, $\mathrm{PSL}(2, 2^n)$ is
the projective special linear group of $2 \times 2$ matrices over the Galois field
$\mathrm{GF}(2^n)$. For $n = 0$ the same construction is taken over $\mathrm{GF}(2)$ instead.

articles.title: The group $\mathrm{PSU}(3, 2^n)$
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$, let $q = 2^n$ and let $J$ be the
$3 \times 3$ matrix with ones on the antidiagonal and zeros elsewhere. Then $\mathrm{PSU}(3, q)$
is the image in the projective general linear group $\mathrm{PGL}(3, \mathrm{GF}(q^2))$ of the
group of matrices $A \in \mathrm{GL}(3, \mathrm{GF}(q^2))$ with $\det A = 1$ and
$\bar{A}^{\mathsf{T}} J A = J$, where $\bar{A}$ is obtained from $A$ by applying $z \mapsto z^q$ to
every entry. For $n = 0$ the same construction is taken over $\mathrm{GF}(2)$ instead, with
$z \mapsto z^q$ the identity.

The map $z \mapsto z^q$ is the involution of $\mathrm{GF}(q^2)$ whose fixed field is
$\mathrm{GF}(q)$, so these are the isometries of determinant one of the Hermitian form with Gram
matrix $J$, taken modulo scalars.

articles.title: Generators of the Suzuki group
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number, $q = 2^{2n+1}$,
$\theta = 2^{n+1}$ and $F = \mathrm{GF}(q)$. The generating set of $\mathrm{Sz}(q)$ is the set of
$4 \times 4$ matrices over $F$ of the following three kinds: for $a, b \in F$, the root element
with rows $(1, a, b, a^{2+\theta} + ab + b^{\theta})$, $(0, 1, a^{\theta}, a^{1+\theta} + b)$,
$(0, 0, 1, a)$ and $(0, 0, 0, 1)$; for nonzero $x \in F$, the torus element with diagonal entries
$x^{1+2^n}$, $x^{2^n}$, $x^{-2^n}$, $x^{-(1+2^n)}$ and zeros elsewhere; and the Weyl element, the
matrix with ones on the antidiagonal and zeros elsewhere.

The map $z \mapsto z^{\theta}$ is the Tits automorphism of $F$: its square is $z \mapsto z^2$.

articles.title: The Suzuki group $\mathrm{Sz}(2^{2n+1})$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the Suzuki group
$\mathrm{Sz}(2^{2n+1})$ is the subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}(4, \mathrm{GF}(2^{2n+1}))$ generated by
