Algebra 478 (2017), 153-173, Kourovka Archive, Problem 18.52: Yes, it is (mod CFSG); moreover every finite simple group is generated by an involution and an element of prime order, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 18.52 (generation by two elements of prime-power order)
articles.statement:
The statement
that every finite simple group $G$ is generated by two elements $x, y \in G$ whose orders are prime
powers, that is, each of the form $p^k$ with $p$ prime and $k \ge 1$ (the primes and exponents may
differ between $x$ and $y$ and depend on the group). The problem is due to J. Krempa.

articles.title: Generator number of almost simple groups (Kourovka 11.27)
articles.statement:
Let $S$
be a finite non-abelian simple group, identified with its inner automorphism group
$\mathrm{Inn}(S) \le \mathrm{Aut}(S)$. For every subgroup $G$ of $\mathrm{Aut}(S)$ containing $S$,
$d(G) = \max(2, d(G / S))$, where $d(G)$ is the minimal number of generators of $G$ and
$d(G / S)$, the minimal number of generators of $G / S$, is taken to be the least number of
elements of $G$ that together with $S$ generate $G$.

Dalla Volta and Lucchini proved this using the classification of finite simple groups.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.27 (K. Gruenberg); resolution: F. Dalla Volta and A. Lucchini, J. Algebra 178, no. 1 (1995), 194-223, Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.27: "The number `d(G)` is found (mod CFSG) for every such a group `G`. In particular, `d(G) = max {2, d(G/S)}` and `d(G) ≤ 3`", https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: The generator-number formula for almost simple groups (Kourovka 11.27)
articles.statement:
The proposition
that for every finite non-abelian simple group $S$, identified with its inner automorphism group
$\mathrm{Inn}(S) \le \mathrm{Aut}(S)$, and every subgroup $G$ of $\mathrm{Aut}(S)$ containing $S$,
$d(G) = \max(2, d(G / S))$. Here $d(G)$ is the minimal number of generators of $G$, and
$d(G / S)$, the minimal number of generators of $G / S$, is taken to be the least number of
elements of $G$ that together with $S$ generate $G$.

articles.title: Almost simple groups are generated by 3 elements (Kourovka 11.27)
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a finite
non-abelian simple group, identified with its inner automorphism group
$\mathrm{Inn}(S) \le \mathrm{Aut}(S)$. Every subgroup $G$ of $\mathrm{Aut}(S)$ containing $S$ is
generated by at most $3$ elements.

Dalla Volta and Lucchini proved this using the classification of finite simple groups.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.27 (K. Gruenberg); resolution: F. Dalla Volta and A. Lucchini, J. Algebra 178, no. 1 (1995), 194-223, Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.27: "The number `d(G)` is found (mod CFSG) for every such a group `G`. In particular, `d(G) = max {2, d(G/S)}` and `d(G) ≤ 3`", https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: The 3-generator bound for almost simple groups (Kourovka 11.27)
articles.statement:
The proposition that for
every finite non-abelian simple group $S$, identified with its inner automorphism group
$\mathrm{Inn}(S) \le \mathrm{Aut}(S)$, every subgroup $G$ of $\mathrm{Aut}(S)$ containing $S$ is
generated by at most $3$ elements.

articles.title: Almost simple groups
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is almost simple when there is a nonabelian finite simple
group $S$ such that $G$ is isomorphic to a subgroup $A$ of the automorphism group $\mathrm{Aut}(S)$
that contains the inner automorphism group $\mathrm{Inn}(S)$.

articles.title: Relative generator number
articles.statement:
For subgroups $G$ and $N$ of a group $A$, the relative generator
number of $G$ modulo $N$ is the least $k$ such that some $k$ elements of $A$ together with $N$
generate $G$, and $0$ if no finite set of elements does. For a normal subgroup $N \le G$ with
$G / N$ finitely generated it is $d(G / N)$, the minimal number of generators of $G / N$.

articles.title: Generator counts of groups generated by two subgroups are not always additive (Kourovka 12.71)
articles.statement:
Write $d(X)$ for the minimal number of generators of a finite group $X$. There are finite groups
$A$ and $B$ such that for every finite group $G$ and all subgroups $H, K \le G$ with $H \cong A$,
$K \cong B$ and $\langle H, K \rangle = G$, we have $d(G) \ne d(A) + d(B)$.

Resolved false: the Kourovka Archive answers 12.71 "No, not always" (A. Lucchini, 2001). Since
$d(G) \le d(A) + d(B)$ always holds for such $G$, every finite group generated by subgroups
isomorphic to $A$ and $B$ needs fewer than $d(A) + d(B)$ generators (Kovács and Sim had shown this
within soluble groups).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 12.71 (L. Ribes); resolution: A. Lucchini, J. Group Theory 4 (2001), no. 1, 53-58, Kourovka Archive, Problem 12.71: No, not always.

articles.title: Ribes' question on generator counts (Kourovka 12.71)
articles.statement:
Write $d(X)$ for the minimal number
of generators of a finite group $X$. This is the proposition that for all finite groups $A$ and
$B$ there are a finite group $G$ and subgroups $H, K \le G$ with $H \cong A$, $K \cong B$ and
$\langle H, K \rangle = G$ such that $d(G) = d(A) + d(B)$.

articles.title: There is a group of spread exactly one
articles.statement:
There exists a group $G$ of spread exactly $1$:
for every nontrivial $x \in G$ there is $y \in G$ with $\langle x, y \rangle = G$, but for every
natural number $m > 1$ there are nontrivial elements $x_1, \dots, x_m \in G$ such that no single
$y \in G$ satisfies $\langle x_i, y \rangle = G$ for all $i$. This answers Kourovka Problem 21.38
affirmatively.

The Nilradical note A group of spread one (17 September 2026, Kourovka Notebook site), Theorem 1,
shows that the subgroup $\{f \in F : f'(0^+) = f'(1^-)\}$ of Thompson's group $F$ is infinite and
has spread exactly one. The note is not refereed; the Kourovka Notebook (arXiv:1401.0300v49) marks
Problem 21.38 solved (AI solution confirmed by S. Corson).

## Sources

- Nilradical, A group of spread one (note of 17 September 2026, Kourovka Notebook site), https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/nilradical-kourovka-21-38.pdf; E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (20 October 2026), Problem 21.38, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Existence of a group of spread exactly one (Kourovka 21.38)
articles.statement:
The conjecture that there
exists a group of spread exactly $1$.

articles.title: Spread at least $k$
articles.statement:
A group $G$ has spread at least $k$, for a natural number $k$, when for
every family $x_1, \dots, x_k$ of nontrivial elements of $G$, not necessarily distinct, there is an
element $y \in G$ such that the subgroup $\langle x_i, y \rangle$ generated by $x_i$ and $y$ is
all of $G$ for every $i$.

articles.title: Spread exactly $k$
articles.statement:
A group $G$ has spread exactly $k$, for a natural number $k$, when $G$
has spread at least $k$ and, for every natural number $m > k$, $G$ does not have spread at
least $m$.

articles.title: Spread of a group
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group. The spread $s(G)$ of $G$ is the supremum in
$\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ of the natural numbers $k$ such that for any non-trivial elements
$x_1, \dots, x_k$ of $G$ (not necessarily distinct) there exists $y \in G$ such that the
subgroup $\langle x_i, y \rangle$ generated by $x_i$ and $y$ is all of $G$ for every $i$. In
particular $s(G) = \infty$ when there is no largest such $k$.

articles.title: Burness–Guralnick–Harper spread theorem
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group. Then the spread $s(G)$
is at least $2$ if and only if every proper quotient of $G$ is cyclic, that is, $G/N$ is cyclic
for every non-trivial normal subgroup $N$ of $G$.

## Sources

- T. C. Burness, R. M. Guralnick, and S. Harper, `The spread of a finite group`, Annals of Math, 193 (2) 2021. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_spread_of_a_finite_group` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Maróti–Tamburini bound for two-generated direct powers
articles.statement:
For every non-abelian finite simple
group $G$ there is a natural number $n$ with $n^2 > 4|G|$, that is, $n > 2\sqrt{|G|}$, such that
the direct power $G^n$ is generated by two elements. This answers Kourovka Problem 17.116
positively.

Maróti and Tamburini (Theorem 1.1) prove $2\sqrt{|G|} < h(G)$ for every non-abelian finite simple
group $G$, where $h(G)$ is the largest $n$ such that $G^n$ is 2-generated; writing $n(G)$ for this
same $h(G)$, the Kourovka Archive answers 17.116 "Yes, it is, even with $n(G) > 2\sqrt{|G|}$".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 17.116 (A. Erfanian, J. Wiegold); resolution: A. Maróti and M. C. Tamburini Bellani, A solution to a problem of Wiegold, Comm. Algebra 41 (2013), 34-49, Theorem 1.1 (for any non-abelian finite simple group G, 2√|G| < h(G), the largest n with G^n 2-generated); Kourovka Archive, Problem 17.116 (Yes, it is, even with n(G) > 2√|G|), https://www.renyi.hu/~maroti/centralizer12.pdf.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 17.116 (two-generated direct powers of simple groups)
articles.statement:
The statement, in
the form of its resolution, that for every non-abelian finite simple group $G$ there is a natural
number $n$ with $n^2 > 4|G|$, that is, $n > 2\sqrt{|G|}$, such that the direct power $G^n$ is
generated by two elements. The problem is due to A. Erfanian and J. Wiegold.

Since $G^n$ maps onto $G^m$ for $m \le n$, this says that the largest $n(G)$ such that $G^{n(G)}$ is
2-generated satisfies $n(G) > 2\sqrt{|G|}$.

articles.title: Finite groups are amenable
articles.statement:
Every finite group is amenable.

The whole group $F = G$ is invariant under left translation, so it is a Følner set whose
symmetric-difference ratio is $0$.

articles.title: Trivial groups are amenable
articles.statement:
Every group with at most one element is amenable; the set
$F = \{1\}$ witnesses the Følner condition.

articles.title: Amenable group (Følner condition)
articles.statement:
A discrete group $G$ is *amenable* if it satisfies the
Følner condition: for every finite subset $K \subseteq G$ and every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is
a finite nonempty subset $F \subseteq G$ such that
$|sF \mathbin{\triangle} F| / |F| < \varepsilon$ for every $s \in K$. Here
$sF = \{sf : f \in F\}$ is the left translate of $F$ by $s$, $\triangle$ is symmetric difference
and $|\cdot|$ is cardinality.

articles.title: Groups containing a free subgroup of rank two
articles.statement:
A group $G$ contains a free subgroup of
rank $2$ when there is an injective group homomorphism from the free group $F_2$ on two
generators into $G$.

articles.title: Branch groups containing free subgroups exist (Kourovka 15.14(c))
articles.statement:
There is a finitely
generated branch group that contains a free subgroup of rank $2$.

The Kourovka Archive answers 15.14(c) "Such groups do exist": Sidki and Wilson constructed
finitely generated branch groups containing free subgroups of rank $2$.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 15.14(c): branch groups containing free subgroups
articles.statement:
The statement that
there exists a finitely generated branch group that contains a free subgroup of rank $2$.

articles.title: Branch groups of exponential growth exist (Kourovka 15.14(d))
articles.statement:
There is a finitely generated
branch group of exponential growth.

The Kourovka Archive answers 15.14(d) "Such groups do exist" (Sidki and Wilson); a finitely

The statement that there

articles.title: Non-amenable branch groups exist (Kourovka 15.14(a))
articles.statement:
There is a finitely generated branch
group that is not amenable.

The Kourovka Archive answers 15.14(a) "Such groups do exist" (Sidki and Wilson): their finitely

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 15.14(b): non-amenable branch groups without free subgroups
articles.statement:
The
statement that there exists a finitely generated branch group that is not amenable and contains
no free subgroup of rank $2$.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 15.14(a): non-amenable branch groups
articles.statement:
The statement that there exists a
finitely generated branch group that is not amenable.

articles.title: Growth rate of a finitely generated group
articles.statement:
The growth rate `ω(G, P) = limsup β_P(n)^(1/n)` of a finite generating family `P`, where
`β_P(n)` is the number of elements that are products of at most `n` generators and their
inverses.

articles.title: Groups of exponential growth
articles.statement:
A group $G$ has exponential growth when it is finitely
generated and every finite generating family $P$ of $G$ has growth rate $\omega(G, P) > 1$.

articles.title: Branch groups (Kourovka 15.14 version)
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is a branch group (Kourovka 15.12) if
there are a sequence $m$ of natural numbers with $m(i) \ge 2$ for every $i$ and an action $\rho$ of
$G$ by permutations of the vertices of the spherically homogeneous rooted tree with branching
sequence $m$ such that: $\rho$ is faithful; each $\rho(g)$ is a tree automorphism, that is, for all
vertices $v$ and $w$, $v$ is a prefix of $w$ if and only if $\rho(g)(v)$ is a prefix of
$\rho(g)(w)$; the action is level-transitive, that is, for any two vertices $v$ and $w$ of the same
level some $g \in G$ has $\rho(g)(v) = w$; and for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ the $n$-th rigid level
stabilizer of $\rho$ has finite index in $G$.

articles.title: Rigid level stabilizers (Kourovka 15.14 version)
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group acting by permutations
$\rho$ on the vertices of the rooted tree with branching sequence $m$, and let $n$ be a natural
number. The $n$-th rigid level stabilizer of $\rho$ is the subgroup of $G$ generated by the rigid
vertex stabilizers of all vertices at level $n$, the words of length $n$.

articles.title: Rigid vertex stabilizers (Kourovka 15.14 version)
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group acting by permutations
$\rho$ on the vertices of the rooted tree with branching sequence $m$, and let $v$ be a vertex. The
rigid vertex stabilizer of $v$ is the set of elements $g \in G$ whose support lies in the subtree
rooted at $v$: $\rho(g)$ fixes every vertex $w$ of which $v$ is not a prefix.

articles.title: Vertices of a spherically homogeneous rooted tree (Kourovka 15.14 version)
articles.statement:
For a sequence
$m$ of natural numbers, the vertices of the spherically homogeneous rooted tree with branching
sequence $m$ are the finite words $l_0 l_1 \cdots l_{k-1}$ of natural numbers with $l_i < m(i)$ for
every $i < k$. The length of a word is its level and its prefixes are its ancestors.

articles.title: Faithful actions by finite-state tree automorphisms
articles.statement:
A group $G$ acts faithfully on a
regular rooted tree by finite-state automorphisms when there are a natural number $d \ge 2$ and an
injective group homomorphism $\varphi$ from $G$ to the group of permutations of the set of finite
words over $\{0, \dots, d-1\}$ such that $\varphi(g)$ is a finite-state automorphism of the
$d$-regular rooted tree for every $g \in G$.

articles.title: Lavrenyuk's theorem on irreducible generators of finite-state automorphism groups
articles.statement:
For every
integer $d \ge 2$, the group of finite-state automorphisms of the $d$-regular rooted tree has an
irreducible system of generators: a set $S$ of elements of the group that generates the group and
no proper subset of which generates the group.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 16.86 (V. I. Sushchanskiĭ); resolution: Ya. Lavrenyuk, The group of all finite-state automorphisms of a regular rooted tree has a minimal generating set, Geom. Dedicata 183 (2016), 59-67 (preprint: Minimal generating sets in wreath products, arXiv:1210.0150), arXiv:1210.0150, Theorem 3.8 (for a regular rooted tree over any alphabet of at least two letters, the group of finite-state automorphisms has a minimal generating set); Kourovka Archive, Problem 16.86 (Yes, it does), https://arxiv.org/abs/1210.0150.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 16.86 (Sushchanskiĭ): irreducible generators of finite-state automorphism groups
articles.statement:
**Kourovka Problem 16.86 (Sushchanskiĭ): irreducible generators of finite-state automorphism
groups.** The statement that for every integer $d \ge 2$ the group of finite-state automorphisms of
the $d$-regular rooted tree has an irreducible system of generators: a set $S$ of elements of the
group that generates the group and no proper subset of which generates the group.

articles.title: Finite-state automorphisms of a regular rooted tree
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, consider the
$d$-regular rooted tree whose vertices are the finite words over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, d-1\}$.
The group of finite-state automorphisms of this tree is the subgroup of the group of all
permutations of the words generated by the tree automorphisms that have only finitely many
distinct sections.

These automorphisms are closed under products and inverses, so the subgroup consists of exactly
them.

articles.title: Finite-state tree automorphism groups with undecidable conjugacy problem
articles.statement:
The answer
to Kourovka Problem 16.34 is negative: there exist $d, k \in \mathbb{N}$ and finite-state
automorphisms $g_0, \dots, g_{k-1}$ of the $d$-regular rooted tree such that no algorithm
decides, given two words in the $g_i$ and their inverses, whether the elements they spell are
conjugate in the group generated by $g_0, \dots, g_{k-1}$.

Šunić and Ventura (Theorem 1.1) construct automaton groups, finitely generated groups
generated by finite self-similar sets of finite-state automorphisms of a regular rooted tree,
with unsolvable conjugacy problem; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) answers 16.34 "No, not
always".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 16.34 (R. I. Grigorchuk, V. V. Nekrashevich, V. I. Sushchanskiĭ); resolution: Z. Šunić and E. Ventura, The conjugacy problem in automaton groups is not solvable, J. Algebra 364 (2012), 148-154, arXiv:1010.1993, Theorem 1.1 (there exist automaton groups with unsolvable conjugacy problem; the examples are (free abelian)-by-free groups generated by finite self-similar sets of tree automorphisms); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 16.34 solved (No, not always), https://arxiv.org/abs/1010.1993.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 16.34: conjugacy in finite-state automorphism groups
articles.statement:
The proposition
that every finitely generated group of finite-state automorphisms of a regular rooted tree has
decidable conjugacy problem: for all $d, k \in \mathbb{N}$ and all finite-state automorphisms
$g_0, \dots, g_{k-1}$ of the $d$-regular rooted tree, some algorithm decides, given two words
in the $g_i$ and their inverses, whether the elements they spell are conjugate in the group
generated by $g_0, \dots, g_{k-1}$.

The problem was posed by R. I. Grigorchuk, V. V. Nekrashevich and V. I. Sushchanskiĭ.

articles.title: Fedorova–Oliynyk theorem (Kourovka Problem 16.85)
articles.statement:
For all groups $G$ and $H$, if $G$ and $H$
each act faithfully on a regular rooted tree by finite-state automorphisms, then their free product
$G \ast H$ acts faithfully on some regular rooted tree by finite-state automorphisms.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 16.85 (V. I. Sushchanskiĭ); resolution: M. Fedorova and A. Oliynyk, Finite automaton actions of free products of groups, Algebra Discrete Math. 23 (2017), no. 2, 230-236, abstract (for groups G and H that act faithfully by finite state automorphisms on regular rooted trees, G ∗ H admits a faithful action by finite state automorphisms on some regular rooted tree) and Theorem 1 (FAut T_n ∗ FAut T_n is isomorphic to a subgroup of FAut T_3n); Kourovka Archive, Problem 16.85 (Yes, it can), https://admjournal.luguniv.edu.ua/index.php/adm/article/view/477.

articles.title: Finite-state actions of free products (Kourovka Problem 16.85)
articles.statement:
The statement that for all
groups $G$ and $H$, if $G$ and $H$ each act faithfully on a regular rooted tree by finite-state
automorphisms (the two trees may have different degrees), then so does their free product
$G \ast H$.

articles.title: Finite-state automorphisms of the regular rooted tree (Kourovka 16.85)
articles.statement:
For a natural
number $d$, let $X^*$ be the set of finite words over $X = \{0, \dots, d-1\}$. A permutation $f$
of $X^*$ is a finite-state automorphism when it is an automorphism of the $d$-regular rooted tree
and its sections at the vertices $u \in X^*$ form a finite set of maps $X^* \to X^*$.

articles.title: Finite-state automorphism of the regular rooted tree
articles.statement:
For $d \in \mathbb{N}$, a
permutation $f$ of the finite words over $\{0, \dots, d-1\}$ is a finite-state automorphism of
the $d$-regular rooted tree when it is an automorphism of the tree and the sections of $f$ at
all vertices $u$ form a finite set of maps.

articles.title: Automorphisms of the regular rooted tree (Kourovka 16.85)
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a natural number and
let $X^*$ be the set of finite words over the alphabet $X = \{0, \dots, d-1\}$, the vertices of the
$d$-regular rooted tree. A permutation $f$ of $X^*$ is a tree automorphism when, for all words $u$
and $v$, the word $f(u)$ has the same length $|u|$ as $u$ and the first $|u|$ letters of $f(uv)$
form the word $f(u)$, where $uv$ denotes concatenation.

articles.title: Automorphism of the regular rooted tree
articles.statement:
For $d \in \mathbb{N}$, the vertices of the
$d$-regular rooted tree are the finite words over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, d-1\}$. A
permutation $f$ of this set of words is a tree automorphism when, for all words $u$ and $v$,
writing $|u|$ for the length of $u$ and $uv$ for the concatenation of $u$ and $v$, the word
$f(u)$ has length $|u|$ and the first $|u|$ letters of $f(uv)$ form $f(u)$.

articles.title: Automorphisms of the regular rooted tree
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, the $d$-regular rooted
tree has as vertices the finite words over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, d-1\}$; write $vw$ for the
concatenation of words $v$ and $w$. The root is the empty word and the children of a word $v$ are
the words $vi$ for letters $i$. A permutation $g$ of the words is a tree automorphism when for all
words $v$ and $w$ there is a word $u$ of the same length as $w$ with $g(vw) = g(v)u$.

For a permutation of the words this says that $g$ preserves lengths and the prefix order, so it is
an automorphism of the tree as a graph.

articles.title: Section of a permutation of the tree at a vertex (Kourovka 16.85)
articles.statement:
For a natural number
$d$, let $X^*$ be the set of finite words over $X = \{0, \dots, d-1\}$, let $f$ be a permutation of
$X^*$ and let $u \in X^*$, of length $|u|$. The section (state) of $f$ at $u$ is the map
$X^* \to X^*$ sending a word $w$ to the word obtained from $f(uw)$ by deleting its first $|u|$
letters (all of them if it has fewer), where $uw$ denotes concatenation.

articles.title: Section of a word permutation at a vertex
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, let $g$ be a
permutation of the finite words over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, d-1\}$ and let $v$ be a word. The
section (state) of $g$ at $v$ is the map sending a word $w$ to the word obtained from $g(vw)$ by
deleting its first $|g(v)|$ letters, where $vw$ is the concatenation of $v$ and $w$ and $|g(v)|$ is
the length of $g(v)$. When $g$ is a tree automorphism, the image of $w$ is the word $u$ with
$g(vw) = g(v)u$.

articles.title: Section of a map of the regular rooted tree at a vertex
articles.statement:
For $d \in \mathbb{N}$, let
$f$ be a permutation of the finite words over $\{0, \dots, d-1\}$ (the vertices of the
$d$-regular rooted tree) and let $u$ be a word, of length $|u|$. The section (state) of $f$ at
$u$ is the map sending each word $w$ to the word obtained from $f(uw)$ by deleting its first
$|u|$ letters, where $uw$ is the concatenation of $u$ and $w$.

articles.title: Value of a word in the generators
articles.statement:
For $d, k \in \mathbb{N}$, let $g_0, \dots, g_{k-1}$
be permutations of the finite words over $\{0, \dots, d-1\}$, and let $w$ be a word whose
letters are pairs $(i, b)$ with $i < k$ and $b$ a boolean. The value of $w$ is the element of
the group generated by $g_0, \dots, g_{k-1}$ obtained by multiplying, from left to right, $g_i$
for each letter $(i, \mathrm{true})$ and $g_i^{-1}$ for each letter $(i, \mathrm{false})$.

articles.title: Cleary's golden-ratio Thompson group
articles.statement:
Let $\tau = (1 + \sqrt{5})/2$ be the golden
ratio. Cleary's group $F_\tau$ is the set of permutations $f$ of $\mathbb{R}$ such that
$f(x) = x$ for every $x \notin [0, 1]$, and there are a natural number $n$ and points
$0 = t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_{n+1} = 1$, each of the form $a + b\tau$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}$,
such that on each interval $[t_i, t_{i+1}]$ the map $f$ is affine with slope $\tau^k$ for some
integer $k$, that is, $f(x) = f(t_i) + \tau^k (x - t_i)$ for all $x \in [t_i, t_{i+1}]$.

articles.title: Cleary's golden-ratio group does not embed in Thompson's group F
articles.statement:
There is no map $\varphi$
from permutations of $\mathbb{R}$ to permutations of $\mathbb{R}$ that sends every element of
Cleary's golden-ratio Thompson group $F_\tau$ into Thompson's group $F$, is injective on
$F_\tau$, and satisfies $\varphi(g h) = \varphi(g) \varphi(h)$ for all $g, h \in F_\tau$, where
the product of permutations is composition. In other words, the golden-ratio Thompson embedding
conjecture is false: $F_\tau$ does not embed in $F$ as a group.

Hyde and Moore proved this by introducing F-obstructions (Corollary 1.4; Corollary 1 in arXiv v1).

## Sources

- J. Hyde, J. T. Moore, Subgroups of PL+I which do not embed into Thompson's group F, Groups, Geometry, and Dynamics 17 (2023) 533-554, arXiv:2103.14911, https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.14911.

articles.title: Golden-ratio Thompson embedding conjecture
articles.statement:
The proposition that there is a map
$\varphi$ from permutations of $\mathbb{R}$ to permutations of $\mathbb{R}$ that sends every
element of Cleary's golden-ratio Thompson group $F_\tau$ into Thompson's group $F$, is injective
on $F_\tau$, and satisfies $\varphi(g h) = \varphi(g) \varphi(h)$ for all $g, h \in F_\tau$,
where the product of permutations is composition.

Since $F_\tau$ is a group under composition, this says that $F_\tau$ embeds in $F$ as a group.

## Sources

- record OWR-16167-018.

articles.title: Dyadic rationals
articles.statement:
A real number $x$ is dyadic when $x = a / 2^n$ for some integer $a$ and
some natural number $n$, that is, when $x$ lies in $\mathbb{Z}[1/2]$.

articles.title: Golden integers
articles.statement:
Let $\tau = (1 + \sqrt{5})/2$ be the golden ratio. A real number $x$ is a
golden integer when $x = a + b\tau$ for some integers $a$ and $b$. Since $\tau^2 = \tau + 1$, these
are exactly the elements of $\mathbb{Z}[\tau]$.

articles.title: Piecewise-linear maps with prescribed breakpoints and slopes
articles.statement:
Let $B$ and $S$ be sets of
real numbers. A permutation $f$ of $\mathbb{R}$ is piecewise linear with breakpoints in $B$ and
slopes in $S$ when $f(x) = x$ for every $x \notin [0, 1]$, and there are a natural number $n$
and points $0 = t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_{n+1} = 1$, all in $B$, such that for each $i \le n$ there
is $s \in S$ with $f(x) = f(t_i) + s (x - t_i)$ for all $x \in [t_i, t_{i+1}]$.

Adjacent pieces agree at the shared point, so $f$ restricts to a piecewise-linear homeomorphism
of $[0, 1]$ when the slopes are positive.

articles.title: Thompson's group F
articles.statement:
Thompson's group $F$ is the set of permutations $f$ of $\mathbb{R}$
such that $f(x) = x$ for every $x \notin [0, 1]$, and there are a natural number $n$ and points
$0 = t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_{n+1} = 1$, each of the form $a / 2^m$ with $a \in \mathbb{Z}$ and
$m \in \mathbb{N}$, such that on each interval $[t_i, t_{i+1}]$ the map $f$ is affine with slope
$2^k$ for some integer $k$, that is, $f(x) = f(t_i) + 2^k (x - t_i)$ for all
$x \in [t_i, t_{i+1}]$.

articles.title: Not every finitely generated hereditarily just infinite group is linear
articles.statement:
There is a finitely
generated hereditarily just infinite group $G$ such that for no field $K$ and no natural number
$n$ is there an injective group homomorphism $G \to \mathrm{GL}_n(K)$.

This answers Kourovka 15.18(b) negatively, as recorded in the Kourovka Archive ("No, not every";
Ershov and Jaikin-Zapirain). As the problem notes, a positive answer to (b) would contradict (a):
a finitely generated linear torsion group is finite, while a just infinite group is infinite.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 15.18 (L. Bartholdi, R. I. Grigorchuk, Z. Šunić); resolution: M. Ershov and A. Jaikin-Zapirain, Groups of positive weighted deficiency and their applications, J. Reine Angew. Math. 677 (2013), 71-134, arXiv:1007.1489, Kourovka Archive, Problem 15.18 ((a) Yes, such groups exist; (b) No, not every); the abstract constructs finitely generated residually finite p-torsion groups and shows that every group of positive weighted deficiency has a hereditarily just infinite quotient, https://arxiv.org/abs/1007.1489.

articles.title: Kourovka 15.18(b): linearity of hereditarily just infinite groups
articles.statement:
The proposition that
every finitely generated hereditarily just infinite group $G$ is linear, i.e. that there are a
field $K$, a natural number $n$ and an injective group homomorphism $G \to \mathrm{GL}_n(K)$.

articles.title: Finitely generated hereditarily just infinite torsion groups exist
articles.statement:
There is a finitely
generated hereditarily just infinite group $G$ in which every element has finite order.

This answers Kourovka 15.18(a) positively, as recorded in the Kourovka Archive ("Yes, such groups
exist"; Ershov and Jaikin-Zapirain).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 15.18 (L. Bartholdi, R. I. Grigorchuk, Z. Šunić); resolution: M. Ershov and A. Jaikin-Zapirain, Groups of positive weighted deficiency and their applications, J. Reine Angew. Math. 677 (2013), 71-134, arXiv:1007.1489, Kourovka Archive, Problem 15.18 ((a) Yes, such groups exist; (b) No, not every); the abstract constructs finitely generated residually finite p-torsion groups and shows that every group of positive weighted deficiency has a hereditarily just infinite quotient, https://arxiv.org/abs/1007.1489.

articles.title: Kourovka 15.18(a): hereditarily just infinite torsion groups
articles.statement:
The proposition that there
exists a finitely generated hereditarily just infinite group $G$ that is a torsion group, i.e.
every element of $G$ has finite order.

articles.title: Growth rate of a finite generating family
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a generating family of a group $G$
indexed by $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$, and let $\beta_P(n)$ be the number of elements of $G$ whose word
length with respect to $P$ is at most $n$, that is, which are products of at most $n$ members of
$P$ and their inverses. The growth rate of $P$ is the real number
$\omega(G, P) = \limsup_{n \to \infty} \beta_P(n)^{1/n}$.

articles.title: Groups of intermediate growth
articles.statement:
A group $G$ has intermediate growth if it is finitely
generated and, for every natural number $k$ and every generating family $P$ of $G$ indexed by
$\{0, \dots, k-1\}$, the growth rate of $P$ is at most $1$ (subexponential growth) and $P$ does
not have polynomial growth.

articles.title: Branch groups
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is a branch group (Kourovka 15.12) if there are a sequence
$m : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $m(i) \ge 2$ for all $i$ and a homomorphism $\rho$ from $G$ to
the group of permutations of the vertices of the rooted tree with branching sequence $m$ such that
$\rho$ is injective; every $\rho(g)$ is a tree automorphism, that is, for all vertices $v$ and $w$,
$v$ is a prefix of $w$ if and only if $\rho(g)(v)$ is a prefix of $\rho(g)(w)$; the action is
level-transitive, that is, for any two vertices $v$ and $w$ of the same level there is $g \in G$
with $\rho(g)(v) = w$; and for every $n$ the $n$-th rigid level stabilizer has finite index in
$G$.

articles.title: Hereditarily just infinite groups
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is hereditarily just infinite (in the
sense of Kourovka 15.18) if it is infinite, residually finite, and every nontrivial normal
subgroup of $G$, viewed as a group in its own right, is just infinite.

articles.title: Just infinite groups
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is just infinite if it is infinite and every nontrivial
normal subgroup of $G$ has finite index, that is, all proper quotients of $G$ are finite.

articles.title: Just infinite groups
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is just infinite if it is infinite and every nontrivial
normal subgroup of $G$ has finite index in $G$.

articles.title: Residually finite groups
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is residually finite if every element $g \ne 1$ of
$G$ lies outside some normal subgroup of finite index in $G$.

articles.title: Just infinite groups of intermediate growth need not be branch groups
articles.statement:
It is not the case
that every finitely generated just infinite group of intermediate growth is a branch group: the
Kourovka Archive answers Problem 15.17 "No, not every".

Nekrashevych constructed infinite finitely generated simple groups of intermediate growth. Such a
group is just infinite, and it is not a branch group: its rigid level stabilizers, nontrivial normal
subgroups of finite index, would be the whole group, which they split as a direct product of at
least two nontrivial factors.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 15.17 (L. Bartholdi, R. I. Grigorchuk, Z. Šunić); resolution: V. Nekrashevych, Palindromic subshifts and simple periodic groups of intermediate growth, Ann. of Math. (2) 187 (2018), no. 3, 667-719, abstract (infinite finitely generated periodic groups of intermediate growth, among them the first simple groups of intermediate growth); Kourovka Archive, Problem 15.17 (answer: No, not every; there exist simple finitely generated groups of intermediate growth; the Archive prints the volume as 87), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.01033.

articles.title: The branch question for just infinite groups of intermediate growth
articles.statement:
Kourovka
Problem 15.17 (L. Bartholdi, R. I. Grigorchuk, Z. Šunić) is the assertion that every finitely
generated just infinite group of intermediate growth is a branch group.

articles.title: Rigid level stabilizer
articles.statement:
Let $\rho$ be a homomorphism from a group $G$ to the group of
permutations of the vertices of the rooted tree with branching sequence $m$. For a natural number
$n$, the $n$-th rigid level stabilizer is the subgroup of $G$ generated by the union of the rigid
vertex stabilizers of all vertices at level $n$, that is, of all words of length $n$.

articles.title: Rigid vertex stabilizer
articles.statement:
Let $\rho$ be a homomorphism from a group $G$ to the group of
permutations of the vertices of the rooted tree with branching sequence $m$, and let $v$ be a
vertex. The rigid vertex stabilizer of $v$ is the set of elements $g \in G$ such that $\rho(g)$
fixes every vertex that does not have $v$ as a prefix, that is, the elements whose support (the set
of vertices they move) lies in the subtree rooted at $v$.

articles.title: Vertices of a spherically homogeneous rooted tree
articles.statement:
For a sequence $m : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{N}$ of branching indices, the vertices of the spherically homogeneous rooted tree with
branching sequence $m$ are the finite words $x_0 x_1 \cdots x_{\ell-1}$ of natural numbers with
$x_i < m(i)$ for every $i < \ell$. The length of a word is its level and its prefixes are its
ancestors.

articles.title: A finitely generated branch group with a non-normal maximal subgroup of finite index
articles.statement:
The
Kourovka 20.101 statement that every maximal subgroup of finite index of a finitely generated
branch group is normal is false: some finitely generated branch group has a maximal subgroup of
finite index that is not normal.

Garciarena and Petschick (2024, Theorem 4.1) construct a finitely generated branch group all of
whose maximal subgroups have finite index, one of which is not normal.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 20.101 (A. Thillaisundaram); resolution: M. E. Garciarena and J. M. Petschick, Maximal subgroups in torsion branch groups, preprint, arXiv:2410.06783 (2024); P. M. Neumann, Illinois J. Math. 30 (1986), 301-316, Garciarena-Petschick, Theorem 4.1: there exists a finitely generated branch group that is in MF (all maximal subgroups of finite index) but not in MN (all maximal subgroups normal); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 20.101 solved, "No, not necessarily" (P. Neumann), https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.06783.

articles.title: Kourovka 20.101: finite-index maximal subgroups of finitely generated branch groups are normal
articles.statement:
**Kourovka 20.101: finite-index maximal subgroups of finitely generated branch groups are
normal.** The statement (A. Thillaisundaram) that in every finitely generated branch group every
maximal subgroup of finite index is normal.

articles.title: A finitely generated branch group with a maximal subgroup of infinite index
articles.statement:
The
Kourovka 15.15 statement that every maximal subgroup of a finitely generated branch group has
finite index is false: some finitely generated branch group has a maximal subgroup of infinite
index.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 15.15 (L. Bartholdi, R. I. Grigorchuk, Z. Šunić); resolution: I. V. Bondarenko, Finite generation of iterated wreath products, Arch. Math. (Basel) 95 (2010), no. 4, 301-308, arXiv:1002.0320, abstract and the example after Corollary 3 (a finitely generated branch group with maximal subgroups of infinite index, answering Question 14 of Bartholdi, Grigorchuk and Šunić, Branch groups); Kourovka Archive, Problem 15.15 (answer: No, not necessarily), https://arxiv.org/abs/1002.0320.

articles.title: Kourovka 15.15: maximal subgroups of finitely generated branch groups have finite index
articles.statement:
The statement (L. Bartholdi, R. I. Grigorchuk, Z. Šunić) that every maximal subgroup of every
finitely generated branch group has finite index.

articles.title: Branch action
articles.statement:
A faithful level-transitive action of a group $G$ on a rooted tree $T$ is a
branch action when, for every level $n$, the rigid stabilizer of level $n$ has finite index in
$G$.

articles.title: Branch group
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is a branch group when there exist a rooted tree $T$ (locally
finite, with every vertex having at least two children) and a faithful level-transitive action of
$G$ on $T$ by tree automorphisms that is a branch action.

articles.title: Branch group (Kourovka 15.15)
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is a branch group if there are a sequence
$m \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $m(i) \ge 2$ for all $i$ and an injective homomorphism
$\rho$ from $G$ to the permutations of the vertices of the spherically homogeneous rooted tree with
branching sequence $m$ such that each $\rho(g)$ is a tree automorphism (for all vertices $v$ and
$w$, $v$ is a prefix of $w$ if and only if $\rho(g)(v)$ is a prefix of $\rho(g)(w)$), the action is
level-transitive (for any two vertices $v$ and $w$ at the same level some $g \in G$ has
$\rho(g)(v) = w$), and for every $n$ the $n$-th rigid level stabilizer has finite index in $G$.

articles.title: Descendants in a rooted tree
articles.statement:
For vertices $v$ at level $n$ and $w$ at level $m$ of a
rooted tree $T$, $w$ is a descendant of $v$ when $w$ is reached from $v$ by moving from a vertex
to one of its children zero or more times: $v$ is a descendant of itself, and a vertex at level
$k + 1$ is a descendant of $v$ whenever its parent is.

articles.title: Rigid vertex stabilizer
articles.statement:
Given a faithful level-transitive action of a group $G$ on a
rooted tree $T$ and a vertex $v$ of $T$, an element $g \in G$ lies in the rigid stabilizer of $v$
when $g$ fixes every vertex of $T$ that is not a descendant of $v$.

articles.title: Faithful level-transitive action on a rooted tree
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a rooted tree with vertex
sets $V_n$ at the levels $n \ge 0$ and parent maps $V_{n+1} \to V_n$, and let $G$ be a group. A
faithful level-transitive action of $G$ on $T$ consists of an action of $G$ on each level $V_n$ by
permutations, that is, a homomorphism $G \to \mathrm{Sym}(V_n)$ for every $n$, such that the
actions commute with the parent maps (so $G$ acts by tree automorphisms), only the identity of $G$
fixes every vertex of $T$, and $G$ acts transitively on every level $V_n$.

articles.title: Rigid stabilizer of a level
articles.statement:
Given a faithful level-transitive action of a group $G$ on a
rooted tree $T$ and a level $n$, the rigid stabilizer of level $n$ is the subgroup of $G$ generated
by the rigid stabilizers of all vertices of $T$ at level $n$.

articles.title: Rigid level stabilizer (Kourovka 15.15)
articles.statement:
Let $\rho$ be a homomorphism from a group $G$ to
the permutations of the vertices of the tree with branching sequence $m$, and let $n$ be a natural
number. The $n$-th rigid level stabilizer is the subgroup of $G$ generated by the rigid vertex
stabilizers of all vertices at level $n$.

articles.title: Rigid vertex stabilizer (Kourovka 15.15)
articles.statement:
Let $\rho$ be a homomorphism from a group $G$ to
the permutations of the vertices of the tree with branching sequence $m$, and let $v$ be a vertex.
The rigid vertex stabilizer of $v$ is the set of $g \in G$ such that $\rho(g)$ fixes every vertex
$w$ of which $v$ is not a prefix, that is, every vertex outside the subtree rooted at $v$.

articles.title: Rooted tree given by levels
articles.statement:
A locally finite rooted tree is given by finite sets $V_n$ for
$n \ge 0$, the vertices at level $n$, where $V_0$ consists of the root alone, together with parent
maps $V_{n+1} \to V_n$, such that every vertex has at least two children: for every $v \in V_n$
there are distinct $x, y \in V_{n+1}$ whose parent is $v$.

articles.title: Vertices of the spherically homogeneous rooted tree (Kourovka 15.15)
articles.statement:
For a branching
sequence $m \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, the vertices of the spherically homogeneous rooted
tree are the finite words $(x_0, \dots, x_{k-1})$ of natural numbers with $x_i < m(i)$ for every
$i < k$. The length $k$ of a word is its level and its prefixes are its ancestors.

articles.title: Thompson's group $F$ by its standard presentation
articles.statement:
Thompson's group $F$ is the group with
generators $x_0, x_1$ and relations $[x_0 x_1^{-1}, x_0^{-1} x_1 x_0] = 1$ and
$[x_0 x_1^{-1}, x_0^{-2} x_1 x_0^2] = 1$, where $[a, b] = a b a^{-1} b^{-1}$; that is, the
quotient of the free group on $x_0, x_1$ by the normal subgroup generated by these two
relators.

articles.title: Thompson's group $F$ does not have the Howson property
articles.statement:
It is not the case that the
intersection of any two finitely generated subgroups of Thompson's group $F$ is finitely
generated: there are finitely generated subgroups $H$ and $K$ of $F$ such that $H \cap K$ is not
finitely generated.

Resolved false: the Kourovka Archive answers 19.40 "No": $\mathbb{Z} \wr \mathbb{Z}$ fails the
Howson property (Kirkinskiĭ) and embeds in $F$ (Cleary), and the property is inherited by
subgroups.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 19.40 (I. Kapovich); resolution: A. S. Kirkinskiĭ, Algebra Logic 20 (1981), no. 1, 24-36; S. Cleary, Pacific J. Math. 228 (2006), no. 1, 53-61; D. Robertson, letter of 24 April 2018, Kourovka Archive, Problem 19.40: No; ℤ ≀ ℤ does not have the Howson property (Kirkinskiĭ) and embeds in F (Cleary), and the Howson property passes to subgroups, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Howson property for Thompson's group $F$
articles.statement:
The statement that Thompson's group $F$ has the
Howson property: for all finitely generated subgroups $H$ and $K$ of $F$, the intersection
$H \cap K$ is finitely generated.

This is Kourovka Notebook Problem 19.40 (I. Kapovich).

articles.title: Relators of Thompson's group $F$
articles.statement:
In the free group on two generators $x_0$ and $x_1$,
this is the set of the two elements $[x_0 x_1^{-1}, x_0^{-1} x_1 x_0]$ and
$[x_0 x_1^{-1}, x_0^{-2} x_1 x_0^2]$, where $[a, b] = a b a^{-1} b^{-1}$. They are the relators
of the standard presentation of Thompson's group $F$.

articles.title: Finitely presented elementary amenable groups need not be virtually solvable
articles.statement:
There is a
finitely presented elementary amenable group $G$ that is not solvable-by-finite: no subgroup of
finite index in $G$ is solvable. This answers Kourovka Problem 16.52 (P. Linnell, T. Schick) in
the negative.

As Belegradek and Cornulier observed, Houghton's groups $H_n$, finitely presented for $n \ge 3$
by Brown, are elementary amenable (the locally finite group of finitary permutations extended by
$\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$) but not virtually solvable.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 16.52 (P. Linnell, T. Schick); resolution: C. H. Houghton, Arch. Math. (Basel) 31 (1978/79), 254-258; K. S. Brown, J. Pure Appl. Algebra 44 (1987), 45-75; observation of I. Belegradek and Y. Cornulier, MathOverflow question 107996, Kourovka Archive, Problem 16.52 (No, not every: Houghton's groups are finitely presented (Brown) and elementary amenable, but not virtually solvable), https://mathoverflow.net/questions/107996.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 16.52 (Linnell–Schick)
articles.statement:
The statement that every finitely presented
elementary amenable group $G$ is solvable-by-finite, that is, $G$ has a solvable subgroup of finite
index.

articles.title: Elementary amenable groups
articles.statement:
The class of elementary amenable groups is the smallest class
of groups that contains every finite group and every abelian group and is closed under
isomorphisms, subgroups, quotients, extensions and directed unions. Closure under extensions means
that a group $G$ with a normal subgroup $N$ is elementary amenable whenever $N$ and $G/N$ are;
closure under directed unions means that $G$ is elementary amenable whenever it is the union of a
family of elementary amenable subgroups that is directed under inclusion.

articles.title: Boundary of a finite subset of a group
articles.statement:
For a group $\Gamma$ and finite subsets $S$ and $F$
of $\Gamma$, the boundary of $F$ with respect to $S$ is the set
$\partial F = \{\gamma \in \Gamma \setminus F : \gamma s \in F \text{ for some } s \in S\}$.

articles.title: Polynomial growth with respect to a finite subset
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a finite subset of a group
$\Gamma$, and let $B_S(n)$ be the ball of radius $n$ for $S$, the set of products of at most $n$
elements of $S \cup S^{-1}$. Then $\Gamma$ has polynomial growth with respect to $S$ if there are
natural numbers $C$ and $d$ such that for every natural number $n$ the ball $B_S(n)$ has at most
$C\,(n + 1)^d$ elements.

articles.title: Følner exhaustions of polynomial size need not give polynomial growth
articles.statement:
There exist a group
$\Gamma$ generated by a finite subset $S$ and finite subsets
$F_0 \subsetneq F_1 \subsetneq F_2 \subsetneq \cdots$ of $\Gamma$ whose union is $\Gamma$ such that
$|\partial F_k| / |F_k| \to 0$ as $k \to \infty$, where $\partial F_k$ is the boundary of $F_k$
with respect to $S$, and such that for some real $c \ge 0$ and some natural number $d \ge 1$ we
have $|F_k| \le c\,(k + 1)^d$ for every $k$, while $\Gamma$ does not have polynomial growth with
respect to $S$. That is, the answer to Kourovka Problem 14.27 is negative.

By Bardakov, every finitely generated group of intermediate growth (such groups exist by
Grigorchuk) has such a sequence of subsets.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 14.27 (A. G. Vaillant); resolution: V. G. Bardakov, Algebra and Logic 40 (2001), no. 1, 12-16, Kourovka Archive, Problem 14.27: every group of intermediate growth has such a sequence (answer: No, not always).

articles.title: Vaillant's question on Følner exhaustions of polynomial size (Kourovka 14.27)
articles.statement:
The statement
that for every group $\Gamma$ generated by a finite subset $S$ the following holds: if there are
finite subsets $F_0 \subsetneq F_1 \subsetneq F_2 \subsetneq \cdots$ of $\Gamma$ whose union is
$\Gamma$ such that $|\partial F_k| / |F_k| \to 0$ as $k \to \infty$, where $\partial F_k$ is the
boundary of $F_k$ with respect to $S$, and such that for some real $c \ge 0$ and some natural
number $d \ge 1$ we have $|F_k| \le c\,(k + 1)^d$ for every $k$, then $\Gamma$ has polynomial
growth with respect to $S$.

The Kourovka Notebook indexes the sets from $F_1$, so its size condition $|F_k| \le c\,k^d$ reads
$|F_k| \le c\,(k + 1)^d$ here.

articles.title: Ball in the word metric
articles.statement:
For a finite subset $S$ of a group $\Gamma$ and a natural number
$n$, the ball $B_S(n)$ of radius $n$ is the set of products of at most $n$ elements of
$S \cup S^{-1}$, the empty product $1$ included.

articles.title: Juschenko–Monod theorem (Kourovka Problem 15.5)
articles.statement:
There exists a group $G$ that is infinite,
finitely generated, simple and amenable, where amenable means that $G$ satisfies the Følner
condition.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 15.5 (P. de la Harpe); resolution: K. Juschenko and N. Monod, Cantor systems, piecewise translations and simple amenable groups, Ann. of Math. (2) 178 (2013), no. 2, 775-787, arXiv:1204.2132, abstract (the first examples of finitely generated simple groups that are amenable and infinite); Kourovka Archive, Problem 15.5 (answer: Yes, it does; another example in V. Nekrashevych, Ann. of Math. 187 (2018), 667-719), https://arxiv.org/abs/1204.2132.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 15.5 (statement): infinite finitely generated simple amenable groups
articles.statement:
The statement that there exists a group $G$ that is infinite, finitely generated, simple and
amenable, where amenable means that $G$ satisfies the Følner condition.

articles.title: The growth function is bounded by the order of the group
articles.statement:
For every generating family $P$
of a finite group $G$ and every natural number $n$, the value of the growth function of $P$ at $n$
is at most the order of $G$, since every ball is a subset of $G$.

articles.title: Polynomial growth makes the growth function positive
articles.statement:
If a generating family $P$ of a
group $G$ has polynomial growth, then the growth function of $P$ is positive at every natural
number $n$.

articles.title: The growth function of a finite group is positive
articles.statement:
For every generating family $P$ of a
finite group $G$ and every natural number $n$, the growth function of $P$ is positive at $n$: the
ball of radius $n$ contains the identity.

articles.title: The growth function at radius zero
articles.statement:
For every generating family $P$ of a group $G$, the
growth function of $P$ takes the value $1$ at $0$: the ball of radius $0$ consists of the identity
element alone.

articles.title: Growth function of a generating family
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a generating family of a group $G$.
The growth function $\gamma_P$ of $P$ assigns to each natural number $n$ the number of elements
$g \in G$ whose word length with respect to $P$ is at most $n$, that is, the cardinality of the
ball of radius $n$ in the word metric of $P$; when this ball is infinite, $\gamma_P(n)$ is taken
to be $0$.

articles.title: Finite groups have polynomial growth
articles.statement:
Every generating family of a finite group has
polynomial growth: its growth function is bounded by the order of the group, a polynomial of
degree $0$.

articles.title: Polynomial growth
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a generating family of a group $G$, with growth function
$\gamma_P$. Then $P$ has polynomial growth if, for every natural number $n$, the ball of radius
$n$ (the set of elements of $G$ of word length at most $n$ with respect to $P$) is finite, and
there are natural numbers $C$ and $d$ such that $\gamma_P(n) \le C (n + 1)^d$ for every
natural number $n$.

articles.title: Growth rate of a $k$-element generating family (Kourovka 14.7)
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a group
and $S = (s_1, \dots, s_k)$ a family of $k$ elements generating $\Gamma$. For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ let
$\beta_S(n)$ be the number of elements of $\Gamma$ that are products of at most $n$ elements of
$S \cup S^{-1}$. The growth rate of $\Gamma$ with respect to $S$ is the real number
$\omega(\Gamma, S) = \limsup_{n \to \infty} \beta_S(n)^{1/n}$.

articles.title: Amenable groups with growth rate close to $2k - 1$ (Kourovka 15.4 refuted)
articles.statement:
For a group
$\Gamma$ generated by a family $S$ of $k$ elements and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\beta_S(n)$ be the
number of elements of $\Gamma$ that are products of at most $n$ elements of $S \cup S^{-1}$, and
let $\omega(\Gamma, S) = \limsup_{n \to \infty} \beta_S(n)^{1/n}$ be the growth rate. For every
$k \ge 2$ and every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there are an amenable group $\Gamma$ (amenability being
the Følner condition) and a family $S$ of $k$ distinct elements generating $\Gamma$ such that
$\omega(\Gamma, S) \ge 2k - 1 - \varepsilon$. Equivalently, there are no $k \ge 2$ and
$\varepsilon > 0$ such that every group generated by a family of $k$ distinct elements with growth
rate at least $2k - 1 - \varepsilon$ is non-amenable.

Arzhantseva, Guba and Guyot showed that for every $m \ge 2$, with $F_m$ the free group of rank
$m$, $R$ a normal subgroup of $F_m$ and $R'$ its commutator subgroup, the growth rate of $F_m/R'$
tends to $2m - 1$ as the shortest relation in $R$ gets longer, so $m$-generated amenable groups
(abelian-by-nilpotent ones, for instance) have growth rates arbitrarily close to $2m - 1$; the
Kourovka Archive answers 15.4 "No, it does not".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 15.4 (P. de la Harpe); resolution: G. N. Arzhantseva, V. S. Guba and L. Guyot, Growth rates of amenable groups, J. Group Theory 8 (2005), 389-394, arXiv:math/0406013, abstract and main result (the growth rate of an m-generated amenable group, already in the abelian-by-nilpotent and metabelian-by-finite classes, can be arbitrarily close to 2m - 1); Kourovka Archive, Problem 15.4 (answer: No, it does not), https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0406013.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 15.4 (large growth rate implies non-amenability)
articles.statement:
The proposition, asked
by P. de la Harpe, that there are $k \ge 2$ and a real $\varepsilon > 0$ such that every group
$\Gamma$ generated by a family $S$ of $k$ distinct elements whose growth rate satisfies
$\omega(\Gamma, S) \ge 2k - 1 - \varepsilon$ is non-amenable (amenability being the Følner
condition).

articles.title: Word-hyperbolic groups are finitely generated
articles.statement:
Every word-hyperbolic group is finitely
generated.

articles.title: Word-hyperbolic groups
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is word-hyperbolic if there are a finite index set
$\iota$ and a family $(s_i)_{i \in \iota}$ of elements generating $G$ such that $G$, equipped with
the word metric of this generating family, is $\delta$-hyperbolic for some real number $\delta$.

articles.title: The trivial group is word-hyperbolic
articles.statement:
Every trivial group is word-hyperbolic: the empty
family generates it, and its word metric is $0$-hyperbolic.

articles.title: Flexible Hamming distance
articles.statement:
Let $n \le m$ be natural numbers, $\sigma$ a permutation of
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and $\tau$ a permutation of $\{0, \dots, m-1\}$. The flexible Hamming distance
of $\sigma$ and $\tau$ is the real number

$$
d^{\mathrm{flex}}_n(\sigma, \tau) = \frac{\#\{i < n : \sigma(i) \ne \tau(i)\} + (m - n)}{n}.
$$

For $n = 0$ this quotient is taken to be $0$; this single value does not affect statements about
limits as $n \to \infty$.

## Sources

- Kourovka Notebook 21.84. The source is internally inconsistent about the argument order: it first defines the distance with the small permutation first, `d_n^flex(σ, τ)` for `σ ∈ S_n`, `τ ∈ S_m`, but later writes the convergence expression with `ρ_n(g)` first. This formalization follows the definition site (small first), which is also the type-correct order for the embedding `Fin n → Fin m`.

articles.title: Flexible permutation stability
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is flexibly permutation stable when every
almost-homomorphism $(f_n)$ from $G$ to the symmetric groups is flexibly close to homomorphisms.

articles.title: Almost-homomorphisms to symmetric groups
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group and, for each natural number
$n$, let $f_n \colon G \to S_n$ be an arbitrary map, where $S_n$ is the group of permutations of
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. The sequence $(f_n)$ is an almost-homomorphism when for all $g, h \in G$ the
normalized Hamming distance $d_n(f_n(g) f_n(h), f_n(gh))$ tends to $0$ as $n \to \infty$.

Following the source, no condition such as $f_n(1) = 1$ is imposed.

articles.title: Closeness to homomorphisms
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group and let $f_n \colon G \to S_n$
($n \in \mathbb{N}$) be maps into the symmetric groups $S_n$ of permutations of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$.
The sequence $(f_n)$ is close to homomorphisms when there are group homomorphisms
$\rho_n \colon G \to S_n$ such that for every $g \in G$ the normalized Hamming distance
$d_n(\rho_n(g), f_n(g))$ tends to $0$ as $n \to \infty$.

articles.title: Flexible closeness to homomorphisms
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group and let $f_n \colon G \to S_n$
($n \in \mathbb{N}$) be maps into the symmetric groups $S_n$ of permutations of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$.
The sequence $(f_n)$ is flexibly close to homomorphisms when there are natural numbers $m_n \ge n$
and group homomorphisms $\rho_n \colon G \to S_{m_n}$ such that for every $g \in G$ the flexible
Hamming distance $d^{\mathrm{flex}}_n(f_n(g), \rho_n(g))$ tends to $0$ as $n \to \infty$.

articles.title: Metabelian groups
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group and let $G' = [G, G]$ be its commutator subgroup.
Then $G$ is metabelian when its second derived subgroup $G'' = [G', G']$ is trivial.

articles.title: Normalized Hamming distance
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and permutations $\sigma$, $\tau$ of
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the normalized Hamming distance $d_n(\sigma, \tau)$ is the number of points
$i < n$ with $\sigma(i) \ne \tau(i)$, divided by $n$, as a real number. For $n = 0$ it is $0$;
this single value does not affect statements about limits as $n \to \infty$.

articles.title: Permutation stability
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is permutation stable when every
almost-homomorphism $(f_n)$ from $G$ to the symmetric groups $S_n$ is close to
homomorphisms.

articles.title: Non-elementary hyperbolic groups have infinite power quotients
articles.statement:
For every word-hyperbolic group
$G$ that is not virtually cyclic, there is an integer $n \ge 1$ such that the subgroup $G^n$
generated by the $n$-th powers of the elements of $G$ has infinite index in $G$, i.e. the quotient
$G / G^n$ is infinite.

This answers Kourovka Problem 11.74(a) ("Yes, it is"); the proof is due to Ivanov and Olshanskii.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.74 (A. Yu. Olshanskii); resolution: S. V. Ivanov and A. Yu. Olshanskii, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 348, no. 6 (1996), 2091-2138, Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.74: "a) Yes, it is; b) Yes, it is", https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 11.74(a) (infinite power quotients of hyperbolic groups)
articles.statement:
For every
word-hyperbolic group $G$ that is not virtually cyclic (non-elementary), there is an integer
$n \ge 1$ such that the subgroup $G^n$ generated by the $n$-th powers of the elements of $G$ has
infinite index in $G$, i.e. the quotient $G / G^n$ is infinite.

The problem is due to M. Gromov and A. Yu. Olshanskii.

articles.title: Power subgroup
articles.statement:
For a group $G$ and a natural number $n$, $G^n$ is the subgroup of $G$
generated by the $n$-th powers $g^n$ of all elements $g \in G$.

articles.title: Power subgroups of a non-elementary hyperbolic group intersect trivially
articles.statement:
For every
word-hyperbolic group $G$ that is not virtually cyclic, the only element of $G$ lying in the
subgroup $G^n$ generated by the $n$-th powers for every integer $n \ge 1$ is the identity, i.e.
$\bigcap_{n \ge 1} G^n = 1$.

This answers Kourovka Problem 11.74(b) ("Yes, it is"); the proof is due to Ivanov and Olshanskii.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.74 (A. Yu. Olshanskii); resolution: S. V. Ivanov and A. Yu. Olshanskii, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 348, no. 6 (1996), 2091-2138, Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.74: "a) Yes, it is; b) Yes, it is", https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 11.74(b) (trivial intersection of power subgroups)
articles.statement:
For every
word-hyperbolic group $G$ that is not virtually cyclic (non-elementary), the only element of $G$
lying in the subgroup $G^n$ generated by the $n$-th powers for every integer $n \ge 1$ is the
identity, i.e. $\bigcap_{n \ge 1} G^n = 1$.

The problem is due to A. Yu. Olshanskii.

articles.title: Involution of the real group ring
articles.statement:
For a group $G$, the involution of the real group ring
$\mathbb{R}G$ is the $\mathbb{R}$-linear map $\mathbb{R}G \to \mathbb{R}G$ that sends
$\sum_{g \in G} a_g g$ to $\sum_{g \in G} a_g g^{-1}$, that is, the linear extension of inversion
on $G$.

articles.title: Laplacian of a finite subset of a group
articles.statement:
For a group $G$ and a finite subset
$S \subseteq G$, the Laplacian of $S$ is the element $\Delta_S = |S| - \sum_{s \in S} s$ of the
real group ring $\mathbb{R}G$, where $|S|$ is the number of elements of $S$, taken as $|S|$ times
the identity element of $\mathbb{R}G$. When $S$ is a symmetric generating set of $G$, this is the
Laplacian of Equation (1) in the paper of Kaluba, Kielak and Nowak on property (T) for
$\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)$ and $\operatorname{SL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$.

articles.title: Property (T)
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group. For a finite subset $S \subseteq G$, write
$\Delta_S = |S| - \sum_{s \in S} s$ for the Laplacian of $S$ in the real group ring $\mathbb{R}G$,
and write $\xi \mapsto \xi^{\star}$ for the involution of $\mathbb{R}G$ that extends inversion on
$G$ linearly. The group $G$ has Kazhdan's property (T) when there exist a finite subset
$S \subseteq G$ with $S^{-1} = S$ that generates $G$, a real number $\lambda > 0$, and a finite set
$\Xi$ of elements of $\mathbb{R}G$ such that
$\Delta_S^2 - \lambda \Delta_S = \sum_{\xi \in \Xi} \xi^{\star} \xi$.

This is Ozawa's characterization of property (T) for finitely generated groups, used as the
definition in Equation (2) of Kaluba, Kielak and Nowak.

articles.title: Property (T) for automorphism groups of free groups of rank at least 6
articles.statement:
For every natural
number $n \ge 6$, the automorphism group $\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)$ of the free group $F_n$ on $n$
generators has property (T).

## Sources

- M. Kaluba, D. Kielak, and P. W. Nowak, `On property (T) for Aut(F_n) and SL_n(Z)`, Annals of Math, 193 (2) 2021. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_on_property_t` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Not every group is sofic
articles.statement:
The soficity problem (Kourovka Notebook Problem 21.86) has a
negative answer: there exists a group that is not sofic.

OpenAI announced the first example, the unit group of the binary Leavitt algebra. G. Kun and
A. Thom (Theorems A and E) prove that $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}) \wr_{G/\Gamma} G$ and
$G *_\Gamma G$ are not sofic for explicit residually finite Kazhdan pairs $\Gamma < G$. The
Kourovka Notebook (arXiv:1401.0300v49) marks Problem 21.86 solved.

## Sources

- G. Kun and A. Thom, Nonsofic wreath products of residually finite groups, arXiv:2608.06222 (2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06222; OpenAI, A counterexample to the soficity conjecture, in Ten advances in mathematics and theoretical computer science, Chapter 3, 2026, https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/ten-proofs-oai.pdf; E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (20 October 2026), Problem 21.86, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Soficity problem (Kourovka Notebook Problem 21.86)
articles.statement:
The statement that every group $G$ is
sofic [KOU-21.86].

articles.title: Sofic groups
articles.statement:
Let $d$ denote the normalized Hamming distance on permutations. A group
$G$ is sofic if for every finite subset $F \subseteq G$ with $1 \in F$ and every real
$\varepsilon > 0$ there are an integer $n \ge 1$ and a map $\varphi$ from $F$ to the permutations
of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ such that $\varphi(1)$ is the identity,
$d(\varphi(gh), \varphi(g)\varphi(h)) < \varepsilon$ for all $g, h \in F$ with $gh \in F$, and
$\varphi(g)$ has no fixed point for every $g \in F$ with $g \ne 1$ [KOU-21.86].

articles.title: Hamming distance for sofic approximations
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and permutations
$\sigma$, $\tau$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the normalized Hamming distance $d(\sigma, \tau)$ is the
number of points $i < n$ with $\sigma(i) \ne \tau(i)$, divided by $n$, as a real number; for
$n = 0$ it is $0$. It is used in the definition of sofic groups [KOU-21.86].

articles.title: Augmentation right ideal of a subset
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group, $S \subseteq G$ a subset and
$\mathbb{Z}G$ the integral group ring of $G$. This is the right ideal of $\mathbb{Z}G$ generated by
the elements $g - 1$ with $g \in S$, regarded as a right $\mathbb{Z}G$-submodule of
$\mathbb{Z}G$.

articles.title: Augmentation ideal of the integral group ring
articles.statement:
For a group $G$, the augmentation ideal
$\Delta(G)$ of the integral group ring $\mathbb{Z}G$ is the $\mathbb{Z}$-submodule spanned by the
elements $g - 1$ for $g \in G$. It is the kernel of the augmentation map
$\mathbb{Z}G \to \mathbb{Z}$, $\sum_g a_g g \mapsto \sum_g a_g$.

articles.title: Dimension quotients need not be central
articles.statement:
There exist a group $G$, an integer $n \ge 1$, an
element $x$ of the $n$-th dimension subgroup $D_n(G)$ and an element $g \in G$ such that the
commutator $x g x^{-1} g^{-1}$ does not lie in $\gamma_n(G)$, the $n$-th term of the lower central
series of $G$ (indexed so that $\gamma_1(G) = G$). That is, the answer to Kourovka Problem 12.22(a)
is negative: the image of $D_n(G)$ in $G/\gamma_n(G)$ need not be central.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 12.22 (N. D. Gupta, Yu. V. Kuz'min); resolution: N. D. Gupta and Yu. V. Kuz'min, J. Pure Appl. Algebra 104, no. 1 (1995), 191-197 (part a); L. Bartholdi and R. Mikhailov, J. Topology 16, no. 2 (2023), 822-853 (part b), Kourovka Archive, Problem 12.22: "a) No, not always; moreover, `D_n(G)/γ_n(G)` need not be contained in any term of the upper central series of `G/γ_n(G)` with fixed number" and "b) No, not always", https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Gupta–Kuz'min centrality question (Kourovka 12.22(a))
articles.statement:
The statement that for every group
$G$, every $n \ge 1$, every element $x$ of the $n$-th dimension subgroup $D_n(G)$ and every
$g \in G$, the commutator $x g x^{-1} g^{-1}$ lies in $\gamma_n(G)$, the $n$-th term of the lower
central series of $G$, indexed so that $\gamma_1(G) = G$ and
$\gamma_{k+1}(G) = [\gamma_k(G), G]$. Equivalently, the image of $D_n(G)$ in $G/\gamma_n(G)$ is
central.

articles.title: Dimension quotients need not have exponent dividing 2
articles.statement:
There exist a group $G$, an integer
$n \ge 1$ and an element $x$ of the $n$-th dimension subgroup $D_n(G)$ such that $x^2$ does not lie
in $\gamma_n(G)$, the $n$-th term of the lower central series of $G$ (indexed so that
$\gamma_1(G) = G$). That is, the answer to Kourovka Problem 12.22(b) is negative: the image of
$D_n(G)$ in $G/\gamma_n(G)$ need not have exponent dividing $2$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 12.22 (N. D. Gupta, Yu. V. Kuz'min); resolution: N. D. Gupta and Yu. V. Kuz'min, J. Pure Appl. Algebra 104, no. 1 (1995), 191-197 (part a); L. Bartholdi and R. Mikhailov, J. Topology 16, no. 2 (2023), 822-853 (part b), Kourovka Archive, Problem 12.22: "a) No, not always; moreover, `D_n(G)/γ_n(G)` need not be contained in any term of the upper central series of `G/γ_n(G)` with fixed number" and "b) No, not always", https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Gupta–Kuz'min exponent question (Kourovka 12.22(b))
articles.statement:
The statement that for every group
$G$, every $n \ge 1$ and every element $x$ of the $n$-th dimension subgroup $D_n(G)$, the square
$x^2$ lies in $\gamma_n(G)$, the $n$-th term of the lower central series of $G$, indexed so that
$\gamma_1(G) = G$ and $\gamma_{k+1}(G) = [\gamma_k(G), G]$. Equivalently, the image of $D_n(G)$ in
$G/\gamma_n(G)$ has exponent dividing $2$.

articles.title: Dimension subgroups
articles.statement:
Let $\Delta(G)$ be the augmentation ideal of the integral group ring
$\mathbb{Z}G$ of a group $G$, and for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ let $\Delta(G)^n$ be its $n$-th power, the
$\mathbb{Z}$-span of all products of $n$ elements of $\Delta(G)$. An element $g \in G$ lies in the
$n$-th dimension subgroup $D_n(G) = G \cap (1 + \Delta(G)^n)$ when $g - 1 \in \Delta(G)^n$.

articles.title: Subfields containing all group-ring powers have infinitely many invariants
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a
prime, $F$ an infinite field of characteristic $p$, $G$ a finite group of ring automorphisms of
$F$, and $\xi = \sum_{g \in G} \xi_g \, g$ an element of the group ring $\mathbb{Z}G$ with
$\xi \notin p\mathbb{Z}G$, that is, with some integer coefficient $\xi_g$ not divisible by $p$.
For nonzero $x \in F$ put $x^\xi = \prod_{g \in G} g(x)^{\xi_g}$. If a subfield $K$ of $F$
contains $x^\xi$ for every nonzero $x \in F$, then $K$ contains infinitely many elements $y$ with
$g(y) = y$ for all $g \in G$. This is the positive answer to Kourovka Notebook Problem 11.79,
given by K. N. Ponomarëv (1992).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.79 (K. N. Ponomarëv); resolution: K. N. Ponomarëv, Siberian Math. J. 33 (1992), 1094-1099, Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.79: "Yes", https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Group-ring powers and invariant elements (Kourovka 11.79)
articles.statement:
The proposition that the
following holds for every prime $p$, every infinite field $F$ of characteristic $p$, every finite
group $G$ of ring automorphisms of $F$, and every element $\xi = \sum_{g \in G} \xi_g \, g$ of the
group ring $\mathbb{Z}G$ with $\xi \notin p\mathbb{Z}G$, that is, with some integer coefficient
$\xi_g$ not divisible by $p$. For nonzero $x \in F$ put $x^\xi = \prod_{g \in G} g(x)^{\xi_g}$.
If a subfield $K$ of $F$ contains $x^\xi$ for every nonzero $x \in F$, then $K$ contains
infinitely many elements $y$ with $g(y) = y$ for all $g \in G$.

articles.title: Underlying bijection of the inversion twist
articles.statement:
For every type $A$, the map sending an
element of the inversion twist of $A$ to its underlying element of $A$ is a bijection, whose
inverse sends $a \in A$ to its copy in the twist.

articles.title: Group-ring inversion is an involution
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $G$ a commutative
group and $\iota$ the inversion of the group ring $R[G]$. For every $x \in R[G]$,
$\iota(\iota(x)) = x$.

articles.title: Inversion on basis elements
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $G$ a commutative group.
For every $g \in G$ and $r \in R$, the inversion of the group ring $R[G]$ sends $r\, g$ to
$r\, g^{-1}$.

articles.title: Inversion twist of a group-ring module
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $G$ a commutative
group and $A$ a module over the group ring $R[G]$. The inversion twist of $A$ is a copy of $A$
with the same addition, on which $r \in R[G]$ acts by $a \mapsto \iota(r) \cdot a$, where $\iota$
is the inversion of $R[G]$ and $\cdot$ is the original action on $A$.

As a bare type, the inversion twist of any type $A$ is a copy of $A$; the addition and the
action above are defined when $A$ is an $R[G]$-module.

articles.title: Inversion on a group ring
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $G$ a commutative group.
The inversion of the group ring $R[G]$ is the ring automorphism of $R[G]$ induced by the group
automorphism $g \mapsto g^{-1}$ of $G$: it sends $\sum_g r_g\, g$ to $\sum_g r_g\, g^{-1}$.

articles.title: Twisting twice by inversion recovers the module
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $G$ a
commutative group and $A$ a module over the group ring $R[G]$. The map sending an element of the
inversion twist of the inversion twist of $A$ to its underlying element of $A$ is an
$R[G]$-linear isomorphism.

articles.title: Scalar action on the inversion twist
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $G$ a commutative
group and $A$ a module over the group ring $R[G]$. For every $r \in R[G]$ and every element $a$
of the inversion twist of $A$, with underlying element $\bar a \in A$, the underlying element of
$r \cdot a$ is $\iota(r) \cdot \bar a$, where $\iota$ is the inversion of $R[G]$ and $\cdot$ on
the right is the original action on $A$.

articles.title: Finitely many $2$-groups have MJD but not AJD
articles.statement:
There is a natural number $B$ such that every
finite $2$-group $G$ whose integral group ring $\mathbb{Z}[G]$ has the multiplicative Jordan
decomposition property (MJD) but not the additive Jordan decomposition property (AJD) has order
at most $B$. In particular, only finitely many isomorphism classes of finite $2$-groups have MJD
but not AJD, which answers Kourovka Problem 16.104 in the affirmative.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 16.104 (A. W. Hales, I. B. S. Passi); resolution: A. W. Hales, I. B. S. Passi and L. E. Wilson, The multiplicative Jordan decomposition in group rings, II, J. Algebra 316 (2007), no. 1, 109-132; corrigendum, J. Algebra 371 (2012), 665-666, Kourovka Archive, Problem 16.104 (answer: Yes, it is true).

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 16.104
articles.statement:
The proposition that there is a natural number $B$ such that
every finite $2$-group $G$ whose integral group ring $\mathbb{Z}[G]$ has the multiplicative Jordan
decomposition property (MJD) but not the additive Jordan decomposition property (AJD) has order
at most $B$.

A. W. Hales and I. B. S. Passi asked whether only finitely many isomorphism classes of finite
$2$-groups $G$ have MJD but not AJD for $\mathbb{Z}[G]$; a bound on the orders is equivalent.

articles.title: Additive Jordan decomposition property
articles.statement:
For a group $G$, let $\mathbb{Z}[G]$ be the set
of elements of the rational group algebra $\mathbb{Q}[G]$ all of whose coefficients are integers.
Then $\mathbb{Z}[G]$ has the additive Jordan decomposition property (AJD) when, for all
$a, s, n \in \mathbb{Q}[G]$ such that $a \in \mathbb{Z}[G]$, $a = s + n$, $sn = ns$, $n$ is
nilpotent and the minimal polynomial of $s$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ is squarefree, both $s$ and $n$ lie
in $\mathbb{Z}[G]$.

For finite $G$ every $a \in \mathbb{Q}[G]$ has exactly one such decomposition $a = s + n$, its
Jordan decomposition, so AJD says that the semisimple and nilpotent parts of every
$a \in \mathbb{Z}[G]$ lie in $\mathbb{Z}[G]$.

articles.title: Elements with integer coefficients
articles.statement:
An element $x$ of the monoid algebra $\mathbb{Q}[G]$
lies in $\mathbb{Z}[G]$ when all its coefficients are integers: for every $g \in G$, the
coefficient of $x$ at $g$ is an integer.

articles.title: Multiplicative Jordan decomposition property
articles.statement:
For a group $G$, let $\mathbb{Z}[G]$ be
the set of elements of the rational group algebra $\mathbb{Q}[G]$ all of whose coefficients are
integers. Then $\mathbb{Z}[G]$ has the multiplicative Jordan decomposition property (MJD) when,
for all $a, b, s, u \in \mathbb{Q}[G]$ such that $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}[G]$, $ab = ba = 1$,
