$a = su$, $su = us$, $u - 1$ is nilpotent and the minimal polynomial of $s$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ is
squarefree, both $s$ and $u$ lie in $\mathbb{Z}[G]$.

Equivalently, for every unit $a$ of $\mathbb{Z}[G]$ and every factorization $a = su$ in
$\mathbb{Q}[G]$ into commuting factors with $s$ semisimple over $\mathbb{Q}$ and $u$ unipotent,
both factors lie in $\mathbb{Z}[G]$; for finite $G$ such a factorization exists and is unique.

articles.title: First free generator of Gardam's presentation
articles.statement:
$a$ is the generator $a$, viewed as an
element of the free group on the two generators $a$ and $b$.

articles.title: Second free generator of Gardam's presentation
articles.statement:
$b$ is the generator $b$, viewed as an
element of the free group on the two generators $a$ and $b$.

articles.title: Generators of Gardam's presentation
articles.statement:
This is the two-element set consisting of the
distinct formal symbols $a$ and $b$, which serve as the generators of the group presentation in
Theorem A of Gardam's counterexample to the unit conjecture.

articles.title: Gardam's element p
articles.statement:
In the group ring $\mathbb{F}_2[P]$ of Gardam's group $P$ with
generators $a$ and $b$, let $x = a^2$, $y = b^2$ and $z = (ab)^2$ in $P$, viewed as elements of
$\mathbb{F}_2[P]$. Then $p$ is the element $(1 + x)(1 + y)(1 + z^{-1})$ of $\mathbb{F}_2[P]$.

articles.title: Gardam's group
articles.statement:
$P$ is the group with generators $a$ and $b$ and relators
$b^{-1}a^2ba^2$ and $a^{-1}b^2ab^2$, that is,
$P = \langle a, b \mid b^{-1}a^2b = a^{-2}, a^{-1}b^2a = b^{-2} \rangle$.

This is the group of Theorem A of Gardam's counterexample to the unit conjecture.

articles.title: Gardam's element q
articles.statement:
In the group ring $\mathbb{F}_2[P]$ of Gardam's group $P$ with
generators $a$ and $b$, let $x = a^2$, $y = b^2$ and $z = (ab)^2$ in $P$, viewed as elements of
$\mathbb{F}_2[P]$. Then $q$ is the element $x^{-1}y^{-1} + x + y^{-1}z + z$ of $\mathbb{F}_2[P]$.

articles.title: Gardam's element r
articles.statement:
In the group ring $\mathbb{F}_2[P]$ of Gardam's group $P$ with
generators $a$ and $b$, let $x = a^2$, $y = b^2$ and $z = (ab)^2$ in $P$, viewed as elements of
$\mathbb{F}_2[P]$. Then $r$ is the element $1 + x + y^{-1}z + xyz$ of $\mathbb{F}_2[P]$.

articles.title: Group ring of Gardam's group over the field with two elements
articles.statement:
$\mathbb{F}_2[P]$ is the
group ring of Gardam's group $P$ over the field $\mathbb{F}_2 = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$.

articles.title: Relators of Gardam's group
articles.statement:
In the free group on the generators $a$ and $b$, the relators
are the two elements $b^{-1}a^2ba^2$ and $a^{-1}b^2ab^2$.

Imposing them gives the relations $b^{-1}a^2b = a^{-2}$ and $a^{-1}b^2a = b^{-2}$ of Theorem A of
Gardam's counterexample to the unit conjecture.

articles.title: Gardam's element s
articles.statement:
In the group ring $\mathbb{F}_2[P]$ of Gardam's group $P$ with
generators $a$ and $b$, let $x = a^2$, $y = b^2$ and $z = (ab)^2$ in $P$, viewed as elements of
$\mathbb{F}_2[P]$. Then $s$ is the element $1 + (x + x^{-1} + y + y^{-1})z^{-1}$ of
$\mathbb{F}_2[P]$.

articles.title: Gardam's counterexample to the unit conjecture
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be the group with presentation
$\langle a, b \mid b^{-1}a^2b = a^{-2},\ a^{-1}b^2a = b^{-2} \rangle$, and set $x = a^2$,
$y = b^2$ and $z = (ab)^2$. In the group ring $\mathbb{F}_2[P]$ set
$p = (1 + x)(1 + y)(1 + z^{-1})$, $q = x^{-1}y^{-1} + x + y^{-1}z + z$,
$r = 1 + x + y^{-1}z + xyz$ and $s = 1 + (x + x^{-1} + y + y^{-1})z^{-1}$, and let
$u = p + qa + rb + sab$. Then $P$ is torsion-free (if $g \in P$ and $g^n = 1$ for some
natural number $n \neq 0$, then $g = 1$), $u$ is a unit of $\mathbb{F}_2[P]$, and $u$ is not
equal to any element $g$ of $P$ viewed in $\mathbb{F}_2[P]$; that is, $u$ is a non-trivial unit.

## Sources

- G. Gardam, `A counterexample to the unit conjecture for group rings`, Annals of Math, 194 (3) 2021. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_unit_conjecture` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Gardam's unit
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be the group with presentation
$\langle a, b \mid b^{-1}a^2b = a^{-2},\ a^{-1}b^2a = b^{-2} \rangle$ and set $x = a^2$,
$y = b^2$, $z = (ab)^2$. In the group ring $\mathbb{F}_2[P]$, $u = p + qa + rb + sab$, where
$p = (1 + x)(1 + y)(1 + z^{-1})$, $q = x^{-1}y^{-1} + x + y^{-1}z + z$,
$r = 1 + x + y^{-1}z + xyz$ and $s = 1 + (x + x^{-1} + y + y^{-1})z^{-1}$.

articles.title: The element x of Gardam's group
articles.statement:
In the group $P$ with presentation
$\langle a, b \mid b^{-1}a^2b = a^{-2},\ a^{-1}b^2a = b^{-2} \rangle$, $x = a^2$.

articles.title: The element y of Gardam's group
articles.statement:
In the group $P$ with presentation
$\langle a, b \mid b^{-1}a^2b = a^{-2},\ a^{-1}b^2a = b^{-2} \rangle$, $y = b^2$.

articles.title: The element z of Gardam's group
articles.statement:
In the group $P$ with presentation
$\langle a, b \mid b^{-1}a^2b = a^{-2},\ a^{-1}b^2a = b^{-2} \rangle$, $z = (ab)^2$.

articles.title: Non-zero-divisor
articles.statement:
An element $s$ of a ring $R$ is a non-zero-divisor when it is neither a
left nor a right zero divisor: for every $z \in R$, $zs = 0$ implies $z = 0$ and $sz = 0$ implies
$z = 0$.

articles.title: Right Ore ring
articles.statement:
A ring $R$ satisfies the right Ore condition for its non-zero-divisors, so
that it has a classical right ring of quotients, when for all $s, t \in R$ with $s$ a
non-zero-divisor there are $x, y \in R$ with $x$ a non-zero-divisor and $sy = tx$.

For group algebras the left and right conditions agree.

articles.title: Lamplighter group algebras are not Ore
articles.statement:
For every field $k$ and every prime $p$, the group
algebra $k[\mathbb{Z}/p \wr \mathbb{Z}]$ of the lamplighter group $\mathbb{Z}/p \wr \mathbb{Z}$
does not satisfy the right Ore condition for its non-zero-divisors: there are $s$ and $t$ in it,
with $s$ a non-zero-divisor, such that $sy = tx$ holds for no $x$ and $y$ with $x$ a
non-zero-divisor.

Resolved false: Linnell, Lück and Schick (Theorem 3, with W. Dicks's argument) prove that $kG$ is
not an Ore ring for every field $k$ and every group $G$ containing $H \wr \mathbb{Z}$ with
$H \ne 1$ finite, in particular for $G = \mathbb{Z}/p \wr \mathbb{Z}$ and every prime $p$; the
Kourovka Archive answers 12.47 "No, it does not".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 12.47 (P. A. Linnell); resolution: P. A. Linnell, W. Lück and T. Schick, The Ore condition, affiliated operators, and the lamplighter group, in: High-dimensional manifold topology (Trieste, 2001), World Scientific, 2003, 315-321, Theorem 3: kG is not an Ore ring for every field k and every group G containing H ≀ ℤ with H ≠ 1 finite; Kourovka Archive, Problem 12.47, http://him-lueck.uni-bonn.de/data/lamplighter.pdf.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 12.47: some lamplighter group algebra is Ore
articles.statement:
There are a field $k$ and a
prime $p$ such that the group algebra $k[\mathbb{Z}/p \wr \mathbb{Z}]$ of the lamplighter group
$\mathbb{Z}/p \wr \mathbb{Z}$ satisfies the right Ore condition for its non-zero-divisors, that
is, has a classical right ring of quotients.

Kourovka 12.47 (P. A. Linnell) asks this for a given field and prime; the existential form makes
its refutation cover every field and every prime.

articles.title: Lamplighter group
articles.statement:
For a natural number $p$, the lamplighter group
$\mathbb{Z}/p \wr \mathbb{Z}$ is the semidirect product
$\left(\bigoplus_{i \in \mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Z}/p\right) \rtimes \mathbb{Z}$, in which
$n \in \mathbb{Z}$ acts on the base group by the $n$-th power of the shift
$f \mapsto f(\cdot - 1)$.

articles.title: Shift of the lamplighter base group
articles.statement:
For a natural number $p$, the shift is the
automorphism $f \mapsto f(\cdot - 1)$ of the base group $\bigoplus_{i \in \mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Z}/p$,
the additive group of finitely supported functions $\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}/p$, viewed as a
multiplicative group.

articles.title: Almost polycyclic group
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is almost polycyclic (polycyclic-by-finite) if it
has a subgroup of finite index that is polycyclic.

articles.title: Polycyclic group
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is polycyclic if for some $n \ge 0$ there are subgroups
$1 = H_0 \le H_1 \le \cdots \le H_n = G$ such that for each $i < n$, $H_i$ is normal in
$H_{i+1}$ and the quotient $H_{i+1} / H_i$ is cyclic.

articles.title: Artamonov's freeness question has a negative answer
articles.statement:
It is not the case that for every
commutative ring $k$, every torsion-free almost polycyclic group $G$ (no element $g \ne 1$ of $G$
has finite order) and every finitely generated projective module $P$ over the group ring $kG$
containing two elements that are linearly independent over $kG$, the module $P$ is free over $kG$.

Jayadevan's counterexample takes $k = \mathbb{F}_2 \times \mathbb{F}_2$ and the trivial group $G$,
so that $kG = k$; then $P = k^2 \oplus (\mathbb{F}_2 \times 0)$ is a finitely generated projective
$k$-module containing an independent pair, but $|P| = 32$ is not a power of $4 = |k|$, so $P$ is
not free. The Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 11.5 solved, "No, not always" (AI solution
confirmed by D. Segal); the example gives nothing for field coefficients.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 11.5 (V. A. Artamonov); resolution: A. Jayadevan, A coefficient-ring obstruction to freeness of projective group-ring modules, preprint, Zenodo record 22846603 (2026), main example: `k = 𝔽₂ × 𝔽₂`, `G = 1`, `P = k² ⊕ (𝔽₂ × 0)` is projective with an independent pair but has 32 elements, while finite free `k`-modules have `4ⁿ`; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 11.5 solved (AI solution confirmed by D. Segal), https://zenodo.org/records/22846603.

articles.title: Artamonov's freeness question (Kourovka 11.5)
articles.statement:
This is the proposition that, for every
commutative ring $k$, every torsion-free almost polycyclic group $G$ (no element $g \ne 1$ of $G$
has finite order) and every finitely generated projective module $P$ over the group ring $kG$, if
$P$ contains two elements that are linearly independent over $kG$, then $P$ is a free
$kG$-module.

articles.title: Twisting automorphism of the free group algebra
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be the free group on $x, y$, let
$\mathbb{C}F$ be its complex group algebra, and for nonzero complex numbers $a, b$ let $\chi$ be the
character of $F$ with $\chi(x) = a$ and $\chi(y) = b$. The map $\vartheta_{a,b}$ sends
$\alpha = \sum_{g \in F} c_g\, g \in \mathbb{C}F$ to $\sum_{g \in F} \chi(g)\, c_g\, g$.

Since $\chi$ is a homomorphism, $\vartheta_{a,b}$ is the algebra automorphism of $\mathbb{C}F$ with
$\vartheta_{a,b}(x) = a x$ and $\vartheta_{a,b}(y) = b y$.

articles.title: Twisting character of the free group of rank two
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be the free group on $x, y$. For
nonzero complex numbers $a, b$, this is the homomorphism $\chi \colon F \to \mathbb{C}^\times$ with
$\chi(x) = a$ and $\chi(y) = b$.

articles.title: Linnell's twisted right ideal question has a negative answer (Kourovka 12.46)
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be the
free group on $x, y$, let $\mathbb{C}F$ be its complex group algebra, and for nonzero complex
numbers $a, b$ let $\vartheta_{a,b}$ be the twisting automorphism of $\mathbb{C}F$ with
$\vartheta_{a,b}(x) = a x$ and $\vartheta_{a,b}(y) = b y$. There is a nonzero
$\alpha \in \mathbb{C}F$ such that for all complex numbers $a, b \neq 1$ with $|a| = |b| = 1$
the right ideals $\alpha\,\mathbb{C}F$ and $\vartheta_{a,b}(\alpha)\,\mathbb{C}F$ intersect only in
$0$: whenever $\beta, \gamma \in \mathbb{C}F$ satisfy $\alpha\beta = \vartheta_{a,b}(\alpha)\gamma$,
then $\alpha\beta = 0$.

The Kourovka Archive answers 12.46 "No, not always" (A. V. Tushev, 1995).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 12.46 (P. A. Linnell); resolution: A. V. Tushev, Ukrain. Mat. Zh. 47 (1995), no. 4, 571-572, Kourovka Archive, Problem 12.46: No, not always.

articles.title: Linnell's twisted right ideal question (Kourovka 12.46)
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be the free group on
$x, y$, let $\mathbb{C}F$ be its complex group algebra, and for nonzero complex numbers $a, b$ let
$\vartheta_{a,b}$ be the twisting automorphism of $\mathbb{C}F$ with $\vartheta_{a,b}(x) = a x$ and
$\vartheta_{a,b}(y) = b y$. The assertion is that for every nonzero $\alpha \in \mathbb{C}F$ there
are complex numbers $a, b \neq 1$ with $|a| = |b| = 1$ such that the right ideals
$\alpha\,\mathbb{C}F$ and $\vartheta_{a,b}(\alpha)\,\mathbb{C}F$ intersect nontrivially, that is,
$\alpha\beta = \vartheta_{a,b}(\alpha)\gamma \neq 0$ for some $\beta, \gamma \in \mathbb{C}F$.

articles.title: No exotic units in the integral group ring of $C_2 \times C_2 \times C_2 \times C_6$
articles.statement:
Let
$G = C_2 \times C_2 \times C_2 \times C_6$. Every unit $u$ of the integral group ring
$\mathbb{Z}G$ is trivial: $u = g$ or $u = -g$ for some $g \in G$.

Classical: G. Higman (1940) showed the integral group ring of an abelian group
of exponent dividing 4 or 6 has only the units $\pm g$. Via the cut-group criterion in Bächle
(arXiv:1701.04347, Prop. 2.2), $C_2^3 \times C_6$ (exponent 6) is an abelian cut group, so every
unit of $\mathbb{Z}G$ is trivial and no exotic unit exists.

## Sources

- Andreas Bächle, Integral group rings of solvable groups with trivial central units, Forum Math. 30 (2018), arXiv:1701.04347, https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.04347.

articles.title: Exotic unit conjecture for $C_2 \times C_2 \times C_2 \times C_6$
articles.statement:
Let
$G = C_2 \times C_2 \times C_2 \times C_6$. The statement that the integral group ring
$\mathbb{Z}G$ contains an exotic unit: a unit $u$ with $u \ne g$ and $u \ne -g$ for every
$g \in G$.

## Sources

- the open question of `OWR-11129-005` (Computational Group Theory (2012), Oberwolfach Reports, DOI 10.4171/owr/2011/37).

articles.title: The integral group ring of $C_2 \times C_2 \times C_2 \times C_6$
articles.statement:
The integral group
ring $\mathbb{Z}G$ of $G = C_2 \times C_2 \times C_2 \times C_6$: finitely supported formal
$\mathbb{Z}$-linear combinations of elements of $G$, with the product extending the group
operation of $G$ bilinearly.

## Sources

- `OWR-11129-005` (Computational Group Theory (2012), Oberwolfach Reports, DOI 10.4171/owr/2011/37).

articles.title: The group $C_2 \times C_2 \times C_2 \times C_6$
articles.statement:
The abelian group
$G = C_2 \times C_2 \times C_2 \times C_6$, the product of cyclic groups of orders $2$, $2$, $2$
and $6$, written additively as
$\mathbb{Z}/2 \times \mathbb{Z}/2 \times \mathbb{Z}/2 \times \mathbb{Z}/6$.

## Sources

- `OWR-11129-005` (Computational Group Theory (2012), Oberwolfach Reports, DOI 10.4171/owr/2011/37).

articles.title: Counterexample to the first Zassenhaus conjecture (Kourovka 17.67)
articles.statement:
There exist a finite
group $G$ and a unit $u$ of finite order of the integral group ring $\mathbb{Z}G$ such that for
every unit $v$ of the rational group ring $\mathbb{Q}G$, every $g \in G$ and every sign
$\varepsilon \in \{1, -1\}$, the conjugate $v u v^{-1}$, computed in $\mathbb{Q}G$, is not equal
to $\varepsilon g$. That is, the first Zassenhaus conjecture is false.

Eisele and Margolis (abstract and Theorem A) give a metabelian group $G$ of order
$2^7 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5 \cdot 7^2 \cdot 19^2$ and a unit of order $7 \cdot 19$ in $\mathbb{Z}G$
that is not conjugate in $\mathbb{Q}G$ to any element $\pm g$, $g \in G$; the Kourovka Archive
records for 17.67 "A counterexample was constructed".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 17.67 (V. D. Mazurov); resolution: F. Eisele and L. Margolis, A counterexample to the first Zassenhaus conjecture, Adv. Math. 339 (2018), 599-641, abstract and Theorem A (a metabelian group of order 2⁷·3²·5·7²·19² whose integral group ring contains a unit of order 7·19 not conjugate in the rational group algebra to any ±g); Kourovka Archive, Problem 17.67 (A counterexample was constructed), http://eprints.gla.ac.uk/177223/7/177223.pdf.

articles.title: Zassenhaus conjecture on torsion units
articles.statement:
Kourovka 17.67 (H. Zassenhaus's conjecture, recorded by V. D. Mazurov): every unit of finite
order of the integral group ring `ℤG` of a finite group `G` is conjugate, by a unit of the rational
group ring `ℚG`, to an element `±g` with `g ∈ G`.

articles.title: Diagonalizing elements of $\mathrm{SL}_2(F)$ with distinct eigenvalues
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a field,
let $s \in F$ with $s \ne s^{-1}$, and let $M \in \mathrm{SL}_2(F)$ have eigenvalues $s$ and
$s^{-1}$, that is, characteristic polynomial $(X - s)(X - s^{-1})$. Then there is
$P \in \mathrm{SL}_2(F)$ such that the matrix $P M P^{-1}$ equals the diagonal matrix
$\operatorname{diag}(s, s^{-1})$.

articles.title: Distinct eigenvalues give conjugacy to $\operatorname{diag}(s, s^{-1})$ in $\mathrm{SL}_2(F)$
articles.statement:
**Distinct eigenvalues give conjugacy to $\operatorname{diag}(s, s^{-1})$ in
$\mathrm{SL}_2(F)$.** Let $F$ be a field and let $s \in F$ with $s \ne s^{-1}$ and $s \ne 0$. If
$M \in \mathrm{SL}_2(F)$ has eigenvalues $s$ and $s^{-1}$, that is, characteristic polynomial
$(X - s)(X - s^{-1})$, then $M$ is conjugate in $\mathrm{SL}_2(F)$ to the diagonal matrix
$\operatorname{diag}(s, s^{-1})$.

The proof builds the conjugating matrix from eigenvectors for $s$ and $s^{-1}$: distinct
eigenvalues give linearly independent eigenvectors, so the matrix of eigenvectors has nonzero
determinant, and rescaling its first column makes the determinant $1$.

articles.title: Elements of $\mathrm{SL}_2(F)$ with eigenvalues $s$ and $s^{-1}$
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a field and
let $s \in F$. A matrix $M \in \mathrm{SL}_2(F)$ has eigenvalues $s$ and $s^{-1}$ if its
characteristic polynomial is $(X - s)(X - s^{-1})$.

articles.title: Conjugacy to $\operatorname{diag}(s, s^{-1})$ in terms of a conjugator
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a field,
let $s \in F$ with $s \ne 0$, and let $M \in \mathrm{SL}_2(F)$. Then $M$ is conjugate in
$\mathrm{SL}_2(F)$ to the diagonal matrix $\operatorname{diag}(s, s^{-1})$ if and only if there is
$P \in \mathrm{SL}_2(F)$ such that the matrix $P M P^{-1}$ equals
$\operatorname{diag}(s, s^{-1})$.

articles.title: Matrices with the same distinct eigenvalues lie in the same normal subgroups of $\mathrm{SL}_2(F)$
articles.statement:
**Matrices with the same distinct eigenvalues lie in the same normal subgroups of
$\mathrm{SL}_2(F)$.** Let $F$ be a field, let $N$ be a normal subgroup of $\mathrm{SL}_2(F)$, and
let $s \in F$ with $s \ne s^{-1}$. If $N$ contains a matrix with eigenvalues $s$ and $s^{-1}$, then
$N$ contains every matrix in $\mathrm{SL}_2(F)$ with eigenvalues $s$ and $s^{-1}$.

articles.title: Conjugates of $\operatorname{diag}(s, s^{-1})$ lie in the same normal subgroups of $\mathrm{SL}_2(F)$
articles.statement:
**Conjugates of $\operatorname{diag}(s, s^{-1})$ lie in the same normal subgroups of
$\mathrm{SL}_2(F)$.** Let $F$ be a field, let $N$ be a normal subgroup of $\mathrm{SL}_2(F)$, and
let $s \in F$. Suppose $N$ contains a matrix $B$ for which some $P \in \mathrm{SL}_2(F)$ makes the
matrix $P B P^{-1}$ equal to the diagonal matrix $\operatorname{diag}(s, s^{-1})$. Then $N$
contains every $Q \in \mathrm{SL}_2(F)$ for which some $P \in \mathrm{SL}_2(F)$ makes $P Q P^{-1}$
equal to $\operatorname{diag}(s, s^{-1})$.

The two matrices are conjugate to each other, via the diagonal matrix, and a normal subgroup is
closed under conjugation.

articles.title: Order of $\mathrm{PGL}_2$ over a finite field
articles.statement:
If $F$ is a finite field with $q$ elements,
then the projective general linear group $\mathrm{PGL}_2(F)$ has order $q(q^2 - 1)$.

articles.title: Order of $\mathrm{PSL}_2$ over a finite field of odd characteristic
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite
field with $q$ elements whose characteristic $p$ is not $2$. Then the projective special linear
group $\mathrm{PSL}_2(F)$ has order $q(q^2 - 1)/2$.

articles.title: Dickson's classification, tame case
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime and let $K$ be an algebraic
closure of $\mathbb{F}_p$. Every finite nontrivial subgroup $G$ of $\mathrm{PGL}_2(K)$ whose order
is not divisible by $p$ is cyclic, or isomorphic to the dihedral group of order $2n$ for some
$n \ge 2$, or isomorphic to one of the groups $A_4$, $S_4$, $A_5$.

Proof: Klein's orbit count on the projective line, followed by identification
of the resulting orbit signatures.

## Sources

- L. E. Dickson, *Linear Groups with an Exposition of the Galois Field Theory*, Teubner (1901).

articles.title: Dickson's classification, wild case
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime, let $K$ be an algebraic
closure of $\mathbb{F}_p$, and let $G$ be a finite subgroup of $\mathrm{PGL}_2(K)$ whose order
is divisible by $p$. Then at least one of the following holds. (a) There are natural numbers
$m \ge 1$ and $t$ with $t$ coprime to $p$ and $t \mid p^m - 1$, and an injective homomorphism
$\varphi$ from the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}/t\mathbb{Z}$ to the automorphism group of the
additive group $\mathbb{F}_p^m$ such that $\varphi(c)$ fixes no nonzero vector of
$\mathbb{F}_p^m$ for every $c \ne 0$, and $G$ is isomorphic to the semidirect product
$\mathbb{F}_p^m \rtimes_\varphi \mathbb{Z}/t\mathbb{Z}$. (b) $G$ is isomorphic to
$\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_{p^m})$ for some $m \ge 1$, where $\mathbb{F}_{p^m}$ is the field
with $p^m$ elements. (c) $G$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{PGL}_2(\mathbb{F}_{p^m})$ for some
$m \ge 1$. (d) $p = 3$ and $G$ is isomorphic to the alternating group $A_5$.

In the source, the first case is a group of maps $z \mapsto az + b$ with $a$ a root of unity;
only the resulting abstract group structure is recorded here.

Proof: We follow X. Faber, *Finite p-irregular subgroups of $\mathrm{PGL}_2(k)$*,
arXiv:1112.1999, §6, using the Sylow normal form, exceptional-orbit count, and projective-line
actions to identify the $\mathrm{PSL}_2$, $\mathrm{PGL}_2$, and $A_5$ cases.

## Sources

- L. E. Dickson, *Linear Groups with an Exposition of the Galois Field Theory*, Teubner (1901).

articles.title: Algebraic closure of the field with p elements
articles.statement:
For a prime $p$, $K_p$ denotes a fixed
algebraic closure of the finite field $\mathbb{F}_p = \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$.

articles.title: Elements of $\mathrm{PGL}_2$ of order divisible by the characteristic
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd
prime and let $F$ be a field of characteristic $p$. If an element $g$ of $\mathrm{PGL}_2(F)$ has
finite order and $p$ divides the order of $g$, then the order of $g$ is $p$.

articles.title: Projective general linear group of degree two
articles.statement:
For a prime $p$, $\mathrm{PGL}_2(K_p)$ is
the quotient of the group $\mathrm{GL}_2(K_p)$ of invertible $2 \times 2$ matrices over the
algebraic closure $K_p$ of $\mathbb{F}_p$ by its center.

articles.title: Injective ring maps induce injective maps of $\mathrm{PGL}_n$
articles.statement:
Let $f : R \to S$ be an
injective homomorphism of commutative rings and let $n$ be a finite index set. Then the
homomorphism $\mathrm{PGL}_n(R) \to \mathrm{PGL}_n(S)$ induced by applying $f$ to matrix entries
is injective, where $\mathrm{PGL}_n(R)$ denotes $\mathrm{GL}_n(R)$ modulo its center.

articles.title: Projective special linear group of degree two
articles.statement:
For a prime $p$, $\mathrm{PSL}_2(K_p)$ is
the quotient of the group $\mathrm{SL}_2(K_p)$ of $2 \times 2$ matrices of determinant $1$ over
the algebraic closure $K_p$ of $\mathbb{F}_p$ by its center.

articles.title: Petechuk's double commutator question has a negative answer (Kourovka 10.46)
articles.statement:
There are a
nontrivial associative ring $R$ with identity, an integer $n \ge 3$ and a matrix
$\sigma \in \mathrm{GL}_n(R)$ such that for all elementary transvections
$\tau_1, \tau_2 \in \mathrm{GL}_n(R)$ the matrix $[[\sigma, \tau_1], \tau_2] - 1$ is not nilpotent,
that is, $[[\sigma, \tau_1], \tau_2]$ is not unipotent. Here $[x, y] = x y x^{-1} y^{-1}$, and an
elementary transvection is a matrix $1 + r e_{ij}$ with $i \ne j$ and $r \in R$ nonzero, where
$e_{ij}$ is the matrix unit with $1$ in position $(i, j)$ and $0$ elsewhere.

Muliarchyk (Theorem 1.1) shows the following for every field $k$ and $n \ge 2$. Let $R$ be the
free associative $k$-algebra on generators $x_{ij}, y_{ij}$ ($1 \le i, j \le n$) modulo the
relations $XY = YX = I$, where $X = (x_{ij})$, $Y = (y_{ij})$ and $I$ is the $n \times n$ identity
matrix; $R$ is nonzero. Then every nonempty iterated commutator of $X \in \mathrm{GL}_n(R)$ with
nonidentity unipotent matrices is nonunipotent.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 10.46 (V. M. Petechuk); resolution: K. Muliarchyk, A counterexample to Kourovka Notebook Problem 10.46: unipotent commutators over noncommutative algebras, preprint (2026), Theorem 1.1 (over R = k⟨x_ij, y_ij⟩ / (XY = YX = I) every nonempty iterated commutator of X with nonidentity unipotent matrices is nonunipotent); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 10.46 solved, https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/kourovka_10.46_solution.pdf.

articles.title: Petechuk's double commutator question (Kourovka 10.46)
articles.statement:
The statement that for every
nontrivial associative ring $R$ with identity, every $n \ge 3$ and every
$\sigma \in \mathrm{GL}_n(R)$ there are elementary transvections
$\tau_1, \tau_2 \in \mathrm{GL}_n(R)$ such that $[[\sigma, \tau_1], \tau_2]$ is unipotent, that
is, $[[\sigma, \tau_1], \tau_2] - 1$ is a nilpotent matrix, where $[x, y] = x y x^{-1} y^{-1}$.

In the problem, transvections are read as elementary transvections.

articles.title: Elementary transvection
articles.statement:
For a ring $R$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, a matrix
$\tau \in \mathrm{GL}_n(R)$ is an elementary transvection when $\tau = 1 + r e_{ij}$ for some
indices $i \ne j$ and some nonzero $r \in R$, where $e_{ij}$ is the matrix unit with $1$ in
position $(i, j)$ and $0$ elsewhere.

articles.title: Robinson's theorem on eigenvalues of elements of prime order
articles.statement:
For every $n$, if $H$ is a finite
subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ and $h \in H$ has prime order $p$ and lies in no abelian
normal subgroup of $H$, then $h$ has at least $(p - 1)/2$ distinct eigenvalues, that is,
$p - 1 \le 2k$ where $k$ is the number of distinct roots of the characteristic polynomial of $h$.
This answers Kourovka Notebook Problem 11.35 (A. E. Zalesskiĭ) in the affirmative.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.35 (A. E. Zalesskiĭ); resolution: G. R. Robinson, J. Algebra 178, no. 2 (1995), 635-642, Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.35: "Yes, it is", https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Zalesskiĭ's problem on eigenvalues of elements of prime order (Kourovka 11.35)
articles.statement:
The
statement that for every $n$, every finite subgroup $H$ of $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ and every
$h \in H$ of prime order $p$ that lies in no abelian normal subgroup of $H$, the element $h$ has at
least $(p - 1)/2$ distinct eigenvalues, that is, $p - 1 \le 2k$ where $k$ is the number of distinct
roots of the characteristic polynomial of $h$.

articles.title: Exponent of the general linear group over a prime field
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and let
$m \ge 1$. The exponent of the group $\mathrm{GL}_m(\mathbb{F}_p)$ of invertible $m \times m$
matrices over $\mathbb{F}_p = \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ is

$$p^{\lceil \log_p m \rceil} \cdot \operatorname{lcm}(p - 1, p^2 - 1, \dots, p^m - 1),$$

and this number equals $p^{\lceil \log_p m \rceil} \prod_{k=1}^{m} \Phi_k(p)$, where $\Phi_k$
denotes the $k$-th cyclotomic polynomial.

## Sources

- Eugene Karolinsky and Dmytro Seliutin, *Carmichael Numbers for GL(m)*, Journal of Integer Sequences 23 (2020), Article 20.10.6, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL23/Karolinsky/kar2.tex>, Theorem `fermat_matr` (quoting J. B. Marshall, *On the extension of Fermat's theorem to matrices of order n*, Proc. Edinb. Math. Soc. 6 (1939), and I. Niven, *Fermat's theorem for matrices*, Duke Math. J. 15 (1948)), lines 139-144; the lcm/cyclotomic identity is the paper's Proposition, lines 113-118.

articles.title: Stable sets of linear automorphisms
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $K$. A set $S$
of $K$-linear automorphisms of $V$ is stable when there are a natural number $m$ and subspaces
$0 = W_0 \le W_1 \le \cdots \le W_m = V$ of $V$ such that $g(w) - w \in W_i$ for every $i < m$,
every $g \in S$ and every $w \in W_{i+1}$.

articles.title: Jordan's theorem on finite linear groups
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ there is a natural
number $J$ such that every finite subgroup $G$ of $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ contains an abelian
subgroup $A$ that is normal in $G$ and has index $[G : A] \le J$.

## Sources

- C. Jordan, J. Reine Angew. Math. 84 (1878); Lean states complex GL_n specialization `GL_n(ℂ)` while general theorem holds over any char-zero field with bound depending only on n.

articles.title: SL(2, ℚ) does not embed in a division ring
articles.statement:
There is no division ring $D$ with an injective
group homomorphism $\mathrm{SL}(2, \mathbb{Q}) \to D^\times$: the group $\mathrm{SL}(2, \mathbb{Q})$
does not embed in the multiplicative group of any division ring.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.110 (B. Hartley); resolution: W. Dicks and B. Hartley, Commun. Algebra 19 (1991), 1919-1943, Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.110 ("No, it is not").

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 11.110 (B. Hartley)
articles.statement:
The group $\mathrm{SL}(2, \mathbb{Q})$ embeds in the
multiplicative group of some division ring: there are a division ring $D$ and an injective group
homomorphism $\mathrm{SL}(2, \mathbb{Q}) \to D^\times$.

articles.title: The one-relator group of Kourovka Problem 18.86 is linear
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be the group with generators
$a, b$ and the single defining relation $[[a, b], b] = 1$, where $[x, y] = x^{-1} y^{-1} x y$. Then
$G$ is linear: there are a field $K$, a natural number $n$ and an injective group homomorphism
$G \to \mathrm{GL}_n(K)$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 18.86 (V. A. Roman'kov); resolution: V. G. Bardakov and O. V. Bryukhanov, Vestnik Novosibirsk Univ. Ser. Mat. Mekh. Inf. 7 (2007), no. 3, 45-58 (Russian); V. A. Roman'kov, J. Siberian Federal Univ. Math. Phys. 6 (2013), no. 4, 516-520, Kourovka Archive, Problem 18.86: Yes, it is linear, since it embeds in Hol F_2 (adding c = [a, b] gives G = ⟨a, b, c | a^b = ac, c^b = c⟩), and Hol F_2 is linear by Corollary 3 of Bardakov-Bryukhanov; another proof by Roman'kov, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 18.86 (statement)
articles.statement:
The statement that the group $G$ with generators $a, b$
and the single defining relation $[[a, b], b] = 1$, where $[x, y] = x^{-1} y^{-1} x y$, is linear:
there are a field $K$, a natural number $n$ and an injective group homomorphism
$G \to \mathrm{GL}_n(K)$.

articles.title: The one-relator group of Kourovka Problem 18.86
articles.statement:
This is the group
$G = \langle a, b \mid [[a, b], b] = 1 \rangle$ with generators $a, b$ and the single defining
relation $[[a, b], b] = 1$, where $[x, y] = x^{-1} y^{-1} x y$; that is, $G$ is the quotient of the
free group on $a$ and $b$ by the normal subgroup generated by $[[a, b], b]$.

articles.title: The relator of Kourovka Problem 18.86
articles.statement:
This is the element $[[a, b], b]$ of the free group
on two generators $a$ and $b$, where $[x, y] = x^{-1} y^{-1} x y$; explicitly,
$[[a, b], b] = c^{-1} b^{-1} c b$ with $c = a^{-1} b^{-1} a b$.

articles.title: Sapir's group is linear over the integers
articles.statement:
The group
$\langle a, b, t \mid a^t = ab, b^t = ba \rangle$, where $a^t = t^{-1} a t$, embeds in
$\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$ for some natural number $n$. That is, Kourovka Problem 17.108 has a
positive answer.

The Kourovka Archive answers 17.108 "Yes, this group is linear" (M. F. Hagen, letter of 6
August 2018): the group is the mapping torus of an irreducible atoroidal self-monomorphism of a
free group, so it is virtually special and hence $\mathbb{Z}$-linear by Theorem B of Hagen and
Wise (2016).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 17.108 (M. Sapir); resolution: M. F. Hagen, letter of 6 August 2018, as recorded in the Kourovka Archive; M. F. Hagen and D. T. Wise, Duke Math. J. 165 (2016), 1753-1813, Kourovka Archive, Problem 17.108 (Yes, this group is linear: as noticed by M. Sapir it is the mapping torus of an irreducible atoroidal self-monomorphism of a free group, hence virtually special, hence Z-linear by Theorem B of Hagen-Wise).

articles.title: Linearity of Sapir's group over the integers (Kourovka 17.108)
articles.statement:
The statement that the
group $\langle a, b, t \mid a^t = ab, b^t = ba \rangle$, where $a^t = t^{-1} a t$, embeds in
$\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$ for some natural number $n$, that is, that it is linear over
$\mathbb{Z}$.

This is the form of the Kourovka Archive's resolution of M. Sapir's question whether the group is
linear.

articles.title: Sapir's group
articles.statement:
Sapir's group is the group with presentation
$\langle a, b, t \mid a^t = ab, b^t = ba \rangle$, where $a^t = t^{-1} a t$: the quotient of the
free group on $a$, $b$, $t$ by the normal subgroup generated by $t^{-1} a t (ab)^{-1}$ and
$t^{-1} b t (ba)^{-1}$.

articles.title: Malcev's theorem on linear groups
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field and $n$ a natural number. Every finitely
generated subgroup of the general linear group $\mathrm{GL}_n(K)$ is residually finite.

## Sources

- A. I. Malcev, Mat. Sb. 8 (1940) 405–422; Wehrfritz, Infinite Linear Groups; Lean states subgroup `G ≤ GL_n(K)` with `Group.FG G`.

articles.title: Selberg's lemma
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field of characteristic zero and let $n$ be a natural number.
Every finitely generated subgroup $G$ of $\mathrm{GL}_n(K)$ has a subgroup $H$ of finite index in
$G$ that is torsion-free: the identity is the only element of finite order in $H$.

## Sources

- A. Selberg, Contributions to Function Theory (1960) Selberg's lemma; Alperin, Proc. AMS 1969; Lean states char-zero case with H not required normal.

articles.title: The matrix with rows $(0, 1)$ and $(-1, 0)$ is special unitary
articles.statement:
The complex $2 \times 2$
matrix with rows $(0, 1)$ and $(-1, 0)$ lies in the special unitary group $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ of
complex $2 \times 2$ matrices.

articles.title: The matrix $\operatorname{diag}(i, -i)$ is special unitary
articles.statement:
The complex diagonal matrix
$\operatorname{diag}(i, -i)$, where $i$ is the imaginary unit, lies in the special unitary group
$\mathrm{SU}(2)$ of complex $2 \times 2$ matrices.

articles.title: Diagonal rotations are $2\pi$-periodic
articles.statement:
For every real number $\theta$ and every integer
$n$, the diagonal rotation through $\theta + 2\pi n$ equals the diagonal rotation through
$\theta$.

articles.title: When two diagonal rotations are equal
articles.statement:
For real numbers $a$ and $b$, the diagonal
rotations through $a$ and through $b$ are equal if and only if $a = b + 2\pi n$ for some
integer $n$.

articles.title: Diagonal rotations as diagonal matrices
articles.statement:
For every real number $\theta$, the diagonal
rotation through $\theta$ is the diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are $e^{i\theta}$ and
$e^{-i\theta}$, in that order.

articles.title: Diagonal rotation through a multiple of $2\pi$
articles.statement:
For every integer $n$, the diagonal
rotation through $2\pi n$ is the $2 \times 2$ identity matrix.

articles.title: Diagonal rotations lie in $\mathrm{SU}(2)$
articles.statement:
For every real number $\theta$, the
diagonal rotation through $\theta$ is a $2 \times 2$ complex matrix that is unitary and has
determinant $1$, that is, it lies in $\mathrm{SU}(2)$.

articles.title: Equal rotation matrices give equal longitude elements
articles.statement:
For real numbers $a$ and $b$, if
the diagonal rotations through $a$ and through $b$ are equal as matrices, then the elements of
the longitude subgroup given by the diagonal rotations through $a$ and through $b$ are
equal.

articles.title: The angle homomorphism into the longitude subgroup
articles.statement:
The homomorphism from the additive
group $\mathbb{R}$ to the longitude subgroup, written additively, that sends a real number
$\theta$ to the diagonal rotation through $\theta$, regarded as an element of the longitude
subgroup.

articles.title: Longitude elements multiply by adding angles
articles.statement:
For real numbers $a$ and $b$, in the
longitude subgroup the product of the diagonal rotations through $a$ and through $b$ is the
diagonal rotation through $a + b$.

articles.title: Diagonal rotation as a longitude element
articles.statement:
For a real number $\theta$, the diagonal
rotation through $\theta$, regarded as an element of the longitude subgroup of
$\mathrm{SU}(2)$.

articles.title: Diagonal rotation
articles.statement:
For a real number $\theta$, the diagonal rotation through $\theta$ is
the $2 \times 2$ complex diagonal matrix $\operatorname{diag}(e^{i\theta}, e^{-i\theta})$.

articles.title: Matrix form of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a complex $2 \times 2$ matrix in the special
unitary group $\mathrm{SU}(2)$, that is, $M$ is unitary with determinant $1$. Then there are
complex numbers $a, b$ with $|a|^2 + |b|^2 = 1$ such that the first row of $M$ is $(a, b)$ and the
second row of $M$ is $(-\bar b, \bar a)$.

articles.title: Every point of $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ comes from a real angle
articles.statement:
Every element $x$ of
the circle group $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$, written multiplicatively, is the class of some real
number $a$.

articles.title: The longitude map on the class of an angle
articles.statement:
For every real number $\theta$, the longitude
map sends the class of $\theta$ in $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ to the diagonal rotation through
$\theta$, regarded as an element of the longitude subgroup.

articles.title: The longitude map is bijective
articles.statement:
The longitude map from the circle group
$\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$, written multiplicatively, to the longitude subgroup of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$
is bijective.

articles.title: The longitude map is injective
articles.statement:
The longitude map from the circle group
$\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$, written multiplicatively, to the longitude subgroup of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$
is injective.

The angle class is recovered from the diagonal rotation via the complex exponential.

articles.title: The longitude map is surjective
articles.statement:
The longitude map from the circle group
$\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$, written multiplicatively, to the longitude subgroup of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$
is surjective: every element of the longitude subgroup is the image of some class.

articles.title: Longitude map
articles.statement:
The longitude map is the group homomorphism from the circle group
$\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$, written multiplicatively, to the longitude subgroup of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$
that sends the class of a real number $\theta$ to the diagonal rotation through $\theta$, that is,
to $\cos\theta \cdot I + \sin\theta \cdot \operatorname{diag}(i, -i) =
\operatorname{diag}(e^{i\theta}, e^{-i\theta})$, where $I$ is the $2 \times 2$ identity matrix.
It is well defined because diagonal rotations are $2\pi$-periodic.

articles.title: Isomorphism of the circle group with the longitude subgroup
articles.statement:
The group isomorphism from
the circle group $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$, written multiplicatively, onto the longitude
subgroup of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ given by the longitude map, which sends the class of a real number
$\theta$ to the diagonal rotation through $\theta$.

articles.title: Longitude subgroup
articles.statement:
The longitude subgroup of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is the subgroup of those
elements of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ that are the diagonal rotation through $\theta$ for some real number
$\theta$.

It is the longitude $\mathrm{Long}_i$ at the equator point $i$.

articles.title: The center of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$
articles.statement:
An element $M$ of the special unitary group
$\mathrm{SU}(2)$ of complex $2 \times 2$ matrices lies in the center of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ if and
only if $M$ is the identity matrix $I$ or $M = -I$.

articles.title: Characterization of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$
articles.statement:
A complex $2 \times 2$ matrix $M$ lies in the
special unitary group $\mathrm{SU}(2)$, that is, $M$ is unitary with determinant $1$, if and
only if there are complex numbers $\alpha, \beta$ with $|\alpha|^2 + |\beta|^2 = 1$ such that
the first row of $M$ is $(\alpha, \beta)$ and the second row is $(-\bar\beta, \bar\alpha)$.

articles.title: The trace of an $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ matrix has absolute value at most two
articles.statement:
For every complex
$2 \times 2$ matrix $M$ in the special unitary group $\mathrm{SU}(2)$, the trace of $M$ satisfies
$|\operatorname{tr} M| \le 2$.

articles.title: Conjugate transpose of a diagonal rotation
articles.statement:
For every real number $\theta$, the conjugate
transpose of the diagonal rotation through $\theta$ is the diagonal rotation through $-\theta$.

articles.title: The center of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is proper
articles.statement:
The center of the special unitary group
$\mathrm{SU}(2)$ of complex $2 \times 2$ matrices is not all of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$.

The matrix $\operatorname{diag}(i, -i)$, where $i$ is the imaginary unit, lies in
$\mathrm{SU}(2)$ but is not central.

articles.title: Conjugacy in `SU₂` is determined by the trace
articles.statement:
Two elements of `SU₂`
with the same trace are conjugate in `SU₂`.

articles.title: Diagonalization in $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ up to conjugacy
articles.statement:
Every element of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is
conjugate in $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ to an element of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ that is the diagonal matrix
$\operatorname{diag}(z, \bar z)$ for some complex number $z$ with $z \bar z = 1$.

articles.title: Diagonal elements of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ with equal trace are conjugate
articles.statement:
Let $z_1, z_2$ be
complex numbers with $z_1 \bar z_1 = 1$ and $z_2 \bar z_2 = 1$, and let $D_1, D_2$ be elements of
$\mathrm{SU}(2)$ equal to the diagonal matrices $\operatorname{diag}(z_1, \bar z_1)$ and
$\operatorname{diag}(z_2, \bar z_2)$. If $D_1$ and $D_2$ have the same trace, then they are
conjugate in $\mathrm{SU}(2)$.

In the proof, either $z_1 = z_2$, or $z_1 = \bar z_2$ and conjugation by the anti-diagonal matrix
with rows $(0, 1)$ and $(-1, 0)$ swaps the diagonal entries.

articles.title: Trace is invariant under conjugation in $\mathrm{SU}(2)$
articles.statement:
For all $P$ and $A$ in
$\mathrm{SU}(2)$, the trace of $P A P^{-1}$ equals the trace of $A$.

articles.title: The trace of an $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ matrix is real
articles.statement:
For every complex $2 \times 2$ matrix
$M$ in the special unitary group $\mathrm{SU}(2)$, the imaginary part of the trace of $M$ is $0$.

articles.title: Free products of groups without generalized torsion have no generalized torsion
articles.statement:
For every
family of groups $(G_i)_{i \in I}$ none of which contains a generalized torsion element (an element
$h \ne 1$ such that some nonempty product of conjugates of $h$ is trivial), the free product of the
family contains no generalized torsion element.

The Kourovka Archive answers 16.49 "Yes, it is true", citing Ito, Motegi and Teragaito (2019),
whose Theorem 1.5 shows that a generalized torsion element of a free product
$G_1 \ast \cdots \ast G_n$ of torsion-free groups is conjugate to a generalized torsion element of
some factor.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 16.49 (V. M. Kopytov, N. Ya. Medvedev); resolution: T. Ito, K. Motegi and M. Teragaito, Generalized torsion and decomposition of 3-manifolds, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 147 (2019), no. 11, 4999-5008, arXiv:1811.07532, Theorem 1.5 (a generalized torsion element of a free product G_1 ∗ ⋯ ∗ G_n of torsion-free groups is conjugate to a generalized torsion element of some factor); Kourovka Archive, Problem 16.49 (Yes; moreover the generalized torsion in a free product of torsion-free groups is conjugate to a generalized torsion of one of its factor groups), https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.07532.

articles.title: Kopytov–Medvedev question on generalized torsion in free products (Kourovka 16.49)
articles.statement:
The
statement that for every family of groups $(G_i)_{i \in I}$ none of which contains a generalized
torsion element (an element $h \ne 1$ such that some nonempty product of conjugates of $h$ is
trivial), the free product of the family contains no generalized torsion element either.

articles.title: Generalized torsion elements (Kourovka 16.48)
articles.statement:
An element $h$ of a group $H$ is a
generalized torsion element if $h \ne 1$ and there are $n \ge 1$ elements
$x_1, \dots, x_n \in H$, not necessarily distinct, such that
$(x_1^{-1} h x_1)(x_2^{-1} h x_2) \cdots (x_n^{-1} h x_n) = 1$.

articles.title: Generalized torsion element (Kourovka 16.49)
articles.statement:
An element $h$ of a group $H$ is a generalized
torsion element when $h \ne 1$ and some nonempty product of conjugates of $h$ is trivial, that is,
$x_1^{-1} h x_1 \cdots x_k^{-1} h x_k = 1$ for some $k \ge 1$ and some $x_1, \dots, x_k \in H$.

articles.title: Some group without generalized torsion is not right-orderable (Kourovka 16.48)
articles.statement:
The
Kopytov–Medvedev proposition is false: there is a group $H$ with no generalized torsion element
that admits no right order.

Resolved false: Cai and Clay give a condition ensuring that an amalgam is generalized torsion-free
and use it to construct a group that is generalized torsion-free but not left-orderable (their
Theorem 1.3, proved in Section 7), hence not right-orderable; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue)
answers 16.48 "No, not every".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 16.48 (V. M. Kopytov, N. Ya. Medvedev); resolution: T. W. Cai and A. Clay, Generalized torsion in amalgams, preprint, arXiv:2504.08084 (2025), Theorem 1.3 (there exists a group which is generalized torsion-free and not left-orderable; Definition 7.1 and Theorem 7.2); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 16.48 solved (No, not every), https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08084.

articles.title: The Kopytov–Medvedev question (Kourovka 16.48)
articles.statement:
This is the proposition that every group
$H$ with no generalized torsion element is right-orderable, that is, admits a right order.

articles.title: Right orders on a group (Kourovka 16.48)
articles.statement:
The right orders of a group $G$ are the binary
relations $\preceq$ on $G$ that are linear orders (reflexive, transitive, antisymmetric and total)
and are invariant under right multiplication: $a \preceq b$ implies $ac \preceq bc$ for all
$a, b, c \in G$.

articles.title: No free group of finite rank at least 2 has an isolated bi-order
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$n \ge 2$ and every finite subset $S$ of the free group $F_n$ on $n$ generators, it is not the case
that exactly one bi-invariant strict total order $<$ on $F_n$ (a strict total order such that
$a < b$ implies $cad < cbd$ for all $a, b, c, d \in F_n$) satisfies $1 < s$ for every $s \in S$.

Resolved false: the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 12.51 solved, "No, it does not". Muliarchyk
(arXiv:2403.14779) proves that a free product of bi-ordered groups admits no isolated bi-ordering;
$F_n$ is the free product of $n \ge 2$ copies of $\mathbb{Z}$ (see also Dovhyi and Muliarchyk,
Groups Geom. Dyn. 17 (2023)).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 12.51 (S. McCleary); resolution: K. Muliarchyk, Free products of bi-orderable groups, preprint (2024), arXiv:2403.14779; S. Dovhyi and K. Muliarchyk, Groups Geom. Dyn. 17 (2023), 613-632, Muliarchyk, main theorem: a free product of bi-ordered groups admits no isolated bi-ordering; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 12.51 solved, https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.14779.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 12.51 (isolated bi-orders of free groups)
articles.statement:
The statement that for some
natural number $n \ge 2$ there is a finite subset $S$ of the free group $F_n$ on $n$ generators
such that exactly one bi-invariant strict total order $<$ on $F_n$ (a strict total order such that
$a < b$ implies $cad < cbd$ for all $a, b, c, d \in F_n$) makes every element of $S$ positive, that
is, satisfies $1 < s$ for all $s \in S$. Such an order is an isolated point of the space of
bi-orders of $F_n$.

articles.title: Bi-invariant strict total orders on a group
articles.statement:
A relation $r$ on a group $G$ is a bi-invariant
order if $r$ is a strict total order on $G$ (irreflexive, transitive and trichotomous) and
$r(a, b)$ implies $r(cad, cbd)$ for all $a, b, c, d \in G$.

articles.title: Left-orderable addition
articles.statement:
The addition of a set $B$ is left-orderable when there is a strict
total order $<$ on $B$ that is invariant under left addition: for all $a, b, c \in B$, if $b < c$
then $a + b < a + c$.

articles.title: Left-orderable multiplication
articles.statement:
The multiplication of a set $B$ is left-orderable when there
is a strict total order $<$ on $B$ that is invariant under left multiplication: for all
$a, b, c \in B$, if $b < c$ then $a b < a c$.

articles.title: A skew brace whose additive group is not left-orderable
articles.statement:
There is a skew brace $B$, that is, a
set with two group structures, an addition $+$ and a multiplication $\cdot$, satisfying
$a \cdot (b + c) = a \cdot b - a + a \cdot c$ for all $a, b, c \in B$, whose multiplication is
left-orderable but whose addition is not left-orderable. That is, the statement of Kourovka
Problem 19.49 fails.

Nasybullov's example (Example 3.1) is $\mathbb{Z}$ with addition $a \oplus b = a + (-1)^a b$ and
multiplication $a \odot b = a + b$: the multiplicative group is infinite cyclic, hence
left-orderable, while the additive group is infinite dihedral and has an element of order $2$, so
it is not left-orderable. The Kourovka Archive answers 19.49 "No, not always".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 19.49 (V. Lebed, L. Vendramin); resolution: T. Nasybullov, Connections between properties of the additive and the multiplicative groups of a two-sided skew brace, J. Algebra 540 (2019), 156-167 (arXiv:1809.09418), Example 3.1: on ℤ, a ⊕ b = a + (−1)^a b and a ⊙ b = a + b define a skew brace with infinite cyclic multiplicative group and infinite dihedral additive group, which has 2-torsion and so is not left-orderable, answering Problem 19.49; Kourovka Archive, Problem 19.49: No, not always, https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.09418.

articles.title: Left-orderability of the additive group of a skew brace (Kourovka 19.49)
articles.statement:
The statement
that for every skew brace $B$, that is, a set with two group structures, an addition $+$ (not
necessarily commutative) and a multiplication $\cdot$, satisfying
$a \cdot (b + c) = a \cdot b - a + a \cdot c$ for all $a, b, c \in B$: if the multiplication of
$B$ is left-orderable, then the addition of $B$ is left-orderable.

articles.title: Bludov–Glass theorem (Kourovka Problem 15.34)
articles.statement:
Let $(G_i)_{i \in I}$ be a family of groups,
each with a linear order invariant under multiplication on both sides ($a \le b$ implies
$ca \le cb$ and $ac \le bc$), let $H$ be a group with such a linear order, and for each $i$ let
$\varphi_i \colon H \to G_i$ be a strictly increasing group homomorphism. Then the free product of
the $G_i$ with $H$ amalgamated along the maps $\varphi_i$ is right-orderable: it admits a linear
order such that $a \le b$ implies $ac \le bc$ for all $a, b, c$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 15.34 (V. V. Bludov); resolution: V. V. Bludov and A. M. W. Glass, On free products of right ordered groups with amalgamated subgroups, Math. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. 146 (2009), 591-601, main theorem (the free product of ordered groups G₁, G₂ with subgroups amalgamated via an order-preserving isomorphism is right orderable; extended to arbitrary families); Kourovka Archive, Problem 15.34 (answer: Yes, it is).

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 15.34 (statement)
articles.statement:
The statement that for every family $(G_i)_{i \in I}$
of groups, each with a linear order invariant under multiplication on both sides, every group $H$
with such a linear order, and all strictly increasing group homomorphisms
$\varphi_i \colon H \to G_i$, the free product of the $G_i$ with $H$ amalgamated along the maps
$\varphi_i$ is right-orderable.

The problem was posed by V. V. Bludov.

articles.title: Right-orderable group
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is right-orderable if it admits a linear order $\le$
that is invariant under right multiplication: $a \le b$ implies $ac \le bc$ for all
$a, b, c \in G$.

articles.title: Boundary-fixing homeomorphisms of the square
articles.statement:
Let $I^2 = [0, 1] \times [0, 1]$ be the
closed square and $\partial I^2$ its boundary. $\mathrm{Homeo}(I^2; \partial I^2)$ is the subgroup
of the group of homeomorphisms of $I^2$ consisting of those homeomorphisms $h$ with $h(x) = x$ for
every $x \in \partial I^2$.

articles.title: Boundary-fixing homeomorphisms of the disc are not right-orderable
articles.statement:
Let
$I^2 = [0, 1] \times [0, 1]$ be the closed square, a model of the closed disc, and let
$\mathrm{Homeo}(I^2; \partial I^2)$ be the group of homeomorphisms of $I^2$ that fix every point of
the boundary $\partial I^2$. There is no linear order $\le$ on $\mathrm{Homeo}(I^2; \partial I^2)$
such that $a \le b$ implies $ac \le bc$ for all $a, b, c$; that is, this group is not
right-orderable.

This answers Kourovka Problem 17.20 negatively: Hyde constructs a finitely generated subgroup of
$\mathrm{Homeo}(I^2; \partial I^2)$ that admits no left order, and left- and right-orderability
are equivalent via $g \mapsto g^{-1}$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 17.20 (G. M. Bergman); resolution: J. Hyde, The group of boundary fixing homeomorphisms of the disc is not left-orderable, Ann. of Math. (2) 190 (2019), 657-661, abstract (a finitely generated subgroup of Homeo(I²; ∂I²) admits no left order, hence neither does Homeo(I²; ∂I²)); Kourovka Archive, Problem 17.20 (No, not always), https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2019/190-2/p05.

articles.title: Right-orderability of the boundary-fixing homeomorphisms of the disc
articles.statement:
The proposition
(Kourovka Problem 17.20, G. M. Bergman, for the closed disc) that the group
$\mathrm{Homeo}(I^2; \partial I^2)$ of homeomorphisms of the closed square
$I^2 = [0, 1] \times [0, 1]$, a model of the closed disc, that fix the boundary $\partial I^2$
pointwise is right-orderable: it carries a linear order $\le$ such that $a \le b$ implies
$ac \le bc$ for all $a, b, c$.

articles.title: Right orders of a group
articles.statement: The right orders of `G`: linear orders (as relations) invariant under right multiplication.

articles.title: Boundary of the square
articles.statement:
The boundary $\partial I^2$ of the closed square
$I^2 = [0, 1] \times [0, 1]$ is the set of points $(x, y) \in I^2$ with $x = 0$, $x = 1$, $y = 0$
or $y = 1$.

articles.title: The closed square
articles.statement:
The closed square $I^2 = [0, 1] \times [0, 1]$, the product of two
copies of the unit interval, used as a model of the closed disc.

articles.title: Not every fully ordered group embeds in one with three conjugacy classes
articles.statement:
There is a fully
ordered group $G$ such that for every fully ordered group $H$ with exactly three conjugacy
classes, no homomorphism $G \to H$ is strictly increasing. Here a fully ordered group is a group
with a linear order $\le$ such that $a \le b$ implies $ca \le cb$ and $ac \le bc$ for all $a$, $b$,
$c$. That is, the answer to Kourovka Problem 11.68 is negative.

The Kourovka Archive records the answer "No, not every", given by Bludov.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.68 (B. Neumann); resolution: V. V. Bludov, Algebra and Logic 44, no. 6 (2005), 370-380, Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.68: "No, not every", https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 11.68 (ordered groups with three conjugacy classes)
articles.statement:
The statement that
for every fully ordered group $G$ there are a fully ordered group $H$ with exactly three conjugacy
classes and a strictly increasing homomorphism $G \to H$ (an order-preserving embedding). Here a
fully ordered group is a group with a linear order $\le$ such that $a \le b$ implies $ca \le cb$
and $ac \le bc$ for all $a$, $b$, $c$.

articles.title: Right-invariant linear order
articles.statement:
A linear order $\le$ on a group $G$ is right-invariant (a
right order) when $a \le b$ implies $ac \le bc$ for all $a, b, c \in G$.

articles.title: Right-relatively convex subgroup
articles.statement:
A subgroup $H$ of a group $G$ is right-relatively convex
when there is a right-invariant linear order $\le$ on $G$ for which $H$ is convex: whenever
$h_1 \le g \le h_2$ with $h_1, h_2 \in H$ and $g \in G$, also $g \in H$.

articles.title: Negative answer to Kourovka Problem 21.147 for non-abelian groups
articles.statement:
It is not the case that for
every non-abelian right-orderable group $G$ and all right-relatively convex subgroups $H$ and $K$ of
$G$, both the intersection $H \cap K$ and the join $H \vee K$ (the subgroup generated by $H$ and
$K$) are right-relatively convex.

In the integer Heisenberg group, which is non-abelian, the cyclic subgroups
$\langle (1, 0, 1) \rangle$ and $\langle (1, 0, -1) \rangle$ are convex for suitable right orders,
but the subgroup $J$ they generate contains $2e$ and not $e = (1, 0, 0)$, and every right order
puts $e$ between $0$ and $2e$, so $J$ is convex for no right order (van Doorn, Judin, Monticone and
Morrison, Theorem 8.1; Monticone's note). The 21st issue of the Kourovka Notebook marks 21.147
solved ("No, not always"; AI solution confirmed by A. V. Zenkov).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 21.147 (V. M. Kopytov, N. Ya. Medvedev; A. V. Zenkov); resolution: P. Monticone, Kourovka Notebook Problem 21.147, solution note (14 May 2026), Kourovka Notebook site; W. van Doorn, E. Judin, P. Monticone and D. Morrison, On some problems from the Kourovka Notebook, preprint, arXiv:2607.17477 (2026), van Doorn-Judin-Monticone-Morrison, Theorem 8.1: in the integer Heisenberg group the subgroups ⟨(1, 0, 1)⟩ and ⟨(1, 0, -1)⟩ are right-relatively convex, while their join contains 2e but not e = (1, 0, 0) and so is not convex for any right order; an AI solution (Aristotle) confirmed by A. V. Zenkov, Kourovka Notebook (21st issue), Problem 21.147: No, not always, https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17477.

articles.title: Sublattice question for right-relatively convex subgroups (Kourovka Problem 21.147, non-abelian case)
articles.statement:
**Sublattice question for right-relatively convex subgroups (Kourovka Problem 21.147,
non-abelian case).** The statement that for every non-abelian right-orderable group $G$ and all
right-relatively convex subgroups $H$ and $K$ of $G$, both the intersection $H \cap K$ and the
join $H \vee K$ (the subgroup generated by $H$ and $K$) are right-relatively convex; that is, the
right-relatively convex subgroups of $G$ form a sublattice of the lattice of subgroups of $G$.

The question is restricted to non-abelian groups, as the proposers meant.

articles.title: Right-orderable groups
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is right-orderable when it admits a linear order $\le$
that is invariant under right multiplication: $a \le b$ implies $ac \le bc$ for all
$a, b, c \in G$.

articles.title: A non-right-orderable group that is residually $p$ for two primes (Linnell)
articles.statement:
There exist a
group $G$ and distinct primes $p$ and $q$ such that $G$ is residually a finite $p$-group and
residually a finite $q$-group but is not right-orderable.

By Rhemtulla, a group that is residually a finite $p$-group for infinitely many primes $p$ is
orderable.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 10.30 (N. Ya. Medvedev); resolution: P. A. Linnell, J. Algebra 248 (2002), 605-607, Kourovka Archive, Problem 10.30 ("Yes, there does").

articles.title: Medvedev's question on right-orderability (Kourovka 10.30)
articles.statement:
The statement that there exist
a group $G$ and distinct primes $p$ and $q$ such that $G$ is residually a finite $p$-group and
residually a finite $q$-group, but $G$ is not right-orderable.

articles.title: Finitely generated simple right-orderable groups exist
articles.statement:
There is a finitely generated simple
group $G$ that admits a right order, that is, a linear order $\le$ on $G$ such that $a \le b$
implies $ac \le bc$ for all $a, b, c \in G$. This answers Kourovka Problem 16.50 positively.

Hyde and Lodha (Theorem 1.3) construct finitely generated simple groups of orientation-preserving
homeomorphisms of the real line, which are finitely generated simple left (or right) orderable
groups (Corollary 1.5 and the abstract). The Kourovka Archive answers 16.50 "Yes, such groups do
exist".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 16.50 (V. M. Kopytov, N. Ya. Medvedev); resolution: J. Hyde and Y. Lodha, Finitely generated infinite simple groups of homeomorphisms of the real line, Invent. Math. 218 (2019), 83-112, arXiv:1807.06478, Theorem 1.3 (G_ρ is a finitely generated simple subgroup of Homeo+(ℝ)) and Corollary 1.5 (finitely generated simple left orderable groups exist; by the abstract, equivalently left or right orderable); Kourovka Archive, Problem 16.50 (Yes, such groups do exist), https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06478.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 16.50 (finitely generated simple right-orderable groups)
articles.statement:
The statement
that there exists a finitely generated simple group $G$ admitting a right order, that is, a linear
order $\le$ on $G$ such that $a \le b$ implies $ac \le bc$ for all $a, b, c \in G$. The problem is
due to V. M. Kopytov and N. Ya. Medvedev.

articles.title: Right orders on a group (Kourovka Problem 16.50)
articles.statement:
The right orders of a group $G$ are the
linear orders $\le$ on $G$, viewed as relations, that are invariant under right multiplication:
$a \le b$ implies $ac \le bc$ for all $a, b, c \in G$.

articles.title: No group has countably infinitely many right orders
articles.statement:
For every group $G$, the set of right
orders on $G$ (linear orders $\le$ on $G$ such that $a \le b$ implies $ac \le bc$ for all
$a, b, c \in G$) is either finite or uncountable. That is, Kourovka Problem 16.51 has a negative
answer.

Linnell proves this for left orders, which correspond to right orders through
$a \le' b \iff b^{-1} \le a^{-1}$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 16.51 (V. M. Kopytov, N. Ya. Medvedev); resolution: P. A. Linnell, Bull. London Math. Soc. 43 (2011), 200-202; A. Clay, preprint, arXiv:0909.0273 (2009); A. Navas and C. Rivas, Algebr. Geom. Topol. 9 (2009), 2079-2100, Linnell, Theorem 1.3 (no group can be left-ordered in a countably infinite number of ways), based on A. V. Zenkov (1997, locally indicable groups); Clay, Corollary 3.10 (the set of left orderings of any group is finite or uncountable); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 16.51 solved (No, there are no such groups), https://arxiv.org/abs/0909.0273.

articles.title: Groups with countably infinitely many right orders (Kourovka 16.51)
articles.statement:
The statement that
some group has a countably infinite set of right orders.

articles.title: Right orders of a group (Kourovka 16.51)
articles.statement:
The right orders of a group $G$ are the linear
orders $\le$ on $G$ that are invariant under right multiplication: $a \le b$ implies $ac \le bc$ for
all $a, b, c \in G$.

articles.title: Left-orderable groups
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is left-orderable if it admits a linear order $\le$ such
that $a \le b$ implies $ca \le cb$ for all $a, b, c \in G$.

articles.title: A unique product group need not be left-orderable
articles.statement:
There exists a group $G$ that has unique
products but is not left-orderable: for all finite nonempty subsets $X, Y \subseteq G$ there are
$x_0 \in X$ and $y_0 \in Y$ such that $(x_0, y_0)$ is the only pair $(x, y) \in X \times Y$ with
$xy = x_0 y_0$, and yet $G$ admits no linear order invariant under left multiplication.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 15.49 (P. Linnell); resolution: N. Dunfield, Appendix B in S. Kionke and J. Raimbault, On geometric aspects of diffuse groups, Doc. Math. 21 (2016), 873-915, arXiv:1411.6449, Section 2.2 and the appendix (diffuse groups have unique products, by Bowditch's observation; the appendix gives a compact hyperbolic 3-manifold group that is diffuse but not left-orderable); Kourovka Archive, Problem 15.49 (answer: Yes, there does), https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.6449.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 15.49 (unique product groups and left orders)
articles.statement:
The statement, asked by
P. Linnell, that there exists a group $G$ with unique products that is not left-orderable. Here $G$
has unique products if for all finite nonempty subsets $X, Y \subseteq G$ there are $x_0 \in X$ and
$y_0 \in Y$ such that $(x_0, y_0)$ is the only pair $(x, y) \in X \times Y$ with $xy = x_0 y_0$.

articles.title: Bi-invariant linear orders on a group
articles.statement:
For a group $G$, the bi-invariant orders of $G$ are
the linear orders $\le$ on $G$ (reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive and total relations) that are
invariant under left and right multiplication: for all $a, b, c \in G$, $a \le b$ implies
$ca \le cb$ and $ac \le bc$.

articles.title: Bludov–Glass: a finitely presented orderable group with insoluble word problem
articles.statement:
There is a
finitely presented group $G$ that admits a bi-invariant linear order and has a finite generating
family $g_1, \dots, g_k$ for which the word problem is insoluble: no algorithm decides, given a word
in the $g_i$ and their inverses, whether it equals $1$ in $G$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 17.29 (V. V. Bludov, A. M. W. Glass); resolution: V. V. Bludov and A. M. W. Glass, Bull. London Math. Soc. 44 (2012), 85-98, Kourovka Archive, Problem 17.29 (Such a group is constructed).

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 17.29 (V. V. Bludov, A. M. W. Glass)
articles.statement:
The statement that there is a
finitely presented group $G$ that admits a bi-invariant linear order and has a finite generating
family $g_1, \dots, g_k$ for which the word problem is insoluble: no algorithm decides, given a word
in the $g_i$ and their inverses, whether it equals $1$ in $G$.

articles.title: Recursively presented group
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group, $k$ a natural number and $\varphi$ a
homomorphism from the free group on $k$ generators to $G$. The group $G$ is recursively presented
with respect to $\varphi$ when the set of words $w$ (finite lists of letters $(i, \varepsilon)$
with $i < k$ and $\varepsilon$ true or false, the letter $(i, \mathrm{false})$ standing for the
inverse of the $i$-th generator) with $\varphi(w) = 1$ in $G$ is recursively enumerable.

When $\varphi$ is surjective, this is the same as a presentation of $G$ on the images of the
generators with a recursively enumerable set of relators; it is the enumerable counterpart of a
solvable word problem.

articles.title: Right orders of a group
articles.statement: The right orders of `G`: linear orders (as relations) invariant under right multiplication.

articles.title: A soluble right-orderable group with insoluble word problem (Kourovka 17.28)
articles.statement:
There exist a
soluble group $G$ that admits a right order, a natural number $k$ and elements
$g_0, \dots, g_{k-1}$ generating $G$ such that, for the homomorphism $\varphi$ from the free group
on $k$ generators to $G$ sending the $i$-th generator to $g_i$, the group $G$ is recursively
presented with respect to $\varphi$ and the word problem for $\varphi$ is not solvable.

Resolved true: Darbinyan constructs a two-generated, recursively presented, bi-orderable (hence
right-orderable) soluble group of derived length 3 with undecidable word problem; the Kourovka
Archive answers 17.28 "Yes, there is".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 17.28 (V. V. Bludov, A. M. W. Glass); resolution: A. Darbinyan, Computability, orders, and solvable groups, J. Symbolic Logic 85 (2020), 1588-1598 (arXiv:1909.05720), abstract, result (2) (a bi-orderable, two-generated, recursively presented solvable group of derived length 3 with undecidable word problem, answering the question of Bludov and Glass); Kourovka Archive, Problem 17.28 (Yes, there is), https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.05720.

articles.title: The Bludov–Glass question (Kourovka 17.28)
articles.statement:
The statement that there exist a soluble group
$G$ that admits a right order, a natural number $k$ and elements $g_0, \dots, g_{k-1}$ generating
$G$ such that, for the homomorphism $\varphi$ from the free group on $k$ generators to $G$ sending
the $i$-th generator to $g_i$, the group $G$ is recursively presented with respect to $\varphi$
and the word problem for $\varphi$ is not solvable. In words: there is a finitely generated,
recursively presented, soluble right-orderable group with insoluble word problem.

articles.title: Counting elements of each order forces prime-power orders
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group such
that for every divisor $d > 1$ of $|G|$ and every subgroup $H$ of $G$ whose order is coprime to
$d$, the order $|H|$ divides the number of elements of $G$ of order $d$. Then every non-identity
element of $G$ has prime-power order.

Buturlakin, Shen and Shi proved this in 2017, answering Kourovka Problem 18.112 (W. J. Shi); the
Kourovka Archive answers 18.112 "Yes, it is true".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 18.112 (W. J. Shi); resolution: A. A. Buturlakin, R. Shen and W. Shi, Siberian Math. J. 58 (2017), 405-407, Kourovka Archive, Problem 18.112 (Yes, it is true).

articles.title: Shi's question on element-order counts (Kourovka 18.112)
articles.statement:
The proposition that if a
finite group $G$ has the property that, for every divisor $d > 1$ of $|G|$ and every subgroup $H$
of $G$ whose order is coprime to $d$, $|H|$ divides the number of elements of $G$ of order $d$,
then every non-identity element of $G$ has prime-power order.

articles.title: Additive groups of squarefree order are cyclic
articles.statement:
An additive commutative group of squarefree cardinality is additively
cyclic.

articles.title: Szele's criterion for cyclic numbers
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a positive integer. Every group of order $n$
is cyclic if and only if $n$ is relatively prime to $\varphi(n)$, that is,
$\gcd(n, \varphi(n)) = 1$, where $\varphi$ is Euler's totient function.

## Sources

- Joel E. Cohen, "Conjectures about Primes and Cyclic Numbers," Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.7, Szele's criterion, lines 107–114, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL28/Cohen/cohen41.tex (citing T. Szele, "Über die endlichen Ordnungszahlen, zu denen nur eine Gruppe gehört," Comment. Math. Helv. 20 (1947), 265–267).

articles.title: Extensions of PSL have a new element order
articles.statement:
Resolved true: the Kourovka Archive answers 14.60 "Yes, it is true": Zavarnitsine proved it for `n ≠
4` and Grechkoseeva and Skresanov for `n = 4` (the editors note that an earlier claim of failure for
`n = 4` was erroneous). Source: E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group
Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems,
Problem 14.60 (V. D. Mazurov); resolution: A. V. Zavarnitsine, Siberian Math. J. 49 (2008), 246-256
(n ≠ 4); M. A. Grechkoseeva and S. V. Skresanov, Siberian Electron. Math. Rep. 17 (2020), 585-589 (n
= 4), Kourovka Archive, Problem 14.60 (answer: Yes, it is true; the editors note that an earlier
claim of failure for n = 4 was erroneous).

articles.title: Kourovka 14.60: new element orders in extensions of projective special linear groups
articles.statement:
The proposition that for every $n \ge 3$, every prime $p$ and every $k \ge 1$, with $q = p^k$ and
$\mathbb{F}_q$ the field with $q$ elements, the following holds: whenever $H$ is a nontrivial normal
subgroup of a finite group $G$ and $G/H$ is isomorphic to the projective special linear group
$\mathrm{PSL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q)$, some element of $G$ has an order that is not the order of any
element of $G/H$.

articles.title: Projective special linear group
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and a field $F$,
$\mathrm{PSL}_n(F)$ is the quotient $\mathrm{SL}_n(F)/Z(\mathrm{SL}_n(F))$ of the special linear
group $\mathrm{SL}_n(F)$ of $n \times n$ matrices over $F$ with determinant $1$ by its centre.

articles.title: Element-order spectrum of a group
articles.statement:
The spectrum $\pi_e(G)$ of a group $G$ is the set of
orders of the elements of $G$, where an element of infinite order counts as having order $0$.

articles.title: Subgroup or quotient of a normal subgroup
articles.statement:
For groups $A$ and $B$, the statement that $A$
is isomorphic to a subgroup of $B$ or to a quotient of a normal subgroup of $B$: there is an
injective homomorphism $A \to B$, or there are a normal subgroup $N$ of $B$ and a surjective
homomorphism $N \to A$.

articles.title: Finite groups with equal spectra, neither a subgroup or normal-subgroup quotient of the other (Kourovka 16.106)
articles.statement:
**Finite groups with equal spectra, neither a subgroup or normal-subgroup quotient of the other
(Kourovka 16.106).** There exist finite groups $G_1$ and $G_2$ such that:

- $G_1$ and $G_2$ have the same spectrum, where the spectrum $\pi_e(G)$ of a group $G$ is the set
  of orders of its elements;
- there is a bound $B$ such that every finite group $G$ with $\pi_e(G) = \pi_e(G_1)$ has order at
  most $B$;
- $G_1$ is not isomorphic to a subgroup of $G_2$ or to a quotient of a normal subgroup of $G_2$,
  and $G_2$ is not isomorphic to a subgroup of $G_1$ or to a quotient of a normal subgroup of $G_1$.

The bound on orders says that only finitely many finite groups have spectrum $\pi_e(G_1)$, up to
isomorphism. The Kourovka Archive gives the example $G_1 = L_{15}(2^{60}).3$ and
$G_2 = L_{15}(2^{60}).5$ (Grechkoseeva).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 16.106 (W. J. Shi); resolution: M. A. Grechkoseeva, Algebra and Logic 47 (2008), no. 4, 229-241, Kourovka Archive, Problem 16.106 (answer: Yes, there do, for example G₁ = L₁₅(2⁶⁰).3 and G₂ = L₁₅(2⁶⁰).5).

articles.title: Finite groups with equal spectra, neither a subgroup or normal-subgroup quotient of the other (problem)
articles.statement:
**Finite groups with equal spectra, neither a subgroup or normal-subgroup quotient of the
other (problem).** The statement that there exist finite groups $G_1$ and $G_2$ with the same
spectrum $\pi_e(G_1) = \pi_e(G_2)$ (the set of orders of elements), such that every finite group
with spectrum $\pi_e(G_1)$ has order at most some fixed bound $B$, and such that neither of $G_1$,
$G_2$ is isomorphic to a subgroup or to a quotient of a normal subgroup of the other.

This is Kourovka Notebook Problem 16.106 (W. J. Shi), which asks for $h(\pi_e(G_1)) < \infty$,
where $h(\Gamma)$ is the number of finite groups with spectrum $\Gamma$ up to isomorphism; the
bound on orders is equivalent, since there are finitely many groups of each order.

articles.title: Exclusive classification of groups of order 10, product form
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group
of order $10$, let $C_n$ denote the cyclic group of order $n$, and let $D_5$ denote the dihedral
group of order $10$. Then exactly one of the following holds: $G$ is isomorphic to the direct
product $C_5 \times C_2$, or $G$ is isomorphic to $D_5$.

The product $C_5 \times C_2$ is cyclic and $D_5$ is not, so the two alternatives cannot both hold.

articles.title: Classification of groups of order 10, product form
articles.statement:
Let $C_n$ denote the cyclic group of
order $n$ and let $D_5$ denote the dihedral group of order $10$. Every finite group of order $10$
