is isomorphic to the direct product $C_5 \times C_2$ or to $D_5$.

articles.title: Exclusive classification of groups of order 10
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group of order $10$.
Then exactly one of the following holds: $G$ is isomorphic to the cyclic group $C_{10}$ of order
$10$, or $G$ is isomorphic to the dihedral group $D_5$ of order $10$.

The two alternatives cannot both hold, since $C_{10}$ is cyclic, $D_5$ is not, and cyclicity is
preserved under isomorphism.

articles.title: Classification of groups of order 10
articles.statement:
Every finite group of order $10$ is isomorphic
either to the cyclic group $C_{10}$ of order $10$ or to the dihedral group $D_5$ of order $10$.

articles.title: Noncyclic groups of order 10 are dihedral
articles.statement:
Every finite group of order $10$ that is not
cyclic is isomorphic to the dihedral group $D_5$ of order $10$.

## Sources

- the generators and inversion argument are adapted from the archived AlgebraNotes source; the final isomorphism uses the shared index-two constructor.

articles.title: Spectrum of a group
articles.statement:
The spectrum $\omega(G)$ of a group $G$ is the set of orders of its
elements, where an element of infinite order is counted as having order $0$.

articles.title: No three non-isomorphic finite non-abelian simple groups are isospectral
articles.statement:
There do not exist
three pairwise non-isomorphic finite non-abelian simple groups $G_1, G_2, G_3$ with
$\omega(G_1) = \omega(G_2) = \omega(G_3)$, where the spectrum $\omega(G)$ of a group $G$ is the
set of orders of its elements.

This answers Kourovka Problem 16.25 (A. V. Vasil'ev) in the negative; the Kourovka Archive cites
Buturlakin (2010).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 16.25 (A. V. Vasil'ev); resolution: A. A. Buturlakin, Sib. Èlektron. Mat. Izv. 7 (2010), 111-114, Kourovka Archive, Problem 16.25 (No).

articles.title: Three isospectral finite simple groups
articles.statement:
Kourovka 16.25 (A. V. Vasil'ev): there are three pairwise non-isomorphic finite non-abelian
simple groups with the same spectrum.

articles.title: Dihedral groups from a cyclic subgroup of index two
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group and let
$H$ be a cyclic subgroup of $G$ of index $2$. If $g^2 = 1$ for every element $g$ of $G$ that is
not in $H$, then $G$ is isomorphic to the dihedral group $D_n$ of order $2n$, where $n = |H|$.

articles.title: At most $k$ isomorphism types with spectrum $\Gamma$
articles.statement:
For a set $\Gamma$ of natural numbers
and a natural number $k$, this property holds when, for any finite groups $G_0, \dots, G_k$ (not
necessarily distinct) whose spectra $\pi_e(G_i)$ (the sets of orders of elements of $G_i$) all
equal $\Gamma$, there are indices $i \ne j$ with $G_i \cong G_j$.

This expresses $h(\Gamma) \le k$, where $h(\Gamma)$ is the number of isomorphism classes of finite
groups with spectrum $\Gamma$, without counting isomorphism classes directly.

articles.title: Spectrum of a group (Kourovka 13.63)
articles.statement:
For a group $G$, the spectrum $\pi_e(G)$ is the set
of orders of elements of $G$, where an element of infinite order counts as having order $0$.

articles.title: The spectrum of a group (Kourovka 12.84)
articles.statement:
The spectrum of a group $G$ is the set
$\{\operatorname{ord}(g) : g \in G\}$ of the orders of its elements, where an element of infinite
order is counted as having order $0$.

articles.title: Infinitely many isomorphism types with spectrum $\Gamma$
articles.statement:
For a set $\Gamma$ of natural
numbers, this property holds when, for every natural number $n$, there are $n$ pairwise
non-isomorphic finite groups $G_0, \dots, G_{n-1}$ whose spectra $\pi_e(G_i)$ (the sets of orders
of elements of $G_i$) all equal $\Gamma$.

This expresses $h(\Gamma) = \infty$, where $h(\Gamma)$ is the number of isomorphism classes of
finite groups with spectrum $\Gamma$.

articles.title: No uniform bound on the number of groups with a given spectrum
articles.statement:
For a set $\Gamma$ of natural
numbers, let $h(\Gamma)$ be the number of isomorphism classes of finite groups $G$ whose spectrum
$\pi_e(G)$ (set of element orders) is $\Gamma$; $h(\Gamma) \le k$ means that among any $k + 1$
finite groups with spectrum $\Gamma$ two are isomorphic, and $h(\Gamma) = \infty$ means that for
every $n$ there are $n$ pairwise non-isomorphic finite groups with spectrum $\Gamma$. Kourovka
Problem 13.63 has a negative answer: there is no natural number $k$ such that for every set
$\Gamma$ of natural numbers, either $h(\Gamma) \le k$ or $h(\Gamma) = \infty$.

Zavarnitsine proves $h(\pi_e(L_3(7^{3^r}))) = r + 1$ for every $r \ge 0$, where $L_3(q)$ is the
projective special linear group $\mathrm{PSL}_3(q)$, so $h$ takes every positive finite value and
no $k$ works.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 13.63 (W. J. Shi); resolution: A. V. Zavarnitsine, J. Group Theory 7 (2004), no. 1, 81-97, h(π_e(L_3(7^(3^r)))) = r + 1 for every r ≥ 0; Kourovka Archive, Problem 13.63 (answer: No, there is no such number).

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 13.63 (bounded or infinite number of groups per spectrum)
articles.statement:
The proposition,
asked about by W. J. Shi, that there is a natural number $k$ such that for every set $\Gamma$ of
natural numbers, either $h(\Gamma) \le k$ or $h(\Gamma) = \infty$, where $h(\Gamma)$ is the number
of isomorphism classes of finite groups $G$ whose spectrum $\pi_e(G)$ (set of element orders) is
$\Gamma$. Here $h(\Gamma) \le k$ means that among any $k + 1$ finite groups with spectrum $\Gamma$
two are isomorphic, and $h(\Gamma) = \infty$ means that for every $n$ there are $n$ pairwise
non-isomorphic finite groups with spectrum $\Gamma$.

articles.title: Two isospectral finite groups do not force infinitely many
articles.statement:
There are a set $\Omega$ of
natural numbers and a natural number $k$ such that two non-isomorphic finite groups have set of
element orders $\Omega$, but there are no $k$ pairwise non-isomorphic finite groups whose set of
element orders is $\Omega$.

For example, by Theorem 2.1(iii) of the survey of Grechkoseeva, Mazurov, Shi, Vasil'ev and Yang,
the finite groups with the set of element orders of $S_6(2)$ are exactly $S_6(2)$ and
$O_8^+(2)$, which have different orders. The Kourovka Archive answers 12.84 "No, it is not"
(V. D. Mazurov, 1994).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 12.84 (well-known problem; S. A. Syskin); resolution: V. D. Mazurov, Algebra and Logic 33 (1994), no. 1, 49-55; M. A. Grechkoseeva, V. D. Mazurov, W. Shi, A. V. Vasil'ev and N. Yang, Finite groups isospectral to simple groups, arXiv:2111.15198, Kourovka Archive, Problem 12.84: No, it is not; Grechkoseeva et al., Theorem 2.1(iii): a finite group has the spectrum of S_6(2) if and only if it is S_6(2) or O_8^+(2), https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.15198.

articles.title: Syskin's question on groups with a given spectrum (Kourovka 12.84)
articles.statement:
The proposition that
for every set $\Omega$ of natural numbers, if two non-isomorphic finite groups both have set of
element orders $\Omega$, then for every natural number $k$ there are $k$ pairwise non-isomorphic
finite groups whose set of element orders is $\Omega$; that is, infinitely many.

articles.title: Amiri's theorem (Kourovka Problem 18.1)
articles.statement:
For every finite group $G$, of order $n$ say, there is
a bijection $f$ from $G$ onto the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ such that for every
$x \in G$ the order of $x$ divides the additive order of $f(x)$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 18.1 (I. M. Isaacs); resolution: M. Amiri, J. Pure Appl. Algebra 228 (2024), no. 7, 107632 (preprint arXiv:2002.11455), abstract (for any finite group G of order n there is a bijection f from G onto C_n with o(x) | o(f(x)) for all x); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 18.1 solved (Yes, it does), https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.11455.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 18.1 (statement)
articles.statement:
The statement that for every finite group $G$, of order
$n$ say, there is a bijection $f$ from $G$ onto the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ such that
for every $x \in G$ the order of $x$ divides the additive order of $f(x)$.

articles.title: Finite soluble groups satisfy a linear prime-divisor bound
articles.statement:
There are natural numbers $a$ and
$b$ such that for every finite soluble group $G$ and every natural number $m$, if the order of
every element of $G$ has at most $m$ distinct prime divisors, then $|G|$ has at most $am + b$
distinct prime divisors. That is, Kourovka Problem 14.66 has a positive answer.

Resolved true: the Kourovka Archive answers 14.66 "Yes, it does", citing Keller.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 14.66 (A. Moretó); resolution: T. M. Keller, J. Algebra 178 (1995), no. 2, 643-652, Kourovka Archive, Problem 14.66 (answer: Yes, it does).

articles.title: Linear bound on the prime divisors of a finite soluble group (Kourovka 14.66)
articles.statement:
The
statement, posed by A. Moretó, that there are natural numbers $a$ and $b$ such that for every
finite soluble group $G$ and every natural number $m$, if the order of every element of $G$ has at
most $m$ distinct prime divisors, then $|G|$ has at most $am + b$ distinct prime divisors.

Equivalently, $|\pi(G)| \le a\,\nu(G) + b$ for every finite soluble group $G$, where $\pi(G)$ is
the set of primes dividing $|G|$ and $\nu(G)$ is the largest number of distinct primes dividing
the order of a single element of $G$.

articles.title: Set of element orders (Kourovka 12.39)
articles.statement:
For a group $G$, the set of natural numbers that
occur as the order of some element of $G$, where an element of infinite order is counted as
having order $0$.

articles.title: Finite simple groups are recognized by order and element orders
articles.statement:
For every finite group $G$
and every finite simple group $S$, if $G$ and $S$ have the same order and the same set of element
orders, then $G$ is isomorphic to $S$. That is, Shi's conjecture (Kourovka Problem 12.39) holds.

Here a simple group may be cyclic of prime order. The Kourovka Archive records the answer "Yes,
they must", proved by Xu and Shi and by Vasil'ev, Grechkoseeva and Mazurov.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 12.39 (W. J. Shi; A. S. Kondratiev); resolution: M. C. Xu and W. J. Shi, Algebra Colloq. 10 (2003), 427-443; A. V. Vasil'ev, M. A. Grechkoseeva and V. D. Mazurov, Algebra Logic 48 (2009), 385-409, Kourovka Archive, Problem 12.39: Yes, they must.

articles.title: Shi's conjecture on recognition by order and element orders (Kourovka 12.39)
articles.statement:
The
statement that for every finite group $G$ and every finite simple group $S$, if $G$ and $S$ have
the same order and the same set of element orders, then $G$ is isomorphic to $S$.

articles.title: Large alternating groups are recognizable by spectrum
articles.statement:
There is a natural number $N$ such that
for every $n \ge N$, every finite group $G$ whose set of element orders equals that of the
alternating group $A_n$ is isomorphic to $A_n$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 16.107 (W. J. Shi); resolution: I. B. Gorshkov, Recognizability of alternating groups by spectrum, Algebra and Logic 52 (2013), no. 1, 41-45, arXiv:1302.4825, abstract (the simple alternating groups Aₙ are recognizable by spectrum for n ≠ 6, 10); Kourovka Archive, Problem 16.107 (answer: Yes, it is), https://arxiv.org/abs/1302.4825.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 16.107 on recognition of alternating groups by spectrum
articles.statement:
This proposition
asserts that there is a natural number $N$ such that for every $n \ge N$, every finite group $G$
with the same spectrum (set of element orders) as the alternating group $A_n$ is isomorphic to
$A_n$.

articles.title: Groups isospectral to an alternating group (Kourovka Problem 16.27)
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural
number and let $G$ be a finite group whose spectrum, the set of orders of its elements, equals the
spectrum of the alternating group $A_n$. Then every composition series of $G$ has at most one
non-abelian factor.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 16.27 (A. V. Vasil'ev and V. D. Mazurov); resolution: I. B. Gorshkov, Algebra and Logic 52 (2013), no. 1, 41-45, Kourovka Archive, Problem 16.27 (Yes, it is).

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 16.27 (statement)
articles.statement:
The statement that for every natural number $n$ and
every finite group $G$ whose spectrum, the set of orders of its elements, equals the spectrum of
the alternating group $A_n$, every composition series of $G$ has at most one non-abelian factor.

The problem was posed by A. V. Vasil'ev and V. D. Mazurov.

articles.title: Spectrum of a group
articles.statement:
The spectrum $\pi_e(G)$ of a group $G$ is the set of orders of the
elements of $G$, where an element of infinite order is assigned order $0$.

articles.title: Finite composition series
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group and $m$ a natural number. A sequence
$s_0, s_1, \dots, s_m$ of subgroups of $G$ is a composition series of length $m$ if $s_0$ is the
trivial subgroup, $s_m = G$, and for each $i < m$ the subgroup $s_i$ is a normal subgroup of
$s_{i+1}$ and the quotient $s_{i+1}/s_i$ is a simple group.

articles.title: Non-abelian factor of a chain of subgroups
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group, let $s_0, s_1, \dots, s_m$
be subgroups of $G$, and let $i < m$. The $i$-th factor of the chain is non-abelian if
$s_i \cap s_{i+1}$ is a normal subgroup of $s_{i+1}$ and the quotient group
$s_{i+1}/(s_i \cap s_{i+1})$ is non-abelian, that is, it has elements $x, y$ with $xy \ne yx$.
When $s_i \le s_{i+1}$, this quotient is $s_{i+1}/s_i$.

articles.title: Groups with element orders $1$ to $7$ are isomorphic to $A_7$
articles.statement:
Every group, finite or
infinite, whose set of element orders is exactly $\{1, 2, \dots, 7\}$ is isomorphic to the
alternating group $A_7$. This answers Kourovka Problem 19.80 positively (Mamontov and Jabara).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 19.80 (W. J. Shi); resolution: A. S. Mamontov and E. Jabara, Recognizing A₇ by its set of element orders, Siberian Math. J. 62 (2021), no. 1, 93-104, doi:10.1134/S0037446621010109, Kourovka Archive, Problem 19.80: Yes, it is true, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 19.80 ($OC_7$-groups)
articles.statement:
The proposition, asked by W. J. Shi, that every
$OC_7$-group, that is, every group whose set of element orders is exactly $\{1, 2, \dots, 7\}$
(such a group is periodic), is isomorphic to the alternating group $A_7$.

articles.title: Spectrum of a group
articles.statement:
The spectrum $\omega(G)$ of a group $G$ is the set of natural numbers
that are orders of elements of $G$, where an element of infinite order is assigned order $0$.

articles.title: Lytkina–Kuznetsov theorem: PSL(2, 7) is recognizable by spectrum
articles.statement:
Every group $G$, finite or
infinite, whose set of element orders $\{\operatorname{ord}(g) : g \in G\}$ equals
$\{1, 2, 3, 4, 7\}$ is isomorphic to $L_2(7) = \mathrm{PSL}(2, 7)$, the projective special linear
group of $2 \times 2$ matrices over the field $\mathbb{Z}/7\mathbb{Z}$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 16.57 (V. D. Mazurov); resolution: D. V. Lytkina and A. A. Kuznetsov, Sib. Èlektron. Mat. Izv. 4 (2007), 136-140, Kourovka Archive, Problem 16.57 (Yes, it is).

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 16.57: recognition of PSL(2, 7) by spectrum
articles.statement:
The statement that every
group $G$, finite or infinite, whose set of element orders $\{\operatorname{ord}(g) : g \in G\}$
equals $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 7\}$ is isomorphic to $L_2(7) = \mathrm{PSL}(2, 7)$, the projective special
linear group of $2 \times 2$ matrices over the field $\mathbb{Z}/7\mathbb{Z}$.

articles.title: Infinitely many simple groups with proper subgroups of equal prime set
articles.statement:
Resolved false: the Kourovka Archive records (V. I. Zenkov) that the symplectic groups `G =
S_{4k}(2^s)` have proper subgroups `H ≅ Ω⁻_{4k}(2^s)` with `π(H) = π(G)`, an infinite family of
non-alternating finite simple groups. Source: E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved
Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of
Solved Problems, Problem 11.64 (V. S. Monakhov); resolution: V. I. Zenkov, letter of 10 March 1994,
Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.64: "No, there are infinitely many such groups. If `G = S_{4k}(2^s)`
and `H ≅ Ω⁻_{4k}(2^s)`, then `π(G) = π(H)`", https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 11.64 (Monakhov)
articles.statement:
The statement that there is a natural number $N$ such
that every finite simple group $G$ that is not isomorphic to the alternating group $A_n$ for any
natural number $n$ and has a proper subgroup $H$ with $\pi(H) = \pi(G)$ satisfies $|G| \le N$,
where $\pi(X)$ denotes the set of prime divisors of the order $|X|$.

Since there are finitely many groups of each order, this says that only finitely many such groups
$G$ exist up to isomorphism.

articles.title: Power-equation type does not characterize almost simple groups
articles.statement:
There exist finite
groups $G$ and $H$ such that $G$ is almost simple, $G$ and $H$ have the same power-equation type,
and $G$ is not isomorphic to $H$. That is, the conjecture of Kourovka Problem 21.134(b) is false.

Kourovka Notebook v46 records that J. G. Thompson had already given a negative answer to part (b).

## Sources

- Yu Li and Wujie Shi, A Note on Thompson Problem, arXiv:2303.09460v1 (2023); published in Ricerche di Matematica 74(1) (2025), 559-563, https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.09460v1; The Kourovka Notebook: Unsolved Problems in Group Theory, 21st edition, Problem 21.134, arXiv:1401.0300v46, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46.

articles.title: Characterization of almost simple groups by power-equation type (Kourovka 21.134(b))
articles.statement:
The conjecture that for all finite groups $G$ and $H$, if $G$ is almost simple and $G$ and $H$
have the same power-equation type, then $G$ is isomorphic to $H$.

articles.title: Almost simple group
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is almost simple when there is a nonabelian finite simple
group $S$ such that $G$ is isomorphic to a subgroup $A$ of the automorphism group
$\mathrm{Aut}(S)$ that contains the inner automorphism group $\mathrm{Inn}(S)$.

articles.title: Same power-equation type
articles.statement:
Two groups $G$ and $H$ have the same power-equation type when,
for every positive integer $n$, the equation $x^n = 1$ has the same number of solutions in $G$ as
in $H$. An infinite set of solutions is counted as $0$, so the notion is meant for finite
groups.

articles.title: Groups of the same type
articles.statement:
Two groups $G$ and $H$ have the same type when, for every integer
$n \ge 1$, the equation $x^n = 1$ has the same number of solutions in $G$ as in $H$, where an
infinite set of solutions counts as having $0$ elements.

articles.title: Solubility is not determined by the type
articles.statement:
The answer to Kourovka Problem 12.37 is negative:
there are finite groups $G$ and $H$ of the same type such that $H$ is soluble and $G$ is not
soluble.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 12.37 (J. G. Thompson; A. S. Kondratiev, W. J. Shi); resolution: P. Piwek, Algebra Number Theory 19 (2025), no. 8, 1663-1670, the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 12.37 solved: No, not always.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 12.37 (J. G. Thompson)
articles.statement:
Every finite group of the same type as a finite
soluble group is soluble: if $G$ and $H$ are finite groups of the same type and $H$ is soluble,
then $G$ is soluble.

articles.title: Order and totient sum do not determine simplicity (Kourovka 19.25)
articles.statement:
There are finite groups
$G$ and $H$ of the same order with $\sum_{g \in G} \varphi(|g|) = \sum_{h \in H} \varphi(|h|)$,
where $|g|$ is the order of $g$ and $\varphi$ is Euler's totient function, such that $G$ is
simple and $H$ is not simple. So the Curtin–Pourgholi question has a negative answer.

Van Doorn, Judin, Monticone and Morrison (Theorem 4.1) take for $G$ the projective special
unitary group $\mathrm{PSU}(3, 3)$, which is simple of order $6048$, and
$H = C_6 \times S_4 \times F$, where $C_6$ is the cyclic group of order $6$, $S_4$ is the symmetric
group on four letters and $F$ is the Frobenius group of order $42$; both totient sums equal
$23984$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 19.25 (B. Curtin, G. R. Pourgholi); resolution: P. Monticone, Kourovka Notebook Problem 19.25, solution note (2026); W. van Doorn, E. Judin, P. Monticone and D. Morrison, On Some Problems from the Kourovka Notebook, preprint, arXiv:2607.17477 (2026), Section 4, Theorem 4.1 with Lemma 4.2 (G = PSU(3, 3) is simple, by Iwasawa's criterion, of order 6048 with totient sum 23984) and Lemma 4.3 (H = C₆ × S₄ × F, F the Frobenius group of order 42, has the same order and totient sum and is not simple); the solution was found and verified in Lean by the AI system Aristotle (abstract and Appendix A); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 19.25 solved: No, it need not be (AI solution confirmed by GAP), https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17477.

articles.title: Curtin–Pourgholi question on totient sums and simplicity (Kourovka 19.25)
articles.statement:
The statement
that for all finite groups $G$ and $H$ of the same order with
$\sum_{g \in G} \varphi(|g|) = \sum_{h \in H} \varphi(|h|)$, where $|g|$ is the order of $g$ and
$\varphi$ is Euler's totient function, if $G$ is simple then $H$ is simple.

articles.title: Centralizer dimension at most $k$
articles.statement:
A group $G$ has $c$-dimension at most $k$ if every
strictly decreasing chain $C_G(X_0) > C_G(X_1) > \cdots > C_G(X_m)$ of centralizers of subsets
$X_0, \dots, X_m$ of $G$ has length $m \le k$.

articles.title: Buturlakin's theorem on locally finite groups of finite $c$-dimension
articles.statement:
There is a function
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that the following holds for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$. Let $G$
be a locally finite group of $c$-dimension at most $k$, let $R$ be a normal locally soluble
subgroup of $G$ that contains every normal locally soluble subgroup of $G$ (the locally soluble
radical), and let $S$ be the preimage in $G$ of the socle of $G/R$. Then there is a subgroup $A$ of
$G$ with $S \le A$ such that $xyx^{-1}y^{-1} \in S$ for all $x, y \in A$ (so $A/S$ is an abelian
subgroup of $G/S$), and the index $|G : A|$ is finite and at most $f(k)$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 19.101 (A. V. Vasil'ev); resolution: A. A. Buturlakin, J. Algebra Appl. 18 (2019), no. 12, 1950223, 12 pp, Kourovka Archive, Problem 19.101: Yes, it is true, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Vasil'ev's abelian section bound (Kourovka 19.101)
articles.statement:
The statement that there is a function
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and every locally finite
group $G$ of $c$-dimension at most $k$ the following holds: if $R$ is a normal locally soluble
subgroup of $G$ containing every normal locally soluble subgroup of $G$ (the locally soluble
radical) and $S$ is the preimage in $G$ of the socle of $G/R$, then there is a subgroup $A$ of $G$
with $S \le A$ such that $xyx^{-1}y^{-1} \in S$ for all $x, y \in A$ (so $A/S$ is an abelian
subgroup of $G/S$), and the index $|G : A|$ is finite and at most $f(k)$.

articles.title: Locally finite groups
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is locally finite if every finitely generated subgroup
of $G$ is finite.

articles.title: Locally soluble subgroups
articles.statement:
A subgroup $H$ of a group $G$ is locally soluble if every
finitely generated subgroup of $H$ is soluble.

articles.title: Minimal normal subgroups
articles.statement:
A subgroup $M$ of a group $Q$ is a minimal normal subgroup if $M$
is normal in $Q$, $M \ne \{1\}$, and every normal subgroup $N$ of $Q$ with $N \le M$ is either
$\{1\}$ or $M$.

articles.title: Preimage of the socle of a quotient
articles.statement:
For a normal subgroup $R$ of a group $G$, the preimage
in $G$ of the socle of $G/R$ under the quotient map $G \to G/R$.

articles.title: Socle
articles.statement:
The socle of a group $Q$ is the subgroup of $Q$ generated by all minimal normal
subgroups of $Q$; it is the trivial subgroup when $Q$ has no minimal normal subgroup.

articles.title: Every periodic group embeds in a simple periodic group
articles.statement:
For every group $G$ in which every
element has finite order, there are a simple group $S$ in which every element has finite order and
an injective homomorphism $G \to S$. This answers Kourovka Problem 11.106 (R. Phillips) in the
affirmative; the result is due to A. Yu. Olshanskii (1992).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.106 (R. Phillips); resolution: A. Yu. Olshanskii, Embedding periodic groups in simple periodic groups, Ukr. Mat. Zh. 44 (1992), 845-847 (Russian); English translation: Ukrain. Math. J. 44 (1992), 761-763, Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.106 ("Yes").

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 11.106 (periodic groups in simple periodic groups)
articles.statement:
The statement, posed
by R. Phillips, that every periodic group embeds in a simple periodic group: for every group $G$ in
which every element has finite order, there are a simple group $S$ in which every element has finite
order and an injective homomorphism $G \to S$.

articles.title: Mazurov's fixed-point question for free Burnside groups has a negative answer
articles.statement:
There exist
primes $q$ and $p$ such that the free Burnside group $B(q, p)$ of rank $q$ and exponent $p$ is
infinite and the automorphism of $B(q, p)$ induced by the cyclic permutation $x_i \mapsto x_{i+1}$
(indices mod $q$) of its free generators $x_0, \dots, x_{q-1}$ fixes no nontrivial element of
$B(q, p)$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 17.70 (V. D. Mazurov); resolution: V. S. Atabekyan, Mazurov's question on fixed points of automorphisms of free Burnside groups, preprint, arXiv:2609.33941 (2026), Theorem 1.1 (for every odd m ≥ 3 there is q_m such that for every prime q > q_m the automorphism of B(m, q) of order m cyclically permuting the free generators has no nontrivial fixed points; B(m, n) is infinite for all odd n ≥ 665 and m > 1 by Adian's theorem, as recalled there); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 17.70 solved (No, it does not for all q ≥ 3 and all sufficiently large p), https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33941.

articles.title: Mazurov's fixed-point question for free Burnside groups (Kourovka 17.70)
articles.statement:
The assertion
that for all primes $q$ and $p$ such that the free Burnside group $B(q, p)$ of rank $q$ and
exponent $p$ is infinite, the automorphism of $B(q, p)$ induced by the cyclic permutation
$x_i \mapsto x_{i+1}$ (indices mod $q$) of its free generators $x_0, \dots, x_{q-1}$ fixes some
nontrivial element of $B(q, p)$.

articles.title: Free Burnside group
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $m$ and $n$, the free Burnside group $B(m, n)$ is
the quotient of the free group $F_m$ on $m$ generators by the normal subgroup generated by all
$n$-th powers $w^n$ with $w \in F_m$.

articles.title: Golod group (Kourovka 11.101)
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a field, $N$ a non-unital associative
$k$-algebra and $y_1, \dots, y_r \in N$. The Golod group of $y$ is the subgroup of the group of
units of the unitization $k \oplus N$ generated by the units that are equal to $1 + y_i$ for some
$i$. When every $1 + y_i$ is invertible (for example when $N$ is nil), this is the subgroup
$\langle 1 + y_1, \dots, 1 + y_r \rangle$ of the adjoint group $1 + N$.

articles.title: There is a Golod group with trivial centre
articles.statement:
There exist a field $k$ of prime characteristic
$p$, an integer $r \ge 2$, a non-unital associative $k$-algebra $N$ and elements
$y_1, \dots, y_r \in N$ such that $N$ is generated by $y_1, \dots, y_r$ as a non-unital
$k$-algebra, every element of $N$ is nilpotent, for every natural number $n$ some product of $n$
elements of $N$ is nonzero, and the Golod group of $y$ has trivial centre. Since a trivial centre
is finite, this answers Kourovka Problem 11.101 (A. V. Timofeenko) positively (V. A. Sereda and
A. I. Sozutov).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.101 (A. V. Timofeenko); resolution: V. A. Sereda and A. I. Sozutov, Algebra and Logic 45, no. 2 (2006), 134-138, Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.101 ("Yes, there is a Golod group with trivial centre").

articles.title: Existence of a Golod group with trivial centre
articles.statement:
Kourovka 11.101 (A. V. Timofeenko), in the strong form proved: some Golod group has trivial
centre (the problem asks for finite centre). A Golod group (9.76) is
`⟨1 + x₁ + I, …, 1 + x_r + I⟩ ≤ 1 + F/I` for `r ≥ 2`, `F` the free associative algebra without
constant term on `x₁, …, x_r` over a field of characteristic `p > 0` and `F/I` a non-nilpotent
nil-algebra; equivalently `N = F/I` is a non-unital algebra generated by `y₁, …, y_r` that is nil
but not nilpotent (some product of `n` elements is nonzero for every `n`).

articles.title: Golod group (Kourovka 12.102)
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a field, $N$ a non-unital associative
$k$-algebra and $y_1, \dots, y_r \in N$. The Golod group of $y$ is the subgroup of the group of
units of the unitization $k \oplus N$ generated by the units that are equal to $1 + y_i$ for some
$i$. When every $1 + y_i$ is invertible (for example when $N$ is nil), this is the subgroup
$\langle 1 + y_1, \dots, 1 + y_r \rangle$ of the adjoint group $1 + N$.

articles.title: Not every proper quotient of a Golod group is residually finite
articles.statement:
The statement that every
proper factor group of a Golod group is residually finite is false: there exist a field $k$ of
prime characteristic $p$, an integer $r \ge 2$, a non-unital associative $k$-algebra $N$ and
elements $y_1, \dots, y_r \in N$ such that $N$ is generated by $y_1, \dots, y_r$ as a non-unital
$k$-algebra, every element of $N$ is nilpotent and for every natural number $n$ some product of
$n$ elements of $N$ is nonzero, together with a nontrivial normal subgroup $K$ of the Golod group
$\Gamma$ of $y$ and an element $x \in \Gamma$ with $x \notin K$, such that every normal subgroup of
finite index in $\Gamma$ that contains $K$ also contains $x$. This answers Kourovka Problem 12.102
(V. P. Shunkov) in the negative (L. Hammoudi).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 12.102 (V. P. Shunkov); resolution: L. Hammoudi, Algebra Colloq. 5 (1998), 371-376, Kourovka Archive, Problem 12.102: "No, not every", https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Residual finiteness of proper quotients of Golod groups (Kourovka 12.102)
articles.statement:
This is the
statement that the following holds for every field $k$ of prime characteristic $p$, every
non-unital associative $k$-algebra $N$, every $r \ge 2$ and all $y_1, \dots, y_r \in N$ such that
$N$ is generated by $y_1, \dots, y_r$ as a non-unital $k$-algebra, every element of $N$ is
nilpotent, and for every natural number $n$ some product of $n$ elements of $N$ is nonzero: if
$\Gamma$ is the Golod group of $y$, then for every nontrivial normal subgroup $K$ of $\Gamma$ and
every $x \in \Gamma$ with $x \notin K$ there is a normal subgroup $M$ of finite index in $\Gamma$
with $K \le M$ and $x \notin M$. In other words, every proper factor group $\Gamma / K$ of a
Golod group $\Gamma$ is residually finite. This is Shunkov's question, Kourovka Problem 12.102.

articles.title: Exponent 4 is not detected on boundedly generated subgroups
articles.statement:
There is no function
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with the following property: for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, every
group $G$ whose $k$-th derived subgroup $G^{(k)}$ is trivial, and every generating set $A$ of $G$,
if $x^4 = 1$ for every element $x$ of every subgroup generated by a finite subset of $A$ with at
most $f(k)$ elements, then $x^4 = 1$ for every $x \in G$. This is the negative answer to Kourovka
Notebook Problem 13.10 (V. V. Bludov), given by G. S. Deryabina and A. N. Krasil'nikov (2003).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 13.10 (V. V. Bludov); resolution: G. S. Deryabina and A. N. Krasil'nikov, Siberian Math. J. 44 (2003), no. 1, 58-60, Kourovka Archive, Problem 13.10: No, there is not.

articles.title: Exponent 4 detected on boundedly generated subgroups (Kourovka 13.10)
articles.statement:
The proposition
that there is a function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with the following property: for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$, every group $G$ whose $k$-th derived subgroup $G^{(k)}$ is trivial (a soluble
group of derived length at most $k$), and every generating set $A$ of $G$, if $x^4 = 1$ for every
element $x$ of every subgroup generated by a finite subset of $A$ with at most $f(k)$ elements,
then $x^4 = 1$ for every $x \in G$. This is Kourovka Notebook Problem 13.10 (V. V. Bludov).

articles.title: Groups finitely presented in a Burnside variety
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $m$ and a
finite set $S$ of elements of the free group on $x_0, \dots, x_{m-1}$, this is the group with
generators $x_0, \dots, x_{m-1}$ and relators $S$ together with $w^n$ for every element $w$ of the
free group: the group finitely presented by $S$ in the Burnside variety $\mathfrak{B}_n$ of groups
of exponent $n$.

articles.title: Higman embedding theorem for Burnside varieties
articles.statement:
There is $n_0$ such that for every odd
$n \ge n_0$, every group of exponent $n$ given by generators $x_0, x_1, \dots$ and a recursively
enumerable set of relators embeds in a group finitely presented in the Burnside variety
$\mathfrak{B}_n$: a group with generators $x_0, \dots, x_{m-1}$ for some $m$ whose relators are a
finite set $S$ together with $w^n$ for every word $w$.

Olshanskii proves this with the ambient group 2-generated; the statement here does not require it.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 12.32 (S. V. Ivanov); resolution: A. Yu. Olshanskii, Groups finitely presented in Burnside varieties, J. Algebra 560 (2020), 960-1052, Theorem 1.1 (finitely generated groups) and Corollary 1.2 (countably many generators; the ambient group can be taken 2-generated), for all odd n ≥ C; Kourovka Archive, Problem 12.32.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 12.32: Higman embedding for Burnside varieties
articles.statement:
There is $n_0$ such that
for every odd $n \ge n_0$ the following holds. Let $G$ be a group given by generators
$x_0, x_1, \dots$ and a recursively enumerable set of relators, and suppose that $g^n = 1$ for
every $g \in G$. Then for some $m$ and some finite set $S$ of elements of the free group on
$x_0, \dots, x_{m-1}$, there is an injective homomorphism from $G$ to the group finitely presented
by $S$ in the Burnside variety $\mathfrak{B}_n$, whose relators are $S$ together with $w^n$ for
every element $w$ of that free group.

The relators are words in the generators, and recursive enumerability refers to these words.

articles.title: Uncountably many infinite 2-group quotients of the (2, 4, 8) triangle group (Kourovka 16.101)
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma = \langle x, y \mid x^2 = y^4 = (xy)^8 = 1 \rangle$. There are an uncountable index set
$I$ and normal subgroups $N_i$ of $\Gamma$, for $i \in I$, such that every quotient $\Gamma / N_i$
is an infinite $2$-group (a group in which every element has order a power of $2$), and
$\Gamma / N_i \cong \Gamma / N_j$ only when $i = j$. So Wiegold's question has a positive answer.

The Kourovka Archive answers 16.101 "Yes, there do" (Grigorchuk; Minasyan, Olshanskii and
Sonkin).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 16.101 (J. Wiegold); resolution: R. I. Grigorchuk, Algebra Discrete Math. 2009, no. 4, 78-96; A. Minasyan, A. Yu. Olshanskii and D. Sonkin, Periodic quotients of hyperbolic and large groups, Groups Geom. Dyn. 3 (2009), no. 3, 423-452, arXiv:0804.3328, Kourovka Archive, Problem 16.101 (answer: Yes, there do); Minasyan, Olshanskii and Sonkin, abstract (continua of pairwise non-isomorphic periodic quotients, with a positive answer to Wiegold's question), https://arxiv.org/abs/0804.3328.

articles.title: Wiegold's question on 2-group quotients of the (2, 4, 8) triangle group (Kourovka 16.101)
articles.statement:
The statement that there are an uncountable index set $I$ and normal subgroups $N_i$ of
$\Gamma = \langle x, y \mid x^2 = y^4 = (xy)^8 = 1 \rangle$, for $i \in I$, such that every
quotient $\Gamma / N_i$ is an infinite $2$-group (a group in which every element has order a
power of $2$), and $\Gamma / N_i \cong \Gamma / N_j$ only when $i = j$.

articles.title: The (2, 4, 8) triangle group
articles.statement:
The $(2, 4, 8)$ triangle group is the group with
presentation $\langle x, y \mid x^2 = y^4 = (xy)^8 = 1 \rangle$.

articles.title: Positive answer to Kourovka Problem 10.62
articles.statement:
There is a periodic group $G$ that has no
subgroup of index $2$ and contains an involution $x$ such that the conjugacy class $X$ of $x$
generates $G$ and the product $yz$ has odd order for all $y, z \in X$.

Kinyon and Urban's 2026 preprint (an AI-generated solution confirmed by M. Amelio; Section 3.7,
Proposition 3.5) constructs, for every sufficiently large odd prime $p$, an infinite
three-generated perfect group of exponent $2p$ whose involutions form one conjugacy class
generating the group, the product of any two distinct involutions having order $p$; being perfect,
it has no subgroup of index $2$. The Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 10.62 solved, "Example
constructed".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 10.62 (A. I. Sozutov); resolution: M. Kinyon and J. Urban (with Codex gpt-6-astra), Results on problems from the Kourovka Notebook, preprint (2026), Section 3.7, Proposition 3.5 (built on Amelio's geometric construction); AI solution confirmed by M. Amelio; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 10.62 solved, https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/kourovka-mathematics.pdf.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 10.62 on involution classes with products of odd order
articles.statement:
The proposition
(Kourovka 10.62, A. I. Sozutov) that there is a periodic group $G$ that has no subgroup of index
$2$ and contains an involution $x$ such that the conjugacy class $X$ of $x$ generates $G$ and the
product $yz$ has odd order for all $y, z \in X$.

The condition includes $y = z$, where $yz = 1$ has order $1$.

articles.title: Composition series in Kurosh's sense
articles.statement:
A set $S$ of subgroups of a group $G$ is a
composition series of $G$ when it contains the trivial subgroup and $G$, it is totally ordered by
inclusion, it contains the join and the intersection of every subset of $S$, and for every jump
$A < B$ of $S$ (members $A \subsetneq B$ of $S$ with no member of $S$ strictly between them) $A$
is normal in $B$ and the quotient $B / A$ is a simple group.

articles.title: Locally finite group
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is locally finite when every subgroup of $G$ generated
by finitely many elements is finite.

articles.title: Locally finite simple groups need not be absolutely simple
articles.statement:
There is a locally finite simple
group $G$ with a composition series, in Kurosh's sense, other than the series consisting of the
trivial subgroup and $G$ alone. That is, the statement of Kourovka Problem 11.108, that every
locally finite simple group is absolutely simple, is false.

The Kourovka Archive answers 11.108 "No, not every", citing Meierfrankenfeld (1995), whose
Section 6 constructs countable locally finite simple groups $G$ that are not absolutely simple,
with an ascending series $M_1 \trianglelefteq M_2 \trianglelefteq \cdots$ of proper subgroups
whose union is $G$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.108 (R. Phillips); resolution: U. Meierfrankenfeld, Non-finitary locally finite simple groups, in: Proc. Int. Conf. Finite and Locally Finite Groups, Istanbul, 1994, Kluwer, 1995, 189-212, Section 6, countable locally finite simple groups that are not absolutely simple; Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.108 ("No, not every"), https://users.math.msu.edu/users/meierfra/Preprints/Nflfsg/nflfsg.pdf.

articles.title: Absolute simplicity of locally finite simple groups (Kourovka 11.108)
articles.statement:
The statement,
asked by R. Phillips, that every locally finite simple group $G$ is absolutely simple: every
composition series of $G$ in Kurosh's sense consists of the trivial subgroup and $G$ alone.

articles.title: Locally finite group
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is locally finite when for every finite subset $S$ of $G$
the subgroup generated by $S$ is finite, that is, every finitely generated subgroup of $G$ is
finite.

articles.title: Minimal condition on centralizers
articles.statement:
For a subset $X$ of a group $G$, write $C_G(X)$ for the
centralizer of $X$ in $G$. The group $G$ satisfies the minimal condition on centralizers when there
is no sequence of subsets $X_0, X_1, X_2, \ldots$ of $G$ whose centralizers form a strictly
descending chain $C_G(X_0) > C_G(X_1) > C_G(X_2) > \cdots$, where $H > K$ means that $K$ is a
proper subgroup of $H$.

articles.title: Every $2$-group with the minimal condition on centralizers is locally finite (Kourovka 11.103)
articles.statement:
Every group $G$ in which every element has order a power of $2$ and which satisfies the minimal
condition on centralizers is locally finite.

Wagner proved that the Sylow $2$-subgroups of a periodic group with the minimal condition on
centralizers are locally finite; a $2$-group is periodic and is its own Sylow $2$-subgroup. The
Kourovka Archive answers 11.103 "Yes, it is".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.103 (John S. Wilson); resolution: F. O. Wagner, Nilpotency in groups with the minimal condition on centralizers, J. Algebra 217, no. 2 (1999), 448-460, abstract: the Sylow 2-subgroups of a periodic group with the minimal condition on centralizers are locally finite and conjugate; Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.103, https://doi.org/10.1006/jabr.1998.7824.

articles.title: Wilson's question on $2$-groups with the minimal condition on centralizers (Kourovka problem 11.103)
articles.statement:
**Wilson's question on $2$-groups with the minimal condition on centralizers (Kourovka
problem 11.103).** The statement that every group $G$ in which every element has order a power of
$2$ and which satisfies the minimal condition on centralizers is locally finite.

articles.title: Monster of the first kind
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is a *monster of the first kind* (V. P. Shunkov)
when $G$ is infinite, $G$ has an element of order greater than $2$, and for every element $a$ of
order greater than $2$ and every proper subgroup $H$ of $G$ there is $g \in G \setminus H$ such
that $a$ and $g^{-1} a g$ generate $G$. Here an element of infinite order counts as having order
greater than $2$.

articles.title: Not every monster of the first kind is a torsion-free group modulo a central cyclic subgroup
articles.statement:
It is not the case that for every monster of the first kind $M$ there are a torsion-free group $E$
and a cyclic subgroup $C$ contained in the center of $E$ with $E / C \cong M$. So Kourovka
Problem 14.104 has a negative answer.

The Kourovka Archive answers 14.104 "No, not always" (A. I. Sozutov): if a torsion-free group $E$
has a central cyclic subgroup $C$ with $E / C \cong M$, then every finite subgroup of $M$ is
cyclic, and some monsters of the first kind have non-cyclic finite subgroups.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 14.104 (V. P. Shunkov); resolution: A. I. Sozutov, letter of 20 November 2001, Kourovka Archive, Problem 14.104: such an extension forces every finite subgroup of the monster to be cyclic, which fails for some monsters (answer: No, not always).

articles.title: Shunkov's question on central extensions of monsters
articles.statement:
Kourovka Problem 14.104
(V. P. Shunkov) asks whether this proposition holds: for every monster of the first kind $M$ there
are a torsion-free group $E$ and a cyclic subgroup $C$ contained in the center of $E$ such that
$E / C \cong M$.

articles.title: Frobenius group with given kernel and complement
articles.statement:
For subgroups $F$ and $H$ of a group $G$,
$G$ is a Frobenius group with kernel $F$ and complement $H$ (Kourovka 6.53) if $G = F \rtimes H$
(that is, $F$ is normal in $G$, $F \cap H = 1$ and $FH = G$), $F \ne 1$, $H \ne 1$,
$H \cap gHg^{-1} = 1$ for every $g \in G \setminus H$, and the non-trivial elements of $F$ are
exactly the elements of $G$ that lie in no conjugate $gHg^{-1}$ of $H$.

articles.title: Lytkina–Mazurov theorem on periodic Frobenius groups
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group in which every element
has finite order, and let $A$ be a normal abelian subgroup of $G$ that is neither trivial nor all of
$G$ and such that for every $a \in A$ with $a \ne 1$ the centralizer $C_G(a)$ of $a$ in $G$ is
contained in $A$. Then there are subgroups $F$ and $H$ of $G$ such that $G$ is a Frobenius group
with kernel $F$ and complement $H$. This answers Kourovka Problem 20.96 (A. I. Sozutov) in the
affirmative.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 20.96 (A. I. Sozutov); resolution: D. V. Lytkina and V. D. Mazurov, Periodic Frobenius groups, Siberian Math. J. 64 (2023), no. 6, 1351-1355 (Sibirsk. Mat. Zh. 64 (2023), no. 6, 1224-1228), abstract: conditions for a strongly isolated normal subgroup of a periodic group to have a complement; Kourovka Notebook (21st issue), Problem 20.96: Yes, it is, https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/smj7826.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 20.96 (periodic Frobenius groups)
articles.statement:
The statement, posed by A. I. Sozutov,
that for every group $G$ in which every element has finite order and every normal abelian subgroup
$A$ of $G$ that is neither trivial nor all of $G$ and such that for every $a \in A$ with $a \ne 1$
the centralizer $C_G(a)$ of $a$ in $G$ is contained in $A$, there are subgroups $F$ and $H$ of $G$
such that $G$ is a Frobenius group with kernel $F$ and complement $H$.

articles.title: Involution
articles.statement:
An element $x$ of a group $G$ is an involution when $x^2 = 1$ and
$x \ne 1$.

articles.title: The projective special unitary group $\mathrm{PSU}_3(4)$
articles.statement:
It is the quotient
$\mathrm{PSU}_3(4) = \mathrm{SU}_3(4) / Z(\mathrm{SU}_3(4))$ of the special unitary group
$\mathrm{SU}_3(4)$ by its centre $Z(\mathrm{SU}_3(4))$.

articles.title: The special unitary group $\mathrm{SU}_3(4)$
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{F}_{16}$ be the field with
$16$ elements and, for a matrix $A$ over $\mathbb{F}_{16}$, let $\bar{A}$ be the matrix obtained by
applying the involutive field automorphism $x \mapsto x^4$ of $\mathbb{F}_{16}$ to each entry.
Then $\mathrm{SU}_3(4)$ is the subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{F}_{16})$ generated by the
invertible $3 \times 3$ matrices $A$ over $\mathbb{F}_{16}$ with $\det A = 1$ and
$\bar{A}^{\top} A = 1$, that is, by the determinant-one isometries of the Hermitian form
$x_1 \bar{y}_1 + x_2 \bar{y}_2 + x_3 \bar{y}_3$.

These matrices already form a subgroup, so $\mathrm{SU}_3(4)$ consists exactly of them.

articles.title: Jabara's conjecture on groups with $\{3, 5\}$-involutions holds
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a periodic group
(every element has finite order) that is generated by its involutions (elements $x \ne 1$ with
$x^2 = 1$). Suppose that the order of $xy$ lies in $\{1, 2, 3, 5\}$ for all involutions $x, y$ of
$G$, and that each of these four values is the order of $xy$ for some involutions $x, y$ of $G$.
Then $G$ is isomorphic to the alternating group $A_5$ or to the projective special unitary group
$\mathrm{PSU}_3(4)$.

Bettio proved this even without the hypothesis that $G$ is periodic; the Kourovka Archive records
the proof.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 19.36 (E. Jabara); resolution: E. Bettio, A proof of a conjecture by Jabara on groups in which all involutions are odd transpositions, J. Group Theory 24 (2021), no. 5, 1055-1067, abstract: a group generated by elements of order two in which the product of any two such elements has order 1, 2, 3 or 5, with all possibilities occurring, is isomorphic to A₅ or to PSU(3, 4), answering Problem 19.36; Kourovka Archive, Problem 19.36: the conjecture is proved, even without using the hypothesis that G is periodic, https://doi.org/10.1515/jgth-2020-0129.

articles.title: Jabara's conjecture on groups with $\{3, 5\}$-involutions
articles.statement:
Kourovka 19.36 (E. Jabara):
let $G$ be a periodic group (every element has finite order) that is generated by its involutions
(elements $x \ne 1$ with $x^2 = 1$). Suppose that the order of $xy$ lies in $\{1, 2, 3, 5\}$ for
all involutions $x, y$ of $G$, and that each of these four values is the order of $xy$ for some
involutions $x, y$ of $G$. Then $G$ is isomorphic to the alternating group $A_5$ or to the
projective special unitary group $\mathrm{PSU}_3(4)$.

articles.title: Products of abelian and locally quaternion groups are soluble
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group with
subgroups $A$ and $B$ such that $A$ is abelian, $B$ is locally quaternion, and $G = AB$, that is,
every element of $G$ is a product $ab$ with $a \in A$ and $b \in B$. Then $G$ is soluble.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 18.95 (A. I. Sozutov); resolution: B. Amberg and Ya. Sysak, On products of groups with abelian subgroups of small index, J. Group Theory 20 (2017), no. 6, 1061-1072, Kourovka Archive, Problem 18.95: Yes, it is; Corollary 1.2 (arXiv:1611.10093): if a group G = AB is the product of an abelian subgroup A and a locally quaternion subgroup B, then G is soluble (Theorem 1.1: derived length at most 3), https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.10093.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 18.95 (Sozutov)
articles.statement:
The proposition that every group $G$ with subgroups $A$
and $B$ such that $A$ is abelian, $B$ is locally quaternion, and $G = AB$ (every element of $G$ is a
product $ab$ with $a \in A$ and $b \in B$) is soluble.

articles.title: Locally quaternion subgroup
articles.statement:
A subgroup $B$ of a group $G$ is locally quaternion if there
is a strictly increasing sequence $C_0 < C_1 < C_2 < \cdots$ of subgroups of $G$, each isomorphic
to a generalized quaternion group $Q_{2^{k+2}}$ of order $2^{k+2}$ for some $k \ge 1$, whose
supremum (for a chain, the union) is $B$. In particular $B$ is infinite.

articles.title: Subgroups inside a product of two periodic subgroups of a soluble group are periodic
articles.statement:
Let $G$
be a soluble group and let $A$ and $B$ be subgroups of $G$ in which every element has finite order.
Then every subgroup $H$ of $G$ contained in the set $AB$ of all products $ab$ with $a \in A$ and
$b \in B$ is periodic: every element of $H$ has finite order. This answers Kourovka Problem 16.38
(F. de Giovanni) in the affirmative; the proof is due to Kinyon and Urban (Proposition 3.8).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 16.38 (F. de Giovanni); resolution: M. Kinyon and J. Urban (with Codex gpt-6-astra), Results on problems from the Kourovka Notebook, preprint, version 4 (19 September 2026), Proposition 3.8 (if G is soluble and A, B ≤ G are periodic, every subgroup contained in the set AB is periodic); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 16.38 solved (Yes, AI solution confirmed by B. Amberg), https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/kourovka-mathematics.pdf.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 16.38 (subgroups inside a product of periodic subgroups)
articles.statement:
The statement,
posed by F. de Giovanni, that for every soluble group $G$ and all subgroups $A$ and $B$ of $G$ in
which every element has finite order, every subgroup $H$ of $G$ contained in the set $AB$ of all
products $ab$ with $a \in A$ and $b \in B$ has every element of finite order.

articles.title: A group with the maximal condition can fail the weak minimal condition
articles.statement:
There is a group $G$
satisfying the maximal condition on subgroups (there is no infinite strictly ascending chain of
subgroups of $G$) that has an infinite descending chain $H_0 \ge H_1 \ge \cdots$ of subgroups in
which every index $|H_i : H_{i+1}|$ is infinite. This answers Kourovka Problem 10.14(b) negatively.

The Kourovka Archive answers 10.14(b) "No, not always", citing Obraztsov (1991).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 10.14 (D. I. Zaitsev); resolution: V. N. Obraztsov, Math. USSR-Sb. 66, no. 2 (1990), 541-553 (a); V. N. Obraztsov, Siberian Math. J. 32, no. 1 (1991), 79-84 (b), Kourovka Archive, Problem 10.14 (both parts "No, not always").

articles.title: Maximal condition implies weak minimal condition
articles.statement:
Kourovka 10.14(b): every group with the maximal condition on subgroups satisfies the weak
minimal condition on subgroups.

articles.title: A group with the minimal condition can fail the weak maximal condition
articles.statement:
There is a group $G$
satisfying the minimal condition on subgroups (there is no infinite strictly descending chain of
subgroups of $G$) that has an infinite ascending chain $H_0 \le H_1 \le \cdots$ of subgroups in
which every index $|H_{i+1} : H_i|$ is infinite. This answers Kourovka Problem 10.14(a) negatively.

The Kourovka Archive answers 10.14(a) "No, not always", citing Obraztsov (1990).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 10.14 (D. I. Zaitsev); resolution: V. N. Obraztsov, Math. USSR-Sb. 66, no. 2 (1990), 541-553 (a); V. N. Obraztsov, Siberian Math. J. 32, no. 1 (1991), 79-84 (b), Kourovka Archive, Problem 10.14 (both parts "No, not always").

articles.title: Minimal condition implies weak maximal condition
articles.statement:
Kourovka 10.14(a) (D. I. Zaitsev): every group with the minimal condition on subgroups
satisfies the weak maximal condition on subgroups.

articles.title: Weak maximal condition on subgroups
articles.statement:
A group $G$ satisfies the weak maximal condition on
subgroups when there is no infinite ascending chain $H_0 \le H_1 \le \cdots$ of subgroups of $G$
in which every index $|H_{i+1} : H_i|$ is infinite.

articles.title: Weak minimal condition on subgroups
articles.statement:
The weak minimal condition on subgroups: there is no infinite descending chain
`H₀ ≥ H₁ ≥ ⋯` of subgroups with every index `|Hᵢ : Hᵢ₊₁|` infinite.

articles.title: A finite insoluble totally 2-closed group with nontrivial Fitting subgroup
articles.statement:
There exists a
finite group $G$ that is not soluble, is totally $2$-closed, and has a nontrivial nilpotent normal
subgroup (equivalently, a nontrivial Fitting subgroup).

The Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) answers Problem 20.1 "Yes, there are". Kinyon and Urban (an
AI-generated solution confirmed by G. Tracey) prove that $J_1 \times C_{13}$ is totally $2$-closed
(Section 3.34, Lemma 3.11), insoluble and has Fitting subgroup $C_{13}$; the Notebook also obtains
$J_1 \times C_p$ for primes $p \in \lbrace 13, 17 \rbrace$ or $p > 19$ from Theorem 1.1 of
Arezoomand-Iranmanesh-Praeger-Tracey and Theorem 2 and Proposition 2 of Abdollahi-Arezoomand.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 20.1 (M. Arezoomand, M. A. Iranmanesh, C. E. Praeger, G. Tracey); resolution: M. Kinyon and J. Urban, Results on problems from the Kourovka Notebook, preprint, version 4, 19 September 2026; M. Arezoomand, M. A. Iranmanesh, C. E. Praeger and G. Tracey, Bull. Math. Sci. 14 (2024), no. 1, 2350004; A. Abdollahi and M. Arezoomand, J. Algebra Appl. 17 (2018), no. 4, 1850065, Kinyon-Urban, Section 3.34 (Problem 20.1): J1 × C13 is totally 2-closed, insoluble, with Fitting subgroup C13 (Lemma 3.11: direct products of totally 2-closed groups of coprime orders are totally 2-closed), an AI solution confirmed by G. Tracey; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) also derives J1 × C_p (p ∈ {13, 17} or p > 19) from Theorem 1.1 of Arezoomand-Iranmanesh-Praeger-Tracey and Theorem 2 and Proposition 2 of Abdollahi-Arezoomand, https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/kourovka-mathematics.pdf.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 20.1 (insoluble totally 2-closed groups)
articles.statement:
The statement, asked by
M. Arezoomand, M. A. Iranmanesh, C. E. Praeger and G. Tracey, that there exists a finite group $G$
that is not soluble, is totally $2$-closed, and has a nontrivial nilpotent normal subgroup
(equivalently, a nontrivial Fitting subgroup).

articles.title: Totally 2-closed groups
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is totally $2$-closed when every faithful action of
$G$ on a set $\Omega$ is $2$-closed; equivalently, in each faithful permutation representation of
$G$ on a set $\Omega$, $G$ is the largest subgroup of $\mathrm{Sym}(\Omega)$ preserving each of
its orbits on $\Omega^2$.

articles.title: 2-closed actions
articles.statement:
An action of a group $G$ on a set $\Omega$ is $2$-closed when every
permutation $\sigma$ of $\Omega$ that preserves each $G$-orbit on ordered pairs (that is, for all
$\alpha, \beta \in \Omega$ some $g \in G$ satisfies $\sigma(\alpha) = g \alpha$ and
$\sigma(\beta) = g \beta$) is induced by an element of $G$: there is $g \in G$ with
$\sigma(\omega) = g \omega$ for all $\omega \in \Omega$.

articles.title: Skresanov's counterexample to Kourovka Problem 19.67
articles.statement:
There exist a finite set $\Omega$, a
solvable subgroup $G$ of the symmetric group $\mathrm{Sym}(\Omega)$, and a composition factor $S$
of the $2$-closure $G^{(2)}$ of $G$ such that $S$ is not cyclic and $S$ is not isomorphic to the
alternating group $A_n$ for any $n$. Here $G^{(2)}$ is the subgroup of $\mathrm{Sym}(\Omega)$
generated by the permutations $\sigma$ such that for all $\alpha, \beta \in \Omega$ some $g \in G$
has $g(\alpha) = \sigma(\alpha)$ and $g(\beta) = \sigma(\beta)$, and a composition factor of
$G^{(2)}$ is a simple group onto which some subnormal subgroup of $G^{(2)}$ maps.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 19.67 (I. Ponomarenko); resolution: S. V. Skresanov, Counterexamples to two conjectures in the Kourovka notebook, Algebra Logic 58 (2019), no. 3, 249-253, abstract: counterexamples to Questions 12.78 and 19.67 of the Kourovka Notebook; Kourovka Archive, Problem 19.67: No, it is not true, https://doi.org/10.1007/s10469-019-09543-1.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 19.67
articles.statement:
The statement that for every finite set $\Omega$ and every
solvable subgroup $G$ of the symmetric group $\mathrm{Sym}(\Omega)$, every composition factor of
the $2$-closure $G^{(2)}$ of $G$ is cyclic or isomorphic to the alternating group $A_n$ for some
natural number $n$.

articles.title: The $2$-closure of a permutation group
articles.statement:
For a subgroup $G$ of the symmetric group
$\mathrm{Sym}(\Omega)$, the $2$-closure $G^{(2)}$ of $G$ is the subgroup of $\mathrm{Sym}(\Omega)$
generated by the permutations $\sigma$ that map every pair of points into its $G$-orbit, that is,
such that for all $\alpha, \beta \in \Omega$ there is $g \in G$ with $g(\alpha) = \sigma(\alpha)$
and $g(\beta) = \sigma(\beta)$.

These permutations already form a subgroup: the largest subgroup of $\mathrm{Sym}(\Omega)$
containing $G$ with the same orbits as $G$ on $\Omega \times \Omega$.

articles.title: Base of a group action
articles.statement:
For a group $G$ acting on a set $\Omega$, a finite set
$B \subseteq \Omega$ is a base when its pointwise stabilizer is trivial: the only $g \in G$ with
$g \cdot \omega = \omega$ for all $\omega \in B$ is $g = 1$.

articles.title: Independent subset of a group
articles.statement:
A finite subset $S$ of a group $G$ is independent when no
element $s \in S$ lies in the subgroup of $G$ generated by $S \setminus \{s\}$.

articles.title: Minimal base
articles.statement:
For a group $G$ acting on a set $\Omega$, a finite set $B \subseteq \Omega$
is a minimal base when it is a base, that is, its pointwise stabilizer in $G$ is trivial, and for
every $\omega \in B$ the set $B \setminus \{\omega\}$ is not a base.

articles.title: Maximal size of an independent set
articles.statement:
For a group $G$, a finite subset $S \subseteq G$ is
independent when no $s \in S$ lies in the subgroup generated by $S \setminus \{s\}$. The number
$\mu'(G)$ is the supremum in $\mathbb{N}$ of the sizes of the finite independent subsets of $G$:
their largest size when these sizes are bounded, as they are for finite $G$, and $0$ when they are
unbounded.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 16.45 has a negative answer
articles.statement:
It is not true that $b(G) = \mu'(G)$ for every
finite group $G$, where $b(G)$ is the largest size of a minimal base of $G$ over all actions of $G$
on a set, and $\mu'(G)$ is the largest size of an independent subset of $G$.

The counterexample in the source is Kriebel's affine group $G = \mathbb{F}_{29}^2 \rtimes
\mathrm{SL}_2(5)$ of order $100920$, for which $b(G) = 3 < 4 = \mu'(G)$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 16.45 (P. J. Cameron); resolution: A. Kriebel, A counterexample to Kourovka Notebook Problem 16.45, preprint, Zenodo record 22929486 (2026), main theorem: G = F_29^2 ⋊ SL_2(5) of order 100920 has b(G) = 3 < 4 = μ'(G); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 16.45 solved (AI solution confirmed by P. J. Cameron), https://zenodo.org/records/22929486.

articles.title: Cameron's question on minimal bases and independent sets
articles.statement:
The statement that
$b(G) = \mu'(G)$ for every finite group $G$, where $b(G)$ is the largest size of a minimal base of
$G$ over all actions of $G$ on a set, and $\mu'(G)$ is the largest size of an independent subset
of $G$ (a subset none of whose elements lies in the subgroup generated by the others).

This is Kourovka Notebook Problem 16.45, posed by P. J. Cameron.

articles.title: Maximal size of a minimal base
articles.statement:
For a group $G$, the number $b(G)$ is the supremum in
$\mathbb{N}$ of the sizes of the minimal bases of $G$ over all actions of $G$ on a set $\Omega$,
where a minimal base is a finite set $B \subseteq \Omega$ whose pointwise stabilizer in $G$ is
trivial while that of $B \setminus \{\omega\}$ is not, for every $\omega \in B$. It is the largest
such size when these sizes are bounded, as they are for finite $G$, and $0$ when they are
unbounded.

articles.title: Burnside's lemma with a uniform fixed-point count
articles.statement:
Let a finite group $G$ act on a finite
set $X$, and let $c$ be a natural number such that every element $g \ne 1$ of $G$ fixes exactly
$c$ points of $X$. Writing $N$ for the number of orbits of $G$ on $X$, we have
$|X| + c\,(|G| - 1) = N \cdot |G|$.

articles.title: A subgroup stabilizing a subset has order dividing its size
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group,
let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$ and let $U$ be a subset of $G$ such that $hu \in U$ for all
$h \in H$ and $u \in U$. Then $|H|$ divides $|U|$.

The $H$-orbits partition $U$ and each orbit has exactly $|H|$ elements, since left
multiplication is injective.

articles.title: Orders of finite $5$-transitive permutation groups
articles.statement:
Let a finite group $G$ act
faithfully on a finite set $X$ with $n = |X| \ge 5$, and suppose that the action is
$5$-transitive: for any two injective maps $a, b \colon \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\} \to X$ there is
$g \in G$ with $g \cdot a(i) = b(i)$ for all $i$. Then $|G| = n!$, or $n \ge 7$ and
$|G| = n!/2$, or $n = 12$ and $|G| = 95040$, or $n = 24$ and $|G| = 244823040$.

## Sources

- Folklore via CFSG; classical work of Mathieu, Jordan; modern accounts in P. Cameron, Permutation Groups (1999). Problem `five_transitive_card_classification` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Frobenius's theorem on the Frobenius kernel
articles.statement:
Let a finite group $G$ act faithfully and
transitively on a finite set $X$ with at least two elements, such that every point stabiliser is
nontrivial and no nonidentity element of $G$ fixes two distinct points of $X$. Then the set
consisting of the identity together with the elements of $G$ that fix no point of $X$ is a normal
subgroup of $G$.

## Sources

- G. Frobenius, Über auflösbare Gruppen IV, Sitzungsber. Akad. Wiss. Berlin (1901). Problem `frobenius_kernel_isNormal` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Two largest orbits force the dihedral group of order eight (Kourovka 18.44)
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a
finite non-abelian group, let $G'$ be its derived subgroup, and let $V$ be a finite faithful
irreducible $G$-module, that is, a nonzero finite abelian group on which $G$ acts faithfully by
automorphisms with no $G$-invariant subgroups other than $0$ and $V$. Write $M = |G/G'|$. If every
orbit of $G$ on $V$ has at most $M$ elements and exactly two orbits have exactly $M$ elements, then
$G$ is isomorphic to the dihedral group of order $8$ and $|V| = 9$.

Jones and Keller (2020), Theorem 3.1, prove this, showing moreover that $V$ is the $2$-dimensional
vector space $V(2, 3)$ over the field with $3$ elements; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) accepts
it as answering 18.44.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 18.44 (T. M. Keller); resolution: N. A. Jones and T. M. Keller, Orbit sizes and the dihedral group of order eight, Ann. Mat. Pura Appl. 199 (2020), 2323-2340, Theorem 3.1: G finite nonabelian, V finite faithful irreducible G-module, M = |G/G'| the largest orbit size with exactly two orbits of size M; then G is dihedral of order 8 and V = V(2, 3), https://doi.org/10.1007/s10231-020-00970-x.

articles.title: Keller's question on two largest orbits and the dihedral group of order eight (Kourovka Problem 18.44)
articles.statement:
**Keller's question on two largest orbits and the dihedral group of order eight (Kourovka
Problem 18.44).** The statement that for every finite non-abelian group $G$, with derived subgroup
$G'$, and every finite faithful irreducible $G$-module $V$ (a nonzero finite abelian group on which
$G$ acts faithfully by automorphisms with no $G$-invariant subgroups other than $0$ and $V$),
writing $M = |G/G'|$: if every orbit of $G$ on $V$ has at most $M$ elements and exactly two orbits
have exactly $M$ elements, then $G$ is isomorphic to the dihedral group of order $8$ and
$|V| = 9$.

articles.title: Bubboloni–Praeger–Spiga conjectured value
Refutation of the Bubboloni–Praeger–Spiga normal covering conjecture
articles.statement:
It is not the case
that there is a natural number $N$ such that, for every $n \ge N$, the normal covering number
$\gamma(S_n)$ of the symmetric group $S_n$ equals the Bubboloni–Praeger–Spiga conjectured value
of $n$. In other words, the conjecture fails for arbitrarily large $n$.

The Kourovka Archive records that A. Maróti showed the conjecture incorrect for odd $n$. His
covering, given in Section 2 of Bubboloni–Praeger–Spiga (2020), yields
$\gamma(S_n) \le n/3 + \varphi(n)/2 + \omega(n)$, where $\varphi$ is Euler's function and
$\omega(n)$ the number of distinct prime factors of $n$. This is below the conjectured value when
$n$ is the product of $r$ consecutive primes starting at a prime $p \ge 43$ and $r$ is large.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 18.23 (D. Bubboloni, C. E. Praeger, P. Spiga); resolution: D. Bubboloni, C. E. Praeger and P. Spiga, Linear bounds for the normal covering number of the symmetric and alternating groups, Monatsh. Math. 191 (2020), 229-247, Section 2, A. Maróti's construction: for n = N(r, p), the product of r consecutive primes starting at p ≥ 43, and r ≥ r*, γ(Sym(n)) < (n/2)(1 - 1/p₁)(1 - 1/p₂) + 2, contradicting the conjecture for infinitely many p and r; Kourovka Archive, Problem 18.23, https://api.research-repository.uwa.edu.au/ws/files/49055019/Bubboloni_et_al_2019_Linear_bounds_for_the_normal_covering.pdf.

articles.title: Bubboloni–Praeger–Spiga normal covering conjecture (eventual form)
articles.statement:
There is a natural
number $N$ such that, for every $n \ge N$, the normal covering number $\gamma(S_n)$ of the
symmetric group $S_n$ equals the Bubboloni–Praeger–Spiga conjectured value of $n$.

This is Kourovka Problem 18.23 (D. Bubboloni, C. E. Praeger, P. Spiga) in the form "for all
sufficiently large $n$" that the proposers single out.

articles.title: Normal covering number of the symmetric group
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the normal
covering number $\gamma(S_n)$ is the least $k$ for which there are proper subgroups
$H_1, \dots, H_k$ of the symmetric group $S_n$ such that every element of $S_n$ is conjugate to an
element of some $H_i$. When no such subgroups exist, as for $n \le 2$, it is $0$.

articles.title: Permutations of prescribed orders with product of prescribed order
articles.statement:
For every natural
number $n$ and all natural numbers $a, b, c$ with $1 < a \le n - 2$, $1 < b \le n - 2$ and
$1 < c \le n - 2$, the symmetric group $S_n$ contains permutations $x$ and $y$ of orders $a$ and
$b$ whose product $xy$ has order $c$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 18.49 (S. Kohl); resolution: G. A. Miller, Amer. J. Math. 22 (1900), no. 2, 185-190; J. König, European J. Combin. 57 (2016), 50-56, Kourovka Archive, Problem 18.49: Yes, it is (Miller); another solution by König, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Kohl's question on orders of products in symmetric groups
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$
and all natural numbers $a, b, c$ with $1 < a \le n - 2$, $1 < b \le n - 2$ and $1 < c \le n - 2$,
the symmetric group $S_n$ contains permutations $x$ and $y$ such that $x$ has order $a$, $y$ has
order $b$ and $xy$ has order $c$.

articles.title: The poles are invariant under the action
articles.statement:
Let a group $G$ act on a set $X$ and let
$P \subseteq X$ be the set of poles of the action. For every $g \in G$, the image of $P$
under the map $x \mapsto g \cdot x$ is $P$.

articles.title: Characterization of poles
articles.statement:
Let a group $G$ act on a set $X$. A point $p \in X$ is
a pole of the action if and only if there is some $g \in G$ with $g \neq 1$ and
$g \cdot p = p$.

articles.title: The poles as a union of fixed-point sets
articles.statement:
Let a group $G$ act on a set $X$. The set
of poles equals $\bigcup_{g \in G,\, g \neq 1} \{x \in X : g \cdot x = x\}$, the union of
the fixed-point sets of the nonidentity elements of $G$.

articles.title: Poles of a group action
articles.statement: A pole of a group action is a point fixed by some nonidentity element.

articles.title: The action sends poles to poles
articles.statement:
Let a group $G$ act on a set $X$. If $p \in X$ is a
pole of the action, then $g \cdot p$ is a pole for every $g \in G$.

If $p$ is fixed by $h \neq 1$, then $g \cdot p$ is fixed by the conjugate $g h g^{-1} \neq 1$.

articles.title: $p$-regular orbits for every prime do not force a regular orbit
articles.statement:
There exist a finite field $F$,
a nonzero finite-dimensional vector space $V$ over $F$ and a finite group $G$ acting faithfully on
$V$ by $F$-linear maps such that the only $G$-invariant subspaces of $V$ are $0$ and $V$ and, for
every prime $p$, some vector of $V$ has a stabilizer in $G$ of order prime to $p$, but no vector of
$V$ has trivial stabilizer in $G$.

Resolved false: the Kourovka Archive answers 12.25 "No, not always" (V. I. Zenkov). Write
$\mathbb{Z}_n$ for the cyclic group of order $n$, $A_4$ for the alternating group of degree $4$ and
$\mathbb{F}_2$ for the field with two elements. Let $H = A_4 \wr \mathbb{Z}_5$ be the wreath
product, let $V = O_2(H)$ be the largest normal $2$-subgroup of $H$, so $V \cong \mathbb{F}_2^{10}$,
and let $G \cong \mathbb{Z}_3 \wr \mathbb{Z}_5$ be a complement to $V$ in $H$. The faithful
irreducible action of $G$ on $V$ by conjugation has orbits with stabilizers of order $5$ and of
order $3$, hence $p$-regular orbits for every prime $p$, but no regular orbit, since
$|G| = 1215 > 1024 = |V|$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 12.25 (Jiping Zhang); resolution: V. I. Zenkov, letter of 11 February 1994, as recorded in the Kourovka Archive, Problem 12.25, Archive answer: No, not always; H = A_4 ≀ Z_5, V = O_2(H), G a complement to V acting by conjugation, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Zhang's question on regular orbits from $p$-regular orbits
articles.statement:
The statement that for every
finite field $F$, every nonzero finite-dimensional vector space $V$ over $F$ and every finite group
$G$ acting faithfully on $V$ by $F$-linear maps, if the only $G$-invariant subspaces of $V$ are $0$
and $V$, and for every prime $p$ some vector of $V$ has a stabilizer in $G$ of order prime to $p$
(a $p$-regular orbit), then some vector of $V$ has trivial stabilizer in $G$ (a regular orbit).

This is Kourovka Notebook Problem 12.25 (Jiping Zhang).

articles.title: Products of two class transpositions have only finitely many orders
articles.statement:
The claim of Kourovka
Problem 18.48 holds: the set of positive integers $k$ such that $\sigma\tau$ has order $k$ for some
class transpositions $\sigma$ and $\tau$ of $\mathbb{Z}$ is finite.

Iskra (2026), accepted in the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue), proves that every finite order of a
product of two class transpositions divides $840$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 18.48 (S. Kohl); resolution: A. Iskra, Finite orders of products of two class transpositions divide 840, preprint, arXiv:2610.01793 (2026), abstract: if the product of two class transpositions has finite order, then its order divides 840 (sharp); this answers Question 18.48 affirmatively, as the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) records, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01793.

articles.title: Claim of Kourovka Problem 18.48
articles.statement:
Only finitely many positive integers occur as orders of
products $\sigma\tau$ of two class transpositions $\sigma$ and $\tau$ of $\mathbb{Z}$.

articles.title: Class transposition of two residue classes
articles.statement:
For integers $r_1, m_1, r_2, m_2$, write
$r_1(m_1) = r_1 + m_1\mathbb{Z}$ and $r_2(m_2) = r_2 + m_2\mathbb{Z}$ for the residue classes. A
permutation $\sigma$ of $\mathbb{Z}$ is the class transposition $\tau_{r_1(m_1), r_2(m_2)}$ when
$0 \le r_1 < m_1$ and $0 \le r_2 < m_2$, the residue classes $r_1(m_1)$ and $r_2(m_2)$ are
disjoint, $\sigma$ interchanges $r_1 + k m_1$ and $r_2 + k m_2$ for every integer $k$, and
$\sigma$ fixes every integer outside $r_1(m_1) \cup r_2(m_2)$.

This is the definition of class transpositions in Kourovka Problem 17.57.

articles.title: Class transpositions of the integers
articles.statement:
A permutation $\sigma$ of $\mathbb{Z}$ is a class
