transposition when it is the class transposition $\tau_{r_1(m_1), r_2(m_2)}$ for some integers
$r_1, m_1, r_2, m_2$.

articles.title: Residue class
articles.statement:
For integers $r$ and $m$, the residue class $r(m)$ is the set
$\{x \in \mathbb{Z} : x \equiv r \pmod{m}\} = \{r + k m : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$.

articles.title: Closed cofinitary permutation groups need not be locally compact
articles.statement:
The claim of Kourovka
Problem 13.28 is false: there are an infinite set $\Omega$ and a subgroup $G$ of the group of
permutations of $\Omega$ such that $G$ is cofinitary (every non-identity element of $G$ fixes only
finitely many points of $\Omega$) and closed in the topology of pointwise convergence, but $G$ is
not locally compact in the subspace topology.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 13.28 (D. M. Evans; P. J. Cameron); resolution: G. Hjorth, J. Algebra 200 (1998), no. 2, 439-448, Kourovka Archive, Problem 13.28: No, not always.

articles.title: Claim of Kourovka Problem 13.28
articles.statement:
For every infinite set $\Omega$, every cofinitary subgroup
$G$ of the group of permutations of $\Omega$ that is closed in the topology of pointwise
convergence is locally compact in the subspace topology.

articles.title: Cofinitary permutation groups
articles.statement:
A subgroup $G$ of the group of permutations of a set
$\Omega$ is cofinitary when every non-identity element of $G$ fixes only finitely many points of
$\Omega$.

articles.title: Lehner's theorem on distinguishing sets of subdegree-finite groups
articles.statement:
Let $\Omega$ be a
countably infinite set and let $G$ be a subgroup of the symmetric group $\mathrm{Sym}(\Omega)$
that is closed in the topology of pointwise convergence and subdegree-finite: for all
$a, b \in \Omega$ the orbit of $b$ under the stabilizer of $a$ in $G$ is finite. If every
non-identity element of $G$ moves infinitely many points of $\Omega$, then there is a subset
$X \subseteq \Omega$ whose setwise stabilizer in $G$ is trivial: the only $g \in G$ with
$g(X) = X$ is the identity.

Lehner proves more generally that every locally compact permutation group on a countable set in
which every non-identity element moves infinitely many points has a subset with trivial setwise
stabilizer; closed subdegree-finite permutation groups are locally compact.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 19.89 (S. M. Smith); resolution: F. Lehner, Asymmetric colouring of locally compact permutation groups, Bull. London Math. Soc. 55 (2023), 1874-1879 (arXiv:2208.08844), Theorem 2: a locally compact permutation group on a countable set with infinite motion (minimal degree) has an asymmetric 2-colouring, a subset with trivial setwise stabiliser; Section 2: every closed, subdegree-finite permutation group is locally compact; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 19.89 solved: the conjecture is proved, https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.08844.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 19.89: Smith's conjecture on distinguishing sets
articles.statement:
The statement that for
every countably infinite set $\Omega$ and every subgroup $G$ of the symmetric group
$\mathrm{Sym}(\Omega)$ that is closed in the topology of pointwise convergence and
subdegree-finite (for all $a, b \in \Omega$ the orbit of $b$ under the stabilizer of $a$ in $G$ is
finite), if every non-identity element of $G$ moves infinitely many points of $\Omega$, then there
is a subset $X \subseteq \Omega$ whose setwise stabilizer in $G$ is trivial: the only $g \in G$
with $g(X) = X$ is the identity.

articles.title: The free group of rank 2 embeds in $\mathrm{Sym}(\mathbb{N})$ with finitely many orbits
articles.statement:
There
is an injective group homomorphism $f$ from the free group $F_2$ of rank $2$ into the symmetric
group $\mathrm{Sym}(\mathbb{N})$ of all permutations of $\mathbb{N}$ such that, for every
non-identity element $w$ of $F_2$, the cyclic subgroup generated by $f(w)$ has only finitely many
orbits on $\mathbb{N}$. This answers Kourovka Problem 12.10 positively.

The Kourovka Archive answers 12.10 "Yes, it can" (Macpherson).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 12.10 (A. M. W. Glass); resolution: H. D. Macpherson, in: Ordered groups and infinite permutation groups (Mathematics and its Applications 354), Kluwer, Dordrecht, 1996, 221-230, Kourovka Archive, Problem 12.10: "Yes, it can", https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Embedding the free group of rank 2 in $\mathrm{Sym}(\mathbb{N})$ with finitely many orbits (Kourovka 12.10)
articles.statement:
**Embedding the free group of rank 2 in $\mathrm{Sym}(\mathbb{N})$ with finitely many orbits
(Kourovka 12.10).** The statement, posed by P. Neumann and A. M. W. Glass, that there is an
injective group homomorphism $f$ from the free group $F_2$ of rank $2$ into the symmetric group
$\mathrm{Sym}(\mathbb{N})$ of all permutations of $\mathbb{N}$ such that, for every non-identity
element $w$ of $F_2$, the cyclic subgroup generated by $f(w)$ has only finitely many orbits on
$\mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: The betweenness group of the rationals is closed and highly homogeneous
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be the
group of permutations $\sigma$ of $\mathbb{Q}$ preserving strict betweenness in both directions:
for all $a, b, c \in \mathbb{Q}$, $b$ lies strictly between $a$ and $c$ (that is, $a < b < c$ or
$c < b < a$) if and only if $\sigma(b)$ lies strictly between $\sigma(a)$ and $\sigma(c)$. Then
$G$ is closed in the topology of pointwise convergence on the permutations of $\mathbb{Q}$, where
$\mathbb{Q}$ carries the discrete topology, and $G$ is highly homogeneous: for every natural
number $k$ it has a single orbit on the $k$-element subsets of $\mathbb{Q}$.

## Sources

- Daniele A. Gewurz and Francesca Merola, "Sequences realized as Parker vectors of oligomorphic permutation groups," Journal of Integer Sequences 6, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL6/Gewurz/gewurz22.tex>, lines 331–359. The source identifies `B` (also `∂C*`) as the rational-order permutations preserving or reversing order and calls Cameron's five representatives closed and highly homogeneous, glossed as one orbit on `k`-sets for all `k`. The source cites Peter J. Cameron, "Transitivity of permutation groups on unordered sets," Math. Z. 148 (1976), 127–139. Interpretation boundary: only the `B` representative is asserted, not exhaustive classification, uniqueness, or conjugacy.

articles.title: The betweenness automorphism group of a linear order
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered
set, and say that $b$ lies strictly between $a$ and $c$ when $a < b < c$ or $c < b < a$. The
betweenness automorphism group of $\alpha$ is the subgroup of the group of permutations of
$\alpha$ consisting of the permutations $\sigma$ such that, for all $a, b, c \in \alpha$, $b$ lies
strictly between $a$ and $c$ if and only if $\sigma(b)$ lies strictly between $\sigma(a)$ and
$\sigma(c)$.

articles.title: The symmetric group of the rationals is closed and highly homogeneous
articles.statement:
Let
$\operatorname{Sym}(\mathbb{Q})$ be the group of all permutations of the set $\mathbb{Q}$. Then
$\operatorname{Sym}(\mathbb{Q})$ is closed in the topology of pointwise convergence on the
permutations of $\mathbb{Q}$, and it is highly homogeneous: for every natural number $k$ it has a
single orbit on the $k$-element subsets of $\mathbb{Q}$.

Here $\mathbb{Q}$ serves only as a countably infinite set; its order, its field structure and its
usual topology play no role.

## Sources

- Daniele A. Gewurz and Francesca Merola, *Sequences realized as Parker vectors of oligomorphic permutation groups*, Journal of Integer Sequences 6, source lines 331--359 at https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL6/Gewurz/gewurz22.tex. Peter J. Cameron, "Transitivity of permutation groups on unordered sets," *Mathematische Zeitschrift* 148(2) (1976), 127--139, DOI 10.1007/BF01214702. Scope: this proves only Cameron's representative S, not Cameron's exhaustive classification, uniqueness, conjugacy, Parker-sequence claims, or the other four representatives.

articles.title: The automorphism group of a countably infinite dense circular order is closed and highly homogeneous
articles.statement:
**The automorphism group of a countably infinite dense circular order is closed and highly
homogeneous.** Let $\alpha$ be a countably infinite set with a circular order, and write
$\operatorname{btw}(a, b, c)$ when $b$ lies between $a$ and $c$ going around from $a$ to $c$.
Suppose the circular order is dense: for all distinct $a, b \in \alpha$ there is some
$c \in \alpha$, different from $a$ and $b$, with $\operatorname{btw}(a, c, b)$. Then the group of
permutations $\sigma$ of $\alpha$ such that $\operatorname{btw}(a, b, c)$ holds if and only if
$\operatorname{btw}(\sigma(a), \sigma(b), \sigma(c))$ holds, for all $a, b, c \in \alpha$, is
closed in the topology of pointwise convergence on the permutations of $\alpha$, where $\alpha$
carries the discrete topology, and it is highly homogeneous: for every natural number $k$ it has
a single orbit on the $k$-element subsets of $\alpha$.

## Sources

- Daniele A. Gewurz and Francesca Merola, "Sequences realized as Parker vectors of oligomorphic permutation groups," JIS 6, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL6/Gewurz/gewurz22.tex, lines 331–359. Interpretation boundary: only Cameron group C is asserted, with standard countable dense infinite circular-order hypotheses, not exhaustive classification, uniqueness, or conjugacy.

articles.title: The automorphism group of a circular order
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a circularly ordered set with
non-strict circular betweenness relation $\operatorname{btw}$. The automorphism group of $\alpha$
is the subgroup of the group of permutations of $\alpha$ consisting of the permutations $\sigma$
such that, for all $a, b, c \in \alpha$, $\operatorname{btw}(a, b, c)$ holds if and only if
$\operatorname{btw}(\sigma(a), \sigma(b), \sigma(c))$ holds.

articles.title: Separation of pairs in a circular order
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a circular order, and write
$\operatorname{sbtw}(x, y, z)$ for its strict betweenness relation ($y$ lies strictly between
$x$ and $z$ going around the circle). For $a, b, c, d \in \alpha$, the pairs $a, b$ and $c, d$
separate each other when either $\operatorname{sbtw}(a, c, b)$ and $\operatorname{sbtw}(b, d, a)$
both hold, or $\operatorname{sbtw}(a, d, b)$ and $\operatorname{sbtw}(b, c, a)$ both hold.

articles.title: Strict betweenness
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a relation $<$ and let $a, b, c \in \alpha$.
Then $b$ lies strictly between $a$ and $c$ when either $a < b$ and $b < c$, or $c < b$ and
$b < a$.

articles.title: The full symmetric group is highly homogeneous
articles.statement:
For every set $\alpha$, the group of all
permutations of $\alpha$ is highly homogeneous: for every natural number $k$, any $k$-element
subset of $\alpha$ can be carried to any other $k$-element subset of $\alpha$ by some permutation
of $\alpha$.

articles.title: Highly homogeneous permutation groups
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group of permutations of a set
$\alpha$. Then $G$ is highly homogeneous when, for every natural number $k$, it acts transitively
on the $k$-element subsets of $\alpha$: for any two $k$-element subsets $X$ and $Y$ of $\alpha$
there is some $g \in G$ with $g(X) = Y$.

articles.title: The order-automorphism group of the rationals is closed and highly homogeneous
articles.statement:
The group of
order automorphisms of $\mathbb{Q}$, that is, of the permutations $\sigma$ of $\mathbb{Q}$ such
that $a < b$ if and only if $\sigma(a) < \sigma(b)$ for all $a, b \in \mathbb{Q}$, is closed in
the topology of pointwise convergence on the permutations of $\mathbb{Q}$, where $\mathbb{Q}$
carries the discrete topology, and it is highly homogeneous: for every natural number $k$ it has
a single orbit on the $k$-element subsets of $\mathbb{Q}$.

## Sources

- Daniele A. Gewurz and Francesca Merola, "Sequences realized as Parker vectors of oligomorphic permutation groups," JIS 6, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL6/Gewurz/gewurz22.tex, lines 331-359. Primary source, cited there: Peter J. Cameron, "Transitivity of permutation groups on unordered sets," *Mathematische Zeitschrift* 148(2) (1976), 127--139, DOI 10.1007/BF01214702.

articles.title: Order automorphism group
articles.statement:
For a type $\alpha$ equipped with a relation $<$, the order
automorphism group of $\alpha$ is the subgroup of the group of permutations of $\alpha$
consisting of the permutations $\sigma$ such that for all $a, b \in \alpha$, $a < b$ holds if and
only if $\sigma(a) < \sigma(b)$ holds.

articles.title: Pointwise convergence topology on permutations
articles.statement:
For a type $\alpha$, the pointwise
convergence topology on the group of permutations of $\alpha$ is the topology induced by the map
sending a permutation $\sigma$ to the underlying function $\sigma \colon \alpha \to \alpha$, where
$\alpha$ carries the discrete topology and the space of functions $\alpha \to \alpha$ carries the
product topology.

articles.title: The separation group of a countably infinite dense circular order is closed and highly homogeneous
articles.statement:
**The separation group of a countably infinite dense circular order is closed and highly
homogeneous.** Let $\alpha$ be a countably infinite set with a circular order, and write
$\operatorname{btw}(a, b, c)$ when $b$ lies between $a$ and $c$ going around from $a$ to $c$.
Suppose the circular order is dense: for all distinct $a, b \in \alpha$ there is some
$c \in \alpha$, different from $a$ and $b$, with $\operatorname{btw}(a, c, b)$. Then the
separation automorphism group of $\alpha$ is closed in the topology of pointwise convergence on
the permutations of $\alpha$, where $\alpha$ carries the discrete topology, and it is highly
homogeneous: for every natural number $k$ it has a single orbit on the $k$-element subsets of
$\alpha$.

## Sources

- Daniele A. Gewurz and Francesca Merola, "Sequences realized as Parker vectors of oligomorphic permutation groups," Journal of Integer Sequences 6, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL6/Gewurz/gewurz22.tex>, lines 331–359. The source identifies `D` (also `C*`) as the cyclic-order permutations preserving or reversing the order and calls Cameron's five representatives closed and highly homogeneous, glossed as one orbit on `k`-sets for all `k`. The source cites Peter J. Cameron, "Transitivity of permutation groups on unordered sets," Math. Z. 148 (1976), 127–139. Interpretation boundary: only the `D` representative is asserted, not exhaustive classification, uniqueness, or conjugacy. The explicit countability, infinitude, and circular-density hypotheses select the intended countable dense circular order.

articles.title: Separation-preserving permutation group
articles.statement:
For a circular order $\alpha$, the
separation-preserving group of $\alpha$ is the subgroup of the group of permutations of $\alpha$
consisting of the permutations $\sigma$ such that for all $a, b, c, d \in \alpha$, the pairs
$a, b$ and $c, d$ separate each other if and only if the pairs $\sigma(a), \sigma(b)$ and
$\sigma(c), \sigma(d)$ separate each other.

articles.title: Product of the reduced incidence algebra
articles.statement:
Let $\Omega$ be a set. For functions $f$ and $g$
from the finite subsets of $\Omega$ to $\mathbb{Q}$, their product $fg$ is the function on finite
subsets given by $(fg)(X) = \sum_{Y \subseteq X} f(Y)\, g(X \setminus Y)$.

If $f$ vanishes off the $n$-element subsets and $g$ vanishes off the $m$-element subsets, this is
the product of Kourovka Problem 13.29, and $fg$ vanishes off the $(n+m)$-element subsets.

articles.title: Cameron's conjecture on invariant incidence algebras holds (Pouzet)
articles.statement:
Let $\Omega$ be an
infinite set and let $G$ be a group of permutations of $\Omega$ all of whose orbits are infinite.
Let $f$ and $g$ be nonzero functions from the finite subsets of $\Omega$ to $\mathbb{Q}$ that are
$G$-invariant ($f(\sigma(X)) = f(X)$ for all $\sigma \in G$ and all finite $X$, and likewise for
$g$) and that each vanish on all subsets of size larger than some bound. Then their product in the
reduced incidence algebra, $(fg)(X) = \sum_{Y \subseteq X} f(Y)\, g(X \setminus Y)$, is not
identically zero. In other words, the algebra $A^G$ of $G$-invariant elements of the reduced
incidence algebra $A$ has no zero divisors.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 13.29 (P. J. Cameron); resolution: M. Pouzet, Theor. Inform. Appl. 42 (2008), no. 1, 83-103, Kourovka Archive, Problem 13.29: the conjecture is proved.

articles.title: Cameron's conjecture on invariant incidence algebras (Kourovka 13.29)
articles.statement:
The statement that
for every infinite set $\Omega$ and every group $G$ of permutations of $\Omega$ all of whose orbits
are infinite, the following holds: if $f$ and $g$ are nonzero functions from the finite subsets of
$\Omega$ to $\mathbb{Q}$ that are $G$-invariant ($f(\sigma(X)) = f(X)$ for all $\sigma \in G$ and
all finite $X$, and likewise for $g$) and that each vanish on all subsets of size larger than some
bound, then their product $fg$ in the reduced incidence algebra, given by
$(fg)(X) = \sum_{Y \subseteq X} f(Y)\, g(X \setminus Y)$, is not identically zero. In other words,
the algebra $A^G$ of $G$-invariant elements of the reduced incidence algebra $A$ has no zero
divisors.

articles.title: Elements of the reduced incidence algebra
articles.statement:
Let $\Omega$ be a set. A function $f$ from the
finite subsets of $\Omega$ to $\mathbb{Q}$ lies in the algebra $A = \bigoplus_n V_n$, where $V_n$
consists of the functions vanishing off the $n$-element subsets, when there is a natural number
$N$ such that $f(X) = 0$ for every finite subset $X$ of $\Omega$ with more than $N$ elements.

articles.title: Invariant functions on finite subsets
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group of permutations of a set
$\Omega$. A function $f$ from the finite subsets of $\Omega$ to $\mathbb{Q}$ is $G$-invariant when
$f(\sigma(X)) = f(X)$ for every $\sigma \in G$ and every finite subset $X$ of $\Omega$, where
$\sigma(X)$ is the image of $X$ under $\sigma$.

articles.title: Permutation groups isomorphic to the rationals have infinite displacement (Kourovka 20.98)
articles.statement:
For every subgroup $G$ of the group of permutations of $\mathbb{N} = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ that is
isomorphic to the additive group $(\mathbb{Q}, +)$, there is an element $g \in G$ such that the
set of displacements $\{a - g(a) : a \in \mathbb{N}\}$, computed in $\mathbb{Z}$, is infinite.
That is, the answer to Kourovka Problem 20.98 is yes.

The 21st issue of the Kourovka Notebook marks 20.98 solved ("Yes, it must"), citing Suchkov,
Shlepkin and Taysnyov (2024).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 20.98 (N. M. Suchkov); resolution: N. M. Suchkov, A. A. Shlepkin and D. A. Taysnyov, On the existence of countable unlimited groups, Siberian Math. J. 65 (2024), no. 6, 1390-1394, abstract: the additive group of the rationals is not isomorphic to a subgroup of the group of all limited permutations of the naturals; Kourovka Notebook (21st issue), Problem 20.98: Yes, it must, https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/smj7921.

articles.title: Suchkov's question on displacements in permutation groups isomorphic to the rationals (Kourovka 20.98)
articles.statement:
**Suchkov's question on displacements in permutation groups isomorphic to the rationals
(Kourovka 20.98).** The statement that for every subgroup $G$ of the group of permutations of
$\mathbb{N} = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ that is isomorphic to the additive group $(\mathbb{Q}, +)$,
there is an element $g \in G$ such that the set of displacements $\{a - g(a) : a \in \mathbb{N}\}$,
computed in $\mathbb{Z}$, is infinite.

Kourovka 20.98 (N. M. Suchkov) is stated for permutations of the positive integers; shifting by
one does not change the displacements.

articles.title: No doubly transitive group has an infinite cyclic point stabilizer (Kourovka 10.63)
articles.statement:
If a group
$G$ acts faithfully on a set $X$ such that for any two ordered pairs of distinct points of $X$
some element of $G$ maps the first to the second, then no point stabilizer of the action is
isomorphic to the infinite cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 10.63 (Ya. P. Sysak); resolution: V. D. Mazurov, Siberian Math. J. 31 (1990), 615-617; Gy. Károlyi, S. J. Kovács and P. P. Pálfy, Aequationes Math. 39, no. 1 (1990), 161-166, Kourovka Archive, Problem 10.63 ("No").

articles.title: Doubly transitive group with infinite cyclic point stabilizer (Kourovka 10.63)
articles.statement:
The
statement that there exist a group $G$ and a faithful action of $G$ on a set $X$ such that for
any two ordered pairs of distinct points of $X$ some element of $G$ maps the first to the second,
and the stabilizer of some point $x \in X$ is isomorphic to the infinite cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}$.

articles.title: A non-periodic doubly transitive group with a periodic point stabilizer (Kourovka 10.64)
articles.statement:
There
exist a group $G$ with an element of infinite order and a faithful action of $G$ on a set $X$
such that for any two ordered pairs of distinct points of $X$ some element of $G$ maps the first
to the second, and every element of the stabilizer of some point $x \in X$ has finite order.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 10.64 (Ya. P. Sysak); resolution: M. Amelio, Non-split sharply 2-transitive groups of bounded exponent, arXiv:2509.11958 (2025), Theorem 1.3 (restated as Theorem 3.5) and Section 3.2: a non-periodic non-split sharply 2-transitive group whose involution centralizers, the point stabilizers of its action on the involutions, have bounded exponent, a positive answer to the paper's Question 2 (Kourovka 10.64); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 10.64 solved, https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11958.

articles.title: Non-periodic doubly transitive group with periodic point stabilizer (Kourovka 10.64)
articles.statement:
The
statement that there exist a group $G$ and a faithful action of $G$ on a set $X$ such that for
any two ordered pairs of distinct points of $X$ some element of $G$ maps the first to the second,
$G$ has an element of infinite order, and every element of the stabilizer of some point $x \in X$
has finite order.

articles.title: Sharply doubly transitive action
articles.statement:
An action of a group $G$ on a set $\Omega$ is sharply
doubly transitive when for all points $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta \in \Omega$ with
$\alpha \ne \beta$ and $\gamma \ne \delta$ there is exactly one $g \in G$ with
$g \cdot \alpha = \gamma$ and $g \cdot \beta = \delta$.

articles.title: A sharply 2-transitive group without nontrivial abelian normal subgroups
articles.statement:
The statement of
Kourovka Problem 11.52 is false: there is a group $G$ acting sharply doubly transitively on a set
$\Omega$ with at least two points such that no nontrivial normal subgroup of $G$ is abelian.

Rips, Segev and Tent construct such a group; the Kourovka Archive answers 11.52 "No, not every".
For finite groups the answer is yes, by Frobenius's theorem.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.52 (V. D. Mazurov); resolution: E. Rips, Y. Segev and K. Tent, J. Eur. Math. Soc. 19, no. 10 (2017), 2895-2910, Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.52: "No, not every", https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Mazurov's question on sharply 2-transitive groups (Kourovka 11.52)
articles.statement:
The statement that every
group $G$ acting sharply doubly transitively on a set $\Omega$ with at least two points has a
nontrivial abelian normal subgroup.

articles.title: The additive group of the reals embeds in the infinite symmetric group
articles.statement:
There is an injective
group homomorphism from the additive group $(\mathbb{R}, +)$ of real numbers into the group
$S_\infty$ of all permutations of the natural numbers.

## Sources

- J. Schreier and S. Ulam, Problem 95 of the Scottish Book; affirmative answer of Schreier and Ulam, November 1935, recorded in the typescript addendum Ad 95. `Multiplicative ℝ` is the additive group `ℝ` viewed multiplicatively, so a monoid homomorphism out of it is an additive homomorphism out of `ℝ`.

articles.title: Separable metrizable groups need not embed in the infinite symmetric group
articles.statement:
The claim of
Kourovka Problem 18.36 is false: there is a group $G$ that admits a metrizable topology
making it a separable topological group but admits no injective group homomorphism into the
group $\mathrm{Sym}(\mathbb{N})$ of all permutations of the natural numbers.

Rosendal and Solecki (2007) give an uncountable connected Polish group (a separable
completely metrizable topological group) every abstract homomorphism of which into
$\mathrm{Sym}(\mathbb{N})$ is trivial, so it has no injective one.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 18.36 (J. D. Dixon); resolution: C. Rosendal and S. Solecki, Israel J. Math. 162 (2007), 349-371, an uncountable connected Polish group whose every abstract homomorphism into Sym(ℕ) is trivial; see also A. Kaïchouh and F. Le Maître, Bull. London Math. Soc. 47 (2015), 996-1009 (S. Corson, letter of 5 June 2024); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 18.36 solved, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Claim of Kourovka Problem 18.36
articles.statement:
The claim (J. D. Dixon) that every group $G$ that
admits a metrizable topology making it a separable topological group admits an injective group
homomorphism into the group $\mathrm{Sym}(\mathbb{N})$ of all permutations of the natural
numbers.

articles.title: Locally finite field (Kourovka 18.60)
articles.statement:
A field $P$ is locally finite when the subfield
generated by any finite subset of $P$ is finite.

articles.title: No field-like transitive automorphism group of a countably infinite elementary abelian $2$-group
articles.statement:
**No field-like transitive automorphism group of a countably infinite elementary abelian
$2$-group.** The conjecture of Kourovka Problem 18.60 holds: for every countably infinite
elementary abelian $2$-group $V$ (an abelian group with $v + v = 0$ for all $v \in V$) there is no
subgroup $G$ of the symmetric group $\mathrm{Sym}(V)$ consisting of additive bijections such that
(a) $G$ is transitive on $V \setminus \{0\}$, and (b) for every nonzero $v \in V$, writing
$H = G_v$ for the stabilizer of $v$ in $G$, there are a subgroup $V_v$ of $V$ with
$V = \langle v \rangle \oplus V_v$ that every element of $H$ maps into itself, a locally finite
field $P$ of characteristic $2$, a group isomorphism $\psi : H \to P^\times$ onto the
multiplicative group of $P$, and a bijection $\theta : V_v \to P$ such that
$\theta(h w) = \psi(h)\,\theta(w)$ for all $h \in H$ and $w \in V_v$.

Muliarchyk's Theorem 1 excludes a group transitive on the nonzero vectors of an
$\mathbb{F}_2$-space of dimension at least $4$ whose point stabilizer preserves a complement to
$\mathbb{F}_2 v$ and is transitive on its nonzero vectors; a similarity with $P^\times$ acting on
$P$ gives that transitivity (Corollary 2).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 18.60 (D. V. Lytkina); resolution: K. Muliarchyk, Involution centralizers and a linear obstruction: Kourovka Problems 18.59 and 18.60, preprint, 2026, Theorem 1: for an F_2-space V of dimension at least 4, no K ≤ GL(V) transitive on V ∖ {0} has a point stabilizer preserving a complement W_v to F_2 v and transitive on W_v ∖ {0}; Corollary 2: the nonexistence conjecture of Problem 18.60 holds; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 18.60 solved, https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/kourovka_18_59-18_60_solution.pdf.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 18.60 (field-like transitive automorphism groups)
articles.statement:
The conjecture of
D. V. Lytkina, as a proposition: for every countably infinite elementary abelian $2$-group $V$
(an abelian group with $v + v = 0$ for all $v \in V$) there is no subgroup $G$ of the symmetric
group $\mathrm{Sym}(V)$ consisting of additive bijections such that (a) $G$ is transitive on
$V \setminus \{0\}$, and (b) for every nonzero $v \in V$, writing $H = G_v$ for the stabilizer of
$v$ in $G$, there are a subgroup $V_v$ of $V$ with $V = \langle v \rangle \oplus V_v$ that every
element of $H$ maps into itself, a locally finite field $P$ of characteristic $2$, a group
isomorphism $\psi : H \to P^\times$ onto the multiplicative group of $P$, and a bijection
$\theta : V_v \to P$ such that $\theta(h w) = \psi(h)\,\theta(w)$ for all $h \in H$ and
$w \in V_v$.

articles.title: The Andrews–Curtis groups $AC_n$ are finitely presented for $n \ge 3$ (Kourovka 18.89)
articles.statement:
For
every $n \ge 3$, the Andrews–Curtis group $AC_n$, the subgroup of the permutation group of the set
$F_n^n$ of $n$-tuples of elements of the free group $F_n$ generated by the elementary Andrews–Curtis
moves, is finitely presented.

The Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) records this, deducing it from Kiralis–Krstić–McCool (1996),
Theorem 3.1, through an isomorphism observed by M. Ershov (letter of 2025, using Roman'kov's
Lemma 3.2).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 18.89 (J. Swan, A. Lisitsa); resolution: S. Krstić and J. McCool, J. London Math. Soc. (2) 56 (1997), no. 2, 264-274; V. A. Roman'kov, On the Andrews-Curtis groups: non-finite presentability, preprint, arXiv:2305.11838 (2023); G. Kiralis, S. Krstić and J. McCool, Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) 73 (1996), no. 3, 575-622; M. Ershov, letter of 16 October 2025, AC_2 is not finitely presented (Krstić-McCool, Theorem 1; Roman'kov, Theorem B: AC(F_2) ≅ A_{2,2} is not finitely presented); AC_n, n ≥ 3, is finitely presented by Kiralis-Krstić-McCool, Theorem 3.1, since AC_n ≅ A_{n,n} ≅ Φ_n(F_n) (Ershov's letter); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 18.89 solved, https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/kourovka1889.pdf.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 18.89 for $n \ge 3$
articles.statement:
The proposition that for every $n \ge 3$ the
Andrews–Curtis group $AC_n$ (the subgroup of the permutation group of the set of $n$-tuples of
elements of the free group $F_n$ generated by the elementary Andrews–Curtis moves) is finitely
presented.

articles.title: The Andrews–Curtis group $AC_n$
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ let $F_n$ be the free group on $n$
generators. The Andrews–Curtis group $AC_n$ is the subgroup of the group of permutations of the set
$F_n^n$ of $n$-tuples $(u_1, \dots, u_n)$ of elements of $F_n$ generated by the elementary
Andrews–Curtis moves that are permutations: $u_i \mapsto u_i u_j^{\pm 1}$ and
$u_i \mapsto u_j^{\pm 1} u_i$ for indices $i \ne j$, $u_i \mapsto u_i^{-1}$, and
$u_i \mapsto w u_i w^{-1}$ for $w \in F_n$, all other entries unchanged. Viewing a tuple as the
relators of a balanced presentation $\langle x_1, \dots, x_n \mid u_1, \dots, u_n \rangle$, these
are the Nielsen transformations of the relator tuple together with conjugations of relators.

articles.title: The Andrews–Curtis group $AC_2$ is not finitely presented (Kourovka 18.89)
articles.statement:
The Andrews–Curtis
group $AC_2$, the subgroup of the permutation group of the set $F_2^2$ of pairs of elements of the
free group $F_2$ generated by the elementary Andrews–Curtis moves, is not finitely presented.

The Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) records this, citing Krstić–McCool (1997) and Roman'kov (2023),
who also shows that the group of moves on all relator tuples is isomorphic to the Andrews–Curtis
group of $F_2$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 18.89 (J. Swan, A. Lisitsa); resolution: S. Krstić and J. McCool, J. London Math. Soc. (2) 56 (1997), no. 2, 264-274; V. A. Roman'kov, On the Andrews-Curtis groups: non-finite presentability, preprint, arXiv:2305.11838 (2023); G. Kiralis, S. Krstić and J. McCool, Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) 73 (1996), no. 3, 575-622; M. Ershov, letter of 16 October 2025, AC_2 is not finitely presented (Krstić-McCool, Theorem 1; Roman'kov, Theorem B: AC(F_2) ≅ A_{2,2} is not finitely presented); AC_n, n ≥ 3, is finitely presented by Kiralis-Krstić-McCool, Theorem 3.1, since AC_n ≅ A_{n,n} ≅ Φ_n(F_n) (Ershov's letter); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 18.89 solved, https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/kourovka1889.pdf.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 18.89 for $n = 2$
articles.statement:
The proposition, asked by J. Swan and A. Lisitsa,
that the Andrews–Curtis group $AC_2$ (the subgroup of the permutation group of the set of pairs of
elements of the free group $F_2$ generated by the elementary Andrews–Curtis moves) is finitely
presented.

articles.title: Elementary Andrews–Curtis moves
articles.statement:
Let $F_n$ be the free group on $n$ generators. A map
$f \colon F_n^n \to F_n^n$ on $n$-tuples $(u_1, \dots, u_n)$ of elements of $F_n$ is an elementary
Andrews–Curtis move if there is an index $i$ such that $f$ replaces the entry $u_i$ of every tuple
by $u_i u_j$, $u_i u_j^{-1}$, $u_j u_i$ or $u_j^{-1} u_i$ for a fixed index $j \ne i$, or by
$u_i^{-1}$, or by $w u_i w^{-1}$ for a fixed $w \in F_n$, and leaves all other entries unchanged.

articles.title: Baumslag's germ representation is not faithful
articles.statement:
Let $B$ be Baumslag's group
$\langle a, b \mid (bab^{-1})\, a\, (bab^{-1})^{-1} = a^2 \rangle$, let $f(x) = 2x$ and
$g(x) = 2^x$, and for $w$ in the free group on $a, b$ with reduced word $l_1 l_2 \cdots l_k$ let
$\varphi_w = \varphi_{l_1} \circ \varphi_{l_2} \circ \cdots \circ \varphi_{l_k}$, where
$\varphi_a = f$, $\varphi_{a^{-1}}(x) = x/2$, $\varphi_b = g$ and $\varphi_{b^{-1}}(x) = \log_2 x$.
The representation $a \mapsto f$, $b \mapsto g$ of $B$ by germs at $+\infty$ is not faithful: there
is an element $w$ of the free group on $a, b$ such that $\varphi_w(x) = x$ for all sufficiently
large real $x$, but the image of $w$ in $B$ is not trivial.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 17.99 (A. Yu. Olshanskii); resolution: C.-F. Nyberg-Brodda, The Baumslag-Gersten group and a problem of Olshanskii, preprint, arXiv:2606.27408 (2026), abstract (the representation of BG(1, 2) by germs is not faithful: an explicit non-trivial element of its kernel); the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 17.99 solved (No, it is not), https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27408.

articles.title: Faithfulness of Baumslag's germ representation (Kourovka 17.99)
articles.statement:
Let $B$ be Baumslag's
group $\langle a, b \mid (bab^{-1})\, a\, (bab^{-1})^{-1} = a^2 \rangle$, let $f(x) = 2x$ and
$g(x) = 2^x$, and for $w$ in the free group on $a, b$ let $\varphi_w$ be its word function, the
composite of $f$, $g$ and their inverses along the reduced word of $w$. The representation
$a \mapsto f$, $b \mapsto g$ of $B$ by germs at $+\infty$ is faithful when every $w$ with
$\varphi_w(x) = x$ for all sufficiently large real $x$ is trivial in $B$.

This is Olshanskii's question whether the representation of $B$ in the group of germs at $+\infty$
of increasing continuous functions on $(0, \infty)$ is faithful.

articles.title: Baumslag's group
articles.statement:
Baumslag's group is the one-relator group
$B = \langle a, b \mid (bab^{-1})\, a\, (bab^{-1})^{-1} = a^2 \rangle$, the quotient of the free
group on the two generators $a$ and $b$ by the normal subgroup generated by
$(bab^{-1})\, a\, (bab^{-1})^{-1} a^{-2}$.

articles.title: Letter functions for Baumslag's group
articles.statement:
To each letter of the free group on $a, b$ attach a
function $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$: $a$ gives $f(x) = 2x$, $a^{-1}$ gives $x/2$, $b$ gives
$g(x) = 2^x$ and $b^{-1}$ gives $\log_2 x$.

On $(0, \infty)$ the function $\log_2 x$ is the inverse of $g$, which is all that matters for germs
at $+\infty$.

articles.title: Word functions for Baumslag's group
articles.statement:
To an element $w$ of the free group on $a, b$ with
reduced word $l_1 l_2 \cdots l_n$ attach the composite
$\varphi_w = \varphi_{l_1} \circ \varphi_{l_2} \circ \cdots \circ \varphi_{l_n}$, where
$\varphi_l$ is the function attached to the letter $l$; the first letter is applied last, and
$\varphi_1$ is the identity. With this order products of germs are composites, and $f(x) = 2x$
and $g(x) = 2^x$ satisfy the defining relation of Baumslag's group as germs at $+\infty$.

articles.title: Boone–Higman theorem (easy direction)
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi \colon F_n \to G$ be a surjective
homomorphism from the free group $F_n$ on $n$ generators onto a group $G$. If there are injective
homomorphisms $G \to H$ and $H \to K$, where $H$ is a simple group and $K$ is a finitely presented
group, then the word problem of $G$ with respect to $\varphi$ is solvable.

## Sources

- W. W. Boone & G. Higman, *An algebraic characterization of groups with soluble word problem*, J. Austral. Math. Soc. 18 (1974). Knill, *Some fundamental theorems in mathematics*, §122. Problem `boone_higman_embedding` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Kuznetsov's theorem on finitely presented simple groups
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple group, let
$F_n$ be the free group on $n$ generators, and let $\varphi \colon F_n \to G$ be a surjective
homomorphism whose kernel is the normal closure of finitely many elements. Then the word problem
of $G$ with respect to $\varphi$ is solvable: there is an algorithm that decides, for every word
$w$ in the $n$ generators and their inverses, whether $\varphi(w) = 1$.

## Sources

- A.V. Kuznetsov, 'Algorithms as operations in algebraic systems', Uspekhi Mat. Nauk 13 (1958) 240–241 (Russian); W.W. Boone and G. Higman, 'An algebraic characterization of groups with soluble word problem', J. Austral. Math. Soc. 18 (1974) 41–53. §122 in O. Knill, *Some Fundamental Theorems in Mathematics* (https://people.math.harvard.edu/~knill/graphgeometry/papers/fundamental.pdf). Problem `boone_higman_simple` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Alternating word
articles.statement:
For elements $a$ and $b$ of a monoid and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the
alternating word of length $n$ starting with $a$ is the product $a b a b \cdots$ of $n$ factors
that alternate between $a$ and $b$, beginning with $a$; for $n = 0$ it is the identity.

articles.title: Artin group
articles.statement:
Let $M = (m_{ij})_{i, j \in B}$ be a Coxeter matrix over an index type $B$,
where $m_{ij} = 0$ encodes $m_{ij} = \infty$. The Artin group (Artin–Tits group) of $M$ is the
group presented by generators $s_i$, one for each $i \in B$, subject only to the braid relations:
for every ordered pair of distinct $i, j \in B$ with $m_{ij} \neq 0$, the alternating words
$s_i s_j s_i \cdots$ and $s_j s_i s_j \cdots$ of length $m_{ij}$ are equal. Unlike for the
Coxeter group of $M$, no relations $s_i^2 = 1$ are imposed.

articles.title: Artin relator
articles.statement:
Let $M = (m_{ij})$ be a Coxeter matrix over an index type $B$, and write
$s_i$ for the free generators of the free group on $B$. For $i, j \in B$, let $u$ and $v$ be the
alternating words $s_i s_j s_i \cdots$ and $s_j s_i s_j \cdots$ of length $m_{ij}$. The Artin
relator of the ordered pair $(i, j)$ is the element $u v^{-1}$ of the free group; setting it equal
to $1$ imposes the braid relation $u = v$.

articles.title: Artin relators of a Coxeter matrix
articles.statement:
Let $M = (m_{ij})$ be a Coxeter matrix over an index
type $B$, where $m_{ij} = 0$ encodes $m_{ij} = \infty$, and write $s_i$ for the free generators of
the free group on $B$. The set of Artin relators of $M$ consists of the elements $u v^{-1}$ of the
free group, one for each ordered pair of distinct $i, j \in B$ with $m_{ij} \neq 0$, where $u$ and
$v$ are the alternating words $s_i s_j s_i \cdots$ and $s_j s_i s_j \cdots$ of length $m_{ij}$.
Pairs with $m_{ij} = \infty$ contribute no relator.

articles.title: Braid relations in the Artin group
articles.statement:
Let $M = (m_{ij})$ be a Coxeter matrix over an index
type $B$, where $m_{ij} = 0$ encodes $m_{ij} = \infty$, and let $s_i$ ($i \in B$) be the
generators of the Artin group of $M$. For distinct $i, j \in B$ with $m_{ij} \neq 0$, the
alternating words $s_i s_j s_i \cdots$ and $s_j s_i s_j \cdots$ of length $m_{ij}$ are equal in
the Artin group.

articles.title: The generators generate the Artin group
articles.statement:
For a Coxeter matrix $M$ over an index type $B$,
the subgroup of the Artin group of $M$ generated by its generators $s_i$, $i \in B$, is the whole
group.

articles.title: Monoid homomorphisms preserve alternating words
articles.statement:
Let $f : G \to H$ be a homomorphism of
monoids. For all $a, b \in G$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $f$ maps the alternating word $a b a \cdots$
of length $n$ starting with $a$ to the alternating word $f(a) f(b) f(a) \cdots$ of length $n$
starting with $f(a)$.

articles.title: Generators of the Artin group
articles.statement:
For a Coxeter matrix $M$ over an index type $B$ and
$i \in B$, the generator $s_i$ of the Artin group of $M$ is the image of the free generator $i$
under the quotient map from the free group on $B$ onto the Artin group.

articles.title: Bardakov–Bellingeri: $B_4$ does not embed in $\operatorname{Aut}(F_2)$
articles.statement:
There is no injective
group homomorphism from the braid group $B_4$ on four strands to the automorphism group
$\operatorname{Aut}(F_2)$ of the free group $F_2$ of rank $2$. Kourovka Problem 17.14
(V. G. Bardakov) asks whether, for $n \ge 4$, the braid group $B_n$ embeds in the automorphism
group of the free group $F_{n-2}$ of rank $n - 2$; this answers the case $n = 4$ negatively.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 17.14 (V. G. Bardakov); resolution: V. G. Bardakov and P. Bellingeri, in Knot theory and its applications (ICTS program KTH-2013, IISER Mohali), Contemp. Math. 670, Amer. Math. Soc., 2016, 285-298, Kourovka Archive, Problem 17.14 (No, it cannot for n = 4).

articles.title: Bardakov's question on embedding $B_4$ in $\operatorname{Aut}(F_2)$
articles.statement:
The statement that
there is an injective group homomorphism from the braid group $B_4$ on four strands to the
automorphism group $\operatorname{Aut}(F_2)$ of the free group $F_2$ of rank $2$. Kourovka
Problem 17.14 (V. G. Bardakov) asks whether, for $n \ge 4$, the braid group $B_n$ embeds in the
automorphism group of the free group $F_{n-2}$ of rank $n - 2$; this is the case $n = 4$.

articles.title: The braid group $B_4$
articles.statement:
The braid group on four strands, given by Artin's presentation: the
group generated by $\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3$ subject to the relations
$\sigma_1 \sigma_2 \sigma_1 = \sigma_2 \sigma_1 \sigma_2$, $\sigma_2 \sigma_3 \sigma_2 =
\sigma_3 \sigma_2 \sigma_3$ and $\sigma_1 \sigma_3 = \sigma_3 \sigma_1$.

articles.title: The braid represented by a braid word
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $B_{n+1}$ be the braid
group on $n + 1$ strands, realized as the Artin group of the Coxeter matrix of type $A_n$, with
standard generators $\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_n$. A braid word is an element of the free group on
$\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_n$; the braid it represents is its image under the group homomorphism from
this free group to $B_{n+1}$ that sends each $\sigma_i$ to the generator $\sigma_i$ of $B_{n+1}$.

articles.title: Braid groups have polynomially short conjugators
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $B_{n+1}$ be
the braid group on $n + 1$ strands, realized as the Artin group of the Coxeter matrix of type
$A_n$, with standard generators $\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_n$. A braid word is an element of the
free group on $\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_n$, and its length $|u|$ is the length of its freely reduced
form. For every $n$ there are natural numbers $C$ and $d$ such that for all braid words $u$ and $v$
whose braids are conjugate in $B_{n+1}$ there is a braid word $w$ with
$|w| \le C (\max(|u|, |v|) + 1)^d$ such that $w u w^{-1}$ and $v$ represent the same braid.

This answers the stronger question of Kourovka Problem 19.81 positively: the Kourovka Archive
answers "Yes, there is such a conjugator, even for any mapping class groups", citing Tao's
linearly bounded conjugator property for mapping class groups (Theorem B: a conjugator of length
at most $K(|f| + |g|)$).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 19.81 (V. Shpilrain); resolution: J. Tao, Linearly bounded conjugator property for mapping class groups, Geom. Funct. Anal. 23 (2013), no. 1, 415-466 (arXiv:1106.2341), Theorem B: for a finite generating set of the mapping class group of a surface of finite type there is K such that conjugate f, g have a conjugator ω with |ω| ≤ K(|f| + |g|); Kourovka Archive, Problem 19.81: Yes, there is such a conjugator, even for any mapping class groups, https://arxiv.org/abs/1106.2341.

articles.title: Polynomially short conjugators in braid groups
articles.statement:
The proposition (the stronger question of
Kourovka Problem 19.81, V. Shpilrain) that for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ there are natural numbers
$C$ and $d$ with the following property. Let $B_{n+1}$ be the braid group on $n + 1$ strands,
realized as the Artin group of the Coxeter matrix of type $A_n$, with standard generators
$\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_n$; a braid word is an element of the free group on
$\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_n$, and its length $|u|$ is the length of its freely reduced form. For all
braid words $u$ and $v$ whose braids are conjugate in $B_{n+1}$ there is a braid word $w$ with
$|w| \le C (\max(|u|, |v|) + 1)^d$ such that $w u w^{-1}$ and $v$ represent the same braid.

articles.title: Nontrivial endomorphisms of the braid commutator subgroup on five or more strands are automorphisms
articles.statement:
**Nontrivial endomorphisms of the braid commutator subgroup on five or more strands are
automorphisms.** For every $n > 4$, every endomorphism of the commutator subgroup $[B_n, B_n]$ of
the braid group $B_n$ on $n$ strands other than the trivial endomorphism is bijective, that is, an
automorphism.

This was proved by Kordek and Margalit for $n \ge 7$ and extended by Orevkov to all $n \ge 5$; the
Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) answers 14.102(b) "Yes".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 14.102 (V. Lin; V. Shpilrain); part (c) in the Archive of Solved Problems; resolution: (a) F. Castel, Geometric representations of the braid groups, Astérisque 378 (2016) (n ≥ 6), and L. Chen, K. Kordek and D. Margalit, Homomorphisms between braid groups, arXiv:1910.00712 (n = 5); (b) S. Orevkov, Ann. Fac. Sci. Toulouse Math. 33 (2024), no. 1, 105-121, extending K. Kordek and D. Margalit, Bull. London Math. Soc. 54 (2022), 95-111 (n ≥ 7); (c) P. Linnell and T. Schick, J. Amer. Math. Soc. 20 (2007), no. 4, 1003-1051, the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 14.102(a), (b) solved (for n ≥ 5 every non-injective endomorphism of B_n has cyclic image; every non-trivial endomorphism of [B_n, B_n] is an automorphism); Kourovka Archive, Problem 14.102(c) (Yes), https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.00712.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 14.102(b): endomorphisms of the braid commutator subgroup
articles.statement:
The statement
that for every $n > 4$, every endomorphism of the commutator subgroup $[B_n, B_n]$ of the braid
group $B_n$ on $n$ strands other than the trivial endomorphism is bijective, that is, an
automorphism. Posed by V. Lin and V. Shpilrain.

articles.title: Braid group on n strands
articles.statement: The braid group `Bₙ` on `n` strands, by Artin's presentation.

articles.title: Non-injective endomorphisms of braid groups on five or more strands have cyclic image
articles.statement:
The
answer to Kourovka Problem 14.102(a) is negative: there is no $n > 4$ for which the braid group
$B_n$ on $n$ strands has a non-injective endomorphism whose image is not cyclic. Equivalently, for
every $n \ge 5$, every non-injective endomorphism of $B_n$ has cyclic image.

This was proved by Castel for $n \ge 6$ and by Chen, Kordek and Margalit for $n = 5$; the Kourovka
Notebook (21st issue) answers 14.102(a) "No".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 14.102 (V. Lin; V. Shpilrain); part (c) in the Archive of Solved Problems; resolution: (a) F. Castel, Geometric representations of the braid groups, Astérisque 378 (2016) (n ≥ 6), and L. Chen, K. Kordek and D. Margalit, Homomorphisms between braid groups, arXiv:1910.00712 (n = 5); (b) S. Orevkov, Ann. Fac. Sci. Toulouse Math. 33 (2024), no. 1, 105-121, extending K. Kordek and D. Margalit, Bull. London Math. Soc. 54 (2022), 95-111 (n ≥ 7); (c) P. Linnell and T. Schick, J. Amer. Math. Soc. 20 (2007), no. 4, 1003-1051, the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 14.102(a), (b) solved (for n ≥ 5 every non-injective endomorphism of B_n has cyclic image; every non-trivial endomorphism of [B_n, B_n] is an automorphism); Kourovka Archive, Problem 14.102(c) (Yes), https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.00712.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 14.102(a): non-injective braid endomorphisms with non-cyclic image
articles.statement:
The
statement that for some $n > 4$ the braid group $B_n$ on $n$ strands has a non-injective
endomorphism whose image is not cyclic (in particular not trivial). Posed by V. Lin and
V. Shpilrain.

articles.title: Artin's braid relators
articles.statement:
Artin's relators for the braid group on `n` strands, in the free group on the generators
`σ₀, …, σ_{n-2}` (indexed by `Fin (n - 1)`): `σᵢ σⱼ = σⱼ σᵢ` when `j ≥ i + 2`, and
`σᵢ σᵢ₊₁ σᵢ = σᵢ₊₁ σᵢ σᵢ₊₁`.

articles.title: Braid groups on five or more strands have proper non-abelian torsion-free quotients
articles.statement:
For
every $n > 4$, the braid group $B_n$ on $n$ strands has a nontrivial normal subgroup $N$ such that
the quotient $B_n / N$ is non-abelian and torsion-free (no element other than the identity has
finite order).

The Kourovka Archive answers 14.102(c) "Yes, it does", citing Linnell and Schick (every braid group
is residually torsion-free nilpotent-by-finite); Humphries had constructed such quotients for
$n < 7$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 14.102 (V. Lin; V. Shpilrain); part (c) in the Archive of Solved Problems; resolution: (a) F. Castel, Geometric representations of the braid groups, Astérisque 378 (2016) (n ≥ 6), and L. Chen, K. Kordek and D. Margalit, Homomorphisms between braid groups, arXiv:1910.00712 (n = 5); (b) S. Orevkov, Ann. Fac. Sci. Toulouse Math. 33 (2024), no. 1, 105-121, extending K. Kordek and D. Margalit, Bull. London Math. Soc. 54 (2022), 95-111 (n ≥ 7); (c) P. Linnell and T. Schick, J. Amer. Math. Soc. 20 (2007), no. 4, 1003-1051, the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 14.102(a), (b) solved (for n ≥ 5 every non-injective endomorphism of B_n has cyclic image; every non-trivial endomorphism of [B_n, B_n] is an automorphism); Kourovka Archive, Problem 14.102(c) (Yes), https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.00712.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 14.102(c): torsion-free quotients of braid groups
articles.statement:
The statement that for
every $n > 4$, the braid group $B_n$ on $n$ strands has a nontrivial normal subgroup $N$ such that
the quotient $B_n / N$ is non-abelian and torsion-free (no element other than the identity has
finite order). Posed by V. Lin and V. Shpilrain.

articles.title: Kourovka 11.54: only the trivial pure braid is conjugate to its inverse
articles.statement:
For every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and every pure braid $\beta$ on $n + 1$ strands, if
$\gamma \beta \gamma^{-1} = \beta^{-1}$ for some pure braid $\gamma$ on $n + 1$ strands, then
$\beta = 1$.

The Kourovka Archive answers 11.54 affirmatively (V. A. Roman'kov): the pure braid group embeds in
the IA-automorphism group of a free group, which is residually torsion-free nilpotent, and in a
torsion-free nilpotent group an element conjugate to its inverse is trivial.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.54 (G. S. Makanin); resolution: V. A. Roman'kov, letter of 3 October 1990; see also V. G. Bardakov, Russ. Acad. Sci. Sb. Math. 76, no. 1 (1993), 123-153, Kourovka Archive, Problems 11.54 and 11.55: both affirmative, since the coloured braid group embeds in the group of automorphisms of `F_n` acting trivially modulo `F_n'`, which is residually torsion-free nilpotent, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Kourovka 11.54: pure braids conjugate to their inverses
articles.statement:
The proposition that for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, every pure braid $\beta$ on $n + 1$ strands that is conjugate to its inverse
inside the pure braid group, that is, $\gamma \beta \gamma^{-1} = \beta^{-1}$ for some pure braid
$\gamma$ on $n + 1$ strands, is the identity braid.

This is Kourovka Problem 11.54 (G. S. Makanin).

articles.title: Pure braid group
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the pure (coloured) braid group $P_{n+1}$ on
$n + 1$ strands is the normal closure, in the braid group $B_{n+1}$, of the squares $\sigma_i^2$ of
the standard generators $\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_n$ of $B_{n+1}$, where $B_{n+1}$ is the Artin
group of the Coxeter matrix of type $A_n$.

This is the kernel of the map $B_{n+1} \to S_{n+1}$, since adding the relations $\sigma_i^2 = 1$ to
the braid relations presents the Coxeter group of type $A_n$, the symmetric group $S_{n+1}$.

articles.title: Pure braid group
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the pure (coloured) braid group $P_{n+1}$ on
$n + 1$ strands is the normal closure, in the braid group $B_{n+1}$, of the squares $\sigma_i^2$ of
the standard generators $\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_n$ of $B_{n+1}$, where $B_{n+1}$ is the Artin
group of the Coxeter matrix of type $A_n$.

This is the kernel of the map $B_{n+1} \to S_{n+1}$, since adding the relations $\sigma_i^2 = 1$ to
the braid relations presents the Coxeter group of type $A_n$, the symmetric group $S_{n+1}$.

articles.title: Kourovka 11.55: roots in pure braid groups are unique
articles.statement:
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and every
integer $k \ge 1$, if pure braids $\alpha$ and $\beta$ on $n + 1$ strands satisfy
$\alpha^k = \beta^k$, then $\alpha = \beta$.

The Kourovka Archive answers 11.55 affirmatively (V. A. Roman'kov): the pure braid group embeds in
the IA-automorphism group of a free group, which is residually torsion-free nilpotent, and
torsion-free nilpotent groups have unique roots.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.55 (G. S. Makanin); resolution: V. A. Roman'kov, letter of 3 October 1990; see also V. G. Bardakov, Russ. Acad. Sci. Sb. Math. 76, no. 1 (1993), 123-153, Kourovka Archive, Problems 11.54 and 11.55: both affirmative, since the coloured braid group embeds in the group of automorphisms of `F_n` acting trivially modulo `F_n'`, which is residually torsion-free nilpotent, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Kourovka 11.55: unique roots in pure braid groups
articles.statement:
The proposition that for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and every integer $k \ge 1$, if pure braids $\alpha$ and $\beta$ on $n + 1$
strands satisfy $\alpha^k = \beta^k$, then $\alpha = \beta$.

This is Kourovka Problem 11.55 (G. S. Makanin): extraction of roots in the group of coloured
braids is unique.

articles.title: The braid group $B_n$ by Artin's presentation
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the braid group
$B_n$ on $n$ strands is the group generated by $\sigma_0, \dots, \sigma_{n-2}$ subject to the
relations $\sigma_i \sigma_j = \sigma_j \sigma_i$ for $j \ge i + 2$ and
$\sigma_i \sigma_{i+1} \sigma_i = \sigma_{i+1} \sigma_i \sigma_{i+1}$ for $0 \le i \le n - 3$; it is
the trivial group when $n \le 1$.

articles.title: Artin's braid relators
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the set of Artin's relators for the braid
group on $n$ strands, as elements of the free group on the $n - 1$ generators
$\sigma_0, \dots, \sigma_{n-2}$ (no generators when $n \le 1$): the commutators
$\sigma_i \sigma_j \sigma_i^{-1} \sigma_j^{-1}$ for $0 \le i$ and $i + 2 \le j \le n - 2$, and the
words $\sigma_i \sigma_{i+1} \sigma_i (\sigma_{i+1} \sigma_i \sigma_{i+1})^{-1}$ for
$0 \le i \le n - 3$.

articles.title: Roots in braid groups are unique up to conjugacy (González-Meneses)
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$n$ and every integer $k \ge 1$, if two elements $\alpha, \beta$ of the braid group $B_n$ on $n$
strands satisfy $\alpha^k = \beta^k$, then $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are conjugate in $B_n$. This answers
Kourovka Problem 10.23 (G. S. Makanin) affirmatively.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 10.23 (G. S. Makanin); resolution: J. González-Meneses, The nth root of a braid is unique up to conjugacy, Algebr. Geom. Topol. 3 (2003), 1103-1118, main theorem; Kourovka Archive, Problem 10.23 ("Yes, it is true"), https://doi.org/10.2140/agt.2003.3.1103.

articles.title: Makanin's root-uniqueness question for braid groups
articles.statement:
The statement that for every natural
number $n$ and every integer $k \ge 1$, any two elements $\alpha, \beta$ of the braid group $B_n$ on
$n$ strands with $\alpha^k = \beta^k$ are conjugate in $B_n$. This is Kourovka Problem 10.23
(G. S. Makanin).

articles.title: Coherent ring
articles.statement:
A semiring $R$ is (left) coherent if every finitely generated left ideal
of $R$ is finitely presented as an $R$-module.

articles.title: Coherent group
articles.statement:
A group is coherent if all of its finitely generated subgroups are
finitely presented.

articles.title: One-relator group
articles.statement: A group `G` is called one-relator if it has a presentation with a single relation.

articles.title: Jaikin-Zapirain–Linton theorem: one-relator groups are coherent
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a one-relator
group and $K$ a field. Then $G$ is a coherent group and the group algebra $K[G]$ is a (left)
coherent ring.

## Sources

- A. Jaikin-Zapirain and M. Linton, `On the coherence of one-relator groups and their group algebras`, Annals of Math, 201 (3) 2025. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_on_coherence_of_one_relator_groups` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Kourovka 12.98(b) has a negative answer
articles.statement:
It is not the case that for every natural number $n$
and every recursively enumerable normal subgroup $R$ of the free group $F$ on $n$ generators, with
commutator subgroup $[R, R]$, the conjugacy problem for $F / R$ is solvable if and only if the
conjugacy problem for $F / [R, R]$ is solvable: for some such $n$ and $R$, exactly one of these two
conjugacy problems is solvable.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 12.98 (V. E. Shpil'rain); resolution: M. I. Anokhin, Math. Notes 61 (1997), no. 1-2, 3-8, Kourovka Archive, Problem 12.98: a) Yes, it is; b) No, it is not; c) No, it is not.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 12.98(b) (V. E. Shpil'rain)
articles.statement:
The statement that for every natural
number $n$ and every recursively enumerable normal subgroup $R$ of the free group $F$ on $n$
generators, with commutator subgroup $[R, R]$, the conjugacy problem for $F / R$ is solvable if and
only if the conjugacy problem for $F / [R, R]$ is solvable.

articles.title: Solvable conjugacy problem for a quotient of a free group
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number,
let $F$ be the free group on the generators $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ and let $N$ be a subgroup of $F$.
The conjugacy problem for $F / N$ is solvable when the predicate on pairs of words $(w, v)$ (finite
lists of letters, each a generator together with a sign) that some $u \in F$ satisfies
$u w u^{-1} v^{-1} \in N$, with $w$ and $v$ read as elements of $F$, is computable.

When $N$ is normal, this says that conjugacy of the images of $w$ and $v$ in $F / N$ is
decidable.

articles.title: Recursively enumerable subgroup of a free group
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $F$
be the free group on the generators $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$. A subgroup $N$ of $F$ is recursively
enumerable when the set of words $w$ (finite lists of letters, each a generator together with a
sign) whose image in $F$ lies in $N$ is recursively enumerable.

articles.title: Kourovka 12.98(c) has a negative answer
articles.statement:
It is not the case that for every natural number $n$
and every recursively enumerable normal subgroup $R$ of the free group $F$ on $n$ generators, with
commutator subgroup $[R, R]$, solvability of the word problem for $F / [R, R]$ implies solvability
of the conjugacy problem for $F / [R, R]$: for some such $n$ and $R$, the word problem for
$F / [R, R]$ is solvable but its conjugacy problem is not.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 12.98 (V. E. Shpil'rain); resolution: M. I. Anokhin, Math. Notes 61 (1997), no. 1-2, 3-8, Kourovka Archive, Problem 12.98: a) Yes, it is; b) No, it is not; c) No, it is not.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 12.98(c) (V. E. Shpil'rain)
articles.statement:
The statement that for every natural
number $n$ and every recursively enumerable normal subgroup $R$ of the free group $F$ on $n$
generators, with commutator subgroup $[R, R]$, if the word problem for $F / [R, R]$ is solvable
then the conjugacy problem for $F / [R, R]$ is solvable.

articles.title: Kourovka 12.98(a) has a positive answer
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and every recursively
enumerable normal subgroup $R$ of the free group $F$ on $n$ generators, with commutator subgroup
$[R, R]$, the word problem for $F / R$ is solvable if and only if the word problem for $F / [R, R]$
is solvable.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 12.98 (V. E. Shpil'rain); resolution: M. I. Anokhin, Math. Notes 61 (1997), no. 1-2, 3-8, Kourovka Archive, Problem 12.98: a) Yes, it is; b) No, it is not; c) No, it is not.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 12.98(a) (V. E. Shpil'rain)
articles.statement:
The statement that for every natural
number $n$ and every recursively enumerable normal subgroup $R$ of the free group $F$ on $n$
generators, with commutator subgroup $[R, R]$, the word problem for $F / R$ is solvable if and only
if the word problem for $F / [R, R]$ is solvable.

articles.title: Solvable word problem for a quotient of a free group
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $F$
be the free group on the generators $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ and let $N$ be a subgroup of $F$. The word
problem for $F / N$ is solvable when membership in $N$ is decidable: the predicate on words $w$
(finite lists of letters, each a generator together with a sign) that the image of $w$ in $F$ lies
in $N$ is computable.

articles.title: Finite soluble groups are images of one-relator groups
articles.statement:
Every
finite soluble group $G$ has a natural number $d$ such that for every element $w$ of the free
group on $x_1, \dots, x_d$ there is a surjective homomorphism from the one-relator group
$\langle x_1, \dots, x_d \mid w \rangle$ onto $G$. That is, Kourovka Problem 18.75 has a positive
answer.

Resolved true: the Kourovka Archive answers 18.75 "Yes, it does" (N. Nikolov and D. Segal, 2007).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 18.75 (A. Yu. Olshanskii); resolution: N. Nikolov and D. Segal, Bull. London Math. Soc. 39 (2007), no. 2, 209-213, Kourovka Archive, Problem 18.75: Yes, it does, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Finite soluble groups as images of one-relator groups (Kourovka 18.75)
articles.statement:
The statement,
posed by A. Yu. Olshanskii, that every finite soluble group $G$ has a natural number $d$ such that
for every element $w$ of the free group on $x_1, \dots, x_d$ there is a surjective homomorphism
from the one-relator group $\langle x_1, \dots, x_d \mid w \rangle$ onto $G$.

articles.title: Groves's question (Kourovka 16.35) has a negative answer
articles.statement:
Not every finitely presented
soluble group is (nilpotent-by-nilpotent)-by-finite: there is a finitely presented soluble group
$G$ such that for no normal subgroup $M$ of finite index in $G$ is there a normal subgroup $N$ of
$M$ with $N$ and $M/N$ both nilpotent.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 16.35 (J. R. J. Groves); resolution: V. V. Bludov, letter of 27 April 2007, as recorded in the Kourovka Archive, Kourovka Archive, Problem 16.35 (No: for a prime p, ⟨a, b, c, d | b^a = b^p, c^a = c^p, d^a = d, c^b = c, d^c = d d^b, [d, d^b] = 1, d^p = 1⟩ is soluble of derived length 3 but not metanilpotent-by-finite).

articles.title: Groves's question (Kourovka 16.35)
articles.statement:
The proposition that every finitely presented soluble
group $G$ is (nilpotent-by-nilpotent)-by-finite, that is, $G$ has a normal subgroup $M$ of finite
index and a normal subgroup $N$ of $M$ such that $N$ and $M/N$ are both nilpotent.

articles.title: Metanilpotent-by-finite groups
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is (nilpotent-by-nilpotent)-by-finite when it
has a normal subgroup $M$ of finite index and a normal subgroup $N$ of $M$ such that $N$ and $M/N$
are both nilpotent.

articles.title: One-relator groups with finitely many generators
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is a one-relator group if,
for some $n \ge 0$ and some element $r$ of the free group on $x_1, \dots, x_n$, $G$ is isomorphic
to the group $\langle x_1, \dots, x_n \mid r \rangle$ with generators $x_1, \dots, x_n$ and the
single relator $r$.

articles.title: Surface groups
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is a surface group if either $G$ is isomorphic to
$\langle a_1, b_1, \dots, a_g, b_g \mid [a_1, b_1] \cdots [a_g, b_g] \rangle$ for some $g \ge 1$,
where $[a, b] = a b a^{-1} b^{-1}$, or $G$ is isomorphic to
$\langle a_1, \dots, a_k \mid a_1^2 \cdots a_k^2 \rangle$ for some $k \ge 2$.

These are the standard one-relator presentations of the fundamental groups of the closed
orientable surfaces of genus $g \ge 1$ and the closed non-orientable surfaces of genus $k \ge 2$,
that is, of the closed aspherical surfaces.

articles.title: Non-orientable surface relator
articles.statement:
For $k \ge 0$, the non-orientable surface relator of genus
$k$ is the element $a_1^2 a_2^2 \cdots a_k^2$ of the free group on the $k$ generators
$a_1, \dots, a_k$; for $k = 0$ it is the identity.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 20.41 has a positive answer
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a non-cyclic residually finite group
such that every subgroup of finite index in $G$ (including $G$ itself) is isomorphic to a
one-relator group $\langle x_0, \dots, x_{n-1} \mid r \rangle$ for some natural number $n$ and
some element $r$ of the free group on $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$, and every subgroup of infinite index
in $G$ is free. Then $G$ is free, or $G$ is isomorphic to
$\langle a_0, b_0, \dots, a_{g-1}, b_{g-1} \mid [a_0, b_0] \cdots [a_{g-1}, b_{g-1}] \rangle$ for
some $g \ge 0$, where $[a, b] = a b a^{-1} b^{-1}$, or $G$ is isomorphic to
$\langle c_0, \dots, c_{k-1} \mid c_0^2 \cdots c_{k-1}^2 \rangle$ for some $k \ge 1$.

These presentations are the fundamental groups of the closed orientable surface of genus $g$ and
the closed non-orientable surface of genus $k$; compact surfaces with boundary have free
fundamental groups.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 20.41 (L. Ciobanu, B. Fine, G. Rosenberger); resolution: H. Wilton, Surface groups among cubulated hyperbolic and one-relator groups, preprint, arXiv:2406.02121 (2024, v3 2026), Theorem D: an infinite one-relator group that is neither free nor a surface group has a subgroup of infinite index that is not free (a non-cyclic one-relator group has at least two generators and is infinite); Kourovka Notebook (21st issue), Problem 20.41: Yes, it is true, https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.02121.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 20.41: one-relator groups with free infinite-index subgroups
articles.statement:
The
proposition that every non-cyclic residually finite group $G$ such that every subgroup of finite
index in $G$ (including $G$ itself) is isomorphic to a one-relator group
$\langle x_0, \dots, x_{n-1} \mid r \rangle$ for some natural number $n$ and some element $r$ of
the free group on $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$, and every subgroup of infinite index in $G$ is free, is
free, or is isomorphic to
$\langle a_0, b_0, \dots, a_{g-1}, b_{g-1} \mid [a_0, b_0] \cdots [a_{g-1}, b_{g-1}] \rangle$ for
some $g \ge 0$, where $[a, b] = a b a^{-1} b^{-1}$, or is isomorphic to
$\langle c_0, \dots, c_{k-1} \mid c_0^2 \cdots c_{k-1}^2 \rangle$ for some $k \ge 1$. The problem is
due to L. Ciobanu, B. Fine and G. Rosenberger.

These presentations are the fundamental groups of the closed orientable surface of genus $g$ and
the closed non-orientable surface of genus $k$; compact surfaces with boundary have free
fundamental groups.

articles.title: Wilton's theorem (Kourovka Problem 20.22)
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group isomorphic to
$\langle x_1, \dots, x_n \mid r \rangle$ for some $n \ge 0$ and some element $r$ of the free group
on $x_1, \dots, x_n$. If $G$ is neither free nor cyclic and every subgroup of infinite index in $G$
is free, then $G$ is a surface group: $G$ is isomorphic to
$\langle a_1, b_1, \dots, a_g, b_g \mid [a_1, b_1] \cdots [a_g, b_g] \rangle$ for some $g \ge 1$,
where $[a, b] = a b a^{-1} b^{-1}$, or to $\langle a_1, \dots, a_k \mid a_1^2 \cdots a_k^2 \rangle$
for some $k \ge 2$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 20.22 (B. Fine, G. Rosenberger, L. Wienke); resolution: H. Wilton, Surface groups among cubulated hyperbolic and one-relator groups, preprint, arXiv:2406.02121 (2024), Theorem D: an infinite one-relator group that is neither free nor a surface group has a subgroup of infinite index that is not free; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 20.22 solved, https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.02121.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 20.22 (statement)
articles.statement:
The statement that every group $G$ with the following
properties is a surface group: $G$ is isomorphic to $\langle x_1, \dots, x_n \mid r \rangle$ for
some $n \ge 0$ and some element $r$ of the free group on $x_1, \dots, x_n$; $G$ is neither free nor
cyclic; and every subgroup of infinite index in $G$ is free. Here $G$ is a surface group if it is
isomorphic to $\langle a_1, b_1, \dots, a_g, b_g \mid [a_1, b_1] \cdots [a_g, b_g] \rangle$ for some
$g \ge 1$, where $[a, b] = a b a^{-1} b^{-1}$, or to
$\langle a_1, \dots, a_k \mid a_1^2 \cdots a_k^2 \rangle$ for some $k \ge 2$.

articles.title: Orientable surface relator
articles.statement:
For $g \ge 0$, the orientable surface relator of genus $g$ is
the element $[a_1, b_1] [a_2, b_2] \cdots [a_g, b_g]$ of the free group on the $2g$ generators
$a_1, \dots, a_g, b_1, \dots, b_g$, where $[a, b] = a b a^{-1} b^{-1}$; for $g = 0$ it is the
identity.

articles.title: Generically, subgroups with fewer generators are free (Kourovka 11.75)
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 2$ and
$n \ge 1$ be natural numbers and let $F_m$ be the free group on $x_1, \dots, x_m$. For each $d$,
let $N_d$ be the number of $n$-tuples $(r_1, \dots, r_n)$ of elements of $F_m$ whose reduced words
are cyclically reduced and have total length $|r_1| + \dots + |r_n| = d$, and let $N_d^f$ be the
number of those tuples for which every subgroup of
$\langle x_1, \dots, x_m \mid r_1, \dots, r_n \rangle$ generated by fewer than $m$ elements is free.
Then $N_d^f / N_d \to 1$ as $d \to \infty$.

Resolved true: Arzhantseva and Olshanskii prove this; the Kourovka Archive records 11.75 as proved
by this paper.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.75 (A. Yu. Olshanskii); resolution: G. N. Arzhantseva and A. Yu. Olshanskii, The class of groups all of whose subgroups with lesser number of generators are free is generic, Math. Notes 59 (1996), no. 4, 350-355 (Mat. Zametki 59 (1996), 489-496), Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.75: This is proved (Arzhantseva-Olshanskii); paper, abstract ("this solves Problem 11.75 from the Kourovka Notebook") and main theorem as summarized in zbMATH Zbl 0877.20021 (lim N_d^f / N_d = 1 over presentations with cyclically reduced relators of total length d), https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02308683.

articles.title: Olshanskii's genericity problem (Kourovka 11.75)
articles.statement:
This is the proposition, in the form
proved by Arzhantseva and Olshanskii, that the following holds for all natural numbers $m \ge 2$
and $n \ge 1$. Let $F_m$ be the free group on $x_1, \dots, x_m$. For each $d$, let $N_d$ be the
number of $n$-tuples $(r_1, \dots, r_n)$ of elements of $F_m$ whose reduced words are cyclically
reduced and have total length $|r_1| + \dots + |r_n| = d$, and let $N_d^f$ be the number of those
tuples for which every subgroup of $\langle x_1, \dots, x_m \mid r_1, \dots, r_n \rangle$
generated by fewer than $m$ elements is free. Then $N_d^f / N_d \to 1$ as $d \to \infty$.

articles.title: Presentations counted by Arzhantseva and Olshanskii
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $m$, $n$ and $d$,
this is the set of $n$-tuples $(r_1, \dots, r_n)$ of elements of the free group $F_m$ on
generators $x_1, \dots, x_m$ such that the reduced word of each $r_i$ is cyclically reduced (the
empty word counts as cyclically reduced) and the reduced word lengths satisfy
$|r_1| + \dots + |r_n| = d$. Each tuple stands for the presentation
$\langle x_1, \dots, x_m \mid r_1, \dots, r_n \rangle$.

articles.title: Groups whose subgroups with fewer than $m$ generators are free
articles.statement:
For a natural number $m$,
a group $G$ has this property if, for every finite set $S \subseteq G$ with fewer than $m$
elements, the subgroup of $G$ generated by $S$ is a free group.

articles.title: Infinite finitely presented simple groups exist
articles.statement:
There exist a natural number $n$ and a
finite set $R$ of elements of the free group on generators $x_1, \dots, x_n$ such that the group
$\langle x_1, \dots, x_n \mid R \rangle$ presented by these generators and relators is simple
and infinite.

## Sources

- G. Higman, 'A finitely generated infinite simple group', J. London Math. Soc. 26 (1951) 61–64; G. Higman, *Finitely Presented Infinite Simple Groups*, Notes on Pure Mathematics 8, Australian National University, 1974. §122 in O. Knill, *Some Fundamental Theorems in Mathematics* (https://people.math.harvard.edu/~knill/graphgeometry/papers/fundamental.pdf). Problem `higman_infinite_simple` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Higman–Neumann–Neumann embedding theorem
articles.statement:
Every countable group $G$ embeds in a group
generated by two elements: there are a group $H$, elements $a, b \in H$ that generate $H$, and an
injective group homomorphism $f \colon G \to H$.

## Sources

- G. Higman, B. H. Neumann, H. Neumann, J. London Math. Soc. 24 (1949) 247–254 via HNN extensions; Lean states countable embedding into 2-generator group including finite case.

articles.title: Quotients by the normal closure of an odd power of a non-square can have involutions
articles.statement:
There
exist a group $G$ without involutions (if $g^2 = 1$ then $g = 1$), an element $a \in G$ that is
not the square of any element of $G$, and an odd natural number $n$ such that the quotient of $G$
by the normal closure of $a^n$ contains an involution, that is, an element $y \ne 1$ with
$y^2 = 1$. This answers Kourovka Problem 18.94 in the negative.

Besides an example of V. I. Trofimov, the group $G = \langle a, b \mid a^2 = b^2 \rangle$ with
$n = 1$ is an example: its quotient by the normal closure of $a$ has order $2$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 18.94 (A. I. Sozutov); resolution: V. I. Trofimov (example), as recorded in the Kourovka Archive, Problem 18.94, Kourovka Archive, Problem 18.94: No, not always, by an example of V. I. Trofimov; another example: G = ⟨a, b | a² = b²⟩ modulo ⟨a^G⟩ has order 2, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Sozutov's question on involutions in quotients (Kourovka 18.94)
articles.statement:
This is the statement
that whenever $G$ is a group without involutions (if $g^2 = 1$ then $g = 1$), $a \in G$ is not the
