square of any element of $G$, and $n$ is an odd natural number, the quotient of $G$ by the normal
closure of $a^n$ has no involutions: every element $y$ of the quotient with $y^2 = 1$ is $1$.

articles.title: SQ-universal group
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is SQ-universal if every countable group is isomorphic
to a subgroup of a quotient of $G$: for every countable group $C$ there are a group $Q$, a
surjective homomorphism $G \to Q$ and an injective homomorphism $C \to Q$.

articles.title: Every finite group has a just finite presentation
articles.statement:
For every finite group $G$ there are a
natural number $n$ and a finite subset $R$ of the free group on $n$ generators $x_1, \dots, x_n$
such that the group $\langle x_1, \dots, x_n \mid R \rangle$ is isomorphic to $G$ and, for every
$r \in R$, the group $\langle x_1, \dots, x_n \mid R \setminus \{r\} \rangle$ is infinite. That is,
the answer to Kourovka Problem 21.10 is positive.

Lackenby's paper acknowledges assistance from the Google DeepMind AI co-mathematician tool.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 21.10 (Y. Barnea); resolution: M. Lackenby, Every finite group admits a just finite presentation, preprint, arXiv:2605.10402 (2026), Theorem 1: every finite group admits a finite, just finite presentation (a consequence of Theorem 2 on just-(FA) presentations); Kourovka Notebook (21st issue), Problem 21.10: Yes, it is true, https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10402.

articles.title: Barnea's question on just finite presentations (Kourovka 21.10)
articles.statement:
The statement that every
finite group $G$ has a just finite presentation: a presentation $\langle X \mid R \rangle$ with $X$
and $R$ finite that defines $G$ and such that removing any single relator from $R$ gives a
presentation of an infinite group.

articles.title: Finitely presented soluble groups of torsion length greater than two
articles.statement:
Resolved true: the Kourovka Archive answers 19.23 "Yes, such groups exist"; Leary and Minasyan
(Theorem 2.14) construct polycyclic groups, which are finitely presented and soluble, of every
torsion length `n ≥ 1`, in particular of torsion length `3`. Source: E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov
(eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49
(2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 19.23 (M. Chiodo, R. Vyas); resolution: I. J. Leary and
A. Minasyan, A note on torsion length and torsion subgroups, J. Group Theory 26 (2023), no. 4,
741-750 (arXiv:2112.14546), Theorem 2.14: for every integer n ≥ 1 there is a polycyclic group of
torsion length n (their torsion length counts G₀ = G, G_{n+1} = G_n / Tor(G_n) from 0 and agrees
with the Notebook's for n ≥ 1); Kourovka Archive, Problem 19.23: Yes, such groups exist,
https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.14546.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 19.23 (Chiodo–Vyas), finitely presented form
articles.statement:
The statement that there is
a finitely presented soluble group $G$ of torsion length greater than $2$, that is, such that
$G / \mathrm{Tor}_2(G)$ is not torsion-free, where $\mathrm{Tor}_2(G)$ is the second term of the
torsion series of $G$.

articles.title: Torsion length greater than two
articles.statement:
A group $G$ has torsion length greater than $2$ when
$G / \mathrm{Tor}_2(G)$ is not torsion-free, where $\mathrm{Tor}_2(G)$ is the second term of the
torsion series of $G$: some element $g \in G$ outside $\mathrm{Tor}_2(G)$ has a power $g^n$ with
$n > 0$ in $\mathrm{Tor}_2(G)$.

Then $G / \mathrm{Tor}_1(G)$ is not torsion-free either, so neither $1$ nor $2$ is the torsion
length of $G$.

articles.title: Torsion series
articles.statement:
For a group $G$, the torsion series of Chiodo and Vyas is the sequence of
subgroups $\mathrm{Tor}_i(G)$ of $G$ defined by $\mathrm{Tor}_0(G) = 1$, the trivial subgroup,
and, for each $i$, $\mathrm{Tor}_{i+1}(G)$ is the normal closure in $G$ of the set of elements $g$
such that $g^n \in \mathrm{Tor}_i(G)$ for some integer $n > 0$.

This is the preimage of $\mathrm{Tor}_1(G / \mathrm{Tor}_i(G))$, the normal closure of the torsion
elements of $G / \mathrm{Tor}_i(G)$, since normal closures commute with the quotient map and
$\mathrm{Tor}_i(G)$ lies in that set.

articles.title: Torsion quotients of finitely presented groups need not be finitely presented
articles.statement:
There exists
a finitely presented group $G$ such that $G / \mathrm{Tor}(G)$ is not finitely presented, where
$\mathrm{Tor}(G)$ is the normal closure of the set of elements of finite order of $G$.

The Kourovka Archive answers Problem 19.24 "Yes, such groups exist": Leary and Minasyan
(Constructions 3.1 and 3.2) give a soluble example and a virtually torsion-free example.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 19.24 (M. Chiodo, R. Vyas); resolution: I. J. Leary and A. Minasyan, A note on torsion length and torsion subgroups, J. Group Theory 26 (2023), no. 4, 741-750 (arXiv:2112.14546), Section 3, Construction 3.1 (Abels' finitely presented soluble group H modulo an infinite cyclic central subgroup C: G = H / C has G / Tor(G) ≅ H / Z(H), which is not finitely presented) and Construction 3.2 (a virtually torsion-free example built from Bestvina-Brady groups); Kourovka Archive, Problem 19.24: Yes, such groups exist, one soluble and one virtually torsion-free, https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.14546.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 19.24 (torsion quotients of finitely presented groups)
articles.statement:
The statement,
asked by M. Chiodo and R. Vyas, that there exists a finitely presented group $G$ such that
$G / \mathrm{Tor}(G)$ is not finitely presented, where $\mathrm{Tor}(G)$ is the normal closure of
the set of elements of finite order of $G$.

articles.title: Torsion closure
articles.statement:
For a group $G$, $\mathrm{Tor}(G)$ is the normal closure in $G$ of the set
of elements of finite order of $G$.

articles.title: Novikov–Boone theorem (unsolvability of the word problem)
articles.statement:
There exist a natural number
$n$ and a finite set $R$ of elements of the free group $F_n$ on generators $g_1, \dots, g_n$ such
that the word problem of the canonical surjection from $F_n$ onto the presented group
$\langle g_1, \dots, g_n \mid R \rangle$ is not solvable: no algorithm decides, for a word $w$ in
the $g_i$ and their inverses, whether $w$ represents the identity of
$\langle g_1, \dots, g_n \mid R \rangle$.

## Sources

- P.S. Novikov, 'On the algorithmic unsolvability of the word problem in group theory', Trudy Mat. Inst. Steklov. 44 (1955) 1–143 (Russian); W.W. Boone, 'The word problem', Ann. of Math. (2) 70 (1959) 207–265 (announced 1958). §122 in O. Knill, *Some Fundamental Theorems in Mathematics* (https://people.math.harvard.edu/~knill/graphgeometry/papers/fundamental.pdf). Problem `novikov_unsolvable` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Solvable word problem
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group, $n$ a natural number and $\varphi$ a
homomorphism from the free group on $n$ generators to $G$. The word problem is solvable for
$\varphi$ when the predicate on words $w$ (finite lists of letters, each a generator together
with a sign) given by $\varphi(w) = 1$ in $G$ is computable: some algorithm decides, given a
word $w$, whether $\varphi(w) = 1$.

When $\varphi$ is surjective, for instance the quotient map of a presentation of $G$ on $n$
generators, this is the classical word problem for $G$ with respect to these generators.

articles.title: Arcwise connected space
articles.statement:
A topological space $G$ is arcwise connected when for any two
points $x, y \in G$ there is a continuous map $\gamma \colon \mathbb{R} \to G$ with
$\gamma(0) = x$ and $\gamma(1) = y$.

Restricting $\gamma$ to $[0, 1]$ gives a path from $x$ to $y$, and every such path extends
to $\mathbb{R}$, so this says that any two points are joined by a path; the path need not be
injective.

articles.title: Connectedness in the sense of Hausdorff
articles.statement:
A topological space $G$ is connected in the
sense of Hausdorff when it is not the union of two disjoint nonempty closed subsets.

The empty space satisfies this condition.

articles.title: Connected metric groups need not be arcwise connected
articles.statement:
The claim of part (2) of Scottish
Book Problem 160 is false: there is a metric group $G$ (a group with a metric for which
multiplication and inversion are continuous) that is connected in the sense of Hausdorff but
not arcwise connected, that is, there are points $x, y \in G$ such that no continuous map
$\gamma \colon \mathbb{R} \to G$ has $\gamma(0) = x$ and $\gamma(1) = y$.

The $p$-adic solenoid, the inverse limit of circles under $z \mapsto z^p$, is such a group:
it is a compact connected metrizable topological group that is not path connected.

## Sources

- Encyclopedia of Mathematics, "Solenoid" (inverse-limit construction with `fᵢ (z) = z ^ nᵢ`, a topological group, a one-dimensional continuum); E. Hewitt and K. A. Ross, Abstract Harmonic Analysis I (1979), cited there; solenoids are compact metrizable spaces that are connected but not path connected.

articles.title: Claim of Scottish Book Problem 160, part (2)
articles.statement:
The claim that every metric group $G$
(a group with a metric for which multiplication and inversion are continuous) that is
connected in the sense of Hausdorff is arcwise connected.

articles.title: Finite-rank free-by-cyclic groups are conjugacy separable
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and
every automorphism $\varphi$ of the free group $F_n$ of rank $n$, the semidirect product
$F_n \rtimes_\varphi \mathbb{Z}$, in which $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ acts on $F_n$ by $\varphi^k$, is
conjugacy separable: any two of its elements whose images are conjugate in every quotient by a
normal subgroup of finite index are conjugate.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 19.41 (I. Kapovich); resolution: F. Dahmani, S. Hughes, M. Kudlinska and N. Touikan, Free-by-cyclic groups are conjugacy separable, preprint, arXiv:2509.22346v2 (2026), abstract: all finitely generated free-by-cyclic groups are conjugacy separable, resolving Question 19.41; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 19.41 solved: Yes, it is, https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22346.

articles.title: Kapovich's conjugacy separability question (Kourovka 19.41)
articles.statement:
The assertion that for every
natural number $n$ and every automorphism $\varphi$ of the free group $F_n$ of rank $n$, the
semidirect product $F_n \rtimes_\varphi \mathbb{Z}$, in which $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ acts on $F_n$ by
$\varphi^k$, is conjugacy separable.

articles.title: Maximal condition on subgroups
articles.statement:
A group $G$ satisfies the maximal condition on subgroups
when every subgroup of $G$ is finitely generated.

articles.title: Minimal condition on subgroups
articles.statement:
A group $G$ satisfies the minimal condition on subgroups
when the order on subgroups of $G$ by inclusion is well-founded: every nonempty set of subgroups
of $G$ has a minimal element, equivalently there is no infinite strictly descending chain of
subgroups of $G$.

articles.title: Minimax groups
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is a minimax group when it has a finite subnormal series
$1 = H_0 \le H_1 \le \dots \le H_n = G$, with each $H_i$ normal in $H_{i+1}$, such that every
factor $H_{i+1}/H_i$ satisfies the maximal condition on subgroups or the minimal condition on
subgroups.

articles.title: Residually finite groups
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is residually finite when for every element
$g \ne 1$ of $G$ there is a normal subgroup $N$ of finite index in $G$ with $g \notin N$.

articles.title: Finite images determine minimaxity (Mann–Segal)
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finitely generated
soluble minimax group and let $H$ be a finitely generated residually finite group with the same
finite images as $G$: a finite group is a homomorphic image of $G$ exactly when it is a
homomorphic image of $H$. Then $H$ is a minimax group.

This answers Kourovka Problem 12.90 (J. S. Wilson) affirmatively: the Kourovka Archive answers
"Yes, it must" (A. Mann and D. Segal, 1990; see also A. V. Tushev, 1994).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 12.90 (J. S. Wilson); resolution: A. Mann and D. Segal, Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) 61 (1990), 529-545; A. V. Tushev, Math. Notes 56 (1994), no. 5, 1190-1192, Kourovka Archive, Problem 12.90: Yes, it must.

articles.title: Minimax groups and finite images (Kourovka 12.90)
articles.statement:
The statement that for all groups $G$
and $H$, if $G$ is a finitely generated soluble minimax group and $H$ is a finitely generated
residually finite group with the same finite images as $G$ (a finite group is a homomorphic image
of $G$ exactly when it is a homomorphic image of $H$), then $H$ is a minimax group.

articles.title: Groups with the same finite images
articles.statement:
Two groups $G$ and $H$ have the same finite images
when, for every finite group $Q$, there is a surjective homomorphism $G \to Q$ exactly when there
is a surjective homomorphism $H \to Q$.

articles.title: Fixed subgroup of a free pro-p group is finitely generated
articles.statement:
Resolved true: the Kourovka Archive answers 12.70 "Yes, it is finite" (C. Scheiderer, 1999);
moreover, the fixed points of a finite `p`-group of automorphisms of a free pro-`p` group form a
free factor (Herfort, Ribes and Zalesskii, 1999), which has finite rank when `F` does. Source: E. I.
Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st
issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 12.70 (L. Ribes); resolution:
C. Scheiderer, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 127 (1999), no. 3, 695-700; W. N. Herfort, L. Ribes and P. A.
Zalesskii, Forum Math. 11 (1999), no. 1, 49-61, Kourovka Archive, Problem 12.70: Yes, it is finite
(Scheiderer); the fixed points of a finite p-group of automorphisms form a free factor
(Herfort-Ribes-Zalesskii).

articles.title: Ribes's question on fixed subgroups of free pro-$p$ groups (Kourovka 12.70)
articles.statement:
The statement
that for every prime $p$, every free pro-$p$ group $F$ on finitely many generators
$x_1, \dots, x_d$ and every continuous automorphism $\Delta \ne 1$ of $F$ with $\Delta^{p^k} = 1$
for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the fixed subgroup
$\mathrm{Fix}_F(\Delta) = \{z \in F \mid \Delta(z) = z\}$ has finite rank: there is a finite set
$S \subseteq \mathrm{Fix}_F(\Delta)$ such that the closure of the subgroup generated by $S$ equals
$\mathrm{Fix}_F(\Delta)$.

articles.title: Free pro-$p$ group on given generators
articles.statement:
Let $p$ and $d$ be natural numbers, $F$ a
topological group and $x_1, \dots, x_d \in F$. Then $F$ is a free pro-$p$ group on
$x_1, \dots, x_d$ when $F$ is a pro-$p$ group, the closure of the subgroup generated by
$x_1, \dots, x_d$ is all of $F$, and for every finite $p$-group $P$ and all $y_1, \dots, y_d \in P$
there is a group homomorphism $\varphi \colon F \to P$ with open kernel such that
$\varphi(x_i) = y_i$ for every $i$.

articles.title: Pro-$p$ group
articles.statement:
For a natural number $p$, a group $G$ with a topology is a pro-$p$ group
when $G$ is compact, Hausdorff and totally disconnected, and every open normal subgroup of $G$ has
index $p^k$ for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Generator rank
articles.statement:
For a topological group $G$, the generator rank $d(G)$ is the least
natural number $k$ such that some finite subset of $G$ with $k$ elements generates a dense
subgroup of $G$, that is, a subgroup whose closure is all of $G$. If no finite subset of $G$
generates a dense subgroup, then $d(G)$ is defined to be $0$. For a finite discrete group this is
the ordinary minimal number of generators.

articles.title: Golod–Shafarevich inequality
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and let $Q$ be a nontrivial finite
$p$-group, viewed as a topological group with the discrete topology. Then the generator rank
$d(Q)$ and the relation rank $r(Q)$, the dimension over $\mathbb{F}_p$ of the continuous
cohomology group $H^2(Q, \mathbb{F}_p)$ with trivial coefficients, satisfy $d(Q)^2 < 4\, r(Q)$.

## Sources

- NSW (J. Neukirch, A. Schmidt, K. Wingberg, *Cohomology of Number Fields*, 2nd ed., Grundlehren 323, Springer 2008), Theorem 3.9.7; J.-P. Serre, *Galois Cohomology*, Chapter I, Appendix 2, Theorem 1. Lean hypothesis: https://github.com/logical-intelligence/erdos-unit-distance (Hyp_GolodShafarevichInequality). Problem `golod_shafarevich_inequality` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Relation rank
articles.statement:
For a prime $p$ and a topological group $G$, the relation rank $r(G)$
is the dimension over $\mathbb{F}_p = \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ of the continuous cohomology
group $H^2(G, \mathbb{F}_p)$, where $G$ acts trivially on $\mathbb{F}_p$. If this space is
infinite-dimensional, then $r(G)$ is defined to be $0$.

articles.title: Trivial representation on $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $p$ and a
topological group $G$, this is $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, with its discrete topology, regarded as
a continuous representation of $G$ over $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ on which every element of $G$
acts as the identity.

articles.title: A countable nilpotent group with modular lattice of group topologies
articles.statement:
It is not the case that
for every countably infinite non-abelian nilpotent group $G$ the lattice of all (not necessarily
Hausdorff) group topologies on $G$ is not modular; that is, some countably infinite non-abelian
nilpotent group has a modular lattice of group topologies.

Peng constructs (Theorem 1.1) a countably infinite non-abelian nilpotent group whose lattice of
group topologies is modular; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) answers 14.4(b) "No".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 14.4 (V. I. Arnautov); resolution: (a) V. Arnautov and A. Topală, Bul. Acad. Ştiinţe Repub. Mold. Mat. 1998, no. 2(27), 130-131; (b) D. Peng, On the lattice of group topologies, preprint, arXiv:2310.08269 (2023), (b) Theorem 1.1: there is a countably infinite non-abelian nilpotent group whose lattice of all (not necessarily Hausdorff) group topologies is modular; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 14.4 solved: a) Yes; b) No, there are such groups with modular L(G), https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.08269.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 14.4(b) (countable nilpotent groups)
articles.statement:
This proposition states that for
every countably infinite non-abelian nilpotent group $G$, the lattice $\mathcal{L}(G)$ of all (not
necessarily Hausdorff) group topologies on $G$ is not modular.

articles.title: A Hausdorff group topology on the integers in which 2ⁿ + 3ⁿ tends to zero
articles.statement:
There is a
topology on $\mathbb{Z}$ that makes $(\mathbb{Z}, +)$ a Hausdorff topological group and in which
the sequence $(2^n + 3^n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ converges to $0$. That is, Kourovka Problem 15.79 has
a positive answer.

The Kourovka Archive answers 15.79 "Yes, there does", as follows from Theorem 3 of Ruzsa; another
solution is due to Skresanov.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 15.79 (I. V. Protasov); resolution: I. Z. Ruzsa, in: Proc. Conf. Number Theory (Budapest, 1987), Vol. I, Colloq. Math. Soc. János Bolyai 51, North-Holland, Amsterdam, 1990, 473-504; S. V. Skresanov, Group topologies on integers and S-unit equations, Siberian Math. J. 61 (2020), no. 3, 542-544, arXiv:1911.11963, Ruzsa, Theorem 3, as applied in the Kourovka Archive, Problem 15.79 (answer: Yes, there does); another solution by Skresanov, abstract (for a finite set of primes S, a Hausdorff group topology on ℤ in which every growing sequence of S-integers tends to 0; as a corollary, 2ⁿ + 3ⁿ tends to 0 in a Hausdorff group topology), https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.11963.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 15.79 (Protasov's question on the integers)
articles.statement:
The statement that there is a
topology on $\mathbb{Z}$ that makes $(\mathbb{Z}, +)$ a Hausdorff topological group and in which
the sequence $(2^n + 3^n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ converges to $0$.

articles.title: A nilpotent group with non-modular lattice of group topologies
articles.statement:
There is a nilpotent group $G$
whose lattice of all (not necessarily Hausdorff) group topologies is not modular.

Arnautov and Topală found such a group; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) answers 14.4(a) "Yes".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 14.4 (V. I. Arnautov); resolution: (a) V. Arnautov and A. Topală, Bul. Acad. Ştiinţe Repub. Mold. Mat. 1998, no. 2(27), 130-131; (b) D. Peng, On the lattice of group topologies, preprint, arXiv:2310.08269 (2023), (b) Theorem 1.1: there is a countably infinite non-abelian nilpotent group whose lattice of all (not necessarily Hausdorff) group topologies is modular; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 14.4 solved: a) Yes; b) No, there are such groups with modular L(G), https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.08269.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 14.4(a) (nilpotent groups with non-modular topology lattice)
articles.statement:
This
proposition states that some nilpotent group $G$ has a non-modular lattice $\mathcal{L}(G)$ of all
(not necessarily Hausdorff) group topologies.

articles.title: Nottingham condition on automorphisms of power series
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring. A
ring automorphism $\varphi$ of the power series ring $R[[x]]$ satisfies the Nottingham condition
when $\varphi(x) - x$ lies in the ideal generated by $x^2$, that is, when
$\varphi(x) = x(1 + a_1 x + a_2 x^2 + \cdots)$ for some $a_1, a_2, \ldots \in R$.

For a prime $p$ and $R = \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, every ring automorphism of $R[[x]]$ is
$R$-linear and preserves the maximal ideal, so it is the substitution $x \mapsto \varphi(x)$; the
automorphisms satisfying the Nottingham condition then form the Nottingham group $N(R)$.

articles.title: The Nottingham group contains a free subgroup of rank 2
articles.statement:
For every prime $p$ there is an
injective group homomorphism $f$ from the free group $F_2$ on two generators to the group of ring
automorphisms of the power series ring $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})[[x]]$ such that, for every
$g \in F_2$, the automorphism $\varphi = f(g)$ satisfies $\varphi(x) - x \in (x^2)$; that is, the
Nottingham group $N(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})$ contains a copy of $F_2$.

The Kourovka Archive answers 12.24 "Yes, it does" (R. Camina, 1997). Camina embeds, for every
prime $p$, every countably based pro-$p$ group in $N(\mathbb{F}_p)$, where
$\mathbb{F}_p = \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$; the free pro-$p$ group of rank $2$ contains $F_2$, since
free groups are residually $p$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 12.24 (D. L. Johnson); resolution: R. Camina, J. Algebra 196 (1997), no. 1, 101-113, Camina's theorem that every countably based (in particular every finitely generated) pro-p group embeds in N(F_p); Kourovka Archive, Problem 12.24.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 12.24 (free subgroups of the Nottingham group)
articles.statement:
For every prime $p$ there
is an injective group homomorphism from the free group $F_2$ on two generators to the group of
ring automorphisms of $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})[[x]]$ whose image consists of automorphisms
$\varphi$ with $\varphi(x) - x \in (x^2)$, that is, of elements of the Nottingham group
$N(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})$.

articles.title: A finitely generated non-prosoluble profinite CN-group exists
articles.statement:
There is an infinite profinite
group $G$, that is, a compact, Hausdorff, totally disconnected topological group, such that $G$ is
topologically finitely generated (the closure of the subgroup generated by some finite set is $G$),
the centralizer of every non-trivial element of $G$ is pronilpotent, and $G$ is not prosoluble: for
some open normal subgroup $N$ of $G$, the quotient $G/N$ is not soluble. This answers Kourovka
Problem 20.90.

Kinyon and Urban (Section 3.35) give an infinite two-generated closed subgroup of
$\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{F}_4[[t]])$ that maps onto $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{F}_4) \cong A_5$ and in
which every non-identity element has abelian, hence pronilpotent, centralizer.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 20.90 (P. Shumyatsky); resolution: M. Kinyon and J. Urban, Results on problems from the Kourovka Notebook, preprint (September 2026), Kourovka Notebook site, Section 3.35: a two-generated closed subgroup G of SL₂(F₄[[t]]) that is infinite, maps onto SL₂(F₄) ≅ A₅ by reduction modulo t (so it is not prosoluble), and in which the centralizer of every non-identity element is abelian; an AI solution confirmed by P. Shumyatsky, Kourovka Notebook (21st issue), Problem 20.90: An example is found, https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/kourovka-mathematics.pdf.

articles.title: Problem of a finitely generated non-prosoluble profinite CN-group (Kourovka 20.90)
articles.statement:
The
statement that there is an infinite profinite group $G$, that is, a compact, Hausdorff, totally
disconnected topological group, such that $G$ is topologically finitely generated (the closure of
the subgroup generated by some finite set is $G$), the centralizer of every non-trivial element of
$G$ is pronilpotent (so $G$ is a CN-group), and $G$ is not prosoluble: for some open normal
subgroup $N$ of $G$, the quotient $G/N$ is not soluble.

articles.title: Pronilpotent subgroup
articles.statement:
A subgroup $H$ of a group $G$ carrying a topology is pronilpotent
when, for every open normal subgroup $N$ of $G$, the image of $H$ in the quotient $G/N$ is
nilpotent.

For a closed subgroup of a profinite group this says that $H$ is an inverse limit of finite
nilpotent groups, since the subgroups $H \cap N$ are cofinal among the open normal subgroups of
$H$.

articles.title: Bianchi group
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, let $\mathcal{O}_d$ be the ring of integers of
$\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-d})$. The Bianchi group is $\mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathcal{O}_d)$, the projective
special linear group of $2 \times 2$ matrices over $\mathcal{O}_d$.

articles.title: Profinite completion
articles.statement:
The profinite completion of a group $G$ is the inverse limit of the
finite quotient groups $G/N$, where $N$ ranges over the normal subgroups of finite index in $G$
and the maps are the quotient maps $G/N \to G/M$ for $N \le M$. It is a profinite group.

articles.title: Profinitely rigid group
articles.statement:
A group $\Gamma$ is *profinitely rigid* if it is finitely
generated and residually finite, and $\Gamma$ is isomorphic to every finitely generated residually
finite group $\Lambda$ whose profinite completion is isomorphic, as a group, to the profinite
completion of $\Gamma$.

Note that any such isomorphism of profinite completions is automatically a homeomorphism. This is
a consequence of the Nikolov-Segal theorem which states that for a finitely generated group
$\Gamma$, every finite index subgroup of the profinite completion of $\Gamma$ is automatically
open. Conversely, every open subgroup has finite index by compactness, so in this case the open
subgroups (which generate the topology) are exactly the subgroups of finite index. Thus, the
topology on the profinite completion of $\Gamma$ can be characterized algebraically as the
topology generated by the finite index subgroups. In particular, any isomorphism between
profinite completions of finitely generated groups automatically preserves the topology and is
thus a homeomorphism.

articles.title: Ring of integers of a field obtained by adjoining a square root to $\mathbb{Q}$
articles.statement:
For a
natural number $d$, the ring of integers of the number field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-d})$, realized as
the splitting field of $X^2 + d$ over $\mathbb{Q}$.

articles.title: Profinite rigidity of the Bianchi group over the Eisenstein integers
articles.statement:
Let $\omega$ be a
primitive cube root of unity, so that the ring $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ of Eisenstein integers is the
ring of integers of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-3})$. The Bianchi group $\mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{Z}[\omega])$
is profinitely rigid: it is finitely generated and residually finite, and it is isomorphic to
every finitely generated residually finite group whose profinite completion is isomorphic, as a
group, to its own.

This is Theorem 7.1 of the source.

## Sources

- M. R. Bridson, D. B. McReynolds, A. W. Reid, and R. Spitler, `Absolute profinite rigidity and hyperbolic geometry`, Annals of Math, 192 (3) 2020. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_absolute_profinite_rigidity` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Residual $p$-finiteness for all $p$ does not imply residual torsion-free nilpotence
articles.statement:
It is not
the case that every finitely generated group that is residually a finite $p$-group for every prime
$p$ is residually torsion-free nilpotent. Here a group $G$ is residually a finite $p$-group when
every element $g \ne 1$ lies outside some normal subgroup $N$ such that $G/N$ is a finite
$p$-group, and residually torsion-free nilpotent when every element $g \ne 1$ lies outside some
normal subgroup $N$ such that $G/N$ is nilpotent and has no nontrivial elements of finite order.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 14.52 (Yu. V. Kuz'min); resolution: B. Hartley, in: Symposia Mathematica XVII (Convegno sui Gruppi Infiniti, INDAM, Roma, 1973), Academic Press, London, 1976, 225-234, Kourovka Archive, Problem 14.52 (answer: Not always).

articles.title: Kuz'min's question on residually finite $p$-groups (Kourovka 14.52)
articles.statement:
The statement that
every finitely generated group $G$ that is residually a finite $p$-group for every prime $p$ is
residually torsion-free nilpotent. Here $G$ is residually a finite $p$-group when every element
$g \ne 1$ lies outside some normal subgroup $N$ such that $G/N$ is a finite $p$-group, and
residually torsion-free nilpotent when every element $g \ne 1$ lies outside some normal subgroup
$N$ such that $G/N$ is nilpotent and has no nontrivial elements of finite order.

articles.title: Two elements generate a dense subgroup of a connected semisimple Lie group
articles.statement:
Every connected
real analytic Lie group $G$ whose Lie algebra is semisimple contains two elements $a$ and $b$ such
that the subgroup of $G$ generated by $a$ and $b$ is dense in $G$. In particular, for connected
groups the number 4 in Problem 90 of the Scottish Book (four elements generating a dense
subgroup) can be lowered to 2.

## Sources

- S. Ulam and H. Auerbach, Problem 90 of the Scottish Book (every semi-simple Lie group contains four elements generating a dense subgroup; can the number 4 be lowered?); Mauldin commentary: every connected semi-simple Lie group has a free subgroup with two generators, and such a free subgroup can be chosen dense.

articles.title: $p'$-isolated subgroup
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a natural number and let $H$ be a subgroup of a group
$F$. Then $H$ is $p'$-isolated if, for every $x \in F$ and every natural number $n > 0$ that is not
divisible by $p$, $x^n \in H$ implies $x \in H$.

articles.title: Separability in the class of finite $p$-groups
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a natural number and let $H$ be
a subgroup of a group $F$. Then $H$ is separable in the class of finite $p$-groups if for every
$x \in F$ with $x \notin H$ there are a finite $p$-group $Q$ (a finite group in which every element
$g$ satisfies $g^{p^k} = 1$ for some natural number $k$) and a group homomorphism
$f \colon F \to Q$ with $f(x) \notin f(H)$.

articles.title: Isolated subgroups of free groups need not be $p$-separable
articles.statement:
For every prime $p$ there are a
set $\alpha$ and a finitely generated $p'$-isolated subgroup of the free group on $\alpha$ that is
not separable in the class of finite $p$-groups. That is, the statement of Kourovka Problem 15.60
fails for every prime $p$.

Bardakov proved that every nonabelian free group has a finitely generated isolated subgroup $H$
($x^n \in H$ with $n \ne 0$ implies $x \in H$) that is not separable in the class of nilpotent
groups; it is $p'$-isolated for every prime $p$, and finite $p$-groups are nilpotent. The Kourovka
Archive answers 15.60 "No, it is not".

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 15.60 (D. I. Moldavanskiĭ); resolution: V. G. Bardakov, On D. I. Moldavanskii's question about p-separable subgroups of a free group, Siberian Math. J. 45 (2004), no. 3, 416-419, arXiv:math/0404292, abstract (every nonabelian free group has a finitely generated isolated subgroup that is not separable in the class of nilpotent groups); Kourovka Archive, Problem 15.60 (answer: No, it is not), https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0404292.

articles.title: Moldavanskiĭ's question on $p$-separability of isolated subgroups (Kourovka 15.60)
articles.statement:
The
statement that there is a prime $p$ such that, for every set $\alpha$, every finitely generated
$p'$-isolated subgroup of the free group on $\alpha$ is separable in the class of finite
$p$-groups.

articles.title: Finite-index normal subgroups are closed when the completion map is onto
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a
profinite group and let $\hat P$ be the profinite completion of $P$ as an abstract group, that is,
the inverse limit of the finite quotients $P/N$ over all normal subgroups $N$ of finite index in
$P$. If the canonical map $P \to \hat P$ is surjective, then every normal subgroup of finite
index in $P$ is closed in $P$.

articles.title: Finite-index normal subgroups are open when the completion map is onto
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a
profinite group and let $\hat P$ be the profinite completion of $P$ as an abstract group, that is,
the inverse limit of the finite quotients $P/N$ over all normal subgroups $N$ of finite index in
$P$. If the canonical map $P \to \hat P$ is surjective, then every normal subgroup of finite
index in $P$ is open in $P$.

articles.title: Strongly complete profinite groups via the profinite completion
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a profinite
group and let $\hat P$ be the profinite completion of $P$ as an abstract group, that is, the
inverse limit of the finite quotients $P/N$ over all normal subgroups $N$ of finite index in $P$.
Then $P$ is strongly complete if and only if the canonical map $P \to \hat P$ is bijective.

articles.title: Strongly complete group
articles.statement:
A group $G$ equipped with a topology is *strongly complete* when
every subgroup of finite index in $G$ is open.

articles.title: Topologically finitely generated group
articles.statement:
A topological group is topologically finitely
generated if some finite set generates a dense abstract subgroup.

articles.title: Nikolov–Segal strong completeness theorem
articles.statement:
Every finite-index subgroup of a
topologically finitely generated profinite group is open.

## Sources

- Nikolay Nikolov and Dan Segal, *On finitely generated profinite groups, I: strong completeness and uniform bounds*, Annals of Mathematics 165 (2007), no. 1, 171–238, Theorem 1.1, https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2007.165.171; *On finitely generated profinite groups, II: products in quasisimple groups*, Annals of Mathematics 165 (2007), no. 1, 239–273, https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2007.165.239. Problem `nikolov_segal` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: The Baumslag–Solitar group BS(1, n)
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $\mathrm{BS}(1, n)$ is the
group with presentation $\langle a, b \mid b a b^{-1} = a^n \rangle$.

articles.title: Locally subgroup-separable (LERF) group
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is locally subgroup-separable, or
LERF, when every finitely generated subgroup of $G$ is separable.

articles.title: Separable subgroup
articles.statement:
A subgroup $H$ of a group $G$ is separable when for every element
$x \in G$ with $x \notin H$ there are a finite group $F$ and a group homomorphism
$f \colon G \to F$ with $f(x) \notin f(H)$.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 16.2 has a negative answer
articles.statement:
There is a finitely generated solvable group $G$
for which the following two conditions are not equivalent: $G$ is locally subgroup-separable;
there is no $n > 1$ such that $G$ has a subgroup isomorphic to the Baumslag–Solitar group
$\mathrm{BS}(1, n)$.

Button's counterexample is the solvable ascending HNN extension of
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z} = \langle u, v \rangle$ by the injective endomorphism
$u \mapsto u^5 v^{-1}$, $v \mapsto u^2$: it is not locally subgroup-separable but contains no
$\mathrm{BS}(1, m)$ with $m \ne 0, \pm 1$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 16.2 (R. C. Alperin); resolution: J. O. Button, Strictly ascending HNN extensions in soluble groups, Ricerche di Matematica 61 (2012), no. 1, 139-145, arXiv:1004.0197, Theorem 2.1 and the remark after it (the soluble ascending HNN extension G = ⟨t, ℤ × ℤ⟩ with θ(u) = u⁵v⁻¹, θ(v) = u² is not LERF and contains no BS(1, m), m ≠ 0, ±1, so the answer to Problem 16.2 is no); Kourovka Archive, Problem 16.2 (No, it is not), https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.0197.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 16.2 (R. C. Alperin)
articles.statement:
A finitely generated solvable group $G$ is locally
subgroup-separable if and only if there is no $n > 1$ such that $G$ has a subgroup isomorphic to
the Baumslag–Solitar group $\mathrm{BS}(1, n)$.

articles.title: Caprace's class $\mathcal{S}$
articles.statement:
A group $G$ with a topology belongs to the class
$\mathcal{S}$ when it is a topological group that is Hausdorff, totally disconnected, locally
compact and not discrete, is generated as a group by some compact subset, and is topologically
simple: $G$ is nontrivial and its only closed normal subgroups are the trivial subgroup and $G$
itself.

articles.title: Locally isomorphic topological groups
articles.statement:
Two topological groups are locally isomorphic: they contain open subgroups that are isomorphic
as topological groups.

articles.title: Uncountably many local isomorphism classes of simple tdlc groups
articles.statement:
There is a family
$(G_i)_{i \in I}$ of groups in Caprace's class $\mathcal{S}$ (non-discrete, compactly generated,
topologically simple, totally disconnected, locally compact Hausdorff topological groups), indexed
by an uncountable set $I$, such that $G_i$ and $G_j$ are not locally isomorphic whenever $i \ne j$.
This answers Kourovka Notebook Problem 19.22 (P.-E. Caprace) in the affirmative.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 19.22 (P.-E. Caprace); resolution: I. Castellano, J. Fariña-Asategui, M. E. Garciarena, B. Marchionna, M. Quick, C. D. Reid, S. M. Smith, S. Tornier, M. Vannacci and J. S. Wilson, Uncountably many local isomorphism types of compactly generated simple groups, preprint, arXiv:2609.17410 (2026), Theorem A: there exist 2^ℵ₀ many non-discrete compactly generated simple tdlc groups which are not pairwise locally isomorphic; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 19.22 solved: Yes, it is, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17410.

articles.title: Caprace's problem on local isomorphism classes (Kourovka 19.22)
articles.statement:
The statement that the
groups in Caprace's class $\mathcal{S}$ fall into uncountably many local isomorphism classes: there
is a family $(G_i)_{i \in I}$ of groups in $\mathcal{S}$, indexed by an uncountable set $I$, such
that $G_i$ and $G_j$ are not locally isomorphic whenever $i \ne j$.

articles.title: Composition factor of a group (via subnormal subgroups)
articles.statement:
For groups $T$ and $Q$, $T$ is a
composition factor of $Q$ when some subnormal subgroup $H$ of $Q$ maps onto $T$, that is, there is a
surjective group homomorphism $H \to T$. Here $H$ is subnormal in $Q$ when there is a finite chain
of subgroups $H = H_0 \le H_1 \le \dots \le H_k = Q$ in which each $H_j$ is normal in $H_{j+1}$.

For simple $T$ and finite $Q$ this is the same as $T$ occurring as a factor of a composition series
of $Q$ (refine the kernel and the subnormal chain).

articles.title: Upper composition factors
articles.statement:
For groups $T$ and $G$, $T$ is an upper composition factor of $G$
when it is a composition factor of some finite quotient of $G$: there are a finite group $Q$ and a
surjective group homomorphism $G \to Q$ such that $T$ is a composition factor of $Q$, that is, $T$
is a homomorphic image of a subnormal subgroup of $Q$.

articles.title: Segal's theorem on upper composition factors, 3 generators (Kourovka Problem 11.57)
articles.statement:
For every
family $(T_i)_{i \in I}$ of finite non-abelian simple groups there is a group $G$ generated by $3$
elements such that a finite non-abelian simple group $Q$ is an upper composition factor of $G$ (a
composition factor of some finite quotient of $G$) if and only if $Q$ is isomorphic to $T_i$ for
some $i \in I$. Abelian upper composition factors of $G$ are not restricted.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.57 (A. Mann, D. Segal); resolution: D. Segal, Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) 82 (2001), 597-613, Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.57: any set of non-abelian finite simple groups is the set of upper composition factors of a 63-generator group; with abelian upper composition factors allowed, 3 generators suffice, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 11.57, 3-generator form (statement)
articles.statement:
The statement that for every family
$(T_i)_{i \in I}$ of finite non-abelian simple groups there is a group $G$ generated by $3$
elements such that a finite non-abelian simple group $Q$ is an upper composition factor of $G$ if
and only if $Q$ is isomorphic to $T_i$ for some $i \in I$. Abelian upper composition factors of $G$
are not restricted.

articles.title: Segal's theorem on upper composition factors, 63 generators (Kourovka Problem 11.57)
articles.statement:
For every
family $(T_i)_{i \in I}$ of finite non-abelian simple groups there is a group $G$ generated by $63$
elements such that a finite simple group $Q$ is an upper composition factor of $G$ (a composition
factor of some finite quotient of $G$) if and only if $Q$ is isomorphic to $T_i$ for some $i \in I$.
In particular, no cyclic group of prime order is an upper composition factor of $G$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.57 (A. Mann, D. Segal); resolution: D. Segal, Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) 82 (2001), 597-613, Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.57: any set of non-abelian finite simple groups is the set of upper composition factors of a 63-generator group; with abelian upper composition factors allowed, 3 generators suffice, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 11.57, 63-generator form (statement)
articles.statement:
The statement that for every family
$(T_i)_{i \in I}$ of finite non-abelian simple groups there is a group $G$ generated by $63$
elements such that a finite simple group $Q$ is an upper composition factor of $G$ if and only if
$Q$ is isomorphic to $T_i$ for some $i \in I$.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 19.100 has a positive answer
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group and let $A$, $B$,
$C$ be subgroups of $G$, each abnormal in $G$ and supersoluble, such that $G = AB = BC = CA$ as
sets. Then $G$ is supersoluble.

The Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) answers 19.100 "Yes, it is" (L. S. Kazarin and V. N. Tyutyanov,
2023).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 19.100 (A. F. Vasil'ev, T. I. Vasil'eva); resolution: L. S. Kazarin and V. N. Tyutyanov, preprint, 2023 (Russian), the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 19.100 solved: Yes, it is, https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/d09ad0bed183d180d0bed0b2d0bad0b0-19.100-5.pdf.

articles.title: Abnormal supersoluble trifactorizations (Kourovka 19.100)
articles.statement:
The proposition that for every
finite group $G$ and all subgroups $A$, $B$, $C$ of $G$ that are abnormal in $G$ and supersoluble,
if $G = AB = BC = CA$ as sets, then $G$ is supersoluble.

articles.title: Abnormal subgroup
articles.statement:
A subgroup $H$ of a group $G$ is abnormal in $G$ if every element
$g \in G$ lies in the subgroup generated by $H$ and its conjugate $gHg^{-1}$.

articles.title: Supersoluble groups via cyclic normal series
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is supersoluble if there are a
natural number $k$ and subgroups $1 = S_0 \le S_1 \le \cdots \le S_k = G$, each normal in $G$, such
that for every $i < k$ we have $S_i \le S_{i+1}$ and there is an element $x \in S_{i+1}$ such that
$S_{i+1}$ is generated by $x$ and $S_i$; that is, every factor $S_{i+1}/S_i$ is cyclic.

articles.title: Finite Alperin groups have derived length at most six
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group in which, for
all $x, y \in G$, the derived subgroup of the subgroup $\langle x, y \rangle$ generated by $x$ and
$y$ is cyclic (an Alperin group). Then the sixth derived subgroup $G^{(6)}$ of $G$ is trivial,
that is, $G$ has derived length at most $6$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 18.33 (B. M. Veretennikov); resolution: P. Longobardi, M. Maj and H. Smith, Rend. Sem. Mat. Univ. Padova 115 (2006), 29-40; B. Wilkens, J. Group Theory 17 (2014), no. 1, 151-174, Kourovka Archive, Problem 18.33: Yes, it is at most 6: finite Alperin groups of odd order are metabelian and finite Alperin groups are supersoluble (Longobardi-Maj-Smith), so the elements of odd order form a metabelian normal subgroup, and finite Alperin 2-groups have derived length at most 4 (Wilkens), https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 18.33 on the derived length of finite Alperin groups
articles.statement:
This proposition
asserts that every finite Alperin group $G$ has derived length at most $6$, that is, its sixth
derived subgroup $G^{(6)}$ is trivial. Here $G$ is an Alperin group when, for all $x, y \in G$, the
derived subgroup of the subgroup $\langle x, y \rangle$ generated by $x$ and $y$ is cyclic.

Problem 18.33 (B. M. Veretennikov) asks whether such a bound exists; $6$ is the bound given in the
answer.

articles.title: Alperin group
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is an Alperin group when, for all $x, y \in G$, the derived
subgroup $[H, H]$ of the subgroup $H = \langle x, y \rangle$ generated by $x$ and $y$ is
cyclic.

articles.title: A Fitting class of supersoluble groups with a non-central minimal normal subgroup
articles.statement:
There
exist a class $\mathfrak{X}$ of groups that is a Fitting class and all of whose finite members are
supersoluble, a finite group $G \in \mathfrak{X}$, and a minimal normal subgroup $N$ of $G$ that is
not contained in the center of $G$.

This answers Kourovka Problem 12.91 in the negative.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 12.91 (H. Heineken); resolution: H. Heineken, Rend. Sem. Mat. Univ. Padova 98 (1997), 241-251, Kourovka Archive, Problem 12.91: No, it does not.

articles.title: Heineken's question on Fitting classes of supersoluble groups
articles.statement:
The proposition that for
every class $\mathfrak{X}$ of groups that is a Fitting class and all of whose finite members are
supersoluble, every minimal normal subgroup of every finite group $G \in \mathfrak{X}$ is contained
in the center of $G$.

This is Kourovka Problem 12.91 (H. Heineken).

articles.title: Isomorphism-closed classes of groups (Kourovka 12.91)
articles.statement:
A class of groups is a property of
groups (in the lowest type universe) that is closed under isomorphism: whenever a group $H$ has the
property and $H$ is isomorphic to a group $K$, then $K$ has the property. Only the finite members of
a class are used in Kourovka Problem 12.91.

articles.title: Fitting classes (Kourovka 12.91)
articles.statement:
A class $\mathfrak{X}$ of groups is a Fitting class (of
finite groups) if, for every finite group $G$: whenever $G \in \mathfrak{X}$, every normal subgroup
of $G$ belongs to $\mathfrak{X}$; and whenever $N_1$ and $N_2$ are normal subgroups of $G$ that
belong to $\mathfrak{X}$, the subgroup $N_1 N_2$ they generate belongs to $\mathfrak{X}$.

articles.title: Minimal normal subgroups (Kourovka 12.91)
articles.statement:
A subgroup $N$ of a group $G$ is minimal normal
if $N$ is a nontrivial normal subgroup of $G$ and every nontrivial normal subgroup $M$ of $G$ with
$M \le N$ equals $N$.

articles.title: Supersoluble groups (Kourovka 12.91)
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is supersoluble if it has a chain of
subgroups $1 = G_0 \le G_1 \le \cdots \le G_k = G$, each normal in $G$, such that for every $i < k$
there is an element $x \in G_{i+1}$ with $G_{i+1} = \langle x \rangle G_i$; that is, every factor
$G_{i+1}/G_i$ is cyclic.

articles.title: Classes of groups
articles.statement:
A class of groups is a predicate on groups: it assigns to every group
$G$ (in the lowest universe of types) a proposition, read as "$G$ belongs to the class". No
closure under isomorphism is required.

articles.title: Formations of finite groups
articles.statement:
A class $\mathfrak F$ of groups is a formation when every group
in $\mathfrak F$ is finite, $\mathfrak F$ contains at least one group, $\mathfrak F$ is closed under
isomorphism, $\mathfrak F$ is closed under quotients (if $G \in \mathfrak F$ and $N$ is a normal
subgroup of $G$, then $G/N \in \mathfrak F$), and $\mathfrak F$ is closed under subdirect products:
if $G$ is a finite group with normal subgroups $M$ and $N$ such that $G/M \in \mathfrak F$ and
$G/N \in \mathfrak F$, then $G/(M \cap N) \in \mathfrak F$.

articles.title: Groups satisfying a set of laws
articles.statement:
Let $W$ be a set of words in the free group on countably
many generators $x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots$. A group $G$ satisfies the laws in $W$ when every
homomorphism from this free group to $G$ sends every $w \in W$ to $1$. The groups satisfying $W$
form the variety defined by $W$, and every variety arises this way.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 11.21 has a negative answer
articles.statement:
There are a prime $p$ and a formation
$\mathfrak F$ all of whose members are $p$-groups such that for every set $W$ of laws, words in the
free group on countably many generators, some finite $p$-group lies in $\mathfrak F$ and fails a
law in $W$, or satisfies every law in $W$ and does not lie in $\mathfrak F$. Thus $\mathfrak F$ is
not of the form $\mathfrak N_p \cap \mathfrak M$ for any variety $\mathfrak M$, where
$\mathfrak N_p$ is the formation of all finite $p$-groups.

The Kourovka Archive answers 11.21 "No, it is not true" (A. N. Krasil'nikov): formations of finite
$p$-groups correspond bijectively to varieties of pro-$p$ groups, there are continuously many
varieties of nilpotent pro-$p$ groups of class at most $6$ (Zubkov), hence continuously many
formations of finite $p$-groups of class at most $6$, while such a formation of the form
$\mathfrak N_p \cap \mathfrak M$ equals $\mathfrak N_p \cap (\mathfrak M \cap \mathfrak N_6)$, where
$\mathfrak N_6$ is the variety of nilpotent groups of class at most $6$, and there are only
countably many varieties of nilpotent groups of class at most $6$ (all finitely based).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.21 (A. F. Vasil'yev); resolution: A. N. Krasil'nikov, letter of 17 July 1998, using A. N. Zubkov, Siberian Math. J. 29, no. 3 (1988), 491-494, Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.21: "No, it is not true"; formations of finite `p`-groups correspond to varieties of pro-`p` groups, there are continuously many varieties of nilpotent pro-`p` groups of class at most 6 (Zubkov) but only countably many varieties of nilpotent groups of class at most 6, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 11.21 (Vasil'yev's question on formations of $p$-groups)
articles.statement:
The proposition
that for every prime $p$ and every formation $\mathfrak F$ all of whose members are $p$-groups (a
subformation of the formation $\mathfrak N_p$ of all finite $p$-groups), there is a set $W$ of laws,
words in the free group on countably many generators, such that a finite $p$-group lies in
$\mathfrak F$ if and only if it satisfies every law in $W$. In other words, every such
$\mathfrak F$ equals $\mathfrak N_p \cap \mathfrak M$ for the variety $\mathfrak M$ defined by
$W$.

articles.title: Classes of groups
articles.statement:
A class of groups is a property of groups: for each group $G$ it gives
a proposition, read as "$G$ belongs to the class". No closure under isomorphism is required.

articles.title: Skiba's theorem (Kourovka Problem 11.91)
articles.statement:
Let $\mathfrak F$ be a hereditary formation of
finite soluble groups: every group in $\mathfrak F$ is finite and soluble, $\mathfrak F$ is closed
under isomorphisms, subgroups and quotients, and whenever $M$ and $N$ are normal subgroups of a
finite group $G$ with $G/M$ and $G/N$ in $\mathfrak F$, also $G/(M \cap N)$ lies in $\mathfrak F$.
Suppose that every finite soluble group that is not simple and is a minimal non-$\mathfrak F$-group
(it does not lie in $\mathfrak F$, but all of its proper subgroups do) is a Shmidt group, that is,
a finite non-nilpotent group all of whose proper subgroups are nilpotent. Then $\mathfrak F$ is
saturated: every finite soluble group $G$ such that $G/\Phi(G)$ lies in $\mathfrak F$, where
$\Phi(G)$ is the Frattini subgroup of $G$, itself lies in $\mathfrak F$.

The hypothesis forces the trivial group into $\mathfrak F$, and by the Gaschütz–Lubeseder theorem a
nonempty saturated formation of finite soluble groups is local, so $\mathfrak F$ is local.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 11.91 (V. N. Semenchuk); resolution: A. N. Skiba, Dokl. Akad. Nauk Belorus. SSR 34, no. 11 (1990), 982-985 (Russian), Kourovka Archive, Problem 11.91: "This is proved", https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 11.91 (statement)
articles.statement:
The statement that every hereditary formation
$\mathfrak F$ of finite soluble groups such that every finite soluble non-simple minimal
non-$\mathfrak F$-group (a group outside $\mathfrak F$ all of whose proper subgroups lie in
$\mathfrak F$) is a Shmidt group is saturated, that is, every finite soluble group $G$ whose
quotient $G/\Phi(G)$ by its Frattini subgroup $\Phi(G)$ lies in $\mathfrak F$ itself lies in
$\mathfrak F$.

Under this hypothesis $\mathfrak F$ contains the trivial group, so by the Gaschütz–Lubeseder
theorem saturated is the same as local, the property the problem (V. N. Semenchuk) asks for.

articles.title: Hereditary formations of finite soluble groups
articles.statement:
A class $\mathfrak F$ of groups is a
hereditary formation of finite soluble groups if every group in $\mathfrak F$ is finite and
soluble; $\mathfrak F$ is closed under isomorphisms, under taking subgroups and under taking
quotients by normal subgroups; and for every finite group $G$ with normal subgroups $M$ and $N$
such that $G/M$ and $G/N$ lie in $\mathfrak F$, also $G/(M \cap N)$ lies in $\mathfrak F$.

articles.title: Minimal non-members of a class of groups
articles.statement:
Let $\mathfrak F$ be a class of groups. A group
$G$ is a minimal non-$\mathfrak F$-group if $G$ does not lie in $\mathfrak F$ but every proper
subgroup of $G$ lies in $\mathfrak F$.

articles.title: Saturated classes of groups
articles.statement:
A class $\mathfrak F$ of groups is saturated if every finite
soluble group $G$ such that $G/\Phi(G)$ lies in $\mathfrak F$, where $\Phi(G)$ is the Frattini
subgroup of $G$, itself lies in $\mathfrak F$.

By the Gaschütz–Lubeseder theorem, a nonempty formation of finite soluble groups is saturated if
and only if it is local.

articles.title: Shmidt groups
articles.statement:
A group $G$ is a Shmidt group if it is finite and not nilpotent, but every
proper subgroup of $G$ is nilpotent.

articles.title: Groups with a subnormal series whose factors are all isomorphic to a given group
articles.statement:
For
groups $T$ and $G$, the group $G$ lies in the class $\mathfrak{F}_T$ when it has a subnormal series
$1 = H_0 \le H_1 \le \dots \le H_n = G$, each $H_i$ normal in $H_{i+1}$, all of whose factors
$H_{i+1}/H_i$ are isomorphic to $T$. For simple $T$ these are the groups all of whose composition
factors are isomorphic to $T$.

articles.title: Mel'nikov's theorem on Kourovka Problem 12.97
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a finite non-abelian simple group,
and write $\mathfrak{F}_T$ for the class of groups having a subnormal series all of whose factors
are isomorphic to $T$. Let $\mathfrak{M}$ and $\mathfrak{H}$ be formations whose finite members
lie in $\mathfrak{F}_T$, each containing a nontrivial finite group and each missing some finite
group of $\mathfrak{F}_T$. Then it is not true that, for every finite group $G$, $G$ lies in
$\mathfrak{F}_T$ if and only if its $\mathfrak{H}$-residual $G^{\mathfrak{H}}$ lies in
$\mathfrak{M}$: the formation $\mathfrak{F}_T$ is not the Gaschütz product
$\mathfrak{M}\mathfrak{H}$ of two nontrivial proper subformations.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 12.97 (L. A. Shemetkov); resolution: O. V. Mel'nikov, Problems in Algebra 9, Gomel', 1996, 42-47 (Russian), Kourovka Archive, Problem 12.97: it is proved.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 12.97 (Shemetkov)
articles.statement:
For a group $T$, write $\mathfrak{F}_T$ for the class
of groups having a subnormal series all of whose factors are isomorphic to $T$. This is the
proposition that, for every finite non-abelian simple group $T$ and all formations $\mathfrak{M}$
and $\mathfrak{H}$ whose finite members lie in $\mathfrak{F}_T$, each containing a nontrivial
finite group and each missing some finite group of $\mathfrak{F}_T$, it is not the case that every
finite group $G$ satisfies: $G \in \mathfrak{F}_T$ if and only if the $\mathfrak{H}$-residual
$G^{\mathfrak{H}}$ of $G$ lies in $\mathfrak{M}$. In other words, $\mathfrak{F}_T$ is not the
Gaschütz product $\mathfrak{M}\mathfrak{H} = \{G : G^{\mathfrak{H}} \in \mathfrak{M}\}$ of two
nontrivial proper subformations.

articles.title: Isomorphism-closed classes of groups (Kourovka 12.97)
articles.statement:
A class of groups is given by a
membership predicate on groups such that every group isomorphic to a member is again a member.
Only the finite members matter in the formulation of Kourovka Problem 12.97.

articles.title: Class of finite groups (Kourovka 10.72)
articles.statement:
A class of finite groups is given by a
membership predicate: a proposition $X(G)$ for every finite group $G$. It is not required to be
closed under isomorphisms.

articles.title: Formations of finite groups (Kourovka 12.97)
articles.statement:
A class $X$ of groups is a formation when it
contains the trivial group, the quotient $G/N$ lies in $X$ for every finite group $G$ in $X$ and
every normal subgroup $N$ of $G$, and for every finite group $G$ with normal subgroups $N_1$ and
$N_2$ such that $G/N_1$ and $G/N_2$ lie in $X$, the quotient $G/(N_1 \cap N_2)$ lies in $X$.

articles.title: Formation of finite groups (Kourovka 10.72)
articles.statement:
A class $X$ of finite groups is a formation
when it is closed under isomorphisms, contains the trivial group, contains the quotient $G/N$ of
each of its members $G$ by every normal subgroup $N$, and contains $G/(N_1 \cap N_2)$ whenever
$N_1$ and $N_2$ are normal subgroups of a finite group $G$ with $G/N_1$ and $G/N_2$ in $X$. The
last condition is closure under subdirect products.

articles.title: Proper subclass of a formation
articles.statement: `X` is a proper subclass of `𝔉_T`: some finite group of `𝔉_T` does not belong to `X`.

articles.title: Classes containing a nontrivial finite group
articles.statement:
A class $X$ of groups is nontrivial when it
contains a nontrivial finite group; for a formation this means that $X$ is not the trivial
formation.

articles.title: The formation of finite $p$-groups is indecomposable
articles.statement:
For every prime $p$, the class
$\mathfrak{N}_p$ of all finite $p$-groups is not the Gaschütz product $\mathfrak{F} \circ
\mathfrak{G}$ of two formations $\mathfrak{F}$ and $\mathfrak{G}$ that consist of $p$-groups, each
contain a nontrivial group and each omit some finite $p$-group. Here a finite group $G$ lies in
$\mathfrak{F} \circ \mathfrak{G}$ when its $\mathfrak{G}$-residual lies in $\mathfrak{F}$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 10.72 (L. A. Shemetkov); resolution: A. N. Skiba and L. A. Shemetkov, Dokl. Akad. Nauk BSSR 33 (1989), 581-582 (Russian), Kourovka Archive, Problem 10.72 ("This has been proved").

articles.title: Indecomposability of the formation of finite $p$-groups (Kourovka 10.72)
articles.statement:
The statement
that for every prime $p$, the class $\mathfrak{N}_p$ of all finite $p$-groups is not the Gaschütz
product $\mathfrak{F} \circ \mathfrak{G}$ of two formations $\mathfrak{F}$ and $\mathfrak{G}$ that
consist of $p$-groups, each contain a nontrivial group and each omit some finite $p$-group. Here a
finite group $G$ lies in $\mathfrak{F} \circ \mathfrak{G}$ when its $\mathfrak{G}$-residual lies
in $\mathfrak{F}$.

Omitting some finite $p$-group is part of the reading of "non-trivial": for all formations
$\mathfrak{F}, \mathfrak{G}$ consisting of $p$-groups,
$\mathfrak{N}_p \circ \mathfrak{G} = \mathfrak{F} \circ \mathfrak{N}_p = \mathfrak{N}_p$.

articles.title: The residual of a group with respect to a class (Kourovka 12.97)
articles.statement:
For a class $X$ of groups
and a group $G$, the $X$-residual of $G$ is the intersection of all normal subgroups $N$ of $G$
such that the quotient $G/N$ lies in $X$.

articles.title: Residual of a finite group with respect to a class (Kourovka 10.72)
articles.statement:
For a class $X$ of
finite groups and a finite group $G$, the $X$-residual of $G$ is the intersection of all normal
subgroups $N$ of $G$ with $G/N \in X$. When $X$ is a formation, it is the smallest such $N$.

articles.title: A Fitting class with no injectors in a non-soluble group
articles.statement:
There are a Fitting class
$\mathfrak{X}$ of finite groups that contains at least one finite group and a finite non-soluble
group $G$ such that no subgroup of $G$ is an $\mathfrak{X}$-injector of $G$.

This answers Kourovka Problem 12.96 (L. A. Shemetkov) affirmatively: the Kourovka Archive records
that E. Salomon found such a Fitting class and group; the example is presented in Section 7.1 of
Ballester-Bolinches and Ezquerro, Classes of finite groups (2006).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 12.96 (L. A. Shemetkov); resolution: E. Salomon (unpublished), presented in A. Ballester-Bolinches and L. M. Ezquerro, Classes of finite groups, Springer, 2006, Section 7.1, Kourovka Archive, Problem 12.96: found by E. Salomon.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 12.96: a Fitting class without injectors
articles.statement:
The statement that there are a
Fitting class $\mathfrak{X}$ of finite groups that contains at least one finite group and a finite
non-soluble group $G$ such that no subgroup of $G$ is an $\mathfrak{X}$-injector of $G$.

The problem was posed by L. A. Shemetkov.

articles.title: Isomorphism-closed classes of groups (Kourovka 12.96)
articles.statement:
A class of groups is a property of
groups that is closed under isomorphism: if a group $H$ has the property and $K$ is a group
isomorphic to $H$, then $K$ has it too.

Only finite members matter for Fitting classes and for injectors of finite groups.

articles.title: Fitting classes of finite groups
articles.statement:
A class $\mathfrak{X}$ of groups is a Fitting class of
finite groups if, for every finite group $G$, every normal subgroup of $G$ lies in $\mathfrak{X}$
whenever $G$ does, and the product $N_1 N_2$ of two normal subgroups $N_1$ and $N_2$ of $G$ lies in
$\mathfrak{X}$ whenever $N_1$ and $N_2$ do.

articles.title: Injectors
articles.statement:
Let $\mathfrak{X}$ be a class of groups and $G$ a group. A subgroup $V$ of $G$ is
an $\mathfrak{X}$-injector of $G$ if, for every subnormal subgroup $N$ of $G$, the intersection
$V \cap N$ is $\mathfrak{X}$-maximal in $N$.

articles.title: Maximal subgroups within a class of groups
articles.statement:
Let $\mathfrak{X}$ be a class of groups and let
$V$ and $K$ be subgroups of a group $G$. Then $V$ is $\mathfrak{X}$-maximal in $K$ if $V \le K$,
$V$ lies in $\mathfrak{X}$, and no subgroup $W$ of $G$ with $V < W \le K$ lies in $\mathfrak{X}$.

articles.title: Inclusion of classes of finite groups
articles.statement:
For classes $\mathfrak{F}$ and $\mathfrak{G}$ of
finite groups, $\mathfrak{F} \subseteq \mathfrak{G}$ means that every finite group in
$\mathfrak{F}$ belongs to $\mathfrak{G}$.

articles.title: Intersection of classes of finite groups
articles.statement:
For classes $\mathfrak F_1$ and $\mathfrak F_2$ of
finite groups, their intersection $\mathfrak F_1 \cap \mathfrak F_2$ is the class of finite
groups $G$ with $G \in \mathfrak F_1$ and $G \in \mathfrak F_2$. For formations $\mathfrak F_1$
and $\mathfrak F_2$ it is their meet in the lattice of formations.

articles.title: Class of finite groups (Kourovka 13.51)
articles.statement:
A class of finite groups is a property of finite
groups: for each finite group $G$ it states whether $G$ belongs to the class.

Closure under isomorphism is not part of the definition.

articles.title: Not every finite modular lattice embeds in the lattice of formations
articles.statement:
There is a finite modular
lattice $L$ that admits no injective map $f$ from $L$ to the formations of finite groups such that,
for all $a, b \in L$, $f(a \wedge b) = f(a) \cap f(b)$ and $f(a \vee b)$ is the smallest formation
containing $f(a) \cup f(b)$. This answers Kourovka Problem 13.51 (Skiba) in the negative.

Jayadevan constructs a modular lattice with 184 elements that admits no such map (a six-variable
Desargues implication holds for formations and fails in the lattice); the Kourovka Notebook (21st
issue) answers 13.51 "No, not every" (AI solution confirmed by A. N. Skiba).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 13.51 (A. N. Skiba); resolution: A. Jayadevan, A finite modular lattice not embeddable in the lattice of formations of finite groups, preprint, Zenodo record 22863019 (2026), main theorem: a modular lattice with 184 elements (the dual of an incidence lattice with 91 points and 91 lines) admits no injective map preserving binary meets and joins into the lattice of formations; the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) marks 13.51 solved (AI solution confirmed by A. N. Skiba), https://zenodo.org/records/22863019.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 13.51 (Skiba): finite modular lattices embed in the lattice of formations
articles.statement:
For every finite modular lattice $L$ there is an injective map $f$ from $L$ to the formations of
finite groups such that, for all $a, b \in L$, $f(a \wedge b) = f(a) \cap f(b)$ and $f(a \vee
b)$ is the smallest formation containing $f(a) \cup f(b)$.

The map is not required to preserve the least or the greatest element.

articles.title: Formation generated by two classes (Kourovka 10.56)
articles.statement:
For classes $X$ and $Y$ of finite
groups, the formation generated by $X \cup Y$ is the class of finite groups that belong to every
formation containing both $X$ and $Y$. For formations $X$ and $Y$ it is their join in the lattice
of formations.

articles.title: Join of formations (Kourovka 13.51)
articles.statement:
For classes $\mathfrak F_1$ and $\mathfrak F_2$ of
finite groups, their formation join is the class of finite groups $G$ that belong to every
formation containing all groups of $\mathfrak F_1$ and of $\mathfrak F_2$: the intersection of
all formations containing $\mathfrak F_1 \cup \mathfrak F_2$, which is the smallest such
formation. For formations $\mathfrak F_1$ and $\mathfrak F_2$ it is their join in the lattice of
formations.

articles.title: Classes of finite groups (Kourovka 10.56)
articles.statement:
A class of finite groups is given by its
membership predicate: a proposition about each finite group, true exactly for the members of the
class.

articles.title: Isomorphism-closed classes of groups (Kourovka 18.92)
articles.statement:
A class of groups $\mathfrak{X}$ is
given by a membership predicate on groups whose underlying type lies in the lowest universe, such
that whenever a group $H$ belongs to $\mathfrak{X}$ and $K$ is a group isomorphic to $H$, the group
$K$ also belongs to $\mathfrak{X}$.

articles.title: Inclusion of group classes
Algebraic sets of group classes
articles.statement:
A set $\Theta$ of classes of groups is algebraic if every
member $\mathfrak{A}$ of $\Theta$ is the join in $\Theta$ of some subset $S \subseteq \Theta$ all of
whose members are compact in $\Theta$.

articles.title: Compact elements of a set of group classes
articles.statement:
Let $\Theta$ be a set of classes of groups and
$\mathfrak{A}$ a class of groups. Then $\mathfrak{A}$ is compact in $\Theta$ if, for every subset
$S \subseteq \Theta$ and every join $\mathfrak{J}$ of $S$ in $\Theta$ with
$\mathfrak{A} \subseteq \mathfrak{J}$, there are a finite subset $S_1 \subseteq S$ and a join
$\mathfrak{J}_1$ of $S_1$ in $\Theta$ with $\mathfrak{A} \subseteq \mathfrak{J}_1$.

articles.title: Complete lattices of formations
articles.statement:
A set $\Theta$ of classes of groups is a complete lattice
of formations if it is nonempty, every member of $\Theta$ is a formation, for every nonempty subset
$S \subseteq \Theta$ the intersection of the classes in $S$ (the class of groups belonging to every
member of $S$) belongs to $\Theta$, and $\Theta$ has a member that contains every member of
$\Theta$.

articles.title: Formation of finite groups (Kourovka 13.51)
articles.statement:
A class $\mathfrak F$ of finite groups is a
formation when it is closed under homomorphic images (if $G \in \mathfrak F$ and $\varphi : G
\to H$ is a surjective homomorphism of finite groups, then $H \in \mathfrak F$) and, for every
finite group $G$ and normal subgroups $N_1$ and $N_2$ of $G$, $G/N_1 \in \mathfrak F$ and $G/N_2
\in \mathfrak F$ imply $G/(N_1 \cap N_2) \in \mathfrak F$ (closure under finite subdirect
products).

The empty class is a formation.

articles.title: Formations of finite groups (Kourovka 10.56)
articles.statement:
A class $X$ of finite groups is a formation
if it is closed under isomorphism, contains the trivial group, contains $G/N$ whenever it contains
$G$ and $N$ is a normal subgroup of $G$, and is closed under subdirect products: if $N_1$ and
$N_2$ are normal subgroups of a finite group $G$ with $G/N_1 \in X$ and $G/N_2 \in X$, then
$G/(N_1 \cap N_2) \in X$.

articles.title: Formations of finite groups (Kourovka 18.92)
articles.statement:
A class $\mathfrak{X}$ of groups is a
formation if every group in $\mathfrak{X}$ is finite, $\mathfrak{X}$ contains the trivial group,
for every finite group $G$ in $\mathfrak{X}$ and every normal subgroup $N$ of $G$ the quotient
$G/N$ lies in $\mathfrak{X}$, and for every finite group $G$ with normal subgroups $N_1$ and $N_2$
such that $G/N_1$ and $G/N_2$ lie in $\mathfrak{X}$, the quotient $G/(N_1 \cap N_2)$ lies in
$\mathfrak{X}$.

articles.title: Joins in a set of group classes
articles.statement:
Let $\Theta$ and $S$ be sets of classes of groups. A class
$\mathfrak{J}$ is the join of $S$ in $\Theta$ if $\mathfrak{J} \in \Theta$, every member of $S$ is
contained in $\mathfrak{J}$, and $\mathfrak{J}$ is contained in every member of $\Theta$ that
contains every member of $S$.

articles.title: Local formation of finite groups
articles.statement:
A class $\mathfrak{F}$ of finite groups is a local
formation when it is a formation, contains the trivial group, and is saturated: a finite group $G$
belongs to $\mathfrak{F}$ whenever $G/\Phi(G)$ does, where $\Phi(G)$ is the Frattini subgroup of
$G$.

By the Gaschütz-Lubeseder-Schmid theorem a nonempty formation of finite groups is local (defined
by a formation function) iff it is saturated.

articles.title: Modular sets of group classes
articles.statement:
A set $\Theta$ of classes of groups is modular if for all
$\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{C} \in \Theta$ with $\mathfrak{A} \subseteq \mathfrak{C}$
the following holds: whenever $\mathfrak{J}_1$ is the join in $\Theta$ of the set
$\{\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B} \cap \mathfrak{C}\}$ and $\mathfrak{D}$ is the join in $\Theta$ of
the set $\{\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B}\}$, the classes $\mathfrak{J}_1$ and
$\mathfrak{D} \cap \mathfrak{C}$ contain the same groups. This is the modular law
$\mathfrak{A} \vee (\mathfrak{B} \wedge \mathfrak{C}) = (\mathfrak{A} \vee \mathfrak{B}) \wedge
\mathfrak{C}$, with joins taken in $\Theta$ and meets the intersections.

articles.title: Formations of nilpotent groups of class at most 4
articles.statement:
A class $X$ of finite groups is a
formation of nilpotent groups of class at most $4$ if $X$ is a formation and every group $G$ in
$X$ is nilpotent of class at most $4$, that is, the fourth term $\zeta_4(G)$ of the upper central
series of $G$ is all of $G$.

articles.title: Intersection of classes of finite groups (Kourovka 10.56)
articles.statement:
The meet of two classes $X$ and
$Y$ of finite groups is their intersection $X \cap Y$: the class of finite groups that belong to
both $X$ and $Y$.

articles.title: The lattice of nilpotent class-4 formations is not distributive (Kourovka 10.56)
articles.statement:
There
exist formations $A$, $B$, $C$ of finite nilpotent groups of class at most $4$ such that the
classes $A \cap (B \vee C)$ and $(A \cap B) \vee (A \cap C)$ differ, that is, some finite group
lies in exactly one of them; here $X \vee Y$ denotes the formation generated by $X \cup Y$, the
intersection of all formations containing $X$ and $Y$.

The Kourovka Archive answers Problem 10.56 "No": the lattice of varieties of nilpotent $2$-groups
of class at most $4$ is not distributive (Belov; Bryce), and $\mathfrak{V} \mapsto \mathfrak{V}
\cap \mathfrak{F}$, where $\mathfrak{F}$ is the class of finite groups, embeds it in the lattice
of formations (Kovács), with image among the formations of finite nilpotent groups of class at
most $4$.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 10.56 (A. N. Skiba); resolution: Yu. A. Belov, Algebra and Logic 9, no. 6 (1970), 371-374; R. A. Bryce, Philos. Trans. Roy. Soc. London (A) 266 (1970), 281-355, footnote on p. 335; L. Kovács, letter of 12 May 1988, Kourovka Archive, Problem 10.56 ("No"): the lattice of varieties of nilpotent 2-groups of class ≤ 4 is non-distributive, and V ↦ V ∩ F embeds it in the lattice of formations.

articles.title: The distributivity question for nilpotent class-4 formations (Kourovka 10.56)
articles.statement:
For all
formations $A$, $B$, $C$ of finite nilpotent groups of class at most $4$, a finite group lies in
$A \cap (B \vee C)$ if and only if it lies in $(A \cap B) \vee (A \cap C)$, where $X \vee Y$ denotes
the formation generated by $X \cup Y$. That is, the lattice of formations of finite nilpotent
groups of class at most $4$ is distributive (A. N. Skiba).

articles.title: Non-algebraic complete lattices of formations exist
articles.statement:
There is a set $\Theta$ of classes of
groups that is a complete lattice of formations of finite groups and is not algebraic; that is,
Kourovka Problem 18.92(a) has a positive answer.

The Kourovka Notebook (21st issue) answers 18.92(a) "Yes", by an AI-generated solution confirmed by
A. N. Skiba (Kinyon–Urban, 2026): for a set $S$ of primes let $\mathfrak{F}_S$ be the class of
finite groups whose order has all its prime divisors in $S$; the classes $\mathfrak{F}_S$ with $S$
finite, together with the class of all finite groups, form a complete lattice of formations whose
only compact element is the bottom.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Problem 18.92 (A. N. Skiba); resolution: M. Kinyon and J. Urban, Results on problems from the Kourovka Notebook, preprint, version 4, 19 September 2026, Section 3.29 (Problem 18.92): with F_S the finite groups whose order has all prime divisors in S, {F_S : S finite} ∪ {F_P} is not algebraic and the formations with prime sets ∅, {2}, {2, 3}, {5}, P form a pentagon N_5; an AI solution confirmed by A. N. Skiba, accepted in the Kourovka Notebook (21st issue), https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/kourovka-mathematics.pdf.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 18.92(a) (A. N. Skiba)
articles.statement:
The proposition that some set $\Theta$ of classes
of groups is a complete lattice of formations of finite groups and is not algebraic.
